<span class="generated-style">Examining Boxplots</span>

<span class="generated-style">A
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">boxplot</span><span class="generated-style">
is a one-dimensional graph of numerical data based on the five-number
summary, which includes the minimum value, the 25th percentile (known as
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Q</span><span class="zsubscript">1</span><span class="generated-style">),
the median, the 75th percentile
(</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Q</span><span class="zsubscript">3</span><span class="generated-style">),
and the maximum value. In essence, these five descriptive statistics
divide the data set into four parts; each part contains 25% of the data.
(See Chapter 5 for a full discussion of the five-number summary.)</span>

<span class="generated-style">Making a boxplot</span>

<span class="generated-style">To make a boxplot, follow these
steps:</span>

<span class="zcheltbold"> 1. Find the five-number summary of your data
set. (Use the steps outlined in Chapter 5.)</span>

<span class="zcheltbold"> 2. Create a vertical (or horizontal) number
line whose scale includes the numbers in the five-number summary and
uses appropriate units of equal distance from each other.</span>

<span class="zcheltbold"> 3. Mark the location of each number in the
five-number summary just above the number line (for a horizontal
boxplot) or just to the right of the number line (for a vertical
boxplot).</span>

<span class="zcheltbold"> 4. Draw a box around the marks for the 25th
percentile and the 75th percentile.</span>

<span class="zcheltbold"> 5. Draw a line in the box where the median is
located.</span>

<span class="zcheltbold"> 6. Determine whether or not outliers are
present.</span>

<span class="generated-style"> To make this determination, calculate the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">IQR
</span><span class="generated-style">(by
subtracting</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
Q</span><span class="zsubscript">3</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> –
Q</span><span class="zsubscript">1</span><span class="generated-style">);
then multiply by 1.5. Add this amount to the value of
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Q</span><span class="zsubscript">3</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
</span><span class="generated-style">and subtract this amount from
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Q</span><span class="zsubscript">1</span><span class="generated-style">.
This gives you a wider boundary around the median than the box does. Any
data points that fall outside this boundary are determined to be
outliers.</span>

<span class="zcheltbold"> 7. If there are no outliers (according to your
results of Step 6), draw lines from the upper and lower edges of the box
out to the minimum and maximum values in the data set.</span>

<span class="zcheltbold"> 8. If there are outliers (according to your
results of Step 6), indicate their location on the boxplot with \*
signs. Instead of drawing a line from the edge of the box all the way to
the most extreme outlier, stop the line at the last data value that
isn’t an outlier.</span>

![tip.eps](9780470911082/images/tip_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Many if not most software packages indicate outliers in a data set by
using an asterisk (\*) or star symbol and use the procedure outlined in
Step 6 to identify outliers. However, not all packages use these symbols
and procedures; check to see what your package does before analyzing
your data with a boxplot. </span>

<span class="generated-style">A horizontal boxplot for ages of the Best
Actress Oscar award winners from 1928–2009 is shown in Figure 7-7. You
can see the numbers separating sections of the boxplot match the
five-number summary statistics shown in Figure 7-3.</span>

![headsup_lewis.eps](9780470911082/images/headsup_lewis_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Boxplots can be vertical (straight up and down) with the values on the
axis going from bottom (lowest) to top (highest); or they can be
horizontal, with the values on the axis going from left (lowest) to
right (highest). The next section shows you how to interpret a
boxplot.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Interpreting a boxplot</span>

<span class="generated-style">Similar to a histogram (see the section
“Interpreting a histogram”), a boxplot can give you information
regarding the shape, center, and variability of a data set. Boxplots
differ from histograms in terms of their strengths and weaknesses, as
you see in the upcoming sections, but one of their biggest strengths is
how they handle skewed data.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Checking the shape with caution!</span>

<span class="generated-style">A boxplot can show whether a data set is
symmetric (roughly the same on each side when cut down the middle) or
skewed (lopsided). A symmetric data set shows the median roughly in the
middle of the box. Skewed data show a lopsided boxplot, where the median
cuts the box into two unequal pieces. If the longer part of the box is
to the right (or above) the median, the data is said to be
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">skewed
right</span><span class="generated-style">. If the longer part is to the
left (or below) the median, the data is
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">skewed
left</span><span class="generated-style">.</span>

<span class="generated-style">As shown in the boxplot of the data in
Figure 7-7, the ages are skewed right. The part of the box to the left
of the median (representing the younger actresses) is shorter than the
part of the box to the right of the median (representing the older
actresses). That means the ages of the younger actresses are closer
together than the ages of the older actresses. Figure 7-3 shows the
descriptive statistics of the data and confirms the right skewness: the
median age (33 years) is lower than the mean age (35.69 years).</span>

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
If one side of the box is longer than the other, it does not mean that
side contains more data. In fact, you can’t tell the sample size by
looking at a boxplot; it’s based on percentages, not counts. Each
section of the boxplot (the minimum to
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Q</span><span class="zsubscript">1</span><span class="generated-style">,
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Q</span><span class="zsubscript">1</span><span class="generated-style">
to the median, the median to
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Q</span><span class="zsubscript">3</span><span class="generated-style">,
and
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Q</span><span class="zsubscript">3</span><span class="generated-style">
to the maximum) contains 25% of the data no matter what. If one of the
sections is longer than another, it indicates a wider range in the
values of data in that section (meaning the data are more spread out). A
smaller section of the boxplot indicates the data are more condensed
(closer together).</span>

![headsup_lewis.eps](9780470911082/images/headsup_lewis_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Although a boxplot can tell you whether a data set is symmetric (when
the median is in the center of the box), it can’t tell you the shape of
the symmetry the way a histogram can. For example, Figure 7-8 shows
histograms from two different data sets, each one containing 18 values
that vary from 1 to 6. The histogram on the left has an equal number of
values in each group, and the one on the right has two peaks at 2 and 5.
Both histograms show the data are symmetric, but their shapes are
clearly different.</span>

symmetric data sets.</span>

</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Q</span><span class="zsubscript">1</span><span class="generated-style">,
the median, and
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Q</span><span class="zsubscript">3</span><span class="generated-style">.
However, if you just saw the boxplots and not the histograms, you might

<span class="generated-style">Despite its weakness in detecting the type

showing them on the same graph, side by side.</span>

![headsup_lewis.eps](9780470911082/images/headsup_lewis_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
All graphs have strengths and weaknesses; it’s always a good idea to
show more than one graph of your data for that reason.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Measuring variability with IQR</span>

<span class="generated-style">Variability in a data set that is
described by the five-number summary is measured by the interquartile
range
(</span><span class="zcheltitalic">IQR</span><span class="generated-style">).
The
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">IQR</span><span class="generated-style">
is equal to
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Q</span><span class="zsubscript">3</span><span class="generated-style">
–
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Q</span><span class="zsubscript">1</span><span class="generated-style">,
the difference between the 75th percentile and the 25th percentile (the
distance covering the middle 50% of the data). The larger the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">IQR,</span><span class="generated-style">
the more variable the data set is.</span>

<span class="generated-style">From Figure 7-3, the variability in age of
the Best Actress winners as measured by the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">IQR</span><span class="generated-style">
is
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Q</span><span class="zsubscript">3</span><span class="generated-style">
–
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Q</span><span class="zsubscript">1</span><span class="generated-style">
= 39 – 28 = 11 years. Of the group of actresses whose ages were closest
to the median, half of them were within 11 years of each other when they
won their awards.</span>

![headsup_lewis.eps](9780470911082/images/headsup_lewis_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Notice that the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">IQR</span><span class="generated-style">
ignores data below the 25th percentile or above the 75th, which may
contain outliers that could inflate the measure of variability of the
entire data set. So if data is skewed, the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">IQR</span><span class="generated-style">
is a more appropriate measure of variability than the standard
deviation.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Picking out the center using the
median</span>

<span class="generated-style">The median, part of the five-number
summary, is shown by the line that cuts through the box in the boxplot.
This makes it very easy to identify. The mean, however, is not part of
the boxplot and can’t be determined accurately by just looking at the
boxplot.</span>

<span class="generated-style">You don’t see the mean on a boxplot
because boxplots are based completely on percentiles. If data are
skewed, the median is the most appropriate measure of center. Of course
you can calculate the mean separately and add it to your results; it’s
never a bad idea to show both.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Making mistakes when interpreting a

<span class="generated-style">It’s a common mistake to associate the
size of the box in a boxplot with the amount of data in the data set.

places in the data set that separate those sections.</span>

![headsup_lewis.eps](9780470911082/images/headsup_lewis_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
In particular, if the median splits the box into two unequal parts, the
larger part contains data that’s more variable than the other part, in
terms of its range of values. However, there is still the same amount of
data (25%) in the larger part of the box as there is in the smaller
part.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Another common error involves sample size.
A boxplot is a one-dimensional graph with only one axis representing the

and one of them has a very long box and the other has a very short one,
don’t conclude that the longer one has more data in it. The length of
the box represents the variability in the data, not the number of data
values.</span>

![headsup_lewis.eps](9780470911082/images/headsup_lewis_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
When viewing or making a boxplot, always make sure the sample size
(</span><span class="zcheltitalic">n</span><span class="generated-style">)
is included as part of the title. You can’t figure out the sample size
otherwise.</span>

![headsup_lewis.eps](9780470911082/images/headsup_lewis_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Variability in a histogram should not be confused with variability in a

appear flat, the data is spread out uniformly across all the groups,

(crimes per capita) — because the population size of a city changes over

<div id="13_9780470911082-pp03.xhtml_x13_9780470911082-pp03">

<div class="story">

<span class="generated-style">Part III</span>

<span class="generated-style">Distributions and the Central Limit
Theorem</span>

<div class="image">

![9780470911082-pp0301.eps](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-pp0301_fmt.png)

</div>

<span class="generated-style">In this part . . . </span>

Statisticians study populations; that’s their bread and butter. They
measure, count, or classify characteristics of a population (using
random variables); find probabilities and proportions; and create (or
estimate) numerical summaries for the population (that is, param-eters
for the population). Sometimes you know a great deal about a population
from the start; sometimes it’s hazier. This part studies populations
under both scenarios.

If a population fits a specific distribution, tools are available for
studying it. In Chapters 8 through 10, you see three commonly used
distributions: the binomial distribution (for categorical data) and the
normal and t-distributions (for numerical data).

If the specifics about a population are unknown (as happens most of the
time), you take a sample and generalize its results to the population.
However, sample results vary, and you need to take that into account. In
Chapter 11 you investigate sample variability, measure the precision of
your sample results, and find probabilities for their likelihood. From
there you’ll be able to properly estimate parameters and test claims
made about them, but that’s another Part — IV, to be exact.

</div>

</div>

<span id="14_9780470911082-ch08.xhtml"></span>

<div id="14_9780470911082-ch08.xhtml_x14_s9780470911082-ch08">

<div class="story">

<span class="generated-style">Chapter 8</span>

<span class="generated-style">Random Variables and the Binomial
Distribution</span>

<span class="generated-style">In This Chapter</span>

![arrow](9780470911082/images/arrow.png)
<span class="generated-style">Identifying a binomial random
variable</span>

![arrow](9780470911082/images/arrow.png)
<span class="generated-style">Finding probabilities using a formula or
table</span>

![arrow](9780470911082/images/arrow.png)
<span class="generated-style">Calculating the mean and variance</span>

<span class="drop-cap">S</span><span class="generated-style">cientists
and engineers often build models for the phenomena they are studying to
make predictions and decisions. For example, where and when is this
hurricane going to hit when it makes landfall? How many accidents will
occur at this intersection this year if it’s not redone? Or, what will
the deer population be like in a certain region five years from
now?</span>

<span class="generated-style">To answer these questions, scientists
(usually working with statisticians) define a characteristic they are
measuring or counting (such as number of intersections, location and
time when a hurricane hits, population size, and so on) and treat it as
a variable that changes in some random way, according to a certain
pattern. They cleverly call them — you guessed it — random variables. In
this chapter, you find out more about random variables, their types and
characteristics, and why they are important. And you look at the details
of one of the most common random variables: the binomial.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Defining a Random Variable</span>

<span class="generated-style">A </span><span class="zcheltitalic">random
variable</span><span class="generated-style"> is a characteristic,
measurement, or count that changes randomly according to a certain set
or pattern. Its notation is
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">,
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Y</span><span class="generated-style">,
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z</span><span class="generated-style">,
and so on. In this section, you see how different random variables are
characterized and how they behave in the long term in terms of their
means and standard deviations.</span>

![headsup_lewis.eps](9780470911082/images/headsup_lewis_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
In math you have variables like
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">
and
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Y</span><span class="generated-style">
that take on certain values depending on the problem (for example, the
width of a rectangle), but in statistics the variables change in a
random way. By
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">random,</span><span class="generated-style">
statisticians mean that you don’t know exactly what the next outcome
will be but you do know that certain outcomes happen more frequently
than others; everything’s not 50-50. (Like when I try to shoot baskets;
it’s definitely not a 50% chance I’ll make one and 50% chance I’ll miss.
It’s more like 5% chance of making it and a 95% chance of missing it.)
You can use that information to better study data and populations and
make good decisions. (For example, don’t put me in your basketball game
to shoot free throws.)</span>

<span class="generated-style">Data have different types: categorical and
numerical (see Chapter 4). While both types of data are associated with
random variables, I discuss only numerical random variables here (this
falls in line with most intro stat courses as well). For information on
analyzing categorical variables, see Chapters 6 and 19.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Discrete versus continuous</span>

<span class="generated-style">Numerical random variables represent
counts and measurements. They come in two different flavors: discrete
and continuous, depending on the type of outcomes that are
possible.</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="zcheltbold">Discrete random
variables:</span><span class="generated-style"> If the possible outcomes
of a random variable can be listed out using whole numbers (for example,
0, 1, 2 . . . , 10; or 0, 1, 2, 3), the random variable is
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">discrete</span><span class="generated-style">.</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="zcheltbold">Continuous random
variables:</span><span class="generated-style"> If the possible outcomes
of a random variable can only be described using an interval of real
numbers (for example, all real numbers from zero to infinity), the
random variable is
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">continuous</span><span class="generated-style">.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Discrete random variables typically
represent counts — for example, the number of people who voted yes for a
smoking ban out of a random sample of 100 people (possible values are 0,
1, 2, . . . , 100); or the number of accidents at a certain intersection
over one year’s time (possible values are 0, 1, 2, . . .).</span>

![technicalstuff.eps](9780470911082/images/technicalstuff_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Discrete random variables have two classes: finite and countably
infinite. A discrete random variable is
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">finite</span><span class="generated-style">
if its list of possible values has a fixed (finite) number of elements
in it (for example, the number of smoking ban supporters in a random
sample of 100 voters has to be between 0 and 100). One very common
finite random variable is the binomial, which is discussed in this
chapter in detail.</span>

<span class="generated-style">A discrete random variable is
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">countably
infinite</span><span class="generated-style"> if its possible values can
be specifically listed out but they have no specific end. For example,
the number of accidents occurring at a certain intersection over a
10-year period can take on possible values: 0, 1, 2, . . . (you know
they end somewhere but you can’t say where, so you list them
all).</span>

<span class="generated-style">Continuous random variables typically
represent measurements, such as time to complete a task (for example 1
minute 10 seconds, 1 minute 20 seconds, and so on) or the weight of a
newborn. What separates continuous random variables from discrete ones
is that they are </span><span class="zcheltitalic">uncountably
infinite;</span><span class="generated-style"> they have too many
possible values to list out or to count and/or they can be measured to a
high level of precision (such as the level of smog in the air in Los
Angeles on a given day, measured in parts per million).</span>

<span class="generated-style">Examples of commonly used continuous
random variables can be found in Chapter 9 (the normal distribution) and
Chapter 10 (the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="generated-style">-distribution).</span>

<span class="generated-style">Probability distributions</span>

<span class="generated-style">A discrete random variable
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">
can take on a certain set of possible outcomes, and each of those
outcomes has a certain probability of occurring. The notation used for
any specific outcome is a lowercase
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">x</span><span class="generated-style">.
For example, say you roll a die and look at the outcome. The random
variable
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">
is the outcome of the die (which takes on possible values of 1, 2, . . .
, 6). Now if you roll the die and get a 1, that’s a specific outcome, so
you write
“</span><span class="zcheltitalic">x</span><span class="generated-style">
= 1.”</span>

<span class="generated-style">The probability of any specific outcome
occurring is denoted
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">p</span><span class="generated-style">(</span><span class="zcheltitalic">x</span><span class="generated-style">),
which you pronounce “</span><span class="zcheltitalic">p
</span><span class="generated-style">of
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">x.</span><span class="generated-style">”
It signifies the probability that the random variable
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">
takes on a specific value, which you call “little
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">x.</span><span class="generated-style">”
For example, to denote the probability of getting a 1 on a die, you
write
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">p</span><span class="generated-style">(1).</span>

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Statisticians use an uppercase
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">
when they talk about random variables in their general form; for
example, “Let
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">
be the outcome of the roll of a single die.” They use lowercase
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">x</span><span class="generated-style">
when they talk about specific outcomes of the random variable, like
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">x</span><span class="generated-style">
= 1 or
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">x</span><span class="generated-style">
= 2.</span>

<span class="generated-style">A list or function showing all possible

</span><span class="zcheltitalic">p</span><span class="generated-style">(</span><span class="zcheltitalic">x</span><span class="generated-style">).
For example, when you roll a single die, the possible outcomes are 1, 2,

= the number of dogs owned, the probability distribution for
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">
is shown in Table 8-1.</span>

![/Table 8-1](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-tb0801.jpg)

<span class="generated-style">The mean and variance of a discrete random
variable</span>

<span class="generated-style">The
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">mean</span><span class="generated-style">
of a random variable is the average of all the outcomes you would expect

die a billion times and record the outcomes, the average of those
outcomes is 3.5. (Each outcome happens with equal chance, so you average
the numbers 1 through 6 to get 3.5.) However, if the die is loaded and

![tip.eps](9780470911082/images/tip_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
The notation for the mean of a random variable
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">

(pronounced “mu sub

and not
</span>![9780470911082-EQ08003.eps](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-EQ08003_fmt.png)<span class="generated-style">.

</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">

</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Y</span><span class="generated-style">
variable or some other letter).</span>

</span><span class="zcheltitalic">variance</span><span class="generated-style">
of a random variable is roughly interpreted as the average squared

You say “sigma sub
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">x</span><span class="generated-style">,
squared” or just “sigma squared.”</span>

</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">
is the square root of the variance, denoted by

(say “sigma
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">x</span><span class="generated-style">”</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
</span><span class="generated-style">or just “sigma”). It roughly

The variance is in square units, so it can’t be easily interpreted. You

<span class="generated-style">Identifying a Binomial</span>

<span class="generated-style">The most well-known and loved discrete
random variable is the binomial.
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Binomial</span><span class="generated-style">
means </span><span class="zcheltitalic">two
names</span><span class="generated-style"> and is associated with
situations involving two outcomes; for example yes/no, or
success/failure (hitting a red light or not, developing a side effect or
not). This section focuses on the binomial random variable — when you
can use it, finding probabilities for it, and finding its mean and
variance.</span>

<span class="generated-style">A random variable is binomial (that is, it
has a binomial distribution) if the following four conditions are
met:</span>

<span class="generated-style"> 1. There are a fixed number of trials
(</span><span class="zcheltitalic">n</span><span class="generated-style">).</span>

<span class="generated-style"> 2. Each trial has two possible outcomes:
success or failure.</span>

<span class="generated-style"> 3. The probability of success (call it
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">p</span><span class="generated-style">)
is the same for each trial.</span>

<span class="generated-style"> 4. The trials are independent, meaning
the outcome of one trial doesn’t influence that of any other.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Let</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> X
</span><span class="generated-style">equal the total number of successes
in</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> n
</span><span class="generated-style">trials; if all four conditions are
met,
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">
has a binomial distribution with probability of success (on each trial)
equal to
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">p</span><span class="generated-style">.</span>

<span class="generated-style">The lowercase
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">p
</span><span class="generated-style">here stands for the probability of
getting a success on one single (individual) trial. It’s not the same as
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">p</span><span class="generated-style">(</span><span class="zcheltitalic">x</span><span class="generated-style">),</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
</span><span class="generated-style">which means the probability of
getting</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> x
</span><span class="generated-style">successes
in</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> n
</span><span class="generated-style">trials.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Checking binomial conditions step by
step</span>

<span class="generated-style">You flip a fair coin 10 times and count
the number of heads
(</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">).
Does
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">
have a binomial distribution? You can check by reviewing your responses
to the questions and statements in the list that follows:</span>

<span class="zcheltbold"> 1. Are there a fixed number of trials?</span>

<span class="generated-style"> You’re flipping the coin 10 times, which
is a fixed number. Condition 1 is met, and
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">n</span><span class="generated-style">
= 10.</span>

<span class="zcheltbold"> 2. Does each trial have only two possible
outcomes — success or failure?</span>

<span class="generated-style"> The outcome of each flip is either heads
or tails, and you’re interested in counting the number of heads. That
means success = heads, and failure = tails. Condition 2 is met.</span>

<span class="zcheltbold"> 3. Is the probability of success the same for
each trial?</span>

<span class="generated-style"> Because the coin is fair, the probability
of success (getting a head) is
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">p</span><span class="generated-style">
= 1/2 for each trial. You also know that 1 – 1/2 = 1/2 is the
probability of failure (getting a tail) on each trial. Condition 3 is
met.</span>

<span class="zcheltbold"> 4. Are the trials independent?</span>

<span class="generated-style"> You assume the coin is being flipped the
same way each time, which means the outcome of one flip doesn’t affect
the outcome of subsequent flips. Condition 4 is met.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Because the random variable
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">
(the number of successes \[heads\] that occur in 10 trials \[flips\])
meets all four conditions, you conclude it has a binomial distribution
with</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> n
</span><span class="generated-style">= 10
and</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> p
</span><span class="generated-style">= 1/2.</span>

<span class="generated-style">But not every situation that appears
binomial actually is. Read on to see some examples of what I
mean.</span>

<span class="generated-style">No fixed number of trials</span>

<span class="generated-style">Suppose that you’re going to flip a fair
coin until you get four heads and you’ll count how many flips it takes
to get there; in this case
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">
= number of flips. This certainly sounds like a binomial situation:
Condition 2 is met because you have success (heads) and failure (tails)
on each flip; condition 3 is met with the probability of success (heads)
being the same (0.5) on each flip; and the flips are independent, so
condition 4 is met.</span>

<span class="generated-style">However, notice
that</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> X
</span><span class="generated-style">isn’t counting the number of heads,
it counts the number of trials needed to get 4 heads. The number of
successes
(</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">)
is fixed rather than the number of trials
(</span><span class="zcheltitalic">n</span><span class="generated-style">).
Condition 1 is not met, so</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
X</span><span class="generated-style"> does not have a binomial
distribution in this case.</span>

<span class="generated-style">More than success or failure</span>

<span class="generated-style">Some situations involve more than two
possible outcomes, yet they can appear to be binomial. For example,
suppose you roll a fair die 10 times and let
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">
be the outcome of each roll (1, 2, 3, . . . , 6). You have a series
of</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> n
</span><span class="generated-style">= 10 trials, they are independent,
and the probability of each outcome is the same for each roll. However,
on each roll you’re recording the outcome on a six-sided die, a number
from 1 to 6. This is not a success/failure situation, so condition 2 is
not met.</span>

<span class="generated-style">However, depending on what you’re
recording, situations originally having more than two outcomes can fall
under the binomial category. For example, if you roll a fair die 10
times and each time you record whether or not you get a 1, then
condition 2 is met because your two outcomes of interest are getting a 1
(“success”) and not getting a 1 (“failure”). In this
case,</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
p</span><span class="generated-style"> (the probability of success) =
1/6, and 5/6 is the probability of failure. So if
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">
is counting the number of 1s you get in 10 rolls,
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">
is a binomial random variable.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Trials are not independent</span>

<span class="generated-style">The independence condition is violated
when the outcome of one trial affects another trial. Suppose you want to
know opinions of adults in your city regarding a proposed casino.
Instead of taking a random sample of, say, 100 people, to save time you
select 50 married couples and ask each of them what their opinion is. In
this case it’s reasonable to say couples have a higher chance of
agreeing on their opinions than individuals selected at random, so the
independence condition 4 is not met.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Probability of success (p) changes</span>

<span class="generated-style">You have 10 people — 6 women and 4 men —
and you want to form a committee of 2 people at random. Let
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">
be the number of women on the committee of 2. The chance of selecting a
woman at random on the first try is 6/10. Because you can’t select this
same woman again, the chance of selecting another woman is now 5/9. The
value of</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> p
</span><span class="generated-style">has changed, and condition 3 is not
met.</span>

![headsup_lewis.eps](9780470911082/images/headsup_lewis_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
If the population is very large (for example all U.S. adults),
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">p
</span><span class="generated-style">still changes every time you choose
someone, but the change is negligible, so you don’t worry about it. You
still say the trials are independent with the same probability of
success,
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">p.</span><span class="generated-style">
(Life is so much easier that way!)</span>

<div class="story">

<span class="generated-style">Chapter 9</span>

<span class="generated-style">The Normal Distribution</span>

<span class="generated-style">In This Chapter</span>

![arrow](9780470911082/images/arrow.png)
<span class="generated-style">Understanding the normal and standard
normal distributions</span>

![arrow](9780470911082/images/arrow.png)
<span class="generated-style">Going from start to finish when finding
normal probabilities</span>

![arrow](9780470911082/images/arrow.png)
<span class="generated-style">Working backward to find

<span class="drop-cap">I</span><span class="generated-style">n your
statistical travels you’ll come across two major types of random
variables: discrete and continuous.
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Discrete random
variables</span><span class="generated-style"> basically count things
(number of heads on 10 coin flips, number of female Democrats in a
sample, and so on). The most well-known discrete random variable is the
binomial. (See Chapter 8 for more on discrete random variables and
binomials). A </span><span class="zcheltitalic">continuous random
variable</span><span class="generated-style"> is typically based on
measurements; it either takes on an uncountably infinite number of
values (values within an interval on the real line), or it has so many
possible values that it may as well be deemed continuous (for example,
time to complete a task, exam scores, and so on).</span>

<span class="generated-style">In this chapter, you understand and
calculate probabilities for the most famous continuous random variable
of all time — the normal distribution. You also find percentiles for the
normal distribution, where you are given a probability as a percent and
you have to find the value of
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">
that’s associated with it. And you can think how funny it would be to
see a statistician wearing a T-shirt that said “I’d rather be
normal.”</span>

<span class="generated-style">Exploring the Basics of theNormal
Distribution</span>

<span class="generated-style">A continuous random variable
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">
has a normal distribution if its values fall into a smooth (continuous)
curve with a bell-shaped pattern. Each normal distribution has its own
mean, denoted by the Greek letter
</span><span class="zsymbolslant">μ</span><span class="generated-style">
(say “mu”); and its own standard deviation, denoted by the Greek letter
</span><span class="zsymbolslant">σ</span><span class="generated-style">
(say “sigma”). But no matter what their means and standard deviations
are, all normal distributions have the same basic bell shape. Figure 9-1
shows some examples of normal distributions.</span>

<div class="story">

**Figure 9-1:**<span class="generated-style"> Three normal
distributions, with means and standard deviations of a) 90 and 30; b)
120 and 30; and c) 90 and 10, respectively.</span>

</div>

![9780470911082-fg0901.eps](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-fg0901_fmt.png)

<span class="generated-style">Every normal distribution has certain
properties. You use these properties to determine the relative standing
of any particular result on the distribution, and to find probabilities.
The properties of any normal distribution are as follows:</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">Its shape is symmetric (that is, when you
cut it in half the two pieces are mirror images of each other).</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">Its distribution has a bump in the middle,
with tails going down and out to the left and right.</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">The mean and the median are the same and
lie directly in the middle of the distribution (due to symmetry).</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">Its standard deviation measures the
distance on the distribution from the mean to the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">inflection
point</span><span class="generated-style"> (the place where the curve
changes from an “upside-down-bowl” shape to a “right-side-up-bowl”
shape).</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">Because of its unique bell shape,
probabilities for the normal distribution follow the Empirical Rule
(full details in Chapter 5), which says the following:</span>

<span class="generated-style"> • About 68 percent of its values lie
within one standard deviation of the mean. To find this range, take the
value of the standard deviation, then find the mean plus this amount,
and the mean minus this amount.</span>

<span class="generated-style"> • About 95 percent of its values lie
within two standard deviations of the mean. (Here you take 2 times the
standard deviation, then add it to and subtract it from the
mean.)</span>

<span class="generated-style"> • Almost all of its values (about 99.7
percent of them) lie within three standard deviations of the mean. (Take
3 times the standard deviation and add it to and subtract it from the
mean.)</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">Precise probabilities for all possible
intervals of values on the normal distribution (not just for those
within 1, 2, or 3 standard deviations from the mean) are found using a
table with minimal (if any) calculations. (The next section gives you
all the info on this table.)</span>

<span class="generated-style">Take a look again at Figure 9-1. To
compare and contrast the distributions shown in Figure 9-1a, b, and c,
you first see they are all symmetric with the signature bell shape. The
examples in Figure 9-1a and Figure 9-1b have the same standard
deviation, but their means are different; Figure 9-1b is located 30
units to the right of Figure 9-1a because its mean is 120 compared to
90. Figures 9-1a and c have the same mean (90), but Figure 9-1a has more
variability than Figure 9-1c due to its higher standard deviation (30
compared to 10). Because of the increased variability, the values in
Figure 9-1a stretch from 0 to 180 (approximately), while the values in
Figure 9-1c only go from 60 to 120.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Finally, Figures 9-1b and c have different
means and different standard deviations entirely; Figure 9-1b has a
higher mean which shifts it to the right, and Figure 9-1c has a smaller
standard deviation; its values are the most concentrated around the
mean.</span>

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Noting the mean and standard deviation is important so you can properly
interpret numbers located on a particular normal distribution. For
example, you can compare where the number 120 falls on each of the
normal distributions in Figure 9-1. In Figure 9-1a, the number 120 is
one standard deviation above the mean (because the standard deviation is
30, you get 90 + 1
</span><span class="zmathpiltstd">∗</span><span class="generated-style">
30 = 120). So on this first distribution, the number 120 is the upper
value for the range where about 68% of the data are located, according
to the Empirical Rule (see Chapter 5).</span>

<span class="generated-style">In Figure 9-1b, the number 120 lies
directly on the mean, where the values are most concentrated. In
Figure 9-1c, the number 120 is way out on the rightmost fringe, 3
standard deviations above the mean (because the standard deviation this
time is 10, you get 90 + 3\[10\]=120). In Figure 9-1c, values beyond 120
are very unlikely to occur because they are beyond the range where about
99.7% of the values should be, according to the Empirical Rule.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Meeting the Standard Normal (Z-)
Distribution</span>

<span class="generated-style">One very special member of the normal
distribution family is called the standard normal distribution, or
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z</span><span class="generated-style">-distribution.
The
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z</span><span class="generated-style">-distribution
is used to help find probabilities and percentiles for regular normal
distributions
(</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">).
It serves as the standard by which all other normal distributions are
measured.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Checking out Z</span>

<span class="generated-style">The
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z-</span><span class="generated-style">distribution
is a normal distribution with mean zero and standard deviation 1; its
graph is shown in Figure 9-2. Almost all (about 99.7%) of its values lie
between –3 and +3 according to the Empirical Rule. Values on the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z-</span><span class="generated-style">distribution
are called
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">z</span><span class="generated-style">-values,
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">z-</span><span class="generated-style">scores,
or standard scores. A
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">z-value</span><span class="generated-style">
represents the number of standard deviations that a particular value
lies above or below the mean. For example,
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">z</span><span class="generated-style">
= 1 on the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z-</span><span class="generated-style">distribution
represents a value that is 1 standard deviation above the mean.
Similarly,
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">z</span><span class="generated-style">
= –1 represents a value that is one standard deviation below the mean
(indicated by the minus sign on the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">z-</span><span class="generated-style">value).
And a
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">z-</span><span class="generated-style">value
of 0 is — you guessed it — right on the mean. All
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">z-</span><span class="generated-style">values
are universally understood.</span>

<span class="generated-style">If you refer back to Figure 9-1 and the
discussion regarding where the number 120 lies on each normal
distribution in “Exploring the Basics of the Normal Distribution,” you
can now calculate
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">z-</span><span class="generated-style">values
to get a much clearer picture. In Figure 9-1a, the number 120 is located
one standard deviation above the mean, so its
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">z-</span><span class="generated-style">value
is 1. In Figure 9-1b, 120 is equal to the mean, so its
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">z-</span><span class="generated-style">value
is 0. Figure 9-1c shows that 120 is 3 standard deviations above the
mean, so its
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">z-</span><span class="generated-style">value
is 3.</span>

<div class="story">

**Figure 9-2:**<span class="generated-style"> The
</span><span class="zunivitalic">Z-</span><span class="generated-style">distribution
has a mean of 0 and standard deviation of 1.</span>

</div>

![9780470911082-fg0902.eps](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-fg0902_fmt.png)

\
\

![headsup_lewis.eps](9780470911082/images/headsup_lewis_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
High standard scores (z-values) aren’t always the best. For example, if
you’re measuring the amount of time needed to run around the block, a
standard score of +2 is a bad thing because your time was two standard
deviations above (more than) the overall average time. In this case, a
standard score of –2 would be much better, indicating your time was two
standard deviations below (less than) the overall average time.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Standardizing from X to Z</span>

<span class="generated-style">Probabilities for any continuous
distribution are found by finding the area under a curve (if you’re into

don’t worry about it). Although the bell-shaped curve for the normal
distribution looks easy to work with, calculating areas under its curve
turns out to be a nightmare requiring high-level math procedures
(believe me, I won’t be going there in this book!). Plus, every normal
distribution is different, causing you to repeat this process over and
over each time you have to find a new probability.</span>

<span class="generated-style">To help get over this obstacle,
statisticians worked out all the math gymnastics for one particular

distribution they chose to crank out the table for?</span>

<span class="generated-style">Yes, all the basic results you need to
find probabilities for any normal distribution
(</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">)
can be boiled down into one table based on the standard normal
(</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z-</span><span class="generated-style">)
distribution. This table is called the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z-</span><span class="generated-style">table
and is found in the appendix. Now all you need is one formula that
transforms values from your normal distribution (X) to the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z-</span><span class="generated-style">distribution;
from there you can use the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z-</span><span class="generated-style">table
to find any probability you need.</span>

</span><span class="zcheltitalic">x-</span><span class="generated-style">value
to a
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">z-</span><span class="generated-style">value
is called
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">standardizing.</span><span class="generated-style">
The so-called “z-formula” for standardizing an
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">x-</span><span class="generated-style">value
to a
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">z-</span><span class="generated-style">value
is:</span>

![9780470911082-EQ09001.eps](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-EQ09001_fmt.png)

<span class="generated-style">You take your
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">x-</span><span class="generated-style">value,
subtract the mean of
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X,</span><span class="generated-style">
and divide by the standard deviation of
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X.</span><span class="generated-style">
This gives you the corresponding standard score
(</span><span class="zcheltitalic">z-</span><span class="generated-style">value
or
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">z-</span><span class="generated-style">score).</span>

![headsup_lewis.eps](9780470911082/images/headsup_lewis_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Standardizing is just like changing units (for example, from Fahrenheit
to Celsius). It doesn’t affect probabilities for X; that’s why you can

![tip.eps](9780470911082/images/tip_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
You can standardize an
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">x-</span><span class="generated-style">value
from any distribution (not just the normal) using the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">z-</span><span class="generated-style">formula.
Similarly, not all standard scores come from a normal
distribution.</span>

![technicalstuff.eps](9780470911082/images/technicalstuff_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Because you subtract the mean from your

and divide everything by the standard deviation when you standardize,

where negative values indicate being below the mean, positive values

</span>![9780470911082-EQ09018.eps](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-eq09018_fmt.png).

To interpret a standard score, you don’t need to know the original

<span class="generated-style">Finding X When You Know the Percent</span>

<span class="generated-style">Another popular normal distribution
problem involves finding percentiles for
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">
(see Chapter 5 for a detailed rundown on percentiles). That is, you are
given the percentage or probability of being at or below a certain
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">x-</span><span class="generated-style">value,
and you have to find the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">x-</span><span class="generated-style">value
that corresponds to it. For example, if you know that the people whose
golf scores were in the lowest 10% got to go to the tournament, you may
wonder what the cutoff score was; that score would represent the 10th
percentile.</span>

![headsup_lewis.eps](9780470911082/images/headsup_lewis_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
A percentile isn’t a percent. A percent is a number between 0 and 100; a
percentile is a value of
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">
(a height, an IQ, a test score, and so on).</span>

<span class="generated-style">Figuring out a percentile for a normal
distribution</span>

<span class="generated-style">Certain percentiles are so popular that

— the first quartile, or the 25th percentile;
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Q</span><span class="zsubscript">2</span><span class="generated-style">
— the 2nd quartile (also known as the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">median</span><span class="generated-style">
or the 50th percentile); and
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Q</span><span class="zsubscript">3</span><span class="generated-style">
— the 3rd quartile or the 75th percentile. (See Chapter 5 for more
information on quartiles.)</span>

![headsup_lewis.eps](9780470911082/images/headsup_lewis_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Some percentile problems are especially challenging to translate. For
example, suppose the amount of time for a racehorse to run around a

</span><span class="zcheltitalic">above</span><span class="generated-style">
the cutoff must be 90. (It’s an easy mistake to think it’s the other way

on the left tail of the distribution. You now work this problem the same

= –1.28 looking at the</span><span class="zcheltitalic">

seconds. So the cutoff time needed for a racehorse to qualify (that is,

</span><span class="zcheltitalic">z</span><span class="generated-style">-value

![tip.eps](9780470911082/images/tip_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
The
50</span><span class="zsuperscript">th</span><span class="generated-style">
percentile for the normal distribution is the mean (because of symmetry)
and its
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">z</span><span class="generated-style">-score
is zero. Smaller percentiles, like the 10th, lie below the mean and have
negative
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">z</span><span class="generated-style">-scores.
Larger percentiles, like the 75th, lie above the mean and have positive
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">z</span><span class="generated-style">-scores.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Here’s another style of wording that has a

![arrow](9780470911082/images/arrow.png)
<span class="generated-style">Understanding and using the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">table</span>

<span class="drop-cap">T</span><span class="generated-style">he
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">distribution
is one of the mainstays of data analysis. You may have heard of the
“</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">test”
for example, which is often used to compare two groups in medical
studies and scientific experiments.</span>

<span class="generated-style">This short chapter covers the basic
characteristics and uses of the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">distribution.
You find out how it compares to the normal distribution (more on that in
Chapter 9) and how to use the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">table
to find probabilities and percentiles.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Basics of the t-Distribution</span>

<span class="generated-style">In this section, you get an overview of
the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="generated-style">-distribution,
its main characteristics, when it’s used, and how it’s related to the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z</span><span class="generated-style">-distribution
(see Chapter 9).</span>

<span class="generated-style">Comparing the t- and
Z-distributions</span>

<span class="generated-style">The normal distribution is that well-known
bell-shaped distribution whose mean is
</span><span class="zsymbolslant">μ</span><span class="generated-style">
and whose standard deviation is
</span><span class="zsymbolslant">σ</span><span class="generated-style">
(see Chapter 9 for more on the normal distribution). The most common
normal distribution is the standard normal (also called the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z-</span><span class="generated-style">distribution),
whose mean is 0 and standard deviation is 1.</span>

<span class="generated-style">The
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">distribution
can be thought of as a cousin of the standard normal distribution — it
looks similar in that it’s centered at zero and has a basic bell-shape,
but it’s shorter and flatter than the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z-</span><span class="generated-style">distribution.
Its standard deviation is proportionally larger compared to the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z,</span><span class="generated-style">
which is why you see the fatter tails on each side.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Figure 10-1 compares the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">
and standard normal
(</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z-</span><span class="generated-style">)
distributions in their most general forms.</span>

<div class="story">

**Figure 10-1:**<span class="generated-style"> Comparing the standard
normal
(</span><span class="zunivitalic">Z-</span><span class="generated-style">)
distribution to a generic
</span><span class="zunivitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">distribution.</span>

</div>

![9780470911082-fg1001.eps](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-fg1001_fmt.png)

<span class="generated-style">The
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">distribution
is typically used to study the mean of a population, rather than to
study the individuals within a population. In particular, it is used in
many cases when you use data to estimate the population mean — for
example, to estimate the average price of all the new homes in
California. Or when you use data to test someone’s claim about the
population mean — for example, is it true that the mean price of all the
new homes in California is \$500,000?</span>

![tip.eps](9780470911082/images/tip_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
These procedures are called </span><span class="zcheltitalic">confidence
intervals</span><span class="generated-style"> and
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">hypothesis
tests</span><span class="generated-style"> and are discussed in Chapters
13 and 14, respectively.</span>

<span class="generated-style">The connection between the normal
distribution and the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">distribution
is that the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">distribution
is often used for analyzing the mean of a population if the population
has a normal distribution (or fairly close to it). Its role is
especially important if your data set is small or if you don’t know the
standard deviation of the population (which is often the case).</span>

<span class="generated-style">When statisticians use the term
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-distribution,</span><span class="generated-style">
they aren’t talking about just one individual distribution. There is an
entire family of specific
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">distributions,
depending on what sample size is being used to study the population
mean.</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
</span><span class="generated-style">Each
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">distribution
is distinguished by what statisticians call its
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">degrees of
freedom.</span><span class="generated-style"> In situations where you
have one population and your sample size is
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">n,</span><span class="generated-style">
the degrees of freedom for the corresponding
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">distribution
is </span><span class="zcheltitalic">n –
</span><span class="generated-style">1. For example, a sample of size 10
uses a
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">distribution
with 10 – 1, or 9, degrees of freedom, denoted
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="zsubscript">9</span><span class="generated-style">
(pronounced </span><span class="zcheltitalic">tee
sub-nine</span><span class="generated-style">). Situations involving two
populations use different degrees of freedom and are discussed in
Chapter 15.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Discovering the effect of variability on
t-distributions</span>

<span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">distributions
based on smaller sample sizes have larger standard deviations than those
based on larger sample sizes. Their shapes are flatter; their values are
more spread out. That’s because results based on smaller data sets are
more variable than results based on large data sets.</span>

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
The larger the sample size is, the larger the degrees of freedom will
be, and the more the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">distributions
look like the standard normal distribution
(</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z-</span><span class="generated-style">distribution).
A rough cutoff point where the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="generated-style">-
and
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z</span><span class="generated-style">-distributions
become similar (at least similar enough for jazz or government work) is
around
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">n</span><span class="generated-style">
= 30.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Figure 10-2 shows what different
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">distributions
look like for different sample sizes and how they all compare to the
standard normal
(</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z</span><span class="generated-style">-)
distribution.</span>

**Figure 10-2:**<span class="generated-style">

</span><span class="zunivitalic">Z</span><span class="generated-style">-distribution.</span>

</div>

![9780470911082-fg1002.eps](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-fg1002_fmt.png)

<span class="generated-style">Using the t-Table</span>

<span class="generated-style">Each normal distribution has its own mean
and standard deviation that classify it, so finding probabilities for
each normal distribution on its own is not the way to go. Thankfully,
you can standardize the values of any normal distribution to become
values on a standard normal
(</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z-</span><span class="generated-style">)
distribution (whose mean is 0 and standard deviation is 1) and use a
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z-</span><span class="generated-style">table
(in the appendix) to find probabilities. (Chapter 9 has info on normal
distributions.)</span>

<span class="generated-style">In contrast,
a</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
t-</span><span class="generated-style">distribution is not classified by
its mean and standard deviation, but by the sample size of the data set
being used
(</span><span class="zcheltitalic">n</span><span class="generated-style">).
Unfortunately, there is no single
“standard</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
t-</span><span class="generated-style">distribution” that you can use to
transform the numbers and find probabilities on a table. Because it
wouldn’t be humanly possible to create a table of probabilities and
corresponding</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
t-</span><span class="generated-style">values for every possible
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">distribution,
statisticians created one table showing certain values of
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="generated-style">-distributions
for a selection of degrees of freedom and a selection of probabilities.
This table is called the</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
t-table</span><span class="generated-style"> (it appears in the
appendix). In this section, you find out how to find probabilities,
percentiles, and critical values (for confidence intervals) using
the</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
t-</span><span class="generated-style">table.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Finding probabilities with the
t-table</span>

<span class="generated-style">Each row of the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">table
(in the appendix) represents a
different</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
t-</span><span class="generated-style">distribution, classified by its
degrees of freedom
(</span><span class="zcheltitalic">df</span><span class="generated-style">).
The columns represent various common greater-than probabilities, such as
0.40, 0.25, 0.10, and 0.05. The numbers across a row indicate the values
on the</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
t-</span><span class="generated-style">distribution
(the</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
t-</span><span class="generated-style">values) corresponding to the
greater-than probabilities shown at the top of the columns. Rows are
arranged by degrees of freedom.</span>

![headsup_lewis.eps](9780470911082/images/headsup_lewis_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Another term for greater-than probability is
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">right-tail
probability,</span><span class="generated-style"> which indicates that
such probabilities represent areas on the right-most end (tail) of the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="generated-style">-distribution.</span>

For example, the second row of the
<span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span>table is for the
<span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="zsubscript">2
</span>distribution (2 degrees of freedom, pronounced
<span class="zcheltitalic">tee sub-two</span>). You see that the second
number, 0.816, is the value on the
<span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="zsubscript">2</span>
distribution whose area to its right (its right-tail probability) is
0.25 (see the heading for column 2). In other words, the probability
that
<span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="zsubscript">2</span> is
greater than 0.816 equals 0.25. In probability notation, that means
<span class="zcheltitalic">p</span>(<span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="zsubscript">2
</span>\> 0.816) = 0.25.

<span class="generated-style">The next number in row two of the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="generated-style">-table
is 1.886, which lies in the 0.10 column. This means the probablity of
being greater than 1.886 on the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="zsubscript">2</span>
distribution is 0.10. Because 1.886 falls to the right of 0.816, its
right-tail probability is lower.

<span class="generated-style">Figuring percentiles for the
t-distribution</span>

You can also use the <span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span>table (in the
appendix) to find percentiles for a
<span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="generated-style">-distribution.
A
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">percentile</span><span class="generated-style">
is a number on a distribution whose less-than probability is the given
percentage; for example, the 95th percentile of the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">distribution
with
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">n</span><span class="generated-style">
– 1 degrees of freedom is that value of
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="zcheltitalicsub">n
– </span><span class="zsubscript">1</span><span class="generated-style">
whose left-tail (less-than) probability is 0.95 (and whose right-tail
probability is 0.05). (See Chapter 5 for particulars on
percentiles.)</span>

<span class="generated-style">Suppose you have a sample of size 10 and
you want to find the 95th percentile of its corresponding
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">distribution.
You have
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">n</span><span class="generated-style">
– 1= 9 degrees of freedom, so you look at the row for
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">df</span><span class="generated-style">
= 9. The 95th percentile is the number where 95% of the values lie below
it and 5% lie above it, so you want the right-tail area to be 0.05. Move
across the row, find the column for 0.05, and you get
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="zsubscript">9</span><span class="generated-style">
= 1.833. This is the 95th percentile of the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">distribution
with 9 degrees of freedom.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Now, if you increase the sample size to
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">n</span><span class="generated-style">
= 20, the value of the 95th percentile decreases; look at the row for 20
– 1 = 19 degrees of freedom, and in the column for 0.05 (a right-tail
probability of 0.05) you find
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="zsubscript">19</span><span class="generated-style">
= 1.729. Notice that the 95th percentile for the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="zsubscript">19
</span><span class="generated-style">distribution is less than the 95th
percentile for the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="zsubscript">9
</span><span class="generated-style">distribution (1.833). This is
because larger degrees of freedom indicate a smaller standard deviation
and the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="generated-style">-values
are more concentrated about the mean, so you reach the 95th percentile
with a smaller value of
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="generated-style">.
(See the section “Discovering the effect of variability on
t-distributions,” earlier in this chapter.)</span>

<span class="generated-style">Picking out t\*-values for confidence
intervals</span>

<span class="zcheltitalic">Confidence
intervals</span><span class="generated-style"> estimate population
parameters, such as the population mean, by using a statistic (for
example, the sample mean) plus or minus a margin of error. (See Chapter
13 for all the information you need on confidence intervals and more.)
To compute the margin of error for a confidence interval, you need a
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">critical
value</span><span class="generated-style"> (the number of standard
errors you add and subtract to get the margin of error you want; see
Chapter 13). When the sample size is large (at least 30), you use
critical values on the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z</span><span class="generated-style">-distribution
(shown in Chapter 13) to build the margin of error. When the sample size
is small (less than 30) and/or the population standard deviation is
unknown, you use the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">distribution
to find critical values.</span>

<span class="generated-style">To help you find critical values for the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">distribution,
you can use the last row of the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">table,
which lists common confidence levels, such as 80%, 90%, and 95%. To find
a critical value, look up your confidence level in the bottom row of the
table; this tells you which column of the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">table
you need. Intersect this column with the row for your
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">df</span><span class="generated-style">
(see Chapter 13 for degrees of freedom formulas). The number you see is
the critical value (or the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="generated-style">\*-value)
for your confidence interval. For example, if you want a
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="generated-style">\*-value
for a 90% confidence interval when you have 9 degrees of freedom, go to
the bottom of the table, find the column for 90%, and intersect it with
the row for </span><span class="zcheltitalic">df
</span><span class="generated-style">= 9. This gives you a
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="generated-style">\*</span><span class="zcheltitalic">-</span><span class="generated-style">value
of 1.833 (rounded).</span>

![technicalstuff.eps](9780470911082/images/technicalstuff_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Across the top row of the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="generated-style">-table,
you see right-tail probabilities for the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">distribution.
But confidence intervals involve both left- and right-tail probabilities
(because you add and subtract the margin of error). So half of the
probability left from the confidence interval goes into each tail. You
need to take that into account. For example, a
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="generated-style">\*-value
for a 90% confidence interval has 5% for its greater-than probability
and 5% for its less-than probability (taking 100% minus 90% and dividing
by 2). Using the top row of the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="generated-style">-table,
you would have to look for 0.05 (rather than 10%, as you might be
inclined to do.) But using the bottom row of the table, you just look
for 90%. (The result you get using either method ends up being in the
same column.)</span>

![tip.eps](9780470911082/images/tip_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
When looking for
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t\*-</span><span class="generated-style">values
for confidence intervals, use the bottom row of the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="generated-style">-table
as your guide, rather than the headings at the top of the table.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Studying Behavior Using the t-Table</span>

<span class="generated-style">You can use computer software to calculate
any probabilities, percentiles, or critical values you need for any
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">distribution
(or any other distribution) if it’s available to you. (On exams it may
not be available.) However, one of the nice things about using a table
to find probabilities (rather than using computer software) is that the
table can tell you information about the behavior of the distribution
itself — that is, it can give you the big picture. Here are some nuggets
of big-picture information about the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">distribution
you can glean by scanning the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">table
(in the appendix).</span>

<span class="generated-style">In Figure 10-2, as the degrees of freedom
increase, the values on each
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">distribution
become more concentrated around the mean, eventually resembling the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z-</span><span class="generated-style">distribution.
The
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="generated-style">-table
confirms this pattern as well. Because of the way the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">table
is set up, if you choose any column and move down through the numbers in
the column, you’re increasing the degrees of freedom (and sample size)
and keeping the right-tail probability the same. As you do this, you see
the</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
t-</span><span class="generated-style">values getting smaller and
smaller, indicating the</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
t-</span><span class="generated-style">values are becoming closer to
(hence more concentrated around) the mean.</span>

<span class="generated-style">I labeled the second-to-last row of the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">table
with a
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">z</span><span class="generated-style">
in the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">df</span><span class="generated-style">
column. This indicates the “limit” of
the</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
t-</span><span class="generated-style">values as the sample size
(</span><span class="zcheltitalic">n</span><span class="generated-style">)
goes to infinity. The</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
t-</span><span class="generated-style">values in this row are
approximately the same as the</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
z</span><span class="generated-style">-values on the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z</span><span class="generated-style">-table
(in the appendix) that correspond to the same greater-than
probabilities. This confirms what you already know: As the sample size
increases, the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">
and the</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
Z-</span><span class="generated-style">distributions look more and more
alike. For example, the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">value
in row 30</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
</span><span class="generated-style">of the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="generated-style">-table
corresponding to a right-tail probability of 0.05 (column 0.05) is
1.697. This lies close to
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">z</span><span class="generated-style">
= 1.645, the value corresponding to a right-tail area of 0.05 on the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z-</span><span class="generated-style">distribution.
(See row Z of the t-table.)</span>

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
It doesn’t take a super-large sample size for the values on the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">distribution
to get close to the values on a
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z-</span><span class="generated-style">distribution.
For example, when
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">n</span><span class="generated-style">
= 31 and
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">df</span><span class="generated-style">
= 30, the values in the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">table
are already quite close to the corresponding values on the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z-</span><span class="generated-style">table.</span>

</div>
