<div id="17_9780470911082-ch11.xhtml_x17_9780470911082-ch11">

<div class="story">

<span class="generated-style">Chapter 11</span>

<span class="generated-style">Sampling Distributions and the Central
Limit Theorem</span>

<span class="generated-style">In This Chapter</span>

![arrow](9780470911082/images/arrow.png)
<span class="generated-style">Understanding the concept of a sampling
distribution</span>

![arrow](9780470911082/images/arrow.png)
<span class="generated-style">Putting the Central Limit Theorem to
work</span>

![arrow](9780470911082/images/arrow.png)
<span class="generated-style">Determining the factors that affect
precision</span>

<span class="drop-cap">W</span><span class="generated-style">hen you
take a sample of data, it’s important to realize the results will vary
from sample to sample. Statistical results based on samples should
include a measure of how much those results are expected to vary. When
the media reports statistics like the average price of a gallon of gas
in the U.S. or the percentage of homes on the market that were sold over
the last month, you know they didn’t sample every possible gas station
or every possible home sold. The question is, how much would their
results change if another sample was selected?</span>

<span class="generated-style">This chapter addresses this question by
studying the behavior of means for all possible samples, and the
behavior of proportions from all possible samples. By studying the
behavior of all possible samples, you can gauge where your sample
results fall and understand what it means when your sample results fall
outside of certain expectations.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Defining a Sampling Distribution</span>

<span class="generated-style">A </span><span class="zcheltitalic">random
variable</span><span class="generated-style"> is a characteristic of
interest that takes on certain values in a random manner. For example,
the number of red lights you hit on the way to work or school is a
random variable; the number of children a randomly selected family has
is a random variable. You use capital letters such
as</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> X
</span><span class="generated-style">or
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Y</span><span class="generated-style">
to denote random variables and you use small case
letters</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> x
</span><span class="generated-style">or
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">y</span><span class="generated-style">
to denote actual outcomes of random variables. A
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">distribution
</span><span class="generated-style">is a listing, graph, or function of
all possible outcomes of a random variable (such
as</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> X</span><span class="generated-style">)
and how often each actual outcome
(</span><span class="zcheltitalic">x</span><span class="generated-style">),
or set of outcomes, occurs. (See Chapter 8 for more details on random
variables and distributions.)</span>

<span class="generated-style">For example, suppose a million of your
closest friends each rolls a single die and records each actual outcome
(</span><span class="zcheltitalic">x</span><span class="generated-style">).
A table or graph of all these possible outcomes (one through six) and
how often they occurred represents the distribution of the random
variable</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
X</span><span class="generated-style">. A graph of the distribution
of</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> X
</span><span class="generated-style">in this case is shown in Figure
11-1a. It shows the numbers 1–6 appearing with equal frequency (each one
occurring 1/6 of the time), which is what you expect over many rolls if
the die is fair.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Now suppose each of your friends rolls
this single die 50 times
(</span><span class="zcheltitalic">n</span><span class="generated-style">
= 50) and records the average,
</span>![9780470911082-EQ11001.eps](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-EQ11001_fmt.png)<span class="generated-style">.
The graph of all their averages of all their samples represents the
distribution of the random variable
</span>![9780470911082-EQ11002.eps](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-EQ11002_fmt.png)<span class="generated-style">.
Because this distribution is based on sample averages rather than
individual outcomes, this distribution has a special name. It’s called
the </span><span class="zcheltitalic">sampling
distribution</span><span class="generated-style"> of the sample mean,
</span>![9780470911082-EQ11003.eps](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-EQ11003_fmt.png)<span class="generated-style">.
Figure 11-1b shows the sampling distribution of
</span>![9780470911082-EQ11004.eps](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-EQ11004_fmt.png)<span class="generated-style">,
the average of 50 rolls of a die.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Figure 11-1b (average of 50 rolls) shows
the same range (1 through 6) of outcomes as Figure 11-1a (individual
rolls), but Figure 11-1b has more possible outcomes. You could get an
average of 3.3 or 2.8 or 3.9 for 50 rolls, for example, whereas someone
rolling a single die can only get whole numbers from 1 to 6. Also, the
shape of the graphs are different; Figure 11-1a shows a flat shape,
where each outcome is equally likely, and Figure 11-1b has a mound
shape; that is, outcomes near the center (3.5) occur with high frequency
and outcomes near the edges (1 and 6) occur with extremely low
frequency. A detailed look at the differences and similarities in shape,
center, and spread for individuals versus averages, and the reasons
behind them, is the topic of the following sections. (See Chapter 8 if
you need background info on shape, center, and spread of random
variables before diving in.)</span>

<span class="generated-style">The Mean of a Sampling Distribution</span>

<span class="generated-style">Using the die-rolling example from the

</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">
is a random variable denoting the outcome you can get from a single die
(assuming the die is fair). The mean
of</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> X
</span><span class="generated-style">(over all possible outcomes) is
denoted by

(pronounced </span><span class="zcheltitalic">mu
sub-x</span><span class="generated-style">); in this case its value is
3.5 (as shown in Figure 11-1a). If you roll a die 50 times and take the

</span>![9780470911082-EQ11006.eps](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-EQ11006_fmt.png)<span class="generated-style">
represents any outcome you could get. The mean of

<div class="story">

**Figure 11-1:**<span class="generated-style"> Distributions of a)

<span class="generated-style">This result is no coincidence! In general,

It’s a mouthful, but it makes sense that the average of the averages

![tip.eps](9780470911082/images/tip_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Using subscripts on
</span>![9780470911082-EQ11010.eps](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-EQ11010_fmt.png)<span class="generated-style">,

<span class="generated-style">Measuring Standard Error</span>

<span class="generated-style">The values in any population deviate from

</span><span class="zcheltitalic">(sigma
sub-x-bar)</span><span class="generated-style">. Its

is population standard deviation
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">(sigma
sub-x)</span><span class="generated-style">
and</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">n
</span><span class="generated-style">is size of each sample. In the next
sections you see the effect each of these two components has on the

<span class="generated-style">Sample size and standard error</span>

<span class="generated-style">The first component of standard error is
the sample size,
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">n</span><span class="generated-style">.
Because</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> n
</span><span class="generated-style">is in the denominator of the
standard error formula, the standard error decreases

</span><span class="generated-style">increases. It makes sense that

<span class="generated-style">Suppose</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
X </span><span class="generated-style">is the time it takes for a

</span><span class="generated-style">has a normal distribution with mean

minutes (quite a bit less than 3 minutes,
</span><span class="generated-style">the standard deviation of the

clerical workers and find their means; the sampling distribution is
shown in the tallest curve in Figure 11-2.
</span><span class="generated-style">The standard error of
</span>![9780470911082-EQ11020.eps](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-EQ11020_fmt.png)<span class="generated-style">
goes down to
</span>![9780470911082-EQ11021.eps](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-EQ11021_fmt.png)<span class="generated-style">
minutes. You can see </span><span class="generated-style">the average
times for 50 clerical workers are even closer to 10.5 than the ones for
10 clerical workers. By the Empirical Rule, most of the values fall
between 10.5 – 3(.42) = 9.24 and 10.5 + 3(.42) = 11.76. Larger samples
give even more precision around the mean because they change even less
from sample to sample.</span>

![technicalstuff.eps](9780470911082/images/technicalstuff_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Why is having more precision around the mean important? Because
sometimes you don’t know the mean but want to determine what it is, or
at least get as close to it as possible. How can you do that? By taking
a large random sample from the population and finding its mean. You know
that your sample mean will be close to the actual population mean if
your sample is large, as Figure 11-2 shows (assuming your data are
collected correctly; see Chapter 16 for details on collecting good
data).</span>

<span class="generated-style">Population standard deviation and standard
error</span>

<span class="generated-style">The second component of standard error
involves the amount of diversity in the population (measured by standard
deviation). In the standard error
</span><span class="generated-style">formula
</span>![9780470911082-EQ11022.eps](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-EQ11022_fmt.png)<span class="generated-style">
you see the population standard deviation,
</span>![9780470911082-EQ11023.eps](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-EQ11023_fmt.png)<span class="generated-style">,
is in the </span><span class="generated-style">numerator. That means as
the population standard deviation increases, the standard error of the
sample means also increases. Mathematically this makes sense; how about
statistically?</span>

<span class="generated-style">Suppose you have two ponds full of fish
(call them pond \#1 and pond \#2), and you’re interested in the length
of the fish in each pond. Assume the fish lengths in each pond have a
normal distribution (see Chapter 9). You’ve been told that the fish
lengths in pond \#1 have a mean of 20 inches and a standard deviation of
2 inches (see Figure 11-3a). Suppose the fish in pond \#2 also average
20 inches but have a larger standard deviation of 5 inches (see Figure
11-3b).</span>

<span class="generated-style">Comparing Figures 11-3a and 11-3b, you see
the lengths for the two populations of fish have the same shape and
mean, but the distribution in Figure 11-3b (for pond \#2) has more
spread, or variability, than the distribution shown in Figure 11-3a (for
pond \#1). This spread confirms that the fish in pond \#2 vary more in
length than those in pond \#1.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Now suppose you take a random sample of
100 fish from pond \#1, find the mean length of the fish, and repeat
this process over and over. Then you do the same with pond \#2. Because
the lengths of individual fish in pond \#2 have more variability than
the lengths of individual fish in pond \#1, you know the average lengths
of samples from pond \#2 will have more variability than the average
lengths of samples from pond \#1 as well. (In fact, you can calculate
their standard errors using the formula earlier in this section to be
0.20 and 0.50, respectively.)</span>

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Estimating the population average is harder when the population varies a
lot to begin with — estimating the population average is much easier
when the population values are more consistent. The bottom line is the
standard error of the sample mean is larger when the population standard
deviation is larger.</span>

just by chance things won’t even out as well, but that won’t happen very
often with 50 rolls.</span>

it was assumed that the average time for all workers to type up a
recommendation letter was 10.5 minutes. Your sample averaged 9.5
minutes. Because the probability that they would average less than 9.5
minutes was found to be tiny (0.0091), you either got an unusually high
number of fast workers in your sample just by chance, or the assumption
that the average time for all workers is 10.5 minutes was simply too
high. (I’m betting on the latter.) The process of checking assumptions
or challenging claims about a population is called hypothesis testing;
details are in Chapter 14.</span>

<span id="18_9780470911082-pp04.xhtml"></span>

<div id="18_9780470911082-pp04.xhtml_x18_9780470911082-pp04">

<div class="story">

<span class="generated-style">Part IV</span>

<span class="generated-style">Guesstimating and Hypothesizing with
Confidence</span>

<div class="image">

![9780470911082-pp0401.eps](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-pp0401_fmt.png)

</div>

<span class="generated-style">In this part . . .</span>

Anytime you’re given a statistic by itself, you haven’t really gotten
the full story. The statistic alone is missing the most important part:
by how much that statistic is expected to vary. All good estimates of
population parameters contain not just a statistic but also a margin of
error. This combination of a statistic plus or minus a margin of error
is called a confidence interval.

Now suppose you’re already given a claim, assumption, or target value
for the population parameter, and you want to test that claim. You do it
with a hypothesis test based on sample statistics. Because sample
statistics will vary, you need techniques that take this into account.

This part gives you a general, intuitive look at margin of error,
confidence intervals, and hypothesis tests: their function, formulas,
calculations, influential factors, and interpretation. You also get
quick references and examples for the most commonly used confidence
intervals and hypothesis tests.

</div>

</div>

<span id="19_9780470911082-ch12.xhtml"></span>

<div id="19_9780470911082-ch12.xhtml_x19_9780470911082-ch12">

<div class="story">

<span class="generated-style">Chapter 12</span>

<span class="generated-style">Leaving Room for a Margin of Error</span>

<span class="generated-style">In This Chapter</span>

![arrow](9780470911082/images/arrow.png)
<span class="generated-style">Understanding and calculating margin of
error</span>

![arrow](9780470911082/images/arrow.png)
<span class="generated-style">Exploring the effect of sample size</span>

![arrow](9780470911082/images/arrow.png)
<span class="generated-style">Finding out what margin of error doesn’t
measure</span>

<span class="drop-cap">G</span><span class="generated-style">ood survey
and experiment researchers always include some measure of how accurate
their results are so that consumers of the information can put the
results into perspective. This measure is called the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">margin of error
(MOE)</span><span class="generated-style"> — it’s a measure of how close
the sample statistic (one number that summarizes the sample) is expected
to be to the population parameter being studied. (A population parameter
is one number that summarizes the population. Find out more about
statistics and parameters in Chapter 4.)Thankfully, many journalists are
also realizing the importance of the MOE in assessing information, so
reports that include the margin of error are beginning to appear in the
media. But what does the margin of error really mean, and does it tell
the whole story?</span>

<span class="generated-style">This chapter looks at the margin of error
and what it can and can’t do to help you assess the accuracy of
statistical information. It also examines the issue of sample size; you
may be surprised at how small a sample can be used to get a good handle
on the pulse of America — or the world — if the research is done
correctly.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Seeing the Importance of That Plus or
Minus</span>

<span class="generated-style">Margin of error is probably not a new term
to you. You’ve probably heard of it before, most likely in the context
of survey results. For example, you may have heard someone report, “This
survey had a margin of error of plus or minus three percentage points.”
And you may have wondered what you’re supposed to do with that
information and how important it really is. The truth is, the survey
results themselves (with no MOE) are only a measure of how the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">sample</span><span class="generated-style">
of selected individuals felt about the issue; they don’t reflect how the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">entire
population</span><span class="generated-style"> may have felt, had they
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">all</span><span class="generated-style">
been asked. The margin of error helps you estimate how close you are to
the truth about the population based on your sample data.</span>

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Results based on a sample won’t be exactly the same as what you would’ve
found for the entire population, because when you take a sample, you
don’t get information from everyone in the population. However, if the
study is done right (see Chapters 16 and 17 for more about designing
good studies), the results from the sample should be close to and
representative of the actual values for the entire population, with a
high level of confidence.</span>

![technicalstuff.eps](9780470911082/images/technicalstuff_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
The MOE doesn’t mean someone made a mistake; all it means is that you
didn’t get to sample everybody in the population, so you expect your
sample results to vary from that population by a certain amount. In
other words, you acknowledge that your results will change with
subsequent samples and are only accurate to within a certain range —
which can be calculated using the margin of error.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Consider one example of the type of survey
conducted by some of the leading polling organizations, such as the
Gallup Organization. Suppose its latest poll sampled 1,000 people from
the United States, and the results show that 520 people (52%) think the
president is doing a good job, compared to 48% who don’t think so.
Suppose Gallup reports that this survey had a margin of error of plus or
minus 3%. Now, you know that the majority (more than 50%) of the people
in this </span><span class="zcheltitalic">sample
</span><span class="generated-style">approve of the president, but can
you say that the majority of </span><span class="zcheltitalic">all
Americans</span><span class="generated-style"> approve of the president?
In this case, you can’t. Why not?</span>

<span class="generated-style">You need to include the margin of error
(in this case, 3%) in your results. If 52% of
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">those
sampled</span><span class="generated-style"> approve of the president,
you can expect that the percent of the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">population of all
Americans</span><span class="generated-style"> who approve of the
president will be 52%, plus or minus 3%. Therefore, between 49% and 55%
of all Americans approve of the president. That’s as close as you can
get with your sample of 1,000. But notice that 49%, the lower end of
this range, represents a minority, because it’s less than 50%. So you
really can’t say that a majority of the American people support the
president, based on this sample. You can only say you’re confident that
between 49% and 55% of all Americans support the president, which may or
may not be a majority.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Think about the sample size for a moment.
Isn’t it interesting that a sample of only 1,000 Americans out of a
population of well over 310,000,000 can lead you to be within plus or
minus only 3% on your survey results? That’s incredible! That means for
large populations you only need to sample a tiny portion of the total to
get close to the true value (assuming, as always, that you have good
data). Statistics is indeed a powerful tool for finding out how people
feel about issues, which is probably why so many people conduct surveys
and why you’re so often bothered to respond to them as well.</span>

![tip.eps](9780470911082/images/tip_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
When you are working with categorical variables (those that record
certain characteristics that don’t involve measurements or counts; see
Chapter 6), a quick-and-dirty way to get a rough idea of the margin of
error for proportions, for any given sample size
(</span><span class="zcheltitalic">n</span><span class="generated-style">),
is simply to find 1 divided by the square root of
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">n</span><span class="generated-style">.
For the Gallup poll example,</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> n
</span><span class="generated-style">= 1,000, and its square root is
roughly 31.62, so the margin of error is roughly 1 divided by 31.62, or
about 0.03, which is equivalent to 3%. In the remainder of this chapter,
you see how to get a more accurate measure of the margin of
error.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Finding the Margin of Error: A General
Formula</span>

<span class="generated-style">The margin of error is the amount of “plus
or minus” that is attached to your sample result when you move from
discussing the sample itself to discussing the whole population that it
represents. Therefore, you know that the general formula for the margin
of error contains a
“</span><span class="zsymbolmedium">±</span><span class="generated-style">”
in front of it. So, how do you come up with that plus or minus amount
(other than taking a rough estimate, as shown above)? This section shows
you how.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Measuring sample variability</span>

<span class="generated-style">Sample results vary, but by how much?
According to the Central Limit Theorem (see Chapter 11), when sample
sizes are large enough, the so-called sampling distribution of the
sample proportions (or the sample means) follows a bell-shaped curve (or
approximate normal distribution — see Chapter 9). Some of the sample
proportions (or sample means) overestimate the population value and some
underestimate it, but most are close to the middle.</span>

<span class="generated-style">And what’s in the middle of this sampling
distribution? If you average out the results from all the possible
samples you could take, the average is the actual
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">population
proportion,</span><span class="generated-style"> in the case of
categorical data, or the actual
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">population average,
</span><span class="generated-style">in the case of numerical data.
Normally, you don’t know all the values of the population, so you can’t
look at all of the possible sample results and average them out — but
knowing something about all the other sample possibilities does help you
to measure the amount by which you expect your own sample proportion (or
average) to vary. (See Chapter 11 for more on sample means and
proportions.)</span>

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Standard errors are the basic building blocks of the margin of error.
The </span><span class="zcheltitalic">standard
error</span><span class="generated-style"> of a statistic is basically
equal to the standard deviation of the population divided by the square
root of</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> n
</span><span class="generated-style">(the sample size). This reflects
the fact that the sample size greatly affects how much that sample
statistic is going to vary from sample to sample. (See Chapter 11 for
more about standard errors.)</span>

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
The number of standard errors you have to add or subtract to get the MOE
depends on how confident you want to be in your results (this is called
your </span><span class="zcheltitalic">confidence
level</span><span class="generated-style">). Typically, you want to be
about 95% confident, so the basic rule is to add or subtract about 2
standard errors (1.96, to be exact) to get the MOE (you get this from
the Empirical Rule; see Chapter 9). This allows you to account for about
95% of all possible results that may have occurred with repeated
sampling. To be 99% confident, you add and subtract 2.58 standard
errors. (This assumes a normal distribution on large n; standard
deviation known. See Chapter 11.)</span>

<span class="generated-style">You can be more precise about the number
of standard errors you have to add or subtract in order to calculate the

(</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z-</span><span class="generated-style">)
distribution. (See Chapter 13 for details.) For any given confidence
level, a corresponding value on the standard normal distribution (called
a</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
z\*-value</span><span class="generated-style">) represents the number of
standard errors to add and subtract to account for that confidence
level. For 95% confidence, a more
precise</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
z\*</span><span class="generated-style">-value is 1.96 (which is “about”
2), and for 99% confidence, the exact</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
z\*</span><span class="generated-style">-value is 2.58. Some of the more
commonly used confidence levels (also known as percentage confidence),
along with their corresponding</span><span class="zcheltitalic">

12-1.</span>

![/Table 12-1](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-tb1201.jpg)

![headsup_lewis.eps](9780470911082/images/headsup_lewis_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
To find a z\*-value like those in Table 12-1, add to the confidence
level to make it a less-than probability and find its corresponding
z-value on the Z-table. For example, a 95% confidence level means the

2.5% (half of what’s left), or 97.5%. Look up 0.975 in the body of the
Z-table and find z \* = 1.96 for a 95% confidence level.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Sample size and margin of error</span>

and sample size is simple: As the sample size increases, the margin of
error decreases. This relationship is called an inverse because the two
move in opposite directions. If you think about it, it makes sense that
the more information you have, the more accurate your results are going
to get (in other words, the smaller your margin of error will get).
(That assumes, of course, that the data were collected and handled
properly.)</span>

In the previous section, you see that the impact of a larger confidence
level is a larger MOE. But if you increase the sample size, you can
offset the larger MOE and bring it down to a reasonable size! Find out
more about this concept in Chapter 13.</span>

approval rating of the president (see the earlier section “Calculating

only 1,000 people from well over 310,000,000 residents in the United
States could get to within about 3% of what the whole population would
have said, if they had all been asked. </span>

a sample proportion, you can look at how the margin of error changes

= 0.52 for this example.) Therefore the margin of error for 95%

</span>![9780470911082-EQ12019.eps](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-EQ12019_fmt.png)<span class="generated-style">,
which is equivalent to 4.38%.
</span><span class="generated-style">When</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
n </span><span class="generated-style">= 1,000 in the same example, the
margin of error (for 95% confidence)
</span><span class="generated-style">is
</span>![9780470911082-EQ12020.eps](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-EQ12020_fmt.png)<span class="generated-style">,
which is equal to 3.10%. If</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> n
</span><span class="generated-style">is increased to 1,500, the margin
of error (with the same level of confidence)
</span><span class="generated-style">becomes
</span>![9780470911082-EQ12021.eps](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-EQ12021_fmt.png)<span class="generated-style">,
or 2.53%. Finally, when</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">n
</span><span class="generated-style">= 2,000, the margin of error is
</span>![9780470911082-EQ12022.eps](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-EQ12022_fmt.png)<span class="generated-style">,
or 2.19%.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Looking at these different results, you
can see that larger sample sizes decrease the MOE, but after a certain
point, you have a diminished return. Each time you survey one more
person, the cost of your survey increases, and going from a sample size
of, say, 1,500 to a sample size of 2,000 decreases your margin of error
by only 0.34% (one third of one percent!) — from 0.0253 to 0.0219. The
extra cost and trouble to get that small decrease in the MOE may not be
worthwhile. Bigger isn’t always that much better!</span>

<span class="generated-style">But what may really surprise you is that
bigger can actually be worse! I explain this surprising fact in the
following section.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Keeping margin of error in
perspective</span>

<span class="generated-style">The margin of error is a measure of how
close you expect your sample results to represent the entire population
being studied. (Or at least it gives an upper limit for the amount of
error you should have.) Because you’re basing your conclusions about the
population on your one sample, you have to account for how much those
sample results could vary just due to chance.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Another view of margin of error is that it
represents the maximum expected distance between the sample results and
the actual population results (if you’d been able to obtain them through
a census). Of course if you had the absolute truth about the population,
you wouldn’t be trying to do a survey, would you?</span>

<span class="generated-style">Just as important as knowing what the
margin of error measures is realizing what the margin of error does
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">not</span><span class="generated-style">
measure. The margin of error does not measure anything other than chance
variation. That is, it doesn’t measure any bias or errors that happen
during the selection of the participants, the preparation or conduct of
the survey, the data collection and entry process, or the analysis of
the data and the drawing of the final conclusions.</span>

![headsup_lewis.eps](9780470911082/images/headsup_lewis_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
A good slogan to remember when examining statistical results is “garbage
in equals garbage out.” No matter how nice and scientific the margin of
error may look, remember that the formula that was used to calculate it
doesn’t have any idea of the quality of the data that the margin of
error is based on. If the sample proportion or sample mean was based on
a </span><span class="zcheltitalic">biased
sample</span><span class="generated-style"> (one that favored certain
people over others), a bad design, bad data-collection procedures,
biased questions, or systematic errors in recording, then calculating
the margin of error is pointless because it won’t mean a thing.</span>

<span class="generated-style">For example, 50,000 people surveyed sounds
great, but if they were all visitors to a certain Web site, the margin
of error for this result is bogus because the calculation is all based
on biased results! In fact, many extremely large samples are the result
of biased sampling procedures. Of course, some people go ahead and
report them anyway, so you have to find out what went into the formula:
good information or garbage? If it turns out to be garbage, you know
what to do about the margin of error. Ignore it. (For more information
on errors that can take place during a survey or experiment, see
Chapters 16 and 17, respectively.)</span>

<span class="generated-style">The Gallup Organization addresses the
issue of what margin of error does and doesn’t measure in a disclaimer
that it uses to report its survey results. Gallup tells you that besides
sampling error, surveys can have additional errors or bias due to
question wording and some of the logistical issues involved in
conducting surveys (such as missing data due to phone numbers that are
no longer current). </span>

<span class="generated-style">This means that even with the best of
intentions and the most meticulous attention to details and process
control, stuff happens. Nothing is ever perfect. But what you need to
know is that the margin of error can’t measure the extent of those other
types of errors. And if a highly credible polling organization like
Gallup admits to possible bias, imagine what’s really going on with
other people’s studies that aren’t nearly as well designed or
conducted.</span>

<div id="20_9780470911082-ch13.xhtml_x20_9780470911082-ch13">

<div class="story">

<span class="generated-style">Chapter 13</span>

<span class="generated-style">Confidence Intervals: Making Your Best
Guesstimate</span>

<span class="generated-style">In This Chapter</span>

![arrow](9780470911082/images/arrow.png)
<span class="generated-style">Understanding confidence interval pieces,
parts, and interpretation</span>

![arrow](9780470911082/images/arrow.png)
<span class="generated-style">Calculating with confidence</span>

![arrow](9780470911082/images/arrow.png)
<span class="generated-style">Examining factors that influence the width
of a confidence interval</span>

![arrow](9780470911082/images/arrow.png)
<span class="generated-style">Detecting misleading results</span>

<span class="drop-cap">M</span><span class="generated-style">ost
statistics are used to estimate some characteristic about a population
of interest, such as average household income, the percentage of people
who buy birthday gifts online, or the average amount of ice cream
consumed in the United States every year (and the resulting average
weight gain — nah!). Such characteristics of a population are called
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">parameters.</span><span class="generated-style">
Typically, people want to estimate (take a good guess at) the value of a
parameter by taking a sample from the population and using statistics
from the sample that will give them a good estimate. The question is:
How do you define “good estimate”?</span>

<span class="generated-style">As long as the process is done correctly
(and in the media, it often isn’t!), an estimate can often get very
close to the parameter. This chapter gives you an overview of confidence
intervals (the type of estimates used and recommended by statisticians);
why they should be used (as opposed to just a one-number estimate); how
to set up, calculate, and interpret the most commonly used confidence
intervals; and how to spot misleading estimates.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Not All Estimates Are Created Equal</span>

<span class="generated-style">Read any magazine or newspaper or listen
to any newscast, and you hear a number of statistics, many of which are
estimates of some quantity or another. You may wonder how they came up
with those statistics. In some cases, the numbers are well researched;
in other cases, they’re just a shot in the dark. Here are some examples
of estimates that I came across in one single issue of a leading
business magazine. They come from a variety of sources:</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">Even though some jobs are harder to get
these days, some areas are really looking for recruits: Over the next
eight years, 13,000 nurse anesthetists will be needed. Pay starts from

<span class="generated-style">Linking a Statistic to a Parameter</span>

<span class="generated-style">A
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">parameter</span><span class="generated-style">
is a single number that describes a population, such as the median
household income for all households in the U.S. A
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">statistic</span><span class="generated-style">
is a single number that describes a sample, such as the median household
income of a sample of, say, 1,200 households. You typically don’t know
the values of parameters of populations, so you take samples and use
statistics to give your best estimates.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Suppose you want to know the percentage of
vehicles in the U.S. that are pickup trucks (that’s the parameter, in
this case). You can’t look at every single vehicle, so you take a random
sample of 1,000 vehicles over a range of highways at different times of
the day. You find that 7% of the vehicles in your sample are pickup
trucks. Now, you don’t want to say that
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">exactly</span><span class="generated-style">
7% of all vehicles on U.S. roads are pickup trucks, because you know
this is only based on the 1,000 vehicles you sampled. Though you hope 7%
is close to the true percentage, you can’t be sure because you based
your results on a sample of vehicles, not on all the vehicles in the
U.S.</span>

<span class="generated-style">So what to do? You take your sample result
and add and subtract some number to indicate that you are giving a range
of possible values for the population parameter, rather than just
assuming the sample statistic equals the population parameter (which
would not be good, although it’s done in the media all the time). This
number that is added to and subtracted from a statistic is called the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">margin of error
</span><span class="generated-style">(</span><span class="zcheltitalic">MOE</span><span class="generated-style">).
This plus or minus (denoted by
</span><span class="zsymbolmedium">±</span><span class="generated-style">)
that’s added to any estimate helps put the results into perspective.
When you know the margin of error, you have an idea of how much the
sample results could change if you took another sample.</span>

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
The word
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">error</span><span class="generated-style">
in </span><span class="zcheltitalic">margin of
error</span><span class="generated-style"> doesn’t mean a mistake was
made or the quality of the data was bad. It just means the results from
a sample are not exactly equal to what you would have gotten if you had
used the entire population. This gap measures error due to random
chance, the luck of the draw — not due to bias. (That’s why minimizing
bias is so important when you select your sample and collect your data;
see Chapters 16 and 17.)</span>

<span class="generated-style">Getting with the Jargon</span>

<span class="generated-style">A statistic plus or minus a margin of
error is called a </span><span class="zcheltitalic">confidence

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">The word
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">interval</span><span class="generated-style">
is used because your result becomes an interval. For example, say the
percentage of kids who like baseball is 40%, plus or minus 3.5%. That
means the percentage of kids who like baseball is somewhere between 40%

your statistic minus the margin of error, and the upper end is your
statistic plus the margin of error.</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">With all confidence intervals, you have a

<span class="generated-style">You can find formulas and examples for the

<span class="zcheltbold">1. Choose your confidence level and your sample
size.</span>

<span class="zcheltbold"> 2. Select a random sample of individuals from
the population.</span>

<span class="zcheltbold"> 3. Collect reliable and relevant data from the

<span class="zcheltbold">4. Summarize the data into a statistic, such as
a mean or proportion.</span>

<span class="zcheltbold"> 5. Calculate the margin of error.</span>

<span class="zcheltbold"> 6. Take the statistic plus or minus the margin
of error to get your final estimate of the parameter.</span>

<span class="generated-style"> This step calculates the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">confidence
interval</span><span class="generated-style"> for that parameter.</span>

The width of a confidence interval is the distance from the lower end of
the interval (statistic minus margin of error) to the upper end of the
interval (statistic plus margin of error). You can always calculate the
width of a confidence interval quickly by taking two times the margin of
error.</span>

<span class="generated-style">The ultimate goal when making an estimate

price doesn’t justify the marginal difference in accuracy. Most people
are pretty comfortable with a margin of error of 2% to 3% when the
estimate itself is a percentage (like the percentage of women,
Republicans, or smokers).</span>

<span class="generated-style">Figuring Out What Sample Size You
Need</span>

<span class="generated-style">The margin of error of a confidence
interval is affected by size (see the earlier section “Factoring In the

this the other way around, if you want a smaller margin of error (and
doesn’t everyone?), you need a larger sample size. Suppose you are
getting ready to do your own survey to estimate a population mean;
wouldn’t it be nice to see ahead of time what sample size you need to
get the margin of error you want? Thinking ahead will save you money and
time and it will give you results you can live with in terms of the
margin of error — you won’t have any surprises later.</span>

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
The formula for the sample size required to get a desired margin of

</span>![9780470911082-EQ13026.eps](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-EQ13026_fmt.png)<span class="generated-style">
is
</span>![9780470911082-EQ13027.eps](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-EQ13027_fmt.png)<span class="generated-style">;
always round up </span><span class="generated-style"> the sample size no
matter what decimal value you get. (For example, if your calculations

in Vegas, I believe I really saw Elvis; he was driving a van taxi to and
from the airport. . . .)</span>

![tip.eps](9780470911082/images/tip_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Notice that you could get a negative value for
</span>![9780470911082-EQ13087.eps](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-EQ13087_fmt.png)<span class="generated-style">.
For example, if you had switched the males and females, you would have
gotten –0.19 for this difference. That’s okay, but you can avoid
negative differences in the sample proportions by having the group with
the larger sample proportion serve as the first group (here,
females).</span>

<span class="generated-style">Spotting Misleading Confidence
Intervals</span>

<span class="generated-style">When the MOE is small, relatively
speaking, you would like to say that these confidence intervals provide
accurate and credible estimates of their parameters. This is not always
the case, however.</span>

![headsup_lewis.eps](9780470911082/images/headsup_lewis_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Not all estimates are as accurate and reliable as the sources may want
you to think. For example, a Web site survey result based on 20,000 hits
may have a small MOE according to the formula, but the MOE means nothing
if the survey is only given to people who happened to visit that Web
site.</span>

<span class="generated-style">In other words, the sample isn’t even
close to being a random sample (where every sample of equal size
selected from the population has an equal chance of being chosen to
participate). Nevertheless, such results do get reported, along with
their margins of error that make the study seem truly scientific. Beware
of these bogus results! (See Chapter</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
</span><span class="generated-style">12 for more on the limits of
the MOE.)</span>

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Before making any decisions based on someone’s estimate, do the
following:</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">Investigate how the statistic was created;
it should be the result of a scientific process that results in
reliable, unbiased, accurate data.</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">Look for a margin of error. If one isn’t
reported, go to the original source and request it.</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">Remember that if the statistic isn’t
reliable or contains bias, the margin of error will be
meaningless.</span>

<span class="generated-style">(See Chapter 16 for evaluating survey data
and see Chapter 17 for criteria for good data in experiments.)</span>

</div>

</div>

<div id="21_9780470911082-ch14.xhtml_x21_9780470911082-ch14">

<div class="story">

<span class="generated-style">Chapter 14</span>

<span class="generated-style">Claims, Tests, and Conclusions</span>

<span class="generated-style">In This Chapter</span>

![arrow](9780470911082/images/arrow.png)
<span class="generated-style">Testing other people’s claims</span>

![arrow](9780470911082/images/arrow.png)
<span class="generated-style">Using hypothesis tests to weigh evidence
and make decisions</span>

![arrow](9780470911082/images/arrow.png)
<span class="generated-style">Recognizing that your conclusions could be
wrong</span>

<span class="drop-cap">Y</span><span class="generated-style">ou hear
claims involving statistics all the time; the media has no shortage of
them:</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">Twenty-five percent of all women in the
United States have varicose veins. (Wow, are some claims better left
unsaid, or what?)</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">Cigarette use in the U.S. continues to
drop, with the percentage of all American smokers decreasing by about 2%
per year over the last ten years.</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">A 6-month-old baby sleeps an average of 14
to 15 hours in a 24-hour period. (Yeah, right!)</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">A name-brand ready-mix pie takes only 5
minutes to make.</span>

<span class="generated-style">In today’s age of information (and big
money), a great deal rides on being able to back up your claims.
Companies that say their products are better than the leading brand had
better be able to prove it, or they could face lawsuits. Drugs that are
approved by the FDA have to show strong evidence that their products
actually work without producing life-threatening side effects.
Manufacturers have to make sure their products are being produced
according to specifications to avoid recalls, customer complaints, and
loss of business.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Although many claims are backed up by
solid scientific (and statistically sound) research, others are not. In
this chapter, you find out how to use statistics to investigate whether
a claim is actually valid and get the lowdown on the process that
researchers
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">should</span><span class="generated-style">
be using to validate claims that they make.</span>

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">A
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">hypothesis
test</span><span class="generated-style"> is a statistical procedure
that’s designed to test a claim. Before diving into details, I want to
give you the big picture of a hypothesis test by showing the main steps
involved. These steps are discussed in the following sections:</span>

<span class="zcheltbold"> 1. Set up the null and alternative
hypotheses.</span>

<span class="zcheltbold"> 2. Collect good data using a well-designed
study (see Chapters 16 and 17).</span>

<span class="zcheltbold"> 3. Calculate the test statistic based on your
data.</span>

<span class="zcheltbold"> 4. Find the
</span><span class="zcheltbolditalic">p-</span><span class="zcheltbold">value
for your test statistic.</span>

<span class="zcheltbold"> 5. Decide whether or not to reject
H</span><span class="zcheltboldsub">o</span><span class="zcheltbold">
based on your
</span><span class="zcheltbolditalic">p-</span><span class="zcheltbold">value.</span>

<span class="zcheltbold">6. Understand that your conclusion may be
wrong, just by chance.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Setting Up the Hypotheses</span>

<span class="generated-style">Typically in a hypothesis test, the claim
being made is about a population
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">parameter</span><span class="generated-style">
(one number that characterizes the entire population). Because
parameters tend to be unknown quantities, everyone wants to make claims
about what their values may be. For example, the claim that 25% (or
0.25) of all women have varicose veins is a claim about the proportion
(that’s the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">parameter</span><span class="generated-style">)
of all women (that’s the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">population</span><span class="generated-style">)
who have varicose veins (that’s the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">variable</span><span class="generated-style">
— having or not having varicose veins).</span>

<span class="generated-style">Researchers often challenge claims about
population parameters. You may hypothesize, for example, that the actual
proportion of women who have varicose veins is lower than 0.25, based on
your observations. Or you may hypothesize that due to the popularity of
high heeled shoes, the proportion may be higher than 0.25. Or if you’re
simply questioning whether the actual proportion is 0.25, your
alternative hypothesis is: “No, it isn’t 0.25.”</span>

<span class="generated-style">Defining the null</span>

<span class="generated-style">Every hypothesis test contains a set of
two opposing statements, or hypotheses, about a population parameter.
The first hypothesis is called the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">null
hypothesis,</span><span class="generated-style"> denoted
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">.
The null hypothesis always states that the population parameter is
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">equal</span><span class="generated-style">
to the claimed value. For example, if the claim is that the average time
to make a name-brand ready-mix pie is five minutes, the statistical
shorthand notation for the null hypothesis in this case would be as
follows:
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">:
</span><span class="zsymbolslant">μ</span><span class="generated-style">
= 5. (That is, the population mean is 5 minutes.)</span>

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">All
null hypotheses include an equal sign in them; there are no
</span><span class="zsymbolmedium">≤</span><span class="generated-style">
or
</span><span class="zsymbolmedium">≥</span><span class="generated-style">
signs in
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">.
Not to cop out or anything, but the reason it’s always equal is beyond
the scope of this book; let’s just say you wouldn’t pay me to explain it
to you.</span>

<span class="generated-style">What’s the alternative?</span>

<span class="generated-style">Before actually conducting a hypothesis

is, there was sufficient evidence against it), what’s your alternative
going to be? Actually, three possibilities exist for the second (or
alternative) hypothesis, denoted
H</span><span class="zsubscript">a</span><span class="generated-style">.
Here they are, along with their shorthand notations in the context of
the pie example:</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">The population parameter is
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">not
equal</span><span class="generated-style"> to the claimed value
(H</span><span class="zsubscript">a</span><span class="generated-style">:
</span><span class="zsymbolslant">μ</span><span class="generated-style">
</span><span class="zsymbolmedium">≠</span><span class="generated-style">
5).</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">The population parameter is
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">greater
than</span><span class="generated-style"> the claimed value
(H</span><span class="zsubscript">a</span><span class="generated-style">:
</span><span class="zsymbolslant">μ</span><span class="generated-style">
\> 5).</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">The population parameter is
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">less
than</span><span class="generated-style"> the claimed value
(H</span><span class="zsubscript">a</span><span class="generated-style">:
</span><span class="zsymbolslant">μ</span><span class="generated-style">
\< 5).</span>

<span class="generated-style">Which alternative hypothesis you choose in
setting up your hypothesis test depends on what you’re interested in
concluding, should you have enough evidence to refute the null
