<span class="generated-style">For example, if you want to test whether a
company is correct in claiming its pie takes five minutes to make and it
doesn’t matter whether the actual average time is more or less than
that, you use the not-equal-to alternative. Your hypotheses for that
test would be
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">:
</span><span class="zsymbolslant">μ</span><span class="generated-style">
= 5 versus
H</span><span class="zsubscript">a</span><span class="generated-style">:
</span><span class="zsymbolslant">μ</span><span class="generated-style">
</span><span class="zsymbolmedium">≠</span><span class="generated-style">
5.</span>

<span class="generated-style">If you only want to see whether the time
turns out to be greater than what the company claims (that is, whether
the company is falsely advertising its quick prep time), you use the
greater-than alternative, and your two hypotheses are
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">:
</span><span class="zsymbolslant">μ</span><span class="generated-style">
= 5 versus
H</span><span class="zsubscript">a</span><span class="generated-style">:
</span><span class="zsymbolslant">μ</span><span class="generated-style">
\> 5.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Finally, say you work for the company
marketing the pie, and you think the pie can be made in less than five
minutes (and could be marketed by the company as such). The less-than
alternative is the one you want, and your two hypotheses would be
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">:
</span><span class="zsymbolslant">μ</span><span class="generated-style">
= 5 versus
H</span><span class="zsubscript">a</span><span class="generated-style">:
</span><span class="zsymbolslant">μ</span><span class="generated-style">
\< 5.</span>

![tip.eps](9780470911082/images/tip_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
How do you know which hypothesis to put in
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">
and which one to put in
H</span><span class="zsubscript">a</span><span class="generated-style">?
Typically, the null hypothesis says that nothing new is happening; the
previous result is the same now as it was before, or the groups have the
same average (their difference is equal to zero). In general, you assume
that people’s claims are true until proven otherwise. So the question
becomes: Can you prove otherwise? In other words, can you show
sufficient evidence to reject Ho?</span>

<span class="generated-style">Gathering Good Evidence (Data)</span>

<span class="generated-style">After you’ve set up the hypotheses, the
next step is to collect your evidence and determine whether your
evidence goes against the claim made in
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">.
Remember, the claim is made about the population, but you can’t test the
whole population; the best you can usually do is take a sample. As with
any other situation in which statistics are being collected, the quality
of the data is extremely critical. (See Chapter 3 for ways to spot
statistics that have gone wrong.)</span>

<span class="generated-style">Collecting good data starts with selecting
a good sample. Two important issues to consider when selecting your
sample are avoiding bias and being accurate. To avoid bias when
selecting a sample, make it a random sample (one that’s got the same
chance of being selected as every other possible sample of the same
size) and choose a large enough sample size so that the results will be
accurate. (See Chapter 11 for more information on accuracy.)</span>

<span class="generated-style">Data is collected in many different ways,
but the methods used basically boil down to two: surveys (observational
studies) and experiments (controlled studies). Chapter 16 gives all the
information you need to design and critique surveys, as well as
information on selecting samples properly. In Chapter 17, you examine
experiments: what they can do beyond an observational study, the
criteria for a good experiment, and when you can conclude cause and
effect.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Compiling the Evidence: The Test
Statistic</span>

<span class="generated-style">After you select your sample, the
appropriate number-crunching takes place. Your null hypothesis
(H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">)
makes a statement about the population parameter — for example, “The
proportion of all women who have varicose veins is 0.25” (in other
words,
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">:
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">p</span><span class="generated-style">
= 0.25); or the average miles per gallon of a U.S.-built light truck is
27
(H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">:
</span><span class="zsymbolslant">μ</span><span class="generated-style">
= 27). The data you collect from the sample measures the variable of
interest, and the statistics that you calculate will help you test the
claim about the population parameter.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Gathering sample statistics</span>

<span class="generated-style">Say you’re testing a claim about the
proportion of women with varicose veins. You need to calculate the
proportion of women in your sample who have varicose veins, and that
number will be your sample statistic. If you’re testing a claim about
the average miles per gallon of a U.S.-built light truck, your statistic
will be the average miles per gallon of the light trucks in your sample.
And knowing you want to measure the variability in average miles per
gallon for various trucks, you’ll want to calculate the sample standard
deviation. (See Chapter 5 for all the information you need on
calculating sample statistics.)</span>

<span class="generated-style">Measuring variability using standard
errors</span>

<span class="generated-style">After you’ve calculated all the necessary
sample statistics, you may think you’re done with the analysis part and
ready to make your conclusions — but you’re not. The problem is you have
no way to put your results into any kind of perspective just by looking
at them in their regular units. That’s because you know that your
results are based only on a sample and that sample results are going to
vary. That variation needs to be taken into account, or your conclusions
could be completely wrong. (How much do sample results vary? Sample
variation is measured by the standard error; see Chapter 11 for more on
this.)</span>

<span class="generated-style">Suppose the claim is that the percentage
of all women with varicose veins is 25%, and your sample of 100 women
had 20% with varicose veins. The standard error for your sample
percentage is 4% (according to formulas in Chapter 11), which means that
your results are expected to vary by about twice that, or about 8%,
according to the Empirical Rule (see Chapter 12). So a difference of 5%,
for example, between the claim and your sample result (25% – 20% = 5%)
isn’t that much, in these terms, because it represents a distance of
less than 2 standard errors away from the claim.</span>

<span class="generated-style">However, suppose your sample percentage
was based on a sample of 1,000 women, not 100. This decreases the amount
by which you expect your results to vary, because you have more
information. Again using formulas from Chapter 11, I calculate the
standard error to be 0.013 or 1.3%. The margin of error (MOE) is about
twice that, or 2.6% on either side. Now a difference of 5% between your
sample result (20%) and the claim in
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">
(25%) is a more meaningful difference; it’s way more than 2 standard
errors.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Exactly how meaningful are your results?
In the next section, you get more specific about measuring exactly how
far apart your sample results are from the claim in terms of the number
of standard errors. This leads you to a specific conclusion as to how
much evidence you have against the claim in
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Understanding standard scores</span>

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
The number of standard errors that a statistic lies above or below the
mean is called a </span><span class="zcheltitalic">standard
score</span><span class="generated-style"> (for example, a
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">z</span><span class="generated-style">-value
is a type of standard score; see Chapter 9). In order to interpret your
statistic, you need to convert it from original units to a standard
score. When finding a standard score, you take your statistic, subtract
the mean, and divide the result by the standard error.</span>

<span class="generated-style">In the case of hypothesis tests, you use
the value in
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">
as the mean. (That’s what you go with unless/until you have enough
evidence against it.) The standardized version of your statistic is
called a </span><span class="zcheltitalic">test statistic,
</span><span class="generated-style">and it’s the main component of a
hypothesis test. (Chapter 15 contains the formulas for the most common
hypothesis tests.)</span>

<span class="generated-style">Calculating and interpreting the test
statistic</span>

<span class="generated-style">The general procedure for converting a
statistic to a test statistic (standard score) is as follows:</span>

<span class="zcheltbold"> 1. Take your statistic minus the claimed value
(the number stated in
H</span><span class="zcheltboldsub">o</span><span class="zcheltbold">).</span>

<span class="zcheltbold"> 2. Divide by the standard error of the
statistic. </span><span class="generated-style">(Different formulas for
standard error exist for different problems; see Chapter 13 for detailed
formulas for standard error and Chapter 15 for formulas for various test
statistics.)</span>

<span class="generated-style">Your test statistic represents the
distance between your actual sample results and the claimed population
value, in terms of number of standard errors. In the case of a single
population mean or proportion, you know that these standardized
distances should at least have an approximate standard normal
distribution if your sample size is large enough (see Chapter 11). So,
to interpret your test statistic in these cases, you can see where it
stands on the standard normal distribution
(</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z</span><span class="generated-style">-distribution).</span>

<span class="generated-style">Using the numbers from the varicose veins
example in the previous section, the test statistic is found by taking
the proportion in the sample with varicose veins, 0.20, subtracting the
claimed proportion of all women with varicose veins, 0.25, and then
dividing the result by the standard error, 0.04. These calculations give
you a test statistic (standard score) of –0.05 ÷ 0.04 = –1.25. This
tells you that your sample results and the population claim in
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">
are 1.25 standard errors apart; in particular, your sample results are
1.25 standard errors below the claim. Now is this enough evidence to
reject the claim? The next section addresses that issue.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Weighing the Evidence and Making
Decisions: p-Values</span>

<span class="generated-style">After you find your test statistic, you
use it to make a decision about whether to reject
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">.
You make this decision by coming up with a number that measures the
strength of this evidence (your test statistic) against the claim in
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">.
That is, how likely is it that your test statistic could have occurred
while the claim was still true? This number you calculate is called the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">p-value;</span><span class="generated-style">
it’s the chance that someone could have gotten results as extreme as
yours while
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">
was still true. Similarly in a jury trial, the jury discusses how likely
it is that all the evidence came out the way it did assuming the
defendant was innocent.</span>

<span class="generated-style">This section shows all the ins and outs of
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">p</span><span class="generated-style">-values,
including how to calculate them and use them to make decisions regarding
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Connecting test statistics and
p-values</span>

<span class="generated-style">To test whether a claim in
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">
should be rejected (after all, it’s all about Ho) you look at your test
statistic taken from your sample and see whether you have enough
evidence to reject the claim. If the test statistic is large (in either
the positive or negative directions), your data is far from the claim;
the larger the test statistic, the more evidence you have against the
claim. You determine “how far is far” by looking at where your test
statistic ends up on the distribution that it came from. When testing
one population mean, under certain conditions the distribution of
comparison is the standard normal
(</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z-</span><span class="generated-style">)
distribution, which has a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1; I use
it throughout this section as an example. (See Chapter 9 to find out
more about the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z</span><span class="generated-style">-distribution.)</span>

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
If your test statistic is close to 0, or at least within that range
where most of the results should fall, then you don’t have much evidence
against the claim
(H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">)
based on your data. If your test statistic is out in the tails of the
standard normal distribution (see Chapter 9 for more on tails), then
your evidence against the claim
(H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">)
is great; this result has a very small chance of happening if the claim
is true. In other words, you have sufficient evidence against the claim
(H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">),
and you reject
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">.</span>

<span class="generated-style">But how far is “too far” from 0? As long
as you have a normal distribution or a large enough sample size, you
know that your test statistic falls somewhere on a standard normal
distribution (see Chapter 11). If the null hypothesis
(H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">)
is true, most (about 95%) of the samples will result in test statistics
that lie roughly within 2 standard errors of the claim. If
H</span><span class="zsubscript">a</span><span class="generated-style">
is the not-equal-to alternative, any test statistic outside this range
will result in
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">
being rejected. See Figure 14-1 for a picture showing the locations of
your test statistic and their corresponding conclusions. In the next
section, you see how to quantify the amount of evidence you have against
Ho.</span>

<div class="story">

**Figure 14-1:**<span class="generated-style"> Decisions for Ha:
not-equal-to.</span>

</div>

![9780470911082-fg1401.eps](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-fg1401_fmt.png)

![tip.eps](9780470911082/images/tip_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Note that if the alternative hypothesis is the less-than alternative,
you reject
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">
only if the test statistic falls in the left tail of the distribution
(below –1.64). Similarly, if
H</span><span class="zsubscript">a</span><span class="generated-style">
is the greater-than alternative, you reject
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">
only if the test statistic falls in the right tail (above 1.64).</span>

<span class="generated-style">Defining a p-value</span>

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
A
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">p-</span><span class="generated-style">value
is a probability associated with your test statistic. It measures the
chance of getting results at least as strong as yours if the claim
(H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">)
were true. In the case of testing the population mean, the farther out
your test statistic is on the tails of the standard normal
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">(Z</span><span class="generated-style">-)
distribution, the smaller your</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
p-</span><span class="generated-style">value will be, the less likely
your results were to have occurred, and the more evidence you have
against the claim
(H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">).</span>

<span class="generated-style">Calculating a p-value</span>

<span class="generated-style">To find
the</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
p-</span><span class="generated-style">value for your test
statistic:</span>

<span class="zcheltbold"> 1. Look up your test statistic on the
appropriate distribution — in this case, on the standard normal
(</span><span class="zcheltbolditalic">Z-</span><span class="zcheltbold">)
distribution (see the
</span><span class="zcheltbolditalic">Z</span><span class="zcheltbold">-table
in the appendix).</span>

<span class="zcheltbold"> 2. Find the chance that
</span><span class="zcheltbolditalic">Z</span><span class="zcheltbold">
is beyond (more extreme than) your test statistic:</span>

<span class="generated-style"> • If
H</span><span class="zsubscript">a</span><span class="generated-style">
contains a less-than alternative, find the probability that
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z</span><span class="generated-style">
is less than your test statistic (that is, look up your test statistic
on the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z</span><span class="generated-style">-table
and find its corresponding probability). This is
the</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
p-</span><span class="generated-style">value.</span>

<span class="generated-style"> • If
H</span><span class="zsubscript">a</span><span class="generated-style">
contains a greater-than alternative, find the probability that
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z</span><span class="generated-style">
is greater than your test statistic (look up your test statistic on the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z</span><span class="generated-style">-table,
find its corresponding probability, and subtract it from one). The
result is your</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
p-</span><span class="generated-style">value.</span>

<span class="generated-style"> • If
H</span><span class="zsubscript">a</span><span class="generated-style">
contains a non-equal-to alternative, find the probability that
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z</span><span class="generated-style">
is beyond your test statistic and double it. There are two cases:</span>

<span class="generated-style"> If your test statistic is negative, first
find the probability that
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z</span><span class="generated-style">
is less than your test statistic (look up your test statistic on the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z</span><span class="generated-style">-table
and find its corresponding probability). Then double this probability to
get the</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
p-</span><span class="generated-style">value.</span>

<span class="generated-style">If your test statistic is positive, first
find the probability that </span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z
</span><span class="generated-style">is greater than your test statistic
(look up your test statistic on the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z</span><span class="generated-style">-table,
find its corresponding probability, and subtract it from one). Then
double this result to get the</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
p-</span><span class="generated-style">value.</span>

![technicalstuff.eps](9780470911082/images/technicalstuff_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Why do you double the probabilities if your
H</span><span class="zsubscript">a</span><span class="generated-style">
contains a non-equal-to alternative? Think of the not-equal-to
alternative as the combination of the greater-than alternative and the
less-than alternative. If you’ve got a positive test statistic,
its</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
p-</span><span class="generated-style">value only accounts for the
greater-than portion of the not-equal-to alternative; double it to
account for the less-than portion. (The doubling of
one</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
p-</span><span class="generated-style">value is possible because the
Z-distribution is symmetric.)</span>

<span class="generated-style">Similarly, if you’ve got a negative test
statistic, its</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
p-</span><span class="generated-style">value only accounts for the
less-than portion of the not-equal-to alternative; double it to also
account for the greater-than portion.</span>

<span class="generated-style">When testing
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">:</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
p </span><span class="generated-style">= 0.25 versus
H</span><span class="zsubscript">a</span><span class="generated-style">:</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
p </span><span class="generated-style">\< 0.25 in the varicose veins
example from the previous section, the</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
p-</span><span class="generated-style">value turns out to be 0.1056.
This is because the test statistic (calculated in the previous section)
was –1.25, and when you look this number up on the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z</span><span class="generated-style">-table
(in the appendix) you find a probability of 0.1056 of being less than
this value. If you had been testing the two-sided alternative,
H</span><span class="zsubscript">a</span><span class="generated-style">:
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">p</span><span class="generated-style">
</span><span class="zsymbolmedium">≠</span><span class="generated-style">
0.25, the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">p</span><span class="generated-style">-value
would be 2
</span><span class="zmathpiltstd">∗</span><span class="generated-style">
0.1056, or 0.2112.</span>

![headsup_lewis.eps](9780470911082/images/headsup_lewis_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
If the results are likely to have occurred under the claim, then you
fail to reject
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">
(like a jury decides not guilty). If the results are unlikely to have
occurred under the claim, then you reject
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">
(like a jury decides guilty). The cutoff point between rejecting
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">
and failing to reject
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">
is another whole can of worms that I dissect in the next section (no pun
intended).</span>

<span class="generated-style">Making Conclusions</span>

<span class="generated-style">To draw conclusions about
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">
(reject or fail to reject) based on a</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
p-</span><span class="generated-style">value, you need to set a
predetermined cutoff point where only those
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">p</span><span class="generated-style">-values
less than or equal to the cutoff will result in rejecting Ho. This
cutoff point is called the </span><span class="zcheltitalic">alpha level
(</span><span class="zsymbolslant">α</span><span class="zcheltitalic">),</span><span class="generated-style">
or </span><span class="zcheltitalic">significance
level</span><span class="generated-style"> for the test. While 0.05 is a
very popular cutoff value for rejecting
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">,
cutoff points and resulting decisions can vary — some people use
stricter cutoffs, such as 0.01, requiring more evidence before rejecting
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">,
and others may have less strict cutoffs, such as 0.10, requiring less
evidence.</span>

<span class="generated-style">If
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">
is rejected (that is, the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">p</span><span class="generated-style">-value
is less than or equal to the predetermined significance level), the
researcher can say she’s found a statistically significant result. A
result is </span><span class="zcheltitalic">statistically
significant</span><span class="generated-style"> if it’s too rare to
have occurred by chance assuming
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">
is true. If you get a statistically significant result, you have enough
evidence to reject the claim,
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">,
and conclude that something different or new is in effect (that is,
H</span><span class="zsubscript">a</span><span class="generated-style">).</span>

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
The significance level can be thought of as the highest
possible</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
p-</span><span class="generated-style">value that would reject Ho and
declare the results statistically significant. Following are the general
rules for making a decision about
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">
based on a
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">p-</span><span class="generated-style">value:</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">If the</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
p-</span><span class="generated-style">value is less than or equal to
your significance level, then it meets your requirements for having
enough evidence against
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">;
you reject
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">.</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">If the</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
p-</span><span class="generated-style">value is greater than your
significance level, your data failed to show evidence beyond a
reasonable doubt; you fail to reject
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">.</span>

<span class="generated-style">However, if you plan to make decisions
about
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">
by comparing the</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
p-</span><span class="generated-style">value to your significance level,
you must decide on your significance level ahead of time. It wouldn’t be
fair to change your cutoff point after you’ve got a sneak peak at what’s
happening in the data.</span>

![headsup_lewis.eps](9780470911082/images/headsup_lewis_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
You may be wondering whether it’s okay to say “Accept
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">”
instead of “Fail to reject
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">.”
The answer is a big no. In a hypothesis test, you are
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">not</span><span class="generated-style">
trying to show whether or not
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">
is true (which
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">accept</span><span class="zunivitalic">
</span><span class="generated-style">implies) — indeed, if you knew
whether
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">
was true, you wouldn’t be doing the hypothesis test in the first place.
You’re trying to show whether you have enough evidence to say
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">
is false, based on your data. Either you have enough evidence to say
it’s false (in which case you reject
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">)
or you don’t have enough evidence to say it’s false (in which case you
fail to reject
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">).</span>

<span class="generated-style">Setting boundaries for rejecting
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span>

<span class="generated-style">These guidelines help you make a decision
(reject or fail to reject Ho) based on
a</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
p-</span><span class="generated-style">value when your significance
level is 0.05:</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">If the</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
p-</span><span class="generated-style">value is less than 0.01 (very
small), the results are considered highly statistically significant —
reject
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">.</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">If the</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
p-</span><span class="generated-style">value is between 0.05 and 0.01
(but not super-close to 0.05), the results are considered statistically
significant — reject
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">.</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">If the</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
p-</span><span class="generated-style">value is really close to 0.05
(like 0.051 or 0.049), the results should be considered marginally
significant — the decision could go either way.</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">If the</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
p-</span><span class="generated-style">value is greater than (but not
super-close to) 0.05, the results are considered non-significant — you
fail to reject
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">.</span>

![headsup_lewis.eps](9780470911082/images/headsup_lewis_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
When you hear a researcher say her results are found to be statistically
significant, look for the</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
p-</span><span class="generated-style">value and make your own decision;
the researcher’s predetermined significance level may be different from
yours. If the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">p</span><span class="generated-style">-value
isn’t stated, ask for it.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Testing varicose veins</span>

<span class="generated-style">In the varicose veins example in the last
section, the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">p</span><span class="generated-style">-value
was found to be 0.1056. This
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">p</span><span class="generated-style">-value
is fairly large and indicates very weak evidence against
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">
by almost anyone’s standards because it’s greater than 0.05 and even
slightly greater than 0.10 (considered to be a very large significance
level). In this case you fail to reject
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">.
You didn’t have enough evidence to say the proportion of women with
varicose veins is less than 0.25 (your alternative hypothesis). This
isn’t declared to be a statistically significant result.</span>

<span class="generated-style">But say
your</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
p-</span><span class="generated-style">value had been something like
0.026. A reader with a personal cutoff point of 0.05 would reject
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">
in this case because the</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
p-</span><span class="generated-style">value (of 0.026) is less than
0.05. His conclusion would be that the proportion of women with varicose
veins isn’t equal to 0.25; according to Ha in this case, you conclude
it’s less than 0.25, and the results are statistically significant.
However, a reader whose significance level is 0.01 wouldn’t have enough
evidence (based on your sample) to reject
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">
because the</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
p-</span><span class="generated-style">value of 0.026 is greater than
0.01. These results wouldn’t be statistically significant.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Finally, if
the</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
p-</span><span class="generated-style">value turned out to be 0.049 and
your significance level is 0.05, you can go by the book and say because
it’s less than 0.05 you reject
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">,
but you really should say your results are marginal, and let the reader
decide. (Maybe they can flip a coin or something — “Heads we reject
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">,
tails, we don’t!”)</span>

<span class="generated-style">Assessing the Chance of a Wrong
Decision</span>

<span class="generated-style">After you make a decision to either reject
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">
or fail to reject
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">,
the next step is living with the consequences, in terms of how people
respond to your decision.</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">If you conclude that a claim isn’t true
but it actually
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">is</span><span class="generated-style">,
will that result in a lawsuit, a fine, unnecessary changes in the
product, or consumer boycotts that shouldn’t have happened? It’s
possible.</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">If you can’t disprove a claim that’s
wrong, what happens then? Will products continue to be made in the same
way as they are now? Will no new law be made, no new action taken,
because you showed that nothing was wrong? Missed opportunities to blow
the whistle have been known to occur.</span>

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Whatever decision you make with a hypothesis test, you know there is a
chance of being wrong; that’s life in the statistics world. Knowing the
kinds of errors that can happen and finding out how to curb the chance
of them occurring are key.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Making a false alarm: Type-1 errors</span>

<span class="generated-style">Suppose a company claims that its average
package delivery time is 2 days, and a consumer group tests this
hypothesis, gets a
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">p</span><span class="generated-style">-value
of 0.04, and concludes that the claim is false: They believe that the
average delivery time is actually more than 2 days. This is a big deal.
If the group can stand by its statistics, it has done well to inform the
public about the false advertising issue. But what if the group is
wrong?</span>

![headsup_lewis.eps](9780470911082/images/headsup_lewis_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Even if the group bases their study on a good design, collects good
data, and makes the right analysis, it can still be wrong. Why? Because
its conclusions were based on a sample of packages, not on the entire
population. And as Chapter 11 tells you, sample results vary from sample
to sample.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Just because the results from a sample are
unusual doesn’t mean they’re impossible.
A</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
p-</span><span class="generated-style">value of 0.04 means that the
chance of getting your particular test statistic, even if the claim is
true, is 4% (less than 5%). You reject
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">
in this case because that chance is small. But even a small chance is
still a chance!</span>

<span class="generated-style">Perhaps your sample, though collected
randomly, just happens to be one of those atypical samples whose result
ended up far from what was expected. So,
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">
could be true, but your results lead you to a different conclusion. How
often does that happen? Five percent of the time (or whatever your given
cutoff probability is for rejecting
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">).</span>

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Rejecting
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">
when you shouldn’t is called a </span><span class="zcheltitalic">type-1
error.</span><span class="generated-style"> I don’t really like this
name, because it seems so nondescript. I prefer to call a type-1 error a
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">false
alarm.</span><span class="generated-style"> In the case of the packages,
if the consumer group made a type-1 error when it rejected the company’s
claim, they created a false alarm. What’s the result? A very angry
delivery company, I guarantee that!</span>

![tip.eps](9780470911082/images/tip_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
To reduce the chance of false alarms, set a low cutoff probability
(significance level) for rejecting
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">.
Setting it to 5% or 1% will keep the chance of a type-1 error in
check.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Missing out on a detection: Type-2
errors</span>

<span class="generated-style">On the other hand, suppose the company
really wasn’t delivering on its claim. Who’s to say that the consumer
group’s sample will detect it? If the actual delivery time is 2.1 days
instead of 2 days, the difference would be pretty hard to detect. If the
actual delivery time is 3 days, even a fairly small sample would
probably show that something’s up. The issue lies with those in-between
values, like 2.5 days.</span>

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
If
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">
is indeed false, you want to find out about it and reject
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">.
Not rejecting
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">
when you should have is called a
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">type-2 error.
</span><span class="generated-style">I like to call it a
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">missed detection.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Sample size is the key to being able to
detect situations where
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">
is false and, thus, avoiding type-2 errors. The more information you
have, the less variable your results will be (see Chapter 11) and the
more ability you have to zoom in on detecting problems that exist with a
claim made by Ho.</span>

<span class="generated-style">This ability to detect when
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">
is truly false is called the </span><span class="zcheltitalic">power
</span><span class="generated-style">of a test. Power is a pretty
complicated issue, but what’s important for you to know is that the
higher the sample size, the more powerful a test is. A powerful test has
a small chance for a type-2 error.</span>

![tip.eps](9780470911082/images/tip_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
As a preventative measure to minimize the chances of a type-2 error,
statisticians recommend that you select a large sample size to ensure
that any differences or departures that really exist won’t be
missed.</span>

</div>

</div>

<span id="22_9780470911082-ch15.xhtml"></span>

<div id="22_9780470911082-ch15.xhtml_x22_9780470911082-ch15">

<div class="story">

<span class="generated-style">Chapter 15</span>

<span class="generated-style">Commonly Used Hypothesis Tests: Formulas
and Examples</span>

<span class="generated-style">In This Chapter</span>

![arrow](9780470911082/images/arrow.png)
<span class="generated-style">Breaking down commonly used hypothesis
tests</span>

![arrow](9780470911082/images/arrow.png)
<span class="generated-style">Calculating their test statistics</span>

![arrow](9780470911082/images/arrow.png)
<span class="generated-style">Using the results to make informed
decisions</span>

<span class="drop-cap">F</span><span class="generated-style">rom product
advertisements to media blitzes on recent medical breakthroughs, you
often run across claims made about one or more populations. For example,
“We promise to deliver our packages in two days or less” or “Two recent
studies show that a high-fiber diet may reduce your risk of colon cancer
by 20%.” Whenever someone makes a claim (also called a
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">null
hypothesis</span><span class="generated-style">) about a population
(such as all packages, or all adults) you can test the claim by doing
what statisticians call a </span><span class="zcheltitalic">hypothesis
test.</span>

<span class="generated-style">A hypothesis test involves setting up your
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">hypotheses</span><span class="generated-style">
(a claim and its alternative), selecting a sample (or samples),
collecting data, calculating the relevant statistics, and using those
statistics to decide whether the claim is true. </span>

<span class="generated-style">In this chapter, I outline the formulas
used for some of the most common hypothesis tests, explain the necessary
calculations, and walk you through some examples.</span>

![tip.eps](9780470911082/images/tip_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
If you need more background information on hypothesis testing (such as
setting up hypotheses, understanding test statistics, p-values,
significance levels, and type-1 and type-2 errors), just flip to Chapter
14. All the general concepts of hypothesis testing are developed there.
This chapter focuses on their application.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Testing One Population Mean</span>

<span class="generated-style">When the variable is numerical (for
example, age, income, time, and so on) and only one population or group
(such as all U.S. households or all college students) is being studied,
you use the hypothesis test in this section to examine or challenge a
claim about the population mean. For example, a child psychologist says
that the average time that working mothers spend talking to their
children is 11 minutes per day, on average. (For dads, the claim is 8
minutes.) The variable — time — is numerical, and the population is all
working mothers. Using statistical notation,
</span><span class="zsymbolslant">μ</span><span class="generated-style">
represents the average number of minutes per day that all working
mothers spend talking to their children, on average.</span>

<span class="generated-style">The null hypothesis is that the population
mean,
</span><span class="zsymbolslant">μ</span><span class="generated-style">,
is equal to a certain claimed value,
</span><span class="zsymbolslant">μ</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">.
The notation for the null hypothesis is
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">:
</span><span class="zsymbolslant">μ</span><span class="generated-style">
=
</span><span class="zsymbolslant">μ</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">.
So the null hypothesis in our example is
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">:
</span><span class="zsymbolslant">μ</span><span class="generated-style">
= 11 minutes, and
</span><span class="zsymbolslant">μ</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">
is 11. The three possibilities for the alternative hypothesis,

\> 11.</span>

The big idea of a hypothesis test is to challenge the claim that’s being

\> 11. According to your data, the child psychologist’s claim of 11

<span class="generated-style">In two cases, you can’t use the

In both cases, you have less reliable information on which to base your

including its relationship with the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z</span><span class="generated-style">.)</span>

<span class="generated-style">A hypothesis test for a population mean
that involves the</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
t</span><span class="generated-style"> -distribution is called a
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">test.
The formula for the test statistic in this case is:</span>

where
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="zsubscript">n-1</span>
is a value from the
<span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">distribution
with
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">n</span><span class="generated-style">–1
degrees of freedom.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Note it is just like the test statistic
for the large sample and/or normal distribution case (see the section
“Testing One Population Mean”), except
</span><span class="zsymbolslant">σ</span><span class="generated-style">
is not known, so you substitute the sample standard deviation,
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">s</span><span class="generated-style">,
instead, and use a</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
t</span><span class="generated-style">-value rather than a
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">z</span><span class="generated-style">-value.</span>

![technicalstuff.eps](9780470911082/images/technicalstuff_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Because the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="generated-style">-distribution
has fatter tails than the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z</span><span class="generated-style">-distribution,
you get a larger
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">p-</span><span class="generated-style">value
from the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="generated-style">-distribution
than one that the standard normal
(</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z-</span><span class="generated-style">)
distribution would have given you for the same test statistic. A bigger

means less chance of rejecting
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o.</span><span class="generated-style">
Having less data and/or not knowing the population standard deviation
should create a higher burden of proof.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Suppose a delivery company claims they

</span><span class="zsymbolslant">μ</span><span class="generated-style">
= 2 versus

</span><span class="zsymbolslant">μ</span><span class="generated-style">
\> 2. To test this claim, you take a random sample of 10 packages and

</span>![9780470911082-EQ15008.eps](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-EQ15008_fmt.png)<span class="generated-style">

</span><span class="zsymbolslant">σ</span><span class="generated-style">,

</span><span class="zcheltitalic">s,</span><span class="generated-style">
the sample standard deviation.) This is a job for the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="generated-style">-test.</span>

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Because the sample size is small
(</span><span class="zcheltitalic">n</span><span class="generated-style">
=10 is much less than 30) and the population standard deviation is not
known, your test statistic has a
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">distribution.
Its degrees of freedom is 10 – 1 = 9. The formula for the test statistic
(referred to as the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-value</span><span class="generated-style">)
is:</span>

![9780470911082-EQ15009.eps](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-EQ15009_fmt.png)

<span class="generated-style">To calculate the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">p-</span><span class="generated-style">value,
you look in the row in the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">table
(in the appendix) for
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">df</span><span class="generated-style">
= 9. Your test statistic (2.71) falls between two values in the row for
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">df
</span><span class="generated-style">= 9 in the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="generated-style">-table:
2.26 and 2.82 (rounding to two decimal places). To calculate the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">p-</span><span class="generated-style">value
for your test statistic, find which columns correspond to these two
numbers. The number 2.26 appears in the 0.025 column and the number 2.82
appears in the 0.010 column; you now know the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">p-</span><span class="generated-style">value
for your test statistic lies between 0.025 and 0.010 (that is, 0.010 \<
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">p</span><span class="generated-style">-value
\< 0.025).</span>

<span class="generated-style">Using the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="generated-style">-table
you don’t know the exact number for the

but because 0.010 and 0.025 are both less than your significance level
of 0.05, you reject
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">;
you have enough evidence in your sample to say the packages are not
being delivered in 2 days, and in fact the average delivery time is more

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
The
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">table
(in the appendix) doesn’t include every possible
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="generated-style">-value;
just find the two values closest to yours on either side, look at the
columns they’re in, and report your
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">p-</span><span class="generated-style">value
in relation to theirs. (If your test statistic is greater than all the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="generated-style">-values
in the corresponding row of the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="generated-style">-table,
just use the last one; your
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">p-</span><span class="generated-style">value
will be less than its probability.)</span>

Of course you can use statistical software, if available, to calculate

for any test statistic; using software you get 0.012 for the exact
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">p</span><span class="generated-style">-value.
</span>

<span class="generated-style">Relating t to Z</span>

<span class="generated-style">The next-to-the-last line of the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="generated-style">-table
shows the corresponding values from the standard normal
(</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z-</span><span class="generated-style">)
distribution for the probabilities listed on the top of each column. Now
choose a column in the table and move down the column looking at the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="generated-style">-values.
As the degrees of freedom of the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">distribution
increase, the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="generated-style">-values
get closer and closer to that row of the table where the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">z-</span><span class="generated-style">values
are.</span>

<span class="generated-style">This confirms a result found in Chapter
10: As the sample size (hence degrees of freedom) increases, the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">distribution
becomes more and more like the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Z</span><span class="generated-style">-distribution,
so the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">p-</span><span class="generated-style">values
from their hypothesis tests are virtually equal for large sample sizes.
And those sample sizes don’t even have to be that large to see this
relationship; for </span><span class="zcheltitalic">df
</span><span class="generated-style">= 30 the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="generated-style">-values
are already very similar to the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">z</span><span class="generated-style">-values
shown in the bottom of the table. These results make sense; the more
data you have, the less of a penalty you have to pay. (And of course,
you can use computer technology to calculate more exact
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">p-</span><span class="generated-style">values
for any
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="generated-style">-value
you like.)</span>

<span class="generated-style">Handling negative t-values</span>

<span class="generated-style">For a less-than alternative hypothesis
(H</span><span class="zsubscript">a</span><span class="generated-style">:
xx \< xx), your test statistic would be a negative number (to the left
of 0 on the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">distribution).
In this case, you want to find the percentage below, or to the left of,
your test statistic to get your
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">p-</span><span class="generated-style">value.
Yet negative test statistics don’t appear on the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">table
(in the appendix).</span>

<span class="generated-style">Not to worry! The percentage to the left
(below) a negative
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">value
is the same as the percentage to the right (above) the positive
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t-</span><span class="generated-style">value,
due to symmetry. So to find the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">p-</span><span class="generated-style">value
for your negative test statistic, look up the positive version of your
test statistic on the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="generated-style">-table,
find the corresponding right tail (greater-than) probability, and use
that.</span>

<span class="generated-style">For example, suppose your test statistic
is –2.7105 with 9 degrees of freedom and
H</span><span class="zsubscript">a</span><span class="generated-style">
is the less-than alternative. To find your
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">p</span><span class="generated-style">-value,
first look up +2.7105 on the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="generated-style">-table;
by the work in the previous section, you know its
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">p</span><span class="generated-style">-value
falls between the column headings 0.025 and 0.010. Because the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">t</span><span class="generated-style">-distribution
is symmetric, the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">p</span><span class="generated-style">-value
for –2.7105 also falls somewhere between 0.025 and 0.010. Again you
reject
H</span><span class="zsubscript">o</span><span class="generated-style">
because these values are both less than or equal to 0.05.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Examining the not-equal-to
alternative</span>

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
To find the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">p-</span><span class="generated-style">value
when your alternative hypothesis

is

<span class="generated-style">For example, if your test statistic is

<span class="generated-style">Testing for an Average Difference (The
Paired t-Test)</span>

<span class="generated-style">You can test for an average difference
using the test in this section when the variable is numerical (for
example, income, cholesterol level, or miles per gallon) and the
individuals in the sample are either paired up in some way according to
relevant variables such as age or perhaps weight, or the same people are
used twice (for example, using a pre-test and post-test). Paired tests
are typically used for studies in which someone is testing to see
whether a new treatment, technique, or method works better than an
existing method, without having to worry about other factors about the
subjects that may influence the results (see Chapter 17 for
details).</span>

The average difference (tested in this section) isn’t the same as the
difference in the averages (tested in the previous section):</span>

<span class="generated-style">With the difference in averages, you
compare the difference in the means of two separate samples to test the

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">With the average difference, you match up
the subjects so they are thought of as coming from a single population,

<span id="23_9780470911082-pp05.xhtml"></span>

<div id="23_9780470911082-pp05.xhtml_x23_9780470911082-pp05">

<div class="story">

<span class="generated-style">Part V</span>

<span class="generated-style">Statistical Studies and the Hunt for a
Meaningful Relationship</span>

<div class="image">

![9780470911082-pp0501.eps](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-pp0501_fmt.png)

</div>

<span class="generated-style">In this part . . .</span>

M<span class="generated-style">any statistics you hear and see each day
are based on the results of surveys, experiments, and observational
studies. Unfortunately, you can’t believe everything you read or
hear.</span>

<span class="generated-style">In this part, you look at what actually
happens behind the scenes of these studies — how they are designed and
conducted and how the data is (supposed to be) collected — so that
you’ll be able to spot misleading results. You also see what’s needed to
conduct your own study correctly and effectively.</span>

<span class="generated-style">You also analyze data from good studies to
look for relationships between two variables, where both variables are
categorical (using two-way tables) or both are numerical (using
correlation and regression). In addition, you see how to make proper
conclusions and spot problems.</span>

</div>

</div>

<span id="24_9780470911082-ch16.xhtml"></span>

<div id="24_9780470911082-ch16.xhtml_x24_9780470911082-ch16">

<div class="story">

<span class="generated-style">Chapter 16</span>

<span class="generated-style">Polls, Polls, and More Polls</span>

<span class="generated-style">In This Chapter</span>

![arrow](9780470911082/images/arrow.png)
<span class="generated-style">Realizing the impact of polls and
surveys</span>

![arrow](9780470911082/images/arrow.png)
<span class="generated-style">Going behind the scenes of polls and
surveys</span>

![arrow](9780470911082/images/arrow.png)
<span class="generated-style">Detecting biased and inaccurate survey
results</span>

<span class="drop-cap">S</span><span class="generated-style">urveys are
all the rage amid today’s information explosion. Everyone wants to know
how the public feels about issues from prescription drug prices and
methods of disciplining children to approval ratings of the president
and ratings of reality TV shows. Polls and surveys are a big part of
American life; they’re a vehicle for quickly getting information about
how you feel, what you think, and how you live your life, and they’re a
means of quickly disseminating information about important issues.
Surveys highlight controversial topics, raise awareness, make political
points, stress the importance of an issue, and educate or persuade the
public.</span>

![headsup_lewis.eps](9780470911082/images/headsup_lewis_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Survey results can be powerful, because when many people hear that “such
and such percentage of the American people do this or that,” they accept
these results as the truth, and then make decisions and form opinions
based on that information. But in fact, many surveys
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">don’t</span><span class="generated-style">
provide correct, complete, or even fair or balanced information.</span>

<span class="generated-style">In this chapter, I discuss the impact of
surveys and how they’re used, and I take you behind the scenes of how
surveys are designed and conducted so you know what to watch for when
examining survey results and how to run your own surveys right. I also
talk about how to interpret survey results and how to spot biased and
inaccurate information, so that you can determine for yourself which
results to believe and which to ignore.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Recognizing the Impact of Polls</span>

<span class="generated-style">A
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">survey</span><span class="generated-style">
is an instrument that collects data through questions and answers. It is
used to gather information about the opinions, behaviors, demographics,
lifestyles, and other reportable characteristics of the population of
interest. What’s the difference between a poll and a survey?
Statisticians don’t make a clear distinction between the two, but I’ve
noticed that what people call a
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">poll</span><span class="generated-style">
is typically a short survey containing only a few questions (maybe
that’s how researchers get more people to respond — they call it a poll
rather than a survey!). But for all intents and purposes, surveys and
polls are the same thing.</span>

<span class="generated-style">You come into contact with surveys and
their results on a daily basis. Compared to other types of studies, such
as medical experiments, some surveys can be relatively easy to conduct.
They provide quick results that can often make interesting headlines in
newspapers or eye-catching stories in magazines. People connect with
surveys because they feel that survey results represent the opinions of
people just like themselves (even though they may never have been asked
to participate in a survey). And many people enjoy seeing how other
people feel, what they do, where they go, and what they care about.
Looking at survey results makes people feel linked with a bigger group,
somehow. That’s what </span><span class="zcheltitalic">pollsters
</span><span class="generated-style">(the people who conduct surveys)
bank on, and that’s why they spend so much time doing surveys and polls
and reporting the results of this research.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Getting to the source</span>

<span class="generated-style">Who conducts surveys these days? Pretty
much anyone and everyone who has a question to ask. Some of the groups
that conduct polls and report the results include the following:</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">News organizations</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">Political parties and candidates running
for office</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">Professional polling organizations (such
as the Gallup Organization, the Harris Poll, Zogby International, and
the National Opinion Research Center \[NORC\])</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">Representatives of magazines, TV shows,
and radio programs</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">Professional research organizations (like
the American Medical Association, Smithsonian Institution, and Pew
Research Center for the People and the Press)</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">Special-interest groups (such as the
National Rifle Association, Greenpeace, and American Civil Liberties
Union)</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">Academic researchers</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">The United States government</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">Joe Six-Pack (who can easily conduct his
own survey on the Internet)</span>

<div class="sidebar">

<span class="generated-style">Ranking the worst cars of the
millennium</span>

<span class="generated-style">You may be familiar with a radio show
called </span><span class="zunivitalic">Car
Talk</span><span class="generated-style"> that’s typically aired
Saturday mornings on National Public Radio and is hosted by “Click and
Clack,” two brothers in Cambridge, Massachusetts, who offer wise and
wacky advice to callers with strange car problems. The show’s Web site
regularly offers “just for fun” surveys on a wide range of car-related
topics, such as, “Who has bumper stickers on their cars, and what do
they say?” One of their surveys asked the question, “What do you think
was the worst car of the millennium?” Thousands upon thousands of folks
responded with their votes — but, of course, these folks don’t represent
all car owners. They represent only those who listen to the radio show,
logged on to the Web site, and answered the survey question.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Just so you won’t be left hanging (and I
know you’re dying to find out!), the results of the survey are shown in
the following table. Although you may not be old enough to remember some
of these vehicles, it is certainly an easy exercise to search the
Internet for pictures and stories about them galore. (Remember, though,
that these results represent only the opinions of
</span><span class="zunivitalic">Car
Talk</span><span class="generated-style"> fans who took the time to get
to the Web site and take the survey.) Notice that the percentages won’t
add up to 100% because the results in the table represent only the top
ten vote-getters.</span>

</span><span class="generated-style">sample is one in which every

strongly agree or disagree with the proposed rules. Suppose only 200

that 800 opinions weren’t counted. Suppose none of those 800 people
really cared about the issue either way. If you could count their
opinions, the results would be 800 ÷ 1,000 = 80% “no opinion,” 100 ÷
1,000 = 10% in favor of the new rules, and 100 ÷ 1,000 = 10% against the
new rules. But without the votes of the 800 non-respondents, the
researchers would report, “Of the people who responded, 50% were in
favor of the new rules and 50% were against them.” This gives the
impression of a very different (and a very biased) result from the one
you would’ve gotten if all 1,000 people had responded.</span>

<span class="generated-style">The
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">response
rate</span><span class="generated-style"> of a survey is a ratio found
by taking the number of respondents divided by the number of people who
were originally asked to participate. You of course want to have the
highest response rate you can get with your survey; but how high is high
enough to be minimizing bias? The purest of the pure statisticians feel
that a good response rate is anything over 70%, but I think we need to
be a little more realistic. Today’s fast-paced society is saturated with
surveys; many if not most response rates fall far short of 70%. In fact,
response rates for today’s surveys are more likely to be in the 20% to
30% range, unless the survey is conducted by a professional polling
organization such as Gallup or you are being offered a new car just for
filling one out. </span>

![headsup_lewis.eps](9780470911082/images/headsup_lewis_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Look for the response rate when examining survey results. If the
response rate is too low (much less than 50%) the results are likely to
be biased and should be taken with a grain of salt, or even
ignored.</span>

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Don’t be fooled by a survey that claims to have a large number of
respondents but actually has a low response rate; in this case, many
people may have responded, but many more were asked and didn’t
respond.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Note that statistical formulas at this
level (including the formulas in this book) assume that your sample size
is equal to the number of respondents, so statisticians want you to know
how important it is to follow up with people and not end up with biased
data due to non-response. However, in reality, statisticians know that
you can’t always get everyone to respond, no matter how hard you try;
indeed, even the U.S. Census doesn’t have a 100% response rate. One way
statisticians combat the non-response problem after the data have been
collected is to break down the data to see how well it matches the
target population. If it’s a fairly good match, they can rest easier on
the bias issue.</span>

<span class="generated-style">So which number do you put in for n in all
those statistical formulas you use so often (such as the sample mean in
Chapter 5)? You can’t use the intended sample size (the number of people
contacted). You have to use the final sample size (the number of people
who responded). In the media you most often see only the number of
respondents reported, but you also need the response rate (or the total
number of respondents) to be able to critically evaluate the
results.</span>

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Regarding the quality of results, selecting a smaller initial sample
size and following them up more aggressively is a much better approach
than selecting a larger group of potential respondents and having a low
response rate, because of the bias introduced by non-response.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Interpreting results and finding
problems</span>

<span class="generated-style">The purpose of a survey is to gain
information about your target population; this information can include
opinions, demographic information, or lifestyles and behaviors. If the
survey has been designed and conducted in a fair and accurate manner
with the goals of the survey in mind, the data should provide good
information as to what’s happening with the target population (within
the stated margin of error; see Chapter 12). The next steps are to
organize the data to get a clear picture of what’s happening; to analyze
the data to look for links, differences, or other relationships of
interest; and then to draw conclusions based on the results.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Organizing and analyzing</span>

<span class="generated-style">After a survey has been completed, the
next step is to organize and analyze the data (in other words, crunch
some numbers and make some graphs). Many different types of data
displays and summary statistics can be created and calculated from
survey data, depending on the type of information that was collected.
(Numerical data, such as income, have different characteristics and are
usually presented differently than categorical data, such as gender.)
For more information on how data can be organized and summarized, see
Chapters 5 through 7. Depending on the research question, different
types of analyses can be performed on the data, including coming up with
population estimates, testing a hypothesis about the population, or
looking for relationships, to name a few. See Chapters 13, 14, 15, 18,
and 19 for more on each of these analyses, respectively.</span>

![headsup_lewis.eps](9780470911082/images/headsup_lewis_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Watch for misleading graphs and statistics. Not all survey data are
organized and analyzed fairly and correctly. See Chapter 3 for more
about how statistics can go wrong.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Drawing conclusions</span>

<span class="generated-style">The conclusions are the best part of any
survey — they’re why the researchers do all of the work in the first
place. If the survey was designed and carried out properly — the sample
was selected carefully and the data were organized and summarized
correctly — the results should fairly and accurately represent the
reality of the target population. But, of course, not all surveys are
done right. And even if a survey is done correctly, researchers can
misinterpret or overinterpret results so that they say more than they
really should.</span>

![headsup_lewis.eps](9780470911082/images/headsup_lewis_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
You know the saying “Seeing is believing”? Some researchers are guilty
of the converse, which is “Believing is seeing.” In other words, they
claim to see what they want to believe about the results. All the more
reason for you to know where the line is drawn between reasonable
conclusions and misleading results, and to realize when others have
crossed that line.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Here are some common errors made in
drawing conclusions from surveys:</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">Making projections to a larger population
than the study actually represents</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">Claiming a difference exists between two
groups when a difference isn’t really there (see Chapter 15)</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">Saying, “these results aren’t scientific,
but . . . ,” and then going on to present the results as if they are
scientific</span>

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
To avoid common errors made when drawing conclusions, do the
following:</span>

<span class="zcheltbold">1. Check whether the sample was selected
properly and that the conclusions don’t go beyond the population
presented by that sample.</span>

<span class="zcheltbold"> 2. Look for any disclaimers about the survey
</span><span class="zcheltbolditalic">before</span><span class="zcheltbold">
reading the results.</span>

<span class="generated-style"> That way, if the results aren’t based on
a scientific survey (an accurate and unbiased survey), you’ll be less
likely to be influenced by the results you’re reading. You can judge for
yourself whether the survey results are credible.</span>

<span class="zcheltbold">3. Be on the lookout for statistically
incorrect conclusions.</span>

<span class="generated-style"> If someone reports a difference between
two groups in terms of survey results, be sure that the difference is
larger than the reported margin of error. If the difference is within
the margin of error, you should expect the sample results to vary by
that much just by chance, and the so-called “difference” can’t really be
generalized to the entire population. (See Chapter 14 for more on
this.)</span>

![headsup_lewis.eps](9780470911082/images/headsup_lewis_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Know the limitations of any survey and be wary of any information coming
from surveys in which those limitations aren’t respected. A bad survey
is cheap and easy to do, but you get what you pay for. But don’t let big
expensive surveys fool you either — they can be riddled with bias as
well! Before looking at the results of any survey, investigate how it
was designed and conducted, using the criteria and tips in this chapter,
so you can judge the quality of the results and express yourself
confidently and correctly about what is wrong.</span>
