<div id="25_9780470911082-ch17.xhtml_x25_9780470911082-ch17">

<div class="story">

<span class="generated-style">Chapter 17</span>

<span class="generated-style">Experiments: Medical Breakthroughs or
Misleading Results?</span>

<span class="generated-style">In This Chapter</span>

![arrow](9780470911082/images/arrow.png)
<span class="generated-style">Distinguishing experiments from
observational studies</span>

![arrow](9780470911082/images/arrow.png)
<span class="generated-style">Dissecting the criteria for a good
experiment</span>

![arrow](9780470911082/images/arrow.png)
<span class="generated-style">Watching for misleading results</span>

<span class="drop-cap">M</span><span class="generated-style">edical
breakthroughs seem to come and go quickly. One day you hear about a
promising new treatment for a disease, only to find out later that the
drug didn’t live up to expectations in the last stage of testing.
Pharmaceutical companies bombard TV viewers with commercials for pills,
sending millions of people to their doctors clamoring for the latest and
greatest cures for their ills, sometimes without even knowing what the
drugs are for. Anyone can search the Internet for details about any type
of ailment, disease, or symptom and come up with tons of information and
advice. But how much can you really believe? And how do you decide which
options are best for you if you get sick, need surgery, or have an
emergency?</span>

<span class="generated-style">In this chapter, you go behind the scenes
of experiments, the driving force of medical studies and other
investigations in which comparisons are made — comparisons that test,
for example, which building materials are best, which soft drink teens
prefer, and so on. You find out the difference between experiments and
observational studies and discover what experiments can do for you, how
they’re supposed to be done, how they can go wrong, and how you can spot
misleading results. With so many headlines, sound bites, and pieces of
“expert advice” coming at you from all directions, you need to use all
your critical thinking skills to evaluate the sometimes-conflicting
information you’re presented with on a regular basis.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Boiling Down the Basics of Studies</span>

<span class="generated-style">Although many different types of studies
exist, you can basically boil them down to two types: experiments and
observational studies. This section examines what exactly makes
experiments different from other studies. But before I dive in to the
details, I need to lay some jargon on you.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Looking at the lingo of studies</span>

<span class="generated-style">To understand studies, you need to find
out what their commonly used terms mean:</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="zcheltbold">Subjects:
</span><span class="generated-style">Individuals participating in the
study.</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="zcheltbold">Observational
study:</span><span class="generated-style"> A study in which the
researcher merely observes the subjects and records the information. No
intervention takes place, no changes are introduced, and no restrictions
or controls are imposed.</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="zcheltbold">Experiment:</span><span class="generated-style">
This study doesn’t simply observe subjects in their natural state; it
deliberately applies treatments to them in a controlled situation and
studies their effects on the outcome.</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="zcheltbold">Response:</span><span class="generated-style">
The response is the variable whose outcome is the million dollar
question; it’s the variable whose outcome is of interest. For example,
if researchers want to know what happens to your blood pressure when you
take a large amount of Ibuprofen each day, the response variable is
blood pressure.</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="zcheltbold">Factor:</span><span class="generated-style"> A
factor is the variable whose effect on the response is being studied.
For example, if you want to know whether a particular drug increases
blood pressure, your factor is the amount of the drug taken. If you want
to know which weight loss program is most effective, your factor would
be the type of weight loss program used.</span>

<span class="generated-style"> You can have more than one factor in a
study; however, in this book I stick with discussing one factor only.
For the analysis of two-factor studies, including the use of Analysis of
Variance (ANOVA) and multiple comparisons to compare treatment
combinations, you can check out my book
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Statistics II For
Dummies,</span><span class="generated-style"> also published by
Wiley.</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="zcheltbold">Level:</span><span class="generated-style"> A
level is one possible outcome of a factor. Each factor has a certain
number of levels. In the weight loss example, the factor is the type of
weight loss program and the levels would be the specific programs
studied (for example Weight Watchers, South Beach, or the famous Potato
Diet). Levels need not be ascending in any way; however, in a study like
the drug example, the levels would be the various dosages taken each
day, in increasing amounts.</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="zcheltbold">Treatment:</span><span class="generated-style">
A treatment is a combination of the levels of the factors being studied.
If you only have one factor, the levels and the treatments are the same
thing. If you have more than one factor, each combination of levels of
the factors is called a treatment.</span>

<span class="generated-style"> For example, if you want to study the
effects of the type of weight loss program and the amount of water
consumed daily, you have two factors: 1) the type of program, with 3
levels (Weight Watchers, South Beach, Potato Diet); and 2) the amount of
water consumed, with, say, 3 levels (24, 48, and 64 ounces per day). In
this case, there are 3
</span><span class="zmathpiltstd">∗</span><span class="generated-style">
3 = 9 treatments: Weight Watchers and 24 ounces of water per day; Weight
Watchers and 48 ounces of water per day, . . . all the way up to the
famous Potato Diet and 64 ounces of water per day. Each subject is
assigned to one treatment. (With my luck, I’d get that last
treatment.)</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style"> </span><span class="zcheltbold">Cause and
effect: </span><span class="generated-style">A factor and a response
have a cause-and-effect relationship if a change in the factor results
in a direct change in the response (for example, increasing calorie
intake causes weight gain).</span>

<span class="generated-style">In the following sections, you see the
differences between observational studies and experiments, when each is
used, and what their strengths and/or weaknesses may be.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Observing observational studies</span>

<span class="generated-style">Just like with tools, you want to find the
right type of study for the right job. In certain situations,
observational studies are the optimal way to go. The most common
observational studies are
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">polls</span><span class="generated-style">
and
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">surveys</span><span class="generated-style">
(see Chapter 16). When the goal is simply to find out what people think
and to collect some demographic information (such as gender, age,
income, and so on), surveys and polls can’t be beat, as long as they’re
designed and conducted correctly.</span>

<span class="generated-style">In other situations, especially those
looking for cause-and-effect relationships, observational studies aren’t
optimal. For example, suppose you took a couple of vitamin C pills last
week; is that what helped you avoid getting that cold that’s going
around the office? Maybe the extra sleep you got recently or the extra
hand-washing you’ve been doing helped you ward off the cold. Or maybe
you just got lucky this time. With so many variables in the mix, how can
you tell which one had an influence on the outcome of your not getting a
cold? An experiment that takes these other variables into account is the
way to go.</span>

![tip.eps](9780470911082/images/tip_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
When looking at the results of any study, first determine what the
purpose of the study was and whether the type of study fits the purpose.
For example, if an observational study was done instead of an experiment
to establish a cause-and-effect relationship, any conclusions that are
drawn should be carefully scrutinized.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Examining experiments</span>

<span class="generated-style">The object of an experiment is to see if
the response changes as a result of the factor you are studying; that
is, you are looking for cause and effect. For example, does taking
Ibuprofen cause blood pressure to increase? If so, by how much? But
because results will vary with any experiment, you want to know that
your results have a high chance of being repeatable if you found
something interesting happening. That is, you want to know that your
results were unlikely to be due to chance; statisticians call such
results </span><span class="zcheltitalic">statistically
significant</span><span class="generated-style">. That’s the objective
of any study, observational, or experimental.</span>

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
A good experiment is conducted by creating a very controlled environment
— so controlled that the researcher can pinpoint whether a certain
factor or combination of factors causes a change in the response
variable, and if so, the extent to which that factor (or combination of
factors) influences the response. For example, to gain government
approval for a proposed blood pressure drug, pharmaceutical researchers
set up experiments to determine whether that drug helps lower blood
pressure, what dosage level is most appropriate for each different
population of patients, what side effects (if any) occur, and to what
extent those side effects occur in each population.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Designing a Good Experiment</span>

<span class="generated-style">How an experiment is designed can mean the
difference between good results and garbage. Because most researchers
are going to write the most glowing press releases that they can about
their experiments, you have to be able to sort through the hype to
determine whether to believe the results you’re being told. To decide
whether an experiment is credible, check to see if it meets
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">all</span><span class="generated-style">
the following criteria for a good experiment. A good experiment:</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="zcheltbold">Makes comparisons</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="zcheltbold">Includes a large enough sample size so that the
results are accurate</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="zcheltbold">Chooses subjects that most accurately represent
the target population</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="zcheltbold">Assigns subjects randomly to the treatment
group(s) and the control group</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="zcheltbold">Controls for possible confounding
variables</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png) <span class="zcheltbold">Is
ethical</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="zcheltbold">Collects good data</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="zcheltbold">Applies the proper data analysis</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="zcheltbold">Makes appropriate conclusions</span>

<span class="generated-style">In this section, each of these criteria is
explained and illustrated with examples.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Designing the experiment to make
comparisons</span>

<span class="generated-style">Every experiment has to make bonafide
comparisons to be credible. This seems to go without saying, but
researchers often are so gung-ho to prove their results that they forget
(or just don’t bother) to show that their factor, and not some other
factor(s), including random chance, was the actual cause for any
differences found in the response.</span>

<span class="generated-style">For example, suppose a researcher is
convinced that taking vitamin C prevents colds, and she assigns subjects
to take one vitamin C pill per day and follows them for 6 months.
Suppose the subjects get very few colds during that time. Can she
attribute these results to the vitamin C and nothing else? No; there’s
no way of knowing whether the subjects would have been just as healthy
without the vitamin C, due to some other factor(s), or just by chance.
There’s nothing to compare the results to.</span>

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
To tease out the real effect (if any) that your factor has on the
response, you need a baseline to compare the results to. This baseline
is called the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">control.</span><span class="generated-style">
Different methods exist for creating a control in an experiment;
depending on the situation, one method typically rises to the top as
being the most appropriate. Three common methods for including control
are to administer: 1) a fake treatment; 2) a standard treatment; or 3)
no treatment. The following sections describe each method.</span>

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
When examining the results of an experiment, make sure the researchers
established a baseline by creating a control group. Without a control
group, you have nothing to compare the results to, and you never know
whether the treatment being applied was the real cause of any
differences found in the response.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Fake treatments — the placebo
effect</span>

<span class="generated-style">A fake treatment (also called a
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">placebo</span><span class="generated-style">)
is not distinguishable from a “real” treatment by the subject. For
example, when drugs are administered, a subject assigned to the placebo
will receive a fake pill that looks and tastes exactly like a real pill;
it’s just filled with an inert substance like sugar instead of the
actual drug. A placebo establishes a baseline measure for what responses
would have taken place anyway, in lieu of any treatment (this would have
helped the vitamin C study mentioned under “Designing the experiment to
make comparisons”). But a fake treatment also takes into account what
researchers call the </span><span class="zcheltitalic">placebo
effect,</span><span class="generated-style"> a response that people have
(or think they’re having) because they know they’re getting some type of
“treatment” (even if that treatment is a fake treatment, such as sugar
pills).</span>

<span class="generated-style">Pharmaceutical companies are required to
account for the placebo effect when examining both the positive and
negative effects of a drug. When you see an ad for a drug in a magazine,
you see the positive results of the drug standing out in big, bright,
happy, colorful visuals. Then look at the back of the page and you see
it’s entirely filled in black with words written in 3-point font.
Embedded somewhere on that page, you can find one or more tiny tables
that show the number and nature of side effects reported by each
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">treatment
group</span><span class="generated-style"> (subjects who received an
actual treatment) as well as the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">control
group</span><span class="generated-style"> (subjects who were
administered a placebo).</span>

![headsup_lewis.eps](9780470911082/images/headsup_lewis_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
If the control group is on a placebo, you may expect the subjects not to
report any side effects, but you would be wrong. If you are taking a
pill, you know it could be an actual drug, and you are being asked
whether or not you’re experiencing side effects, you might be surprised
at what your response would be.</span>

<span class="generated-style">If you don’t take the placebo effect into
account, you have to believe that any side effects (or positive results)
reported are actually due to the drug. This gives an artificially high
number of reported side effects because at least some of those reports
are likely due to the placebo effect and not to the drug itself. If you
have a control group to compare with, you can subtract the percentage of
people in the control group who reported the side effects from the
percentage of people in the treatment group that reported the side
effects, and examine the magnitude of the numbers that remain. You’re in
essence looking at the net number of reported side effects due to the
drug, rather than the gross number of side effects, some of which are
due to the placebo effect.</span>

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
The placebo effect has been shown to be real. If you want to be fair
about examining the reported side effects (or positive reactions) of a
treatment, you have to also take into account the side effects (or
positive reactions) that the control group reports — those reactions
that are due to the placebo effect only.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Standard treatments</span>

![headsup_lewis.eps](9780470911082/images/headsup_lewis_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
In some situations, such as when the subjects have very serious
diseases, offering a fake treatment as an option may be unethical. One
famous example of a breech in ethics occurred in 1997. The U.S.
government was harshly criticized for financing an HIV study that
examined new dosage levels of AZT, a drug known at that time to cut the
risk of HIV transmission from pregnant mothers to their babies by
two-thirds. This particular study, in which 12,000 pregnant women with
HIV in Africa, Thailand, and the Dominican Republic participated, had a
deadly design. Researchers gave half of the women various dosages of
AZT, but the other half of the women received sugar pills. Of course,
had the U.S. government realized that a placebo was being given to half
of the subjects, it wouldn’t have supported the HIV study. It’s not
ethical to give a fake treatment to anyone with a deadly disease for
which a standard treatment is available (in this case, the standard
dosage of AZT).</span>

<span class="generated-style">When ethical reasons bar the use of fake
treatments, the new treatment is compared to at least one existing or
standard treatment that is known to be an effective treatment. After
researchers have enough data to see that one of the treatments is
working better than the other, they generally stop the experiment and
put everyone on the better treatment; again, for ethical reasons.</span>

<span class="generated-style">No treatment</span>

<span class="generated-style">“No treatment” means the researcher can’t
help but tell which group the subject is in, due to the nature of the
experiment. The subjects in this case aren’t receiving any type of
intervention in terms of their behavior, but they still serve as a
control, establishing a baseline of data to compare their results with
those in the treatment group(s). For example, if you want to determine
whether speed walking around the block ten times a day lowers a person’s
resting heart rate after six months, the subjects in your control group
know they aren’t going to be speed walking — obviously you can’t do fake
speed walking (although faking exercising and still reaping the benefits
would be great, wouldn’t it?).</span>

![tip.eps](9780470911082/images/tip_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
In situations where the control group receives no treatment, you still
make sure the groups of subjects (speed walkers versus non–speed
walkers) are similar in as many ways as possible, and that the other
criteria for a good experiment are being met. (See “Designing a Good
Experiment” for the list of criteria.)</span>

<span class="generated-style">Selecting the sample size</span>

<span class="generated-style">The size of a (good) sample greatly
affects the accuracy of the results. The larger the sample size, the
more accurate the results, and the more powerful the statistical tests
(in terms of being able to detect real results when they exist). In this
section, I hit the highlights; Chapter 14 has the details.</span>

![tip.eps](9780470911082/images/tip_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
The word
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">sample</span><span class="generated-style">

<span class="zcheltbold"> 3. Check the conclusions made by the

broader population than they actually studied.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Making Informed Decisions</span>

<span class="generated-style">Just because someone says they conducted a
“scientific study” or a “scientific experiment” doesn’t mean it was done
right or that the results are credible (not that I’m saying you should
discount everything that you see and hear). Unfortunately, I’ve come
across a lot of bad experiments in my days as a statistical consultant.
The worst part is that if an experiment was done poorly, you can’t do
anything about it after the fact except ignore the results — and that’s
exactly what you need to do.</span>

![tip.eps](9780470911082/images/tip_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Here are some tips that help you make an informed decision about whether
to believe the results of an experiment, especially one whose results
are very important to you:</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="zcheltbold">When you first hear or see the result, grab a
pencil and write down as much as you can about what you heard or read,
where you heard or read it, who did the research, and what the main
results were.</span><span class="generated-style"> (I keep pencil and
paper in my TV room and in my purse just for this purpose.)</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="zcheltbold">Follow up on your sources until you find the
person who did the original research and then ask them for a copy of the
report or paper.</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png) <span class="zcheltbold">Go
through the report and evaluate the experiment according to the eight
steps for a good experiment described in the “Designing a Good
Experiment” section of this
chapter.</span><span class="generated-style"> (You really don’t have to
understand everything written in a report in order to do that.)</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="zcheltbold">Carefully scrutinize the conclusions that the
researcher makes regarding his or her findings.
</span><span class="generated-style">Many researchers tend to overstate
results, make conclusions beyond the statistical evidence, or try to
apply their results to a broader population than the one they
studied.</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="zcheltbold">Never be afraid to ask questions of the media,
the researchers, and even your own experts.
</span><span class="generated-style">For example, if you have a question
about a medical study, ask your doctor. He or she will be glad that
you’re an empowered and well-informed patient!</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="zcheltbold">And finally, don’t get overly skeptical, just
because you’re now a lot more aware of all the bad practices going on
out there. </span><span class="generated-style">Not everything is bad.
There are many more good researchers, credible results, and
well-informed reporters than not. You have to maintain a sense of being
cautious and ready to spot problems without discounting
everything.</span>

</div>

</div>

<span class="generated-style">Chapter 18</span>

<span class="generated-style">Looking for Links: Correlation and
Regression</span>

<span class="generated-style">In This Chapter</span>

![arrow](9780470911082/images/arrow.png)
<span class="generated-style">Exploring statistical relationships
between numerical variables</span>

![arrow](9780470911082/images/arrow.png)
<span class="generated-style">Looking at correlation and linear

![arrow](9780470911082/images/arrow.png)

![arrow](9780470911082/images/arrow.png)
<span class="generated-style">Considering correlation versus
causation</span>

T<span class="normal">oday’s media provide a steady stream of
information, including reports on all the latest links that have been
found by researchers. </span><span class="generated-style">Just today I
heard that increased video game use can negatively affect a child’s
attention span, the amount of a certain hormone in a woman’s body can
predict when she will enter menopause, and the more depressed you get,
the more chocolate you eat, and the more chocolate you eat, the more
depressed you get (how depressing!).</span>

<span class="generated-style">Some studies are truly legitimate and help
improve the quality and longevity of our lives. Other studies are not so
clear. For example, one study says that exercising 20 minutes three
times a week is better than exercising 60 minutes one time a week,
another study says the opposite, and yet another study says there is no
difference.</span>

<span class="generated-style">If you are a confused consumer when it
comes to links and correlations, take heart; this chapter can help.
You’ll gain the skills to dissect and evaluate research claims and make
your own decisions about those headlines and sound bites that you hear
each day alerting you to the latest correlation. You’ll discover what it
truly means for two variables to be correlated, when a cause-and-effect
relationship can be concluded, and when and how to predict one variable
based on another.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Picturing a Relationship with a
Scatterplot</span>

<span class="generated-style">An article in
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Garden
Gate</span><span class="generated-style"> magazine caught my eye: “Count
Cricket Chirps to Gauge Temperature.” According to the article, all you
have to do is find a cricket, count the number of times it chirps in 15
seconds, add 40, and voilà! You’ve just estimated the temperature in
Fahrenheit.</span>

<span class="generated-style">The National Weather Service Forecast
Office even puts out its own “Cricket Chirp Converter.” You enter the
number of cricket chirps recorded in 15 seconds, and the converter gives
you the estimated temperature in four different units, including
Fahrenheit and Celsius.</span>

<span class="generated-style">A fair amount of research does support the
claim that frequency of cricket chirps is related to temperature. For
the purpose of illustration I’ve taken only a subset of some of the data
(see Table 18-1).</span>

![/Table 18-1](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-tb1801.jpg)

<span class="generated-style">Notice that each observation is composed
of two variables that are tied together: the number of times the cricket

</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">-variable)
and the temperature at the time the data was collected (the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Y</span><span class="generated-style">-variable).
Statisticians call this type of two-dimensional data
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">bivariate
</span><span class="generated-style">data. Each observation contains one
pair of data collected simultaneously. For example, row one of Table
18-1 depicts a pair of data (18, 57).</span>

<span class="generated-style">Bivariate data is typically organized in a
graph that statisticians call a
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">scatterplot.</span><span class="generated-style">
A scatterplot has two dimensions, a horizontal dimension (the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">-axis)
and a vertical dimension (the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Y</span><span class="generated-style">-axis).
Both axes are numerical; each one contains a number line. In the
following sections, I explain how to make and interpret a

<span class="generated-style">Making a scatterplot</span>

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Placing observations (or points) on a scatterplot is similar to playing
the game Battleship. Each observation has two coordinates; the first
corresponds to the first piece of data in the pair (that’s
the</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> X
</span><span class="generated-style">coordinate; the amount that you go
left or right). The second coordinate corresponds to the second piece of
data in the pair (that’s the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Y</span><span class="generated-style">-coordinate;
the amount that you go up or down). You place the point representing
that observation at the intersection of the two coordinates.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Figure 18-1 shows a scatterplot for the
cricket chirps and temperature data listed in Table 18-1. Because I

the points on the scatterplot correspond from left to right to the

<span class="generated-style">One pattern of special interest is a

In this chapter I explore linear relationships only. A
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">linear relationship between X and Y

</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">-

</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Y</span><span class="generated-style">-values
resembles a line, either uphill (with a positive slope) or downhill

![headsup_lewis.eps](9780470911082/images/headsup_lewis_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Scatterplots show possible associations or relationships between two
variables. However, just because your graph or chart shows something is
going on, it doesn’t mean that a cause-and-effect relationship
exists.</span>

<span class="generated-style">For example, a doctor observes that people
who take vitamin C each day seem to have fewer colds. Does this mean

Figure 18-2d shows a correlation of +0.15. Comparing Figures 18-2a and
c, you see Figure 18-2a is a perfect uphill straight line, and Figure
18-2c shows a very strong uphill linear pattern. Figure 18-2b is going
downhill but the points are somewhat scattered in a wider band, showing
a linear relationship is present, but not as strong as in Figures 18-2a
and 18-2c. Figure 18-2d doesn’t show much of anything happening (and it
shouldn’t, since its correlation is very close to 0).</span>

<div class="story">

**Figure 18-2:**<span class="generated-style"> Scatterplots with
correlations of a) +1.00; b) –0.50; c) +0.85; and d) +0.15.</span>

</div>

![9780470911082-fg1802.eps](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-fg1802_fmt.png)

<span class="generated-style">Many folks make the mistake of thinking
that a correlation of –1 is a bad thing, indicating no relationship.
Just the opposite is true! A correlation of –1 means the data are lined
up in a perfect straight line, the strongest linear relationship you can
get. The “–” (minus) sign just happens to indicate a negative
relationship, a downhill line.</span>

![tip.eps](9780470911082/images/tip_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
How close is close enough to –1 or +1 to indicate a strong enough linear
relationship? Most statisticians like to see correlations beyond at
least +0.5 or –0.5 before getting too excited about them. Don’t expect a
correlation to always be 0.99 however; remember, this is real data, and
real data aren’t perfect.</span>

<span class="generated-style">For my subset of the cricket chirps versus
temperature data from the earlier section “Picturing a Relationship with
a Scatterplot,” I calculated a correlation of 0.98, which is almost
unheard of in the real world (these crickets are
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">good!</span><span class="generated-style">).</span>

<span class="generated-style">Examining properties of the
correlation</span>

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Here are several important properties of the correlation
coefficient:</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">The correlation is always between –1 and
+1, as I explain in the preceding section.</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">The correlation is a unitless measure,
which means that if you change the units
of</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> X
</span><span class="generated-style">or
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Y,</span><span class="generated-style">
the correlation won’t change. For example, changing the temperature from
Fahrenheit to Celsius won’t affect the correlation between the frequency
of chirps
(</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">)
and the outside temperature
(</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Y</span><span class="generated-style">).</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">The
variables</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> X
</span><span class="generated-style">and</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
Y </span><span class="generated-style">can be switched in the data set
without changing the correlation. For example, if height and weight have
a correlation of 0.53, weight and height have the same
correlation.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Working with Linear Regression</span>

<span class="generated-style">In the case of two numerical
variables</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> X
</span><span class="generated-style">and
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Y,</span><span class="generated-style">
when at least a moderate correlation has been established through both
the correlation and the scatterplot, you know they have some type of
linear relationship. Researchers often use that relationship to predict
the (average) value of</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> Y
</span><span class="generated-style">for a given value
of</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> X
</span><span class="generated-style">using a straight line.
Statisticians call this line the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">regression
line.</span><span class="generated-style"> If you know the slope and the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">y</span><span class="generated-style">-intercept
of that regression line, then you can plug in a value
for</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> X
</span><span class="generated-style">and predict the average value for
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Y.</span><span class="generated-style">
In other words, you predict (the
average)</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> Y
</span><span class="generated-style">from
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X.</span><span class="generated-style">
In the following sections, I provide the basics of understanding and
using the linear regression equation (I explain how to make predictions
with linear regression later in this chapter).</span>

![headsup_lewis.eps](9780470911082/images/headsup_lewis_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Never do a regression analysis unless you have already found at least a
moderately strong correlation between the two variables. (My rule of
thumb is it should be at or beyond either positive or negative 0.50, but
other statisticians may have different criteria.) I’ve seen cases where
researchers go ahead and make predictions when a correlation is as low
as 0.20! By anyone’s standards, that doesn’t make sense. If the data
don’t resemble a line to begin with, you shouldn’t try to use a line to
fit the data and make predictions (but people still try).</span>

<span class="generated-style">Figuring out which variable is X and which
is Y</span>

<span class="generated-style">Before moving forward to find the equation
for your regression line, you have to identify which of your two
variables is</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> X
</span><span class="generated-style">and which
is</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
Y</span><span class="generated-style">. When doing correlations (as I
explain earlier in this chapter), the choice of which variable
is</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> X
</span><span class="generated-style">and which
is</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> Y
</span><span class="generated-style">doesn’t matter, as long as you’re
consistent for all the data. But when fitting lines and making
predictions, the choice of</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> X
</span><span class="generated-style">and</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
Y </span><span class="generated-style">does make a difference.</span>

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
So how do you determine which variable is which? In
general,</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> Y
</span><span class="generated-style">is the variable that you want to
predict, and
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">
is the variable you are using to make that prediction. In the earlier
cricket chirps example, you are using the number of chirps to predict
the temperature. So in this case the variable
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Y</span><span class="generated-style">
is the temperature, and the variable
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">
is the number of chirps. Hence</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> Y
</span><span class="generated-style">can be predicted
by</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> X
</span><span class="generated-style">using the equation of a line if a
strong enough linear relationship exists.</span>

![tip.eps](9780470911082/images/tip_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Statisticians call the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">-variable
(cricket chirps in my earlier example) the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">explanatory
variable,</span><span class="generated-style"> because
if</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> X
</span><span class="generated-style">changes, the slope tells you (or
explains) how much</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> Y
</span><span class="generated-style">is expected to change in response.
Therefore, the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Y</span><span class="generated-style">
variable is called the </span><span class="zcheltitalic">response
variable.</span><span class="generated-style"> Other names for
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">
and
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Y</span><span class="generated-style">
include the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">independent</span><span class="generated-style">
and
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">dependent</span><span class="generated-style">
variables, respectively.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Checking the conditions</span>

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
In the case of two numerical variables, you can come up with a line that
enables you to predict</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> Y
</span><span class="generated-style">from
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X,</span><span class="generated-style">
if (and only if) the following two conditions from the previous sections
are met:</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">The scatterplot must form a linear
pattern.</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">The correlation,
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">r,</span><span class="generated-style">
is moderate to strong (typically beyond 0.50 or –0.50).</span>

<span class="generated-style">Some researchers actually don’t check
these conditions before making predictions. Their claims are not valid
unless the two conditions are met.</span>

<span class="generated-style">But suppose the correlation is high; do
you still need to look at the scatterplot? Yes. In some situations the
data have a somewhat curved shape, yet the correlation is still strong;
in these cases making predictions using a straight line is still
invalid. Predictions need to be made based on a curve. (This topic is
outside the scope of this book; if you are interested, see
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Statistics II For
Dummies,</span><span class="generated-style"> where I tackle nonlinear
relationships.)</span>

<span class="generated-style">Calculating the regression line</span>

<span class="generated-style">For the crickets and temperature data, you
can see that the scatterplot in Figure 18-1 shows a linear pattern. The
correlation between cricket chirps and temperature was found earlier in
this chapter to be very strong
(</span><span class="zcheltitalic">r</span><span class="generated-style">
= 0.98). You now can find one line that best fits the data (in terms of
having the smallest overall distance to the points). Statisticians call
this technique for finding the best-fitting line a
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">simple
linear</span><span class="generated-style">
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">regression analysis using the least
squares method.</span>

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
The formula for the </span><span class="zcheltitalic">best-fitting
line</span><span class="generated-style"> (or
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">regression
line</span><span class="generated-style">)
is</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> y
</span><span class="generated-style">=
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">mx</span><span class="generated-style"> +
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">b</span><span class="generated-style">,
where
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">m</span><span class="generated-style">
is the slope of the line and
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">b</span><span class="generated-style">
is the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">y</span><span class="generated-style">-intercept.
This equation itself is the same one used to find a line in algebra; but
remember, in statistics the points don’t lie perfectly on a line — the
line is a model around which the data lie if a strong linear pattern
exists.</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">The
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">slope</span><span class="generated-style">
of a line is the change in</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> Y
</span><span class="generated-style">over the change in
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">.
For example, a slope of 10/3 means as the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">x-</span><span class="generated-style">value
increases (moves right) by 3 units, the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">y</span><span class="generated-style">-value
moves up by 10 units on average.</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">The
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">y-intercept</span><span class="generated-style">
is that place on the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">y-</span><span class="generated-style">axis
where the value of
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">x</span><span class="generated-style">
is zero. For example, in the equation
2</span><span class="zcheltitalic">x</span><span class="generated-style">
– 6, the line crosses the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">y</span><span class="generated-style">-axis
at the point –6. The coordinates of this point are (0, –6); when a line
crosses the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">y-</span><span class="generated-style">axis,
the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">x-</span><span class="generated-style">value
is always 0.</span>

![technicalstuff.eps](9780470911082/images/technicalstuff_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
To come up with the best-fitting line, you need to find values for
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">m</span><span class="generated-style">
and
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">b</span><span class="generated-style">
that fit the pattern of data the best, for your given criteria.
Different criteria exist and can lead to other lines, but the criteria I
use in this book (and in all introductory level statistics courses in
general) is to find the line that minimizes what statisticians call the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">sum of squares for error
(SSE)</span><span class="generated-style">. The SSE is the sum of all
the squared differences from the points on the proposed line to the
actual points in the data set. The line with the lowest possible SSE
wins and its equation is used as the best-fitting line. This process is
where the name </span><span class="zcheltitalic">the least-squares
method</span><span class="generated-style"> comes from.</span>

<span class="generated-style">You may be thinking that you have to try
lots and lots of different lines to see which one fits best.

<span class="generated-style">Interpreting the slope</span>

<span class="generated-style">The slope is interpreted in algebra as
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">rise over
run</span><span class="generated-style">. If, for example, the slope is

and say that as you move from point to point on the line,
as</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
</span><span class="generated-style">the</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
</span><span class="generated-style">value of
the</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> X
</span><span class="generated-style">variable</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
</span><span class="generated-style">increases by
1,</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
</span><span class="generated-style">the value of
the</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> Y
</span><span class="generated-style">variable</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
</span><span class="generated-style">increases by 2. In a regression
context, the slope is the heart and soul of the equation because it
tells you how much you can expect</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> Y
</span><span class="generated-style">to change
as</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> X
</span><span class="generated-style">increases.</span>

<span class="generated-style">In general, the units for slope are the
units of the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Y</span><span class="generated-style">
variable per units of the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">
variable. It’s a ratio of change in</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> Y
</span><span class="generated-style">per change in
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X.</span><span class="generated-style">
Suppose in studying the effect of dosage level in milligrams (mg) on
systolic blood pressure (mmHg), a researcher finds that the slope of the
regression line is –2.5. You can write this as
</span><span class="zcheltbold">–2.5/1</span><span class="generated-style">
and say that systolic blood pressure is expected to decrease by 2.5 mmHg
on average per 1 mg increase in drug dosage.</span>

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Always make sure to use proper units when interpreting slope. If you
don’t consider units, you won’t really see the connection between the
two variables at hand. For example if
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Y</span><span class="generated-style">
is exam score and
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">
= study time, and you find the slope of the equation is 5, what does
this mean? Not much without any units to draw from. Including the units,
you see you get an increase of 5 points (change in
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Y</span><span class="generated-style">)
for every 1 hour increase in studying (change in
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">).
Also be sure to watch for variables that have more than one common unit,
such as temperature being in either Fahrenheit or Celsius; know which
unit is being used.</span>

<span class="generated-style">If using a 1 in the denominator of slope
is not super-meaningful to you, you can multiply the top and bottom by
any number (as long as it’s the same number) and interpret it that way
instead. In the systolic blood pressure example, instead of writing
slope as
</span><span class="zcheltbold">–2.5/1</span><span class="generated-style">
and interpreting it as a drop of 2.5 mmHg per 1 mg increase of the drug,
you can multiply the top and bottom by 10 to get
</span><span class="zcheltbold">–25/10</span><span class="generated-style">
and say an increase in dosage of 10 mg results in a decrease in systolic
blood pressure of 25 mmHg.</span>

<span class="generated-style">The
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">y-</span><span class="generated-style">intercept

</span><span class="zcheltitalic">y</span><span class="generated-style">-axis
where
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">x</span><span class="generated-style">
= 0, and is denoted by
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">b</span><span class="generated-style">
(see the earlier section “Finding the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">y-</span><span class="generated-style">intercept”).
Sometimes the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">y-</span><span class="generated-style">intercept
can be interpreted in a meaningful way, and sometimes not. This
uncertainty differs from slope, which is always interpretable. In fact,
between the two elements of slope and
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">y-</span><span class="generated-style">intercept,
the slope is the star of the show, with the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">y-</span><span class="generated-style">intercept
serving as the less-famous but still noticeable sidekick.</span>

![headsup_lewis.eps](9780470911082/images/headsup_lewis_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
At times the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">y-</span><span class="generated-style">intercept
makes no sense. For example, suppose you use rain to predict bushels per
acre of corn. You know if the data set contains a point where rain is 0,
the bushels per acre must be 0 as well. As a result, if the regression
line crosses the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">y-</span><span class="generated-style">axis
somewhere else besides 0 (and there is no guarantee it will cross at 0 —
it depends on the data), the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">y-</span><span class="generated-style">intercept
will make no sense. Similarly, in this context a negative value of
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">y</span><span class="generated-style">
(corn production) cannot be interpreted.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Another situation where you can’t
interpret the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">y-</span><span class="generated-style">intercept
is when data are not present near the point
where</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> x
</span><span class="generated-style">= 0. For example, suppose you want
to use students’ scores on Midterm 1 to predict their scores on Midterm
2. The
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">y-</span><span class="generated-style">intercept
represents a prediction for Midterm 2 when the score on Midterm 1 is 0.
You don’t expect scores on a midterm to be at or near 0 unless someone
didn’t take the exam, in which case her score wouldn’t be included in
the first place.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Many times, however, the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">y-</span><span class="generated-style">intercept
is of interest to you, it has meaning, and you have data collected in
the area where</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> x
</span><span class="generated-style">= 0. For example, if you’re
predicting coffee sales at football games in Green Bay, Wisconsin, using
temperature, some games get cold enough to have temperatures at or even
below 0 degrees Fahrenheit, so predicting coffee sales at these
temperatures makes sense. (As you may guess, they sell more and more
coffee as the temperature dips.)</span>

(</span><span class="zcheltbolditalic">Note:</span><span class="generated-style">
I’m rounding for ease of explanation only.)</span>

![/Table 18-2](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-tb1802.jpg)

<span class="generated-style">The slope,
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">m,</span><span class="generated-style">
for the best-fitting line for the subset of cricket chirps versus

</span>![9780470911082-EQ18021.eps](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-EQ18021_fmt.png)<span class="generated-style">.
So as the number of chirps

<span class="generated-style">Now, to find the

</span><span class="zcheltitalic">b,</span><span class="generated-style">
you take
</span>![9780470911082-EQ18022.eps](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-EQ18022_fmt.png)<span class="generated-style">,
or 67 – (0.90)(26.5) = 43.15. So the best-fitting line for predicting

</span><span class="zmathpiltstd">∗</span><span class="generated-style">
(number of chirps in 15 seconds) + 43.2. Now can you use the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">y-</span><span class="generated-style">intercept

<span class="generated-style">After you have determined a strong linear

line</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
</span><span class="generated-style">using</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
y </span><span class="generated-style">=
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">mx</span><span class="generated-style"> +
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">b</span><span class="generated-style">,
you use that line to predict (the

</span><span class="generated-style">for a given
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">x-</span><span class="generated-style">value.
To make predictions, you plug the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">x-</span><span class="generated-style">value
into the equation and solve for
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">y.</span><span class="generated-style">
For example, if your equation is</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> y
</span><span class="generated-style">=

</span><span class="generated-style">= 2(1) + 1 = 3.</span>

</span><span class="generated-style">(the explanatory variable) that you

the response variable, which totally depends on

By doing this, you are using one variable that you can easily collect

</span><span class="generated-style">variable that is difficult or not

</span><span class="generated-style">and</span><span class="zcheltitalic">

the big idea of regression.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Using the examples from the previous

</span><span class="generated-style">=

</span><span class="generated-style">+ 43.2. Say you’re camping outside,

and find that</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> y

this range you go with your
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">x-</span><span class="generated-style">values,

point they would either pass out or burn up! And what does a negative
number of chirps really mean? (Is this similar to asking what the sound
of one hand clapping is?)</span>

Be aware that not every data point will necessarily fit the regression
line well, even if the correlation is high. A point or two may fall
outside the overall pattern of the rest of the data; such points are
called
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">outliers</span><span class="generated-style">.
One or two outliers probably won’t affect the overall fit of the
regression line much, but in the end you can see that the line didn’t do
well at those specific points.</span>

<span class="generated-style">The numerical difference between the
predicted value of
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">y</span><span class="generated-style">
from the line and the actual
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">y-</span><span class="generated-style">value
you got from your data is called a
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">residual.</span><span class="generated-style">
Outliers have large residuals compared to the rest of the points; they
are worth investigating to see if there was an error in the data at
those points or if there is something particularly interesting in the
data to follow up on. (I give a much more detailed look at residuals in
the book </span><span class="zcheltitalic">Statistics II For
Dummies</span><span class="generated-style">.)</span>

<span class="generated-style">Explaining the Relationship: Correlation
versus Cause and Effect</span>

<span class="generated-style">Scatterplots and correlations identify and
quantify relationships between two variables. However, if a scatterplot
shows a definite pattern and the data are found to have a strong
correlation, that doesn’t necessarily mean that a cause-and-effect
relationship exists between the two variables. A
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">cause-and-effect
relationship</span><span class="generated-style"> is one where a change
in</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
</span><span class="generated-style">one variable (in this case
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">)</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
</span><span class="generated-style">causes a change in another variable
(in this case
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Y</span><span class="generated-style">).
(In other words, the change in</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> Y
</span><span class="generated-style">is not only associated with a
change in
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">,
but also directly caused by
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">X</span><span class="generated-style">.)</span>

<span class="generated-style">For example, suppose a well-controlled
medical experiment is conducted to determine the effects of dosage of a
certain drug on blood pressure. (See a total breakdown of experiments in
Chapter 17.) The researchers look at their scatterplot and see a
definite downhill linear pattern; they calculate the correlation, and
it’s strong. They conclude that increasing the dosage of this drug
causes a decrease in blood pressure. This cause-and-effect conclusion is
okay because they controlled for other variables that could affect blood
pressure in their experiment, such as other drugs taken, age, general
health, and so on.</span>

<span class="generated-style">However, if you made a scatterplot and
examined the correlation between ice cream consumption versus murder
rates in New York City, you would also see a strong linear relationship
(this one is uphill). Yet no one would claim that more ice cream
consumption causes more murders to occur.</span>

<span class="generated-style">What’s going on here? In the first case,
the data were collected through a well-controlled medical experiment,
which minimizes the influence of other factors that may affect blood
pressure. In the second example, the data were based just on
observation, and no other factors were examined. Researchers
subsequently found out that this strong relationship exists because
increases in murder rates and ice cream sales are both related to
increases in temperature. Temperature in this case is called a
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">confounding
variable</span><span class="generated-style">; it affects
both</span><span class="zcheltitalic"> X
</span><span class="generated-style">and</span><span class="zcheltitalic">
Y </span><span class="generated-style">but was not included in the study
(see Chapter 17).</span>

![headsup_lewis.eps](9780470911082/images/headsup_lewis_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Whether two variables are found to be causally associated depends on how
the study was conducted. I’ve seen many instances in which people try to
claim cause-and-effect relationships just by looking at scatterplots or
correlations. Why would they do this? Because they want to believe it
(in other words for them it’s “believing is seeing,” rather than the
other way around). Beware of this tactic. In order to establish cause
and effect, you need to have a well-designed experiment or a boatload of
observational studies. If someone is trying to establish a
cause-and-effect relationship by showing a chart or graph, dig deeper to
find out how the study was designed and how the data were collected, and
evaluate the study appropriately using the criteria outlined in Chapter
17.</span>

<span class="generated-style">The need for a well-designed experiment in
order to claim cause and effect is often ignored by some researchers and
members of the media, who give us headlines such as “Doctors can lower
malpractice lawsuits by spending more time with patients.” In reality,
it was found that doctors who have fewer lawsuits are the type who spend
a lot of time with patients. But that doesn’t mean taking a bad doctor
and having him spend more time with his patients will reduce his
malpractice suits; in fact, spending more time with them may create even
more problems.</span>

</div>

</div>

<span id="27_9780470911082-ch19.xhtml"></span>

<div id="27_9780470911082-ch19.xhtml_x27_9780470911082-ch19">

<div class="story">

<span class="generated-style">Chapter 19</span>

<span class="generated-style">Two-Way Tables and Independence</span>

<span class="generated-style">In This Chapter</span>

![arrow](9780470911082/images/arrow.png)
<span class="generated-style">Setting up two-way tables with categorical
variables</span>

![arrow](9780470911082/images/arrow.png)
<span class="generated-style">Delving into marginal, joint, and
conditional distributions</span>

![arrow](9780470911082/images/arrow.png)
<span class="generated-style">Checking for independence and
dependence</span>

![arrow](9780470911082/images/arrow.png)
<span class="generated-style">Having perspective on the results of
two-way tables</span>

<span class="drop-cap">C</span><span class="zcheltitalic">ategorical
variables</span><span class="generated-style"> place individuals into
groups based on certain characteristics, behaviors, or outcomes, such as
whether you ate breakfast this morning (yes, no) or political
affiliation (Democrat, Republican, Independent, “other”). Oftentimes
people look for relationships between two categorical variables; hardly
a day goes by that you don’t hear about another relationship that’s
reported to have been found.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Here are just a few examples I found on
the Internet recently:</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">Dog owners are more likely to take their
animal to the vet than cat owners.</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">Heavy use of social-networking Web sites
in teens is linked to depression.</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">Children who play more video games do
better in science classes.</span>

<span class="generated-style">With all this information being given to
you about variables that are related, how do you decide what to believe?
For example, does heavy use of social-networking Web sites cause
depression, or is it the other way around? Or perhaps a third variable
out there is related to both of them, such as problems in the
home.</span>

<span class="generated-style">In this chapter, you see how to organize
and analyze data from two categorical variables. You find out how to use
proportions to make comparisons and look at overall patterns and how to
check for independence of two categorical variables. You see how to
describe dependent relationships appropriately and to evaluate results
claiming to indicate cause-and-effect relationships, making predictions,
and/or projecting their results to a population.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Organizing a Two-Way Table</span>

<span class="generated-style">To explore links between two categorical
variables, you first need to organize the data that’s been collected,
and a table is a great way to do that. A
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">two-way
table</span><span class="generated-style"> classifies individuals into
groups based on the outcomes of two categorical variables (for example,
gender and opinion).</span>

<span class="generated-style">Suppose your local community developers
are building a campground, and they’ve decided pets will be allowed as
long as they’re on a leash. They are now trying to decide whether the
campground should have a separate section for pets. You have a hunch
that non–pet campers in the area may be more in favor of a separate pet
area than pet campers, so you decide to find out what the members of the
camping community think. You randomly select 100 campers from the local
area and conduct a pet camping survey, recording each person’s opinion
on having a pet section (yes, no) and if they camp with pets (yes, no).
You now have a spreadsheet with 100 rows of data, one for each person
you surveyed. Each row has two pieces of data: one column for whether
the person is a pet camper (yes, no) and one column for that person’s
opinion on having a pet section (support, oppose). Suppose the first
10 rows of your data set look like what’s shown in Table 19-1.</span>

![/Table 19-1](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-tb1901.jpg)

<span class="generated-style">From this small portion of your data set,
you can start to break it down yourself. For example, looking at column
2 results, you see that half the respondents (5 ÷ 10 = 0.50) camp with
pets and the other half do not. Of those who camp with pets (that is, of
those five people who have a yes in column 2), three of them (60%)
support having a separate section; and the same results are true for
non–pet campers. These results from these 10 campers likely don’t apply
to all 100 campers surveyed; however, if you tried to examine the raw
data from all 100 rows of this data set by hand, you wouldn’t make much
progress in seeing patterns without a lot of hard work.</span>

<span class="generated-style">In order to get a handle on what’s
happening in a large data set when you are examining two categorical
variables, you organize your data into a two-way table. The following
sections take you through it.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Setting up the cells</span>

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
A two-way table organizes categorical data from two variables by using
rows to represent one variable (such as pet camping — yes or no) and
columns to represent the other variable (such as opinion on a pet
section — support or oppose). Each person appears exactly once in the
table.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Continuing with the camping example I
start earlier in this chapter, in Table 19-2 I summarize the results
from all 100 campers surveyed.</span>

![/Table 19-2](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-tb1902.jpg)

<span class="generated-style">Table 19-2 has 2
</span><span class="zmathpiltstd">∗</span><span class="generated-style">
2 = 4 numbers in it. These numbers represent the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">cells</span><span class="generated-style">
of the two-way table; each one represents an intersection of a row and
column. The cell in the upper left corner of the table represents the 20
people who are pet campers supporting a pet section. In the upper right
cell 10 people are pet campers opposing a pet section. In the lower left
are the 55 non–pet campers who want a pet section; the 15 people in the
lower right are non–pet campers opposing a pet section.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Figuring the totals</span>

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
Before getting to the nitty-gritty analysis of a two-way table in the
later section “Interpreting Results from a Two-Way Table,” you calculate
some totals and add them to the table for later reference. You summarize
each variable separately by calculating the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">marginal
totals,</span><span class="generated-style"> which represent the total
number in each row (for the first variable) and the total number in each
column (for the second variable). The
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">marginal row
totals</span><span class="generated-style"> form an additional column on
the right side of the table, and the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">marginal column
totals</span><span class="generated-style"> form an additional row on
the bottom of the table.</span>

<span class="generated-style">For example, in Table 19-2 in the
preceding section, the marginal row total for row 1, the number of pet
campers, is 20 + 10 = 30; the marginal row total for non–pet campers
(row 2) is 55 + 15 = 70. The marginal column total for those wanting a
pet section (column 1) is 20 + 55 = 75; and the marginal column total
for those not wanting a separate section (column 2) is 10 + 15 =
25.</span>

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
The </span><span class="zcheltitalic">grand
total</span><span class="generated-style"> is the total of all the cells
in the table and is equal to the sample size. (Note the marginal totals
are not included in the grand total, only the cells.) The grand total
sits in the lower right-hand corner of the two-way table. In this
example, the grand total is 20 + 10 + 55 + 15 = 100. Table 19-3 shows
the marginal row and column totals and the grand total for the pet
camping survey data.</span>

<span class="generated-style">The marginal row totals always sum to the
grand total, because everyone in the survey either camps with a pet or
they don’t. In the last column of Table 19-3 you see that 30 + 70 = 100.
Similarly the marginal column totals always sum to the grand total;
everyone in the survey either wants a pet section or they don’t; in the
last row of Table 19-3 you see 75 + 25 = 100.</span>

![/Table 19-3](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-tb1903.jpg)

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
When organizing a two-way table, always include the marginal totals and
the grand total. It gets you off on the right foot when analyzing the
data.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Interpreting Two-Way Tables</span>

<span class="generated-style">After the two-way table is set up (with
the help of the information in the previous section), you calculate
percents to explore the data to answer your research questions. Here are
some questions of interest from the camping data earlier in this chapter
(each question will be handled in the following sections,
respectively):</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">What percentage of the campers are in
favor of a pet section?</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">What percentage of the campers are pet
campers who support a pet section?</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">Do more non–pet campers support a pet
section, compared to pet campers?</span>

<span class="generated-style">The answers to these (and any other)
questions about the data come from finding and working with the
proportions, or percentages, of individuals within certain parts of the
table. This process involves calculating and examining what
statisticians call
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">distributions.</span><span class="generated-style">
A distribution in the case of a two-way table is a list of all the
possible outcomes for one variable or a combination of variables, along
with their corresponding proportions (or percentages).</span>

<span class="generated-style">For example, the distribution for the pet
camping variable lists the percentages of people who do and do not camp
with pets. The distribution for the combination of the pet camping
variable (yes, no) and the opinion variable (support, oppose) lists the
percentages of: 1) pet campers who support a pet section; 2) pet campers
who oppose a pet section; 3) non–pet campers who support a pet section;
and 4) the non–pet campers who oppose a pet section.</span>

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
For any distribution, all the percentages must sum to 100%. If you’re
using proportions (decimals), they must sum to 1.00. Each individual has
to be somewhere, and he can’t be in more than one place at one
time.</span>

<span class="generated-style">In the following sections, you see how to
find three types of distributions, each one helping you to answer its
corresponding question in the preceding list.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Singling out variables with marginal
distributions</span>

<span class="generated-style">If you want to examine one variable at a
time in a two-way table, you don’t look in the cells of the table, but
rather in the margins. As seen in the earlier section “Figuring the
totals,” the marginal totals represent the total number in each row (or
column) separately. In the two-way table for the pet camping survey
(refer to Table 19-3), you see the marginal totals for the pet camping
variable (yes/no) in the right-hand column, and you find the marginal
totals for the opinion variable (support/oppose) in the bottom
row.</span>

<span class="generated-style">If you want to make comparisons between
two groups (for example, pet campers versus non–pet campers), however,
the results are easier to interpret if you use proportions instead of
totals. If 350 people were surveyed, visualizing a comparison is easier
if you’re told that 60% are in Group A and 40% are in Group B, rather
than saying 210 people are in Group A and 140 are in Group B.</span>

<span class="generated-style">To examine the results of a two-way table
based on a single variable, you find what statisticians call the
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">marginal
distribution</span><span class="generated-style"> for that variable. In
the following sections, I show you how to calculate and graph marginal
distributions.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Calculating marginal distributions</span>

![remember.eps](9780470911082/images/remember_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
To find a marginal distribution for one variable in a two-way table, you
take the marginal total for each row (or column) divided by the grand
total.</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">If your variable is represented by the
rows (for example, the pet camping variable in Table 19-3), use the
marginal row totals in the numerators and the grand total in the
denominators. Table 19-4 shows the marginal distribution for the pet
camping variable (yes, no).</span>

![check.png](9780470911082/images/check.png)
<span class="generated-style">If your variable is represented by the
columns (for example, opinion on the pet section policy, shown in Table
19-3), use the marginal column totals for the numerators and the grand
total for the denominators. Table 19-5 shows the marginal distribution
for the opinion variable (support, oppose).</span>

![tip.eps](9780470911082/images/tip_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
In either case, the sum of the proportions for any marginal distribution
must be 1 (subject to rounding). All results in a two-way table are
subject to rounding error; to reduce rounding error, keep at least 2
digits after the decimal point throughout.</span>

![/Table 19-4](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-tb1904.jpg)

![/Table 19-5](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-tb1905.jpg)

<span class="generated-style">Graphing marginal distributions</span>

<span class="generated-style">You graph a marginal distribution using
either a pie chart or a bar graph. Each graph shows the proportion of
individuals within each group for a single variable. Figure 19-1a is a
pie chart summarizing the pet camping variable, and Figure 19-1b is a
pie chart showing the breakdown of the opinion variable. You see that
the results of these two pie charts correspond with the marginal
distributions in Tables 19-4 and 19-5, respectively.</span>

marginal distributions for a) pet camping variable; and b) opinion
variable.</span>

![9780470911082-fg1901.eps](9780470911082/images/9780470911082-fg1901_fmt.png)

<span class="generated-style">From the results of the two separate
marginal distributions for the pet camping and opinion variables, you

![headsup_lewis.eps](9780470911082/images/headsup_lewis_fmt.jpeg)<span class="generated-style">
While marginal distributions show us how each variable breaks down on
its own, they don’t tell us about the connection between two variables.
For the camping example, you know what percentage of all campers support
a new pet section, but you can’t distinguish the opinions of the pet
campers from the non–pet campers. Distributions for making such

<span class="generated-style">Examining all groups — a joint

<span class="generated-style">Story time: A certain auto manufacturer

paired with the most popular outcome of the second variable (options on

To figure out which combination of two categorical variables contains

</span><span class="zcheltitalic">joint distribution
</span><span class="generated-style">of both variables in a two-way

show you how to calculate and graph joint distributions.</span>

<span class="generated-style">Comparing groups with conditional
distributions</span>

<span class="generated-style">You need a different type of distribution
other than a joint distribution to compare the results from two groups
(for example comparing opinions of pet campers versus non–pet campers).
</span><span class="zcheltitalic">Conditional
