data, making the results subject to skepticism by statisticians.

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png)
<span class="zCheltBold">Double-check that you clearly understand the
type of data being collected.</span> Is the data categorical or
quantitative? The type of data used drives the approach that you take in
the analysis.

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png)
<span class="zCheltBold">Make sure that the statistical technique you
use is designed to answer the research question.</span> If you want to
make comparisons between two groups and your data is quantitative, use a
hypothesis test for two means. If you want to compare five groups, use
analysis of variance (ANOVA). Use this book as a resource to help you
determine the technique you need.

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png)
<span class="zCheltBold">Look for the limitations of the data
analysis.</span> For example, if the researcher wants to know whether
negative political ads affect the population of voters and she bases her
study on a group of college students, you can find severe limitations
here. For starters, student reactions to negative ads don’t necessarily
carry over to all voters in the population. In this case, it’s best to
limit the conclusions to college students in that class (which no
researcher would ever want to do). Better to take a sample that
represents the intended population of all voters in the first place (a
much more difficult task, but well worth it).

</div>

</div>

<span id="07_466469-ch03.html"></span>

<div id="07_466469-ch03.html_x07_466469-ch03.html">

<div class="Basic-Text-Frame">

Chapter 3

Reviewing Confidence Intervals and Hypothesis Tests

In This Chapter

![arrow](9780470543887/images/arrow.png) Utilizing confidence intervals
to estimate parameters

![arrow](9780470543887/images/arrow.png) Testing models by using
hypothesis tests

![arrow](9780470543887/images/arrow.png) Finding the probability of
getting it right and getting it wrong

![arrow](9780470543887/images/arrow.png) Discovering power in a large
sample size

<span class="char-style-override-1">O</span>ne of the major goals in
statistics is to use the information you collect from a sample to get a
better idea of what’s going on in the entire population you’re studying
(because populations are generally large and exact info is often
unknown). Unknown values that summarize the population are called
<span class="zCheltItalic">population parameters.</span> Researchers
typically want to either get a handle on what those parameters are or
test a hypothesis about the population parameters.

In Stats I, you probably went over confidence intervals and hypothesis
tests for one and two population means and one and two population
proportions. Your instructor hopefully emphasized that no matter which
parameters you’re trying to estimate or test, the general process is the
same. If not, don’t worry; this chapter drives that point home.

This chapter reviews the basic concepts of confidence intervals and
hypothesis tests, including the probabilities of making errors by
chance. I also discuss how statisticians measure the ability of a
statistical procedure to do a good job — of detecting a real difference
in the populations, for example.

Estimating Parameters by Using Confidence Intervals

<span class="zCheltItalic">Confidence intervals</span> are a
statistician’s way of covering his you-know-what when it comes to
estimating a population parameter. For example, instead of just giving a
one-number guess as to what the average household income is in the
United States, a statistician gives a range of likely values for this
number. He does this because

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) All good statisticians know
sample results vary from sample to sample, so a one-number estimate
isn’t any good.

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) Statisticians have
developed some awfully nice formulas to give a range of likely values,
so why not use them?

In this section, you get the general formula for a confidence interval,
including the margin of error, and a good look at the common approach to
building confidence intervals. I also discuss interpretation and the
chance of making an error.

Getting the basics: The general form of a confidence interval

The big idea of a confidence interval is coming up with a range of
likely values for a population parameter. The
<span class="zCheltItalic">confidence level</span> represents the chance
that if you were to repeat your sample-taking over and over, you’d get a
range of likely values that actually contains the actual population
parameter. In other words, the confidence level is the long-term chance
of being correct.

![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png) The general
formula for a confidence interval is

Confidence interval = Sample statistic
<span class="zSymbolMedium">±</span> Margin of error

The confidence interval has a certain level of precision (measured by
the margin of error). Precision measures how close you expect your
results to be to the truth.

For example, suppose you want to know the average amount of time a
student at The Ohio State University spends listening to music on an MP3
player per day. The average time for the entire population of OSU
students who are MP3-player users is the parameter you’re looking for.
You take a random sample of 1,000 students and find that the average
time a student uses an MP3 player per day to listen to music is 2.5
hours, and the standard deviation is 0.5 hours. Is it right to say that
the population of all OSU-student, MP3-player owners use their players
an average of 2.5 hours per day for music listening? You hope and may
assume that the average for the whole population is close to 2.5, but it
probably isn’t exact.

What’s the solution to this problem? The solution is to not only report
the average from your sample but along with it report some measure of
how much you expect that sample average to vary from one sample to the
next, with a certain level of confidence. The number that you use to
represent this level of precision in your results is called the
<span class="zCheltItalic">margin of error.</span>

Finding the confidence interval for a population mean

The sample statistic part of the confidence-interval formula is fairly
straightforward.

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) <span class="zCheltBold">To
estimate the population mean,</span> you use the sample mean plus or
minus a margin of error, which is based on standard error. The sample
mean has a standard error of
![466469-eq0301.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0301_fmt.png). In
this formula, you can see the population standard deviation
<span class="zCheltItalic">(</span><span class="zSymbolMedium">σ</span><span class="zCheltItalic">)</span>
and the sample size <span class="zCheltItalic">(n)</span>.

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) <span class="zCheltBold">To
estimate the population proportion,</span> you use the sample proportion
plus or minus a margin of error.

In many cases, the standard deviation of the population,
<span class="zSymbolMedium">σ</span>, is not known. To estimate the
population mean by using a confidence interval when
<span class="zSymbolMedium">σ</span> is unknown, you use the formula
![466469-eq0302.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0302_fmt.png). This
formula contains the sample standard deviation
<span class="zCheltItalic">(s)</span>, the sample size
<span class="zCheltItalic">(n)</span>, and a
<span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-value representing how many standard
errors you want to add and subtract to get the confidence you need. To
get the margin of error for the mean, you see the standard error,
![466469-eq0303.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0303_fmt.png), is
being multiplied by a factor of <span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>.
Notice that <span class="zCheltItalic">t</span> has
<span class="zCheltItalic">n</span> – 1 as a subscript to indicate which
of the myriad <span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-distributions you use
for your confidence interval. The <span class="zCheltItalic">n</span> –
1 is called <span class="zCheltItalic">degrees of freedom.</span>

The value of <span class="zCheltItalic">t</span> in this case represents
the number of standard errors you add and subtract to or from the sample
mean to get the confidence you want. If you want to be 95 percent
confident, for example, you add and subtract 1.96 of those standard
errors. If you want to be 99.7 percent confident, you add or subtract
about three of them. (See Table A-1 in the appendix to find t-values for
various confidence levels; use
![466469-eq0313.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0313_fmt.png) for the
area to the right and find the t-value that goes with it.)

![tip.eps](9780470543887/images/tip_fmt.png) If you know the population
standard deviation, you should certainly use it. In that case, you use
the corresponding number from the
<span class="zCheltItalic">Z</span>-distribution (standard normal
distribution) in the confidence interval formula. (The
<span class="zCheltItalic">Z</span>-distribution from your Stats I
textbook can give you the numbers you need.) But I would be remiss in
saying that while textbooks and teachers always include problems where
<span class="zSymbolMedium">σ</span> is known, rarely is
<span class="zSymbolMedium">σ</span> known in the real world. Why teach
it this way? This issue is up for debate; for now just go with it, and I
can keep you posted.

For the MP3 player example from the preceding section, a random sample
of 1,000 all OSU students spends an average of 2.5 hours using their MP3
players to listen to music. The standard deviation is 0.5 hours.
Plugging this information into the formula for a confidence interval,
you get
![466469-eq0304.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0304_fmt.png). You
conclude that all OSU-student MP3-owners spend an average of between
2.47 and 2.53 hours listening to music on their players.

What changes the margin of error?

What do you need to know in order to come up with a margin of error?
Margin of error, in general, depends on three elements:

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) The standard deviation of
the population, <span class="zSymbolMedium">σ</span> (or an estimate of
it, denoted by <span class="zCheltItalic">s</span>, the sample standard
deviation)

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) The sample size,
<span class="zCheltItalic">n</span>

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) The level of confidence you
need

You can see these elements in action in the formula for margin of error
of the sample mean:
![466469-eq0305.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0305_fmt.png). Here I
assume that <span class="zSymbolMedium">σ</span> isn’t known;
<span class="zCheltItalic">tn</span> – 1 represents the value on the
<span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-distribution table (see Table A-1 in
the appendix) with <span class="zCheltItalic">n</span> – 1 degrees of
freedom.

Each of these three elements has a major role in determining how large
the margin of error will be when you estimate the mean of a population.
In the following sections, I show how each of the elements of the margin
of error formula work separately and together to affect the size of the
margin of error.

Population standard deviation

The standard deviation of the population is typically combined with the
sample size in the margin of error formula, with the population standard
deviation on top of the fraction and <span class="zCheltItalic">n</span>
on the bottom. (In this case, the standard error of the population,
<span class="zSymbolMedium">σ</span>, is estimated by the standard
deviation of the sample, <span class="zCheltItalic">s</span>, because
<span class="zSymbolMedium">σ</span> is typically unknown.)

This combination of standard deviation of the population and sample size
is known as the <span class="zCheltItalic">standard error</span> of your
statistic. It measures how much the sample statistic deviates from its
mean in the long term.

![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png) How does the
standard deviation of the population
(<span class="zSymbolMedium">σ</span>) affect margin of error? As it
gets larger, the margin of error increases, so your range of likely
values is wider.

Suppose you have two gas stations, one on a busy corner (gas station
\#1) and one farther off the main drag (gas station \#2). You want to
estimate the average time between customers at each station. At the busy
gas station \#1, customers are constantly using the gas pumps, so you
basically have no downtime between customers. At gas station \#2,
customers sometimes come all at once, and sometimes you don’t see a
single person for an hour or more. So the time between customers varies
quite a bit.

For which gas station would it be easier to estimate the overall average
time between customers as a whole? Gas station \#1 has much more
consistency, which represents a smaller standard deviation of time
between customers. Gas station \#2 has much more variability in time
between customers. That means <span class="zSymbolMedium">σ</span> for
gas station \#1 is smaller than <span class="zSymbolMedium">σ</span> for
gas station \#2. So the average time between customers is easier to
estimate at gas station \#1.

Sample size

Sample size affects margin of error in a very intuitive way. Suppose
you’re trying to estimate the average number of pets per household in
your city. Which sample size would give you better information: 10 homes
or 100 homes? I hope you’d agree that 100 homes would give more precise
information (as long as the data on those 100 homes was collected
properly).

If you have more data to base your conclusions on and that data is
collected properly, your results will be more precise. Precision is
measured by margin of error, so as the sample size increases, the margin
of error of your estimate goes down.

![warning_bomb.eps](9780470543887/images/warning_bomb_fmt.png) Bigger is
only better in terms of sample size if the data is collected properly —
that is, with minimal bias. If the quality of the data can’t be
maintained with a larger sample size, it does no good to have it.

Confidence level

For each problem at hand, you have to address how confident you need to
be in your results over the long term, and, of course, more confidence
comes with a price in the margin of error formula. This level of
confidence in your results over the long term is reflected in a number
called the <span class="zCheltItalic">confidence level,</span> which you
report as a percentage. In general, more confidence requires a wider
range of likely values. So, as the confidence level increases, so does
the margin of error.

![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png) Every margin of
error is interpreted as plus or minus a certain number of standard
errors. The number of standard errors added and subtracted is determined
by the confidence level. If you need more confidence, you add and
subtract more standard errors. If you need less confidence, you add and
subtract fewer standard errors. The number that represents how many
standard errors to add and subtract is different from situation to
situation. For one population mean, you use a value on the
<span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-distribution, represented by
<span class="zCheltItalic">tn</span> – 1, where
<span class="zCheltItalic">n</span> is the sample size (see Table A-1 in
the appendix).

Suppose you have a sample size of 20, and you want to estimate the mean
of a population with 90 percent confidence. The number of standard
errors you add and subtract is represented by
<span class="zCheltItalic">tn</span> – 1, which in this case is
<span class="zCheltItalic">t</span><span class="zSubscript">19</span> =
1.73. (To find these values of <span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>, see
Table A-1 in the appendix, with <span class="zCheltItalic">n</span> – 1
degrees of freedom for the row, and
![466469-eq0306.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0306_fmt.png) for the
column.)

Now suppose you want to be 95 percent confident in your results, with
the same sample size of <span class="zCheltItalic">n</span> = 20. The
degrees of freedom are 20 – 1 = 19 (row) and the column is for
![466469-eq0307.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0307_fmt.png). The
t-table gives you the value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">t</span><span class="zSubscript">19</span> =
2.09.

Notice that this value of <span class="zCheltItalic">t</span> is larger
than the value of <span class="zCheltItalic">t</span> for 90 percent
confidence, because in order to be more confident, you need to go out
more standard deviations on the
<span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-distribution table to cover more
possible results.

Large confidence, narrow intervals — just the right size

A narrow confidence interval is much more desirable than a wide one. For
example, claiming that the average cost of a new home is \$150,000 plus
or minus \$100,000 isn’t helpful at all because your estimate is
anywhere between \$50,000 and \$250,000. (Who has an extra \$100,000 to
throw around?) But you <span class="zCheltItalic">do</span> want a high
confidence level, so your statistician has to add and subtract more
standard errors to get there, which makes the interval that much wider
(a downer).

Wait, don’t panic — you can have your cake and eat it too! If you know
you want to have a high level of confidence but you don’t want a wide
confidence interval, just increase your sample size to meet that level
of confidence.

Suppose the standard deviation of the house prices from a previous study
is <span class="zCheltItalic">s</span> = \$15,000, and you want to be 95
percent confident in your estimate of average house price. Using a large
sample size, your value of <span class="zCheltItalic">t</span> (from
Table A-1 in the appendix) is 1.96.

With a sample of 100 homes, your margin of error is
![466469-eq0311.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0311_fmt.png).

If this is too large for you but you still want 95 percent confidence,
crank up your value of <span class="zCheltItalic">n</span>. If you
sample 500 homes, the margin of error decreases to
![466469-eq0312.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0312_fmt.png), which
brings you down to \$1,314.81.

![technicalstuff.eps](9780470543887/images/technicalstuff_fmt.png) You
can use a formula to find the sample size you need to meet a desired
margin of error. That formula is
![466469-eq0308.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0308_fmt.png), where
<span class="zCheltItalic">MOE</span> is the desired margin of error (as
a proportion), <span class="zCheltItalic">s</span> is the sample
standard deviation, and <span class="zCheltItalic">t</span> is the value
on the <span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-distribution that corresponds
with the confidence level you want. (For large sample sizes, the
t-distribution is approximately equal to the Z-distribution; you can use
the last line of Table A-1 in the appendix for the appropriate t-values,
or use a Z-table from your Stats I textbook.)

Interpreting a confidence interval

Interpreting a confidence interval involves a couple of subtle but
important issues. The big idea is that a
<span class="zCheltItalic">confidence interval</span> presents a range
of likely values for the population parameter, based on your sample.
However, you interpret it not in terms of your own sample, but in terms
of an infinite number of other samples out there that could have been
selected, yours just being one of them. For example, suppose 1,000
people each took a sample and they each formed a 95 percent confidence
interval for the mean. The “95 percent confidence” part means that of
those 1,000 confidence intervals, about 950 of them can be expected to
be correct on average. (Correct means the confidence interval actually
contains the true value of the parameter.)

![warning_bomb.eps](9780470543887/images/warning_bomb_fmt.png) A 95
percent confidence interval doesn’t mean that your particular confidence
interval has a 95 percent chance of capturing the actual value of the
parameter; after the sample has been taken, the parameter is either in
the interval or it isn’t. A confidence interval represents the chances
of capturing the actual value of the population parameter over many
different samples.

Suppose a polling organization wants to estimate the percentage of
people in the United States who drive a car with more than 100,000 miles
on it, and it wants to be 95 percent confident in its results. The
organization takes a random sample of 1,200 people and finds that 420 of
them (35 percent) drive a car with that minimum mileage; the margin of
error turns out to be plus or minus 3 percent. (See your Stats I text
for determining margin of error for percentages.)

The meaty part of the interpretation lies in the confidence level — in
this case, the 95 percent. Because the organization took a sample of
1,200 people in the U.S., asked each of them whether his or her car has
more than 100,000 miles on it, and made a confidence interval out of the
results, the polling organization is, in essence, accounting for all the
other samples out there that it could have gotten by building in the
margin of error (<span class="zSymbolMedium">±</span> 3 percent). The
organization wants to cover its bases on 95 percent of those other
situations, and <span class="zSymbolMedium">±</span> 3 percent satisfies
that.

Another way of thinking about the confidence interval is to say that if
the organization sampled 1,200 people over and over again and made a
confidence interval from its results each time, 95 percent of those
confidence intervals would be right. (You just have to hope that yours
is one of those right results.)

![tip.eps](9780470543887/images/tip_fmt.png) Using stat notation, you
can write confidence levels as (1 –
<span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span>)%. So if you want 95 percent
confidence, you write it as 1 – 0.05. Here,
<span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span> represents the chance that your
confidence interval is one of the wrong ones. This number,
<span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span>, is also related to the random
chance of making a certain kind of error with a hypothesis test, which I
explain in the later section “False alarms and missed opportunities:
Type I and II errors.”

What’s the Hype about Hypothesis Tests?

Suppose a shipping company claims that its packages are on time 92
percent of the time, or a campus official claims that 75 percent of
students live off campus. If you’re questioning these claims, how can
you use statistics to investigate?

In this section, you see the big ideas of hypothesis testing that are
the basis for the data-analysis techniques in this book. You review and
expand on the concepts involved in a hypothesis test, including the
hypotheses, the test statistic, and the
<span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-value.

What Ho and Ha really represent

You use a hypothesis test in situations where you have a certain model
in mind and want to see whether that model fits your data. Your model
may be one that just revolves around the population mean (testing
whether that mean is equal to ten, for example). Your model may be
testing the slope of a regression line (whether or not it’s zero, for
example, with zero meaning you find no relationship between
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> and
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>). You may be trying to use several
different variables to predict the marketability of a product, and you
believe a model using customer age, price, and shelf location can help
predict it, so you need to run one or more hypothesis tests to see
whether that model works. (This particular process is called multiple
regression, and you can find more info on it in Chapter 5.)

A hypothesis test is made up of two hypotheses:

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png)
<span class="zCheltBold">The null hypothesis, Ho:</span> Ho symbolizes
the current situation — the one that everyone assumed was true until you
got involved.

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png)
<span class="zCheltBold">The alternative hypothesis, Ha:</span> Ha
represents the alternative model that you want to consider. It stands
for the researcher’s hypothesis, and the burden of proof lies on the
researcher.

![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png) Ho is the model
that’s on trial. If you get enough evidence against it, you conclude Ha,
which is the model you’re claiming is the right one. If you don’t get
enough evidence against Ho, then you can’t say that your model (Ha) is
the right one.

Gathering your evidence into a test statistic

A <span class="zCheltItalic">test statistic</span> is the statistic from
your sample, standardized so you can look it up on a table, basically.
Although each hypothesis test is a little different, the main thought is
the same. Take your statistic and standardize it in the appropriate way
so you can use the corresponding table for it. Then look up your test
statistic on a table to see where it stands. That table may be the
<span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-table (Table A-1 in the appendix),
the Chi-square table (Table A-3 in the appendix), or a different table.
The type of test you need to use on your data dictates which table you
use.

In the case of testing a hypothesis for a population mean,
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span>, you use the sample mean,
![466469-eq0309.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0309_fmt.png), as
your statistic. To standardize it, you take
![466469-eq0309.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0309_fmt.png) and
convert it to a value of <span class="zCheltItalic">t</span> by using
the formula
![466469-eq0310.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0310_fmt.png), where
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span><span class="zSubscript">0</span> is
the value in Ho.

This value is your test statistic, which you compare to the
<span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-distribution.

Determining strength of evidence with a p-value

If you want to know whether your data has the brawn to stand up against
Ho, you need to figure out the <span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-value
and compare it to a predetermined cutoff,
<span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span> (typically 0.05). The
<span class="zCheltItalic">p-value</span> is a measure of the strength
of your evidence against Ho. You calculate the
<span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-value through these steps:

<span class="zCheltBold"> 1. Calculate the test statistic (refer to the
preceding section for more info on this).</span>

<span class="zCheltBold">2. Look up the test statistic on the
appropriate table (such as the
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">t</span><span class="zCheltBold">-table,
Table A-1 in the appendix).</span>

<span class="zCheltBold"> 3. Find the percentage of values on the table
that fall beyond your test statistic. This percentage is the
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">p</span><span class="zCheltBold">-value.</span>

<span class="zCheltBold"> 4. If your Ha is “not equal to,” double the
percentage that you got in step three because your test statistic could
have gone either way before the data was collected. (See your Stats I
textbook or <span class="zCheltBoldItalic">Statistics For Dummies</span>
for full details on obtaining p-values for hypothesis tests.)</span>

![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png) Your friend
<span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span> is the cutoff for your
<span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-value.
(<span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span> is typically set at 0.05, but
sometimes it’s 0.10.) If your <span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-value
is less than your predetermined value of
<span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span>, reject Ho because you have
sufficient evidence against it. If your
<span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-value is greater than or equal to
<span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span>, you can’t reject Ho.

For example, if your <span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-value is 0.002,
your test statistic is so far away from Ho that the chance of getting
this result by chance is only 2 out of 1,000. So, you conclude that Ho
is very likely to be false. If your
<span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-value turns out to be 0.30, this
same result is expected to happen 30 percent of the time anyway, so you
see no red flags there, and you can’t reject Ho. You don’t have enough
evidence against it. If your <span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-value
is close to the cutoff line, say <span class="zCheltItalic">p</span> =
0.049 or 0.51, you say the result is marginal and let the reader make
her own conclusions. That’s the main advantage of the
<span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-value: It lets other folks determine
whether your evidence is strong enough to reject Ho in their minds.

False alarms and missed opportunities: Type I and II errors

Any technique you use in statistics to make a conclusion about a
population based on a sample of data has the chance of making an error.
The errors I am talking about, Type I and Type II errors, are due to
random chance.

![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png) The way you set
up your test can help to reduce these kinds of errors, but they’re
always out there. As a data analyst, you need to know how to measure and
understand the impact of the errors that can occur with a hypothesis
test and what you can do to possibly make those errors smaller. In the
following sections, I show you how you can do just that.

Making false alarms with Type I errors

A <span class="zCheltItalic">Type I error</span> is the conditional
probability of rejecting Ho, given that Ho is true. I think of a Type I
error as a false alarm: You blew the whistle when you shouldn’t have.

The chance of making a Type I error is equal to
<span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span>, which is predetermined before you
begin collecting your data. This <span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span> is
the same <span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span> that represents the chance
of missing the boat in a confidence interval. It makes some sense that
these two probabilities are both equal because the probability of
rejecting Ho when you shouldn’t (a Type I error) is the same as the
chance that the true population parameter falls out of the range of
likely values when it shouldn’t. That chance is
<span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span>.

Suppose someone claims that the mean time to deliver packages for a
company is 3.0 days on average (so Ho is
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span> = 3.0), but you believe it’s not
equal to that (so Ha is <span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span>
<span class="zSymbolMedium">≠</span> 3.0). Your
<span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span> level is 0.05, and because you have
a two-sided test, you have 0.025 on each side. Your sample of 100
packages has a mean of 3.5 days with a standard deviation of 1.5 days.
The test statistic equals
![466469-eq0314.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0314_fmt.png), which
is greater than 1.96 (the value on the last row and the 0.025 column of
the <span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-distribution table — see Table
A-1 in the appendix). So 3.0 is not a likely value for the mean time of
delivery for all packages, and you reject Ho.

But suppose that just by chance, your sample contained some longer than
normal delivery times and that, in reality, the company’s claim is
right. You just made a Type I error. You made a false alarm about the
company’s claim.

![tip.eps](9780470543887/images/tip_fmt.png) To reduce the chance of a
Type I error, reduce your value of <span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span>.
However I don’t recommend reducing it too far. On the positive side,
this reduction makes it harder to reject Ho because you need more
evidence in your data to do so. On the negative side, by reducing your
chance of a false alarm (Type I error) you increase the chance of a
missed opportunity (a Type II error.)

Missing an opportunity with a Type II error

A <span class="zCheltItalic">Type II error</span> is the conditional
probability of not rejecting Ho, given that Ho is false. I call it a
missed opportunity because you were supposed to be able to find a
problem with Ho and reject it, but you didn’t. You didn’t blow the
whistle when you should have.

The chance of making a Type II error depends on a couple of things:

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png)
<span class="zCheltBold">Sample size:</span> If you have more data,
you’re less likely to miss something that’s going on. For example, if a
coin actually is unfair, flipping the coin only ten times may not reveal
the problem. But if you flip the coin 1,000 times, you have a good
chance of seeing a pattern that favors heads over tails, or vice versa.

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png)
<span class="zCheltBold">Actual value of the parameter:</span> A Type II
error is also related to how big the problem is that you’re trying to
uncover. For example, suppose a company claims that the average delivery
time for packages is 3.5 days. If the actual average delivery time is
5.0 days, you won’t have a very hard time detecting that with your
sample (even a small sample). But if the actual average delivery time is
4.0 days, you have to do more work to actually detect the problem.

![tip.eps](9780470543887/images/tip_fmt.png) To reduce the chance of a
Type II error, take a larger sample size. A greater sample size makes it
easier to reject Ho but increases the chance of a Type I error.

![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png) Type I and Type
II errors sit on opposite ends of a seesaw — as one goes up, the other
goes down. Try to meet in the middle by choosing a large sample size
(the bigger, the better; see Figures 3-1 and 3-2) and a small
<span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span> level (0.05 or less) for your
hypothesis test.

The power of a hypothesis test

Type II errors, which I explain in the preceding section, show the
downside of a hypothesis test. But statisticians, despite what many may
think, actually try to look on the bright side once in a while; so
instead of looking at the chance of
<span class="zCheltItalic">missing</span> a difference from Ho that
actually is there, they look at the chance of
<span class="zCheltItalic">detecting</span> a difference that really
<span class="zCheltItalic">is </span>there. This detection is called the
<span class="zCheltItalic">power of a hypothesis test.</span>

![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png) The power of a
hypothesis test is 1 – the probability of making a Type II error. So
<span class="zCheltItalic">power</span> is a number between 0 and 1 that
represents the chance that you rejected Ho when Ho was false. (You can
even sing about it: “If Ho is false and you know it, clap your hands. .
. .”) Remember that power (just like Type II errors) depends on two
elements: the sample size and the actual value of the parameter (see the
preceding section for a description of these elements).

In the following sections, you discover what power means in statistics
(not being one of the bigwigs, mind you); you also find out how to
quantify power by using a power curve.

Throwing a power curve

The specific calculations for the power of a hypothesis test are beyond
the scope of this book (so you can take a sigh of relief), but computer
programs and graphs are available online to show you what the power is
for different hypothesis tests and various sample sizes (just type
“power curve for the \[blah blah blah\] test” into an Internet search
engine).

These graphs are called <span class="zCheltItalic">power curves</span>
for a hypothesis test. A power curve is a special kind of graph that
gives you an idea of how much of a difference from Ho you can detect
with the sample size that you have. Because the precision of your test
statistic increases as your sample size increases, sample size is
directly related to power. But it also depends on how much of a
difference from Ho you’re trying to detect. For example, if a package
delivery company claims that its packages arrive in 2 days or less, do
you want to blow the whistle if it’s actually 2.1 days? Or wait until
it’s 3 days? You need a much larger sample size to detect the 2.1-days
situation versus the 3-days situation just because of the precision
level needed.

In Figure 3-1, you can see the power curve for a particular test of Ho:
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span> = 0 versus Ha:
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span> \> 0. You can assume that
<span class="zSymbolMedium">σ</span> (the standard deviation of the
population) is equal to 2 (I give you this value in each problem) and
doesn’t change. I set the sample size at 10 throughout.

The horizontal <span class="zCheltItalic">(x)</span> axis on the power
curve shows a range of actual values of
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span>. For example, you hypothesize that
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span> is equal to 0, but it may actually
be 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, or any other possible value. If
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span> equals 0, then Ho is true, and the
chance of detecting this (and therefore rejecting Ho) is equal to 0.05,
the set value of <span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span>. You work from
that baseline. (Notice the low power in this situation makes sense
because there’s nothing to detect for values of
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span> that are close to 0.) So, on the
graph in Figure 3-1, when <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> = 0, you
get a <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-value of 0.05.

<div class="story">

**Figure 3-1:** Power curve for Ho: <span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span>
= 0 versus Ha: <span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span> \> 0, for
<span class="zUnivItalic">n</span> = 10 and
<span class="zSymbolMedium">σ</span> = 2.

</div>

![466469-fg0301.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-fg0301_fmt.png)

Suppose that <span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span> is actually 0.5, not
0, as you hypothesized. A computer tells you that the chance of
rejecting Ho (what you’re supposed to do here) is 0.197 = 0.20, which is
the power. So, you have about a 20-percent chance of detecting this
difference with a sample size of 10. As you move to the right, away from
0 on the horizontal <span class="zCheltItalic">(x)</span> axis, you can
see that the power goes up and the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-values get closer and closer to 1.0.

For example, if the actual value of <span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span>
is 1.0, the difference from 0 is easier to detect than if it’s 0.50. In
fact, the power at 1.0 is equal to 0.475 = 0.48, so you have almost a 50
percent chance of catching the difference from Ho in this case. And as
the values of the mean increase, the power gets closer and closer to
1.0. Power never reaches 1.0 because statistics can never prove anything
with 100 percent accuracy, but you can get close to 1.0 if the actual
value is far enough from your hypothesis.

Controlling the sample size

How can you increase the power of your hypothesis test? You don’t have
any control over the actual value of the parameter, because that number
is unknown. So what do you have control over? The sample size. As the
sample size increases, it becomes easier to detect a real difference
from Ho.

Figure 3-2 shows the power curve with the same numbers as Figure 3-1,
except for the sample size <span class="zCheltItalic">(n)</span>, which
is 100 instead of 10. Notice that the curve increases much more quickly
and approaches 1.0 when the actual mean is 1.0, compared to your
hypothesis of 0. You want to see this kind of curve that moves up
quickly toward the value of 1.0, while the actual values of the
parameter increase on the <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>-axis.

<div class="story">

**Figure 3-2:** Power curve for Ho: <span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span>
= 0 versus Ha: <span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span> \> 0, for
<span class="zUnivItalic">n</span> = 100 and
<span class="zSymbolMedium">σ</span> = 2.

</div>

![466469-fg0302.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-fg0302_fmt.png)

If you compare the power of your test when
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span> is 1.0 for the
<span class="zCheltItalic">n</span> = 10 situation (in Figure 3-1)
versus the <span class="zCheltItalic">n</span> = 100 situation (in
Figure 3-2), you see that the power increases from 0.475 to more than
0.999. Table 3-1 shows the different values of power for the
<span class="zCheltItalic">n</span> = 10 case versus the
<span class="zCheltItalic">n</span> = 100 case, when you test Ho:
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span> = 0 versus Ha:
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span> \> 0, assuming a value of
<span class="zSymbolMedium">σ</span> = 2.

<table id="table-1" class="Dummies-Table">
<tbody>
<tr>
<td colspan="3" class="TB-Head"><p>Table 3-1 Comparing the Values of
Power for <span class="zUnivBoldItalic">n</span> = 10 Versus <span
class="zUnivBoldItalic">n</span> = 100 (Ho is <span
class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span> = 0)</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td class="TB-Col-Head"><p>Actual Value of <span
class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span></p></td>

</tr>
<tr>
<td class="TB-Body"><p>0.00</p></td>
<td class="TB-Body"><p>0.050 = 0.05</p></td>
<td class="TB-Body"><p>0.050 = 0.05</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td class="TB-Body"><p>0.50</p></td>
<td class="TB-Body"><p>0.197 = 0.20</p></td>
<td class="TB-Body"><p>0.804 = 0.81</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td class="TB-Body"><p>1.00</p></td>
<td class="TB-Body"><p>0.475 = 0.48</p></td>

</tr>
<tr>
<td class="TB-Body"><p>1.50</p></td>
<td class="TB-Body"><p>0.766 = 0.77</p></td>
<td class="TB-Body"><p>approx. 1.0</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td class="TB-Body"><p>2.00</p></td>
<td class="TB-Body"><p>0.935 = 0.94</p></td>
<td class="TB-Body"><p>approx. 1.0</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td class="TB-Body-Last"><p>3.00</p></td>

</table>

![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png) You can find
power curves for a variety of hypothesis tests under many different
scenarios. Each has the same general look and feel to it: starting at
the value of <span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span> when Ho is true,
increasing in an <span class="zCheltItalic">S</span>-shape as you move
from left to right on the <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>-axis, and
finally approaching the value of 1.0 at some point. Power curves with
large sample sizes approach 1.0 faster than power curves with low sample
sizes.

![warning_bomb.eps](9780470543887/images/warning_bomb_fmt.png) It’s
possible to have too much power. For example, if you make the power
curve for <span class="zCheltItalic">n</span> = 10,000 and compare it to
Figures 3-1 and 3-2, you find that it’s practically at 1.0 already for
any number other than 0.0 for the mean. In other words, the actual mean
could be 0.05 and with your hypothesis Ho:
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span> = 0.00, you would reject Ho because
of your huge sample size. Unless a researcher really wants to detect
very small differences from Ho (such as in medical studies or quality
control situations), inflated values of
<span class="zCheltItalic">n</span> are usually suspect. People
sometimes increase <span class="zCheltItalic">n</span> just to be able
to say they’ve found a difference, no matter how small, so watch for
that. If you zoom in enough, you can always detect something, even if
that something makes no practical difference. Beware of surveys and
experiments with an excessive sample size, such as one in the tens of
thousands. Their results are guaranteed to be inflated.

<div class="sidebar">

Power in manufacturing and medicine

The power of a test plays a role in the manufacturing process.
Manufacturers often have very strict specifications regarding the size,
weight, and/or quality of their products. During the manufacturing
process, manufacturers want to be able to detect deviations from these
specifications, even small ones, so they must determine how much of a
difference from Ho they want to detect, and then figure out the sample
size needed in order to detect that difference when it appears. For
example, if the candy bar is supposed to weigh 2.0 ounces, the
manufacturer may want to blow the whistle if the actual average weight
shifts to 2.2 ounces. Statisticians can work backward in calculating the
power and find the sample size they need to know to stop the process.

Medical scientists also think about power when they set up their studies
(called <span class="zUnivItalic">clinical trials</span>). Suppose
they’re checking to see whether an antidepressant adversely affects
blood pressure (as a side effect of taking the drug). Scientists need to
be able to detect small differences in blood pressure, because for some
patients, any change in blood pressure is important to note and treat.

</div>

</div>

</div>

<span id="08_466469-pp02.html"></span>

<div id="08_466469-pp02.html_x08_466469-pp02.html">

<div class="story">

Part II

Using Different Types of Regression to Make Predictions

<div class="image">

![466469-pp0201.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-pp0201_fmt.png)

</div>

In this part . . .

<span class="char-style-override-1">T</span>his part takes you beyond
using one variable to predict another variable using a straight line
(that’s what simple linear regression is about). Instead, you find ways
to predict one variable using many, and you also discover ways to make
predictions using curves. Finally, you make predictions for
probabilities, not just average values. It’s a one-stop-shopping place
for all things regression. Because these methods allow you to solve more
complex problems, they lend themselves nicely to many real-world
applications.

</div>

</div>

<span id="09_466469-ch04.html"></span>

<div id="09_466469-ch04.html_x09_466469-ch04.html">

<div class="Basic-Text-Frame">

Chapter 4

Getting in Line with Simple Linear Regression

In This Chapter

![arrow](9780470543887/images/arrow.png) Using scatterplots and
correlation coefficients to examine relationships

![arrow](9780470543887/images/arrow.png) Building a simple linear
regression model to estimate <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> from
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>

![arrow](9780470543887/images/arrow.png) Testing how well the model fits

![arrow](9780470543887/images/arrow.png) Interpreting the results and
making good predictions

<span class="char-style-override-1">L</span>ooking for relationships and
making predictions is one of the staples of data analysis. Everyone
wants to answer questions like, “Can I predict how many units I’ll sell
if I spend <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> amount of advertising
dollars?”; or “Does drinking more diet cola really relate to more weight
gain?”; or “Do children’s backpacks seem to get heavier with each year
of school, or is it just me?”

<span class="zCheltItalic">Linear regression</span> tries to find
relationships between two or more variables and comes up with a model
that tries to describe that relationship, much like the way the line
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> =
2<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> + 3 explains the relationship
between <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> and
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>. But unlike in math, where functions
like <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> =
2<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> + 3 tell the entire story about the
two variables, in statistics things don’t come out that perfectly; some
variability and error is involved (that’s what makes it fun!).

This chapter is partly a review of the concepts of simple linear
regression presented in a typical Stats I textbook. But the fun doesn’t
stop there. I expand on the ideas about regression that you picked up in
your Stats I course and set you up for some of the other types of
regression models you see in Chapters 5 through 8.

In this chapter, you see how to build a simple linear regression model
that examines the relationship between two variables. You also see how
simple linear regression works from a model-building standpoint.

Exploring Relationships with Scatterplots and Correlations

Before looking ahead to predicting a value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> from
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> using a line, you need to

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) Establish that you have a
legitimate reason to do so by using a straight line.

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) Feel confident that using a
line to make that prediction will actually work well.

In order to accomplish both of these important steps, you need to first
plot the data in a pairwise fashion so you can visually look for a
relationship; then you need to somehow quantify that relationship in
terms of how well those points follow a line. In this section, you do
just that, using scatterplots and correlations.

Here’s a perfect example of a situation where simple linear regression
is useful: In 2004, the California State Board of Education wrote a
report entitled “Textbook Weight in California: Analysis and
Recommendations.” This report discussed the great concern over the
weight of the textbooks in students’ backpacks and the problems it
presents for students. The board conducted a study where it weighed a
variety of textbooks from each of four core areas studied in grades 1–12
(reading, math, science, and history — where’s statistics?) over a range
of textbook brands and found the average total weight for all four books
for each grade.

The board consulted pediatricians and chiropractors, who recommended
that the weight of a student’s backpack should not exceed 15 percent of
his or her body weight. From there, the board hypothesized that the
total weight of the textbooks in these four areas increases for each
grade level and wanted to see whether it could find a relationship
between the average child’s weight in each grade and the average weight
of his or her books. So along with the average weight of the four
core-area textbooks for each grade, researchers also recorded the
average weight for the students in that grade. The results are shown in
Table 4-1.

In this section, you begin exploring whether or not a relationship
exists between these two quantitative variables. You start by displaying
the pairs of data using a two-dimensional scatterplot to look for a
possible pattern, and you quantify the strength and direction of that
pattern using the correlation coefficient.

Using scatterplots to explore relationships

In order to explore a possible relationship between two variables, such
as textbook weight and student weight, you first plot the data in a
special graph called a <span class="zCheltItalic">scatterplot.</span> A
scatterplot is a two-dimensional graph that displays pairs of data, one
pair per observation in the <span class="zCheltItalic">(x, y)</span>
format. Figure 4-1 shows a scatterplot of the textbook-weight data from
Table 4-1.

You can see that the relationship appears to follow the straight line
that’s included on the graph, except possibly for the last point, where
textbook weight is 16.06 pounds and student weight is 142 pounds (for
grade 12). This point appears to be an
<span class="zCheltItalic">outlier</span> — it’s the only point that
doesn’t fall into the pattern. So overall, an uphill, or
<span class="zCheltItalic">positive</span> linear relationship appears
to exist between textbook weight and student weight; as student weight
increases, so does textbook weight.

<div class="story">

**Figure 4-1:** Scatterplot of average student weight versus average
textbook weight in grades 1–12.

</div>

![466469-fg0401.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-fg0401_fmt.png)

![computeroutput.eps](9780470543887/images/computeroutput_fmt.png) To
make a scatterplot in Minitab, enter the data in columns one and two of
the spreadsheet. Go to Graphs\>Scatterplot. Click Simple and then OK.
Highlight the response variable <span class="zCheltItalic">(y)</span> in
the left-hand box, and click Select. This variable shows up as the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> variable in the scatterplot. Click
on the explanatory <span class="zCheltItalic">(x)</span> variable in the
left-hand box, and click Select. It shows up in the
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variable box. Click OK, and you get
the scatterplot.

Collating the information by using the correlation coefficient

After you’ve displayed the data using a scatterplot (see the preceding
section), the next step is to find a statistic that quantifies the
relationship somehow. The <span class="zCheltItalic">correlation
coefficient</span> (also known as <span class="zCheltItalic">Pearson’s
correlation coefficient,</span> especially in statistical software
packages) measures the strength and direction of the linear relationship
between two quantitative variables <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>
and <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>. It’s a number between –1 and +1
that’s <span class="zCheltItalic">unit-free,</span> which means that if
you change from pounds to ounces, the correlation coefficient doesn’t
change. (What a messed-up world it would be if this wasn’t the case!)

If the relationship between <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> and
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> is uphill, or positive (as
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> increases, so does
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>), the correlation is a positive
number. If the relationship is downhill, or negative (as
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> increases,
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> gets smaller), then the correlation
is negative. The following list translates different correlation values:

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) <span class="zCheltBold">A
correlation value of zero means that you can find no linear relationship
between
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">x</span><span class="zCheltBold">
and
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">y</span><span class="zCheltBold">.</span>
(It may be that a different relationship exists, such as a curve; see
Chapter 7 for more on this.)

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) <span class="zCheltBold">A
correlation value of +1 or –1 indicates that the points fall in a
perfect, straight line.</span> (Negative values indicate a downhill
relationship; positive values indicate an uphill relationship.)

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) <span class="zCheltBold">A
correlation value close to +1 or –1 signifies a strong
relationship.</span> A general rule of thumb is that correlations close
to or beyond 0.7 or –0.7 are considered to be strong.

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) <span class="zCheltBold">A
correlation closer to +0.5 or –0.5 shows a moderate relationship.</span>

You can calculate the correlation coefficient by using a formula
involving the standard deviation of <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>,
the standard deviation of <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>, and the
covariance of <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> and
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>, which measures how
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> and
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> move together in relation to their
means. However, the formula isn’t the focus here (you can find it in
your Stats I textbook or in my other book,
<span class="zCheltItalic">Statistics For Dummies,</span> published by
Wiley); it’s the concept that’s important. Any computer package can
calculate the correlation coefficient for you with a simple click of the
mouse.

![computeroutput.eps](9780470543887/images/computeroutput_fmt.png) To
have Minitab calculate a correlation for you, go to Stat\>Basic
Statistics\>Correlation. Highlight the variables you want correlations
for, and click Select. Then click OK.

The correlation for the textbook-weight example is (can you guess before
looking at it?) 0.926, which is very close to 1.0. This correlation
means that a very strong linear relationship is present between average
textbook weight and average student weight for grades 1–12, and that
relationship is positive and linear (it follows a straight line). This
correlation is confirmed by the scatterplot shown in Figure 4-1.

![warning_bomb.eps](9780470543887/images/warning_bomb_fmt.png) Data
analysts should never make any conclusions about a relationship between
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> and
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> based solely on either the
correlation or the scatterplot alone; the two elements need to be
examined together. It’s possible (but of course not a good idea) to
manipulate graphs to look better or worse than they really are just by
changing the scales on the axes. Because of this, statisticians never go
with the scatterplot alone to determine whether or not a linear
relationship exists between <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> and
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>. A correlation without a scatterplot
is dangerous, too, because the relationship between
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> and
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> may be very strong but just not
linear.

Building a Simple Linear Regression Model

After you have a handle on which <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>
variables may be related to <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> in a
linear way, you go about the business of finding that straight line that
best fits the data. You find the slope and
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept, put them together to make
a line, and you use the equation of that line to make predictions for
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>. All this is part of building a
simple linear regression model.

In this section, you set the foundation for regression models in general
(including those you can find in Chapters 5 through 8). You plot the
data, come up with a model that you think makes sense, assess how well
it fits, and use it to guesstimate the value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> given another variable,
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>.

Finding the best-fitting line to model your data

After you’ve established that <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> and
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> have a strong linear relationship,
as evidenced by both the scatterplot and the correlation coefficient
(close to or beyond 0.7 and –0.7; see the previous sections), you’re
ready to build a model that estimates
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> using
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>. In the textbook-weight case, you
want to estimate average textbook weight using average student weight.

The most basic of all the regression models in the simple linear
regression model that comes in the general form of
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> = α +
β<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> + ε. Here, α represents the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept of the line, β represents
the slope, and ε represents the error in the model due to chance.

![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png) A straight line
that’s used in simple linear regression is just one of an entire family
of models (or functions) that statisticians use to express relationships
between variables. A <span class="zCheltItalic">model</span> is just a
general name for a function that you can use to describe what outcome
will occur based on some given information about one or more related
variables.

Note that you will never know the true model that describes the
relationship perfectly. The best you can do is estimate it based on
data.

To find the right model for your data, the idea is to scour all possible
lines and choose the one that fits the data best. Thankfully, you have
an algorithm that does this for you (computers use it in their
calculations). Formulas also exist for finding the slope and
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept of the best-fitting line
by hand. The best-fitting line based on your data is
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> =
<span class="zCheltItalic">a</span> +
<span class="zCheltItalic">bx,</span> where
<span class="zCheltItalic">a</span> estimates α and
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span> estimates β from the true model.
(You can find those formulas in your Stats I text or in
<span class="zCheltItalic">Statistics For Dummies.</span>)

![computeroutput.eps](9780470543887/images/computeroutput_fmt.png) To
run a linear regression analysis in Minitab, go to
Stat\>Regression\>Regression. Highlight the response
<span class="zCheltItalic">(y)</span> variable in the left-hand box, and
click Select. The variable shows up in the Response Variable box. Then
highlight your explanatory <span class="zCheltItalic">(x)</span>
variable, and click Select. This variable shows up in the Predictor
Variable box. Click OK.

The equation of the line that best describes the relationship between
average textbook weight and average student weight is
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> = 3.69 +
0.113<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>, where
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> is the average student weight for
that grade, and <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> is the average
textbook weight. Figure 4-2 shows the Minitab output of this analysis.

<div class="story">

**Figure 4-2:** Simple linear regression analysis for the
textbook-weight example.

</div>

![466469-fg0402.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-fg0402_fmt.png)

![technicalstuff.eps](9780470543887/images/technicalstuff_fmt.png) By
writing <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> = 3.69 +
0.113<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>, you mean that this equation
represents your estimated value of <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>,
given the value of <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> that you observe
with your data. Statisticians technically write this equation by using a
caret (or <span class="zCheltItalic">hat</span> as statisticians call
it), like ŷ, so everyone can know it’s an estimate, not the actual value
of <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>. This
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-hat is your estimate of the average
value of <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> over the long term, based
on the observed values of <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>. However,
in many Stats I texts, the hat is left off because statisticians have an
unwritten understanding as to what <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>
represents. This issue comes up again in Chapters 5 through 8. (By the
way, if you think <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-hat is a funny
term here, it’s even funnier in Mexico, where statisticians call it
<span class="zCheltItalic">y-sombrero</span> — no kidding!)

The y-intercept of the regression line

Selected parts of that Minitab output shown in Figure 4-2 are of
importance to you at this point. First, you can see that under the Coef
column you have the numerical values on the right side of the equation
of the line — in other words, the slope and
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept. The number 3.69
represents the coefficient of “Constant,” which is a fancy way of saying
that’s the <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept (because the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept is just a constant — it
never changes). The <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept is the
point where the line crosses the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-axis; in other words, it’s the value
of <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> when
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> equals zero.

![tip.eps](9780470543887/images/tip_fmt.png) The
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept of a regression line may
or may not have a practical meaning depending on the situation. To
determine whether the <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept of a
regression line has practical meaning, look at the following:

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) Does the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept fall within the actual
values in the data set? If yes, it has practical meaning.

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) Does the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept fall into negative
territory where negative <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-values
aren’t possible? For example, if the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-values are weights, they can’t be
negative. Then the <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept has no
practical meaning. The <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept is
still needed in the equation though, because it just happens to be the
place where the line, if extended to the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-axis, crosses the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-axis.

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) Does the value
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> = 0 have practical meaning? For
example, if <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> is tem-perature at a
football game in Green Bay, then <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> = 0
is a value that’s relevant to examine. If
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> = 0 has practical meaning, then the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept does too, because it
represents the value of <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> when
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> = 0. If the value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> = 0 doesn’t have practical meaning
in its own right (such as when <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>
represents height of a toddler), then the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept doesn’t either.

In the textbook example, the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept doesn’t really have a
practical meaning because students don’t weigh zero pounds, so you don’t
really care what the estimated textbook weight is for that situation.
But you do need to find a line that fits the data you do have (where
average student weights go from 48.5 to 142 pounds). That best-fitting
line must include a <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept, and
for this problem, that <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept
happens to be 3.69 pounds.

The slope of the regression line

The value 0.113 from Figure 4-2 indicates the coefficient (or number in
front) of the student-weight variable. This number is also known as the
<span class="zCheltItalic">slope.</span> It represents the change in
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> (textbook weight) is associated with
a one-unit increase in <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> (student
weight). As student weight increases by 1 pound, textbook weight
increases by about 0.113 pounds, on average. To make this relationship
more meaningful, you can multiply both quantities by 10 to say that as
student weight increases by 10 pounds, the textbook weight goes up by
about 1.13 pounds on average.

![tip.eps](9780470543887/images/tip_fmt.png) Whenever you get a number
for the slope, take that number and put it over 1 to help you get
started on a proper interpretation of slope. For example, a slope of
0.113 is rewritten as
![466469-eq0411.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0411_fmt.png). Using
the idea that slope equals rise over run, or change in
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> over change in
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>, you can interpret the value of
0.113 in the following way: As <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>
increases on average by 1 pound, <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>
increases by 0.113 pounds.

Making point estimates by using the regression line

When you have a line that estimates <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>
given <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>, you can use it to give a
one-number estimate for the (average) value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> for a given value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>. This is called making a
<span class="zCheltItalic">point estimate.</span> The basic idea is to
take a reasonable value of <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>, plug it
into the equation of the regression line, and see what you get for the
value of <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>.

In the textbook-weight example, the best-fitting line (or model) is the
line <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> = 3.69 +
0.113<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>. For an average student who
weighs 60 pounds, for example, a one-number point estimate of the
average textbook weight is 3.69 + (0.113
<span class="Times-Sign">\*</span> 60) = 10.47 pounds (those poor little
kids!). If the average student weighs 100 pounds, the estimated average
textbook weight is 3.69 + (0.113 <span class="Times-Sign">\*</span> 100)
= 14.99, or nearly 15 pounds, plus or minus something. (You find out
what that something is in the following section.)

No Conclusion Left Behind: Tests and Confidence Intervals for Regression

After you have the slope of the best-fitting regression line for your
data (see the previous sections), you need to step back and take into
account the fact that sample results will vary. You shouldn’t just say,
“Okay, the slope of this line is 2. I’m done!” It won’t be exactly 2 the
next time. This variability is why statistics professors harp on adding
a margin of error to your sample results; you want to be sure to cover
yourself by adding that plus or minus.

In hypothesis testing, you don’t just compare your sample mean to the
population mean and say, “Yep, they’re different alright!” You have to
standardize your sample result using the standard error so that you can
put your results in the proper perspective (see Chapter 3 for a review
of confidence intervals and hypothesis tests).

The same idea applies here with regression. The data were used to figure
out the best-fitting line, and you know it fits well for that data.
That’s not to say that the best-fitting line will work perfectly well
for a new data set taken from the same population. So, in regression,
all your results should involve the standard error with them in order to
allow for the fact that sample results vary. That goes for estimating
and testing for the slope and
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept and for any predictions
that you make.

Many times in Stats I courses the concept of margin of error is skipped
over after the best-fitting regression line is found, But these are very
important ideas and should always be included. (Okay, enough of the soap
box for now. Let’s get out there and do it!)

Scrutinizing the slope

Recall the <span class="zCheltItalic">slope</span> of the regression
line is the amount by which you expect the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> variable to change on average as the
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variable increases by 1 unit — the
old rise-over-run idea (see the section “The slope of the regression
line” earlier in this chapter). Now, how do you deal with knowing the
best-fitting line will change with a new data set? You just apply the
basic ideas of confidence intervals and hypothesis tests (see Chapter
3).

A confidence interval for slope

A <span class="zCheltItalic">confidence interval</span> in general has
this form: your statistic plus or minus a margin of error. The margin of
error includes a certain number of standard deviations (or standard
errors) from your statistic. How many standard errors you add and
subtract depends on what confidence level, 1 –
<span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span>, you want. The size of the standard
error depends on the sample size and other factors.

The equation of the best-fitting simple linear regression line,
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> =
<span class="zCheltItalic">a</span> +
<span class="zCheltItalic">bx,</span> includes a slope
<span class="zCheltItalic">(b)</span> and a
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept
<span class="zCheltItalic">(a)</span>. Because these were found using
the data, they’re only estimates of what’s going on in the population,
and therefore they need to be accompanied by a margin of error.

The formula for a 1 – <span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span> level
confidence interval for the slope of a regression line is
![466469-eq0401.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0401_fmt.png), where
the standard error is denoted
![466469-eq0402.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0402_fmt.png). The
value of <span class="zCheltItalic">t\*</span> comes from the
<span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-distribution with
<span class="zCheltItalic">n</span> – 2 degrees of freedom and area to
its right equal to <span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span> ÷ 2. (See
Chapter 3 regarding the concept of
<span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span>.)

![technicalstuff.eps](9780470543887/images/technicalstuff_fmt.png) In
case you wonder why you see <span class="zCheltItalic">n</span> – 2
degrees of freedom here, as opposed to
<span class="zCheltItalic">n</span> – 1 degrees of freedom used in
<span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-tests for the population mean in
Stats I, here’s the scoop. From Stats I you know that a
<span class="zCheltItalic">parameter</span> is a number that describes
the population; it’s usually known, and it can change from scenario to
scenario. For each parameter in a model, you lose 1 degree of freedom.
The regression line contains two parameters — the slope and the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept — and you lose 1 degree of
freedom for each one. With the <span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-test
from Stats I you only have one parameter, the population mean, to worry
about, hence you use <span class="zCheltItalic">n</span> – 1 degrees of
freedom.

![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png) You can find the
value of <span class="zCheltItalic">t\*</span> in any
<span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-distribution table (check your
textbook for one). For example, suppose you want to find a 95 percent
confidence interval based on sample size
<span class="zCheltItalic">n</span> = 10. The value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">t\*</span> is found in Table A-1 in the
appendix in the row marked 10 – 2 = 8 degrees of freedom, and the column
marked 0.025 (because <span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span> ÷ 2 = 0.05 ÷
2 = 0.025). This value of <span class="zCheltItalic">t\*</span> is
2.306. (<span class="zCheltItalic">Statistics For Dummies</span> can
tell you a lot more about the
<span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-distribution and the
<span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-table.)

To put together a 95 percent confidence interval for the slope using
computer output, you pull off the pieces that you need. For the
textbook-weight example, in Figure 4-2 you see that the slope is equal
to 0.11337. (Recall that slope is the coefficient of the
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variable in the equation, which is
why you see the abbreviation Coef in the output.)

Because the slope changes from sample to sample, it’s a random variable
with its own distribution, its own mean, and its own standard error.
(Recall from Stats I the standard error of a statistic is likened to the
standard deviation of a random variable.) If you look just to the right
of the slope in Figure 4-2, you see SE Coef; this stands for the
standard error of the slope (which is 0.01456 in this case.)

Now all you need is the value of <span class="zCheltItalic">t\*</span>
from the <span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-table (Table A-1 in the
appendix). Because <span class="zCheltItalic">n</span> = 12, you look in
the row where degrees of freedom is 12 – 2 = 10. You want a 95 percent
confidence interval, so you look in the column for (1 – 0.95) ÷ 2 =
0.25. The <span class="zCheltItalic">t\*</span> value you get is 2.228.

Putting these pieces together, a 95 percent confidence interval for the
slope of the best-fitting regression line for the textbook-weight
example is 0.11337 <span class="zSymbolMedium">± </span>2.228
<span class="Times-Sign">\*</span> 0.01456 which goes from 0.0809 to
0.1458. The units are in pounds (textbook) per pounds (child weight).
Note this interval is large due to the small sample size, which
increases the standard error.

A hypothesis test for slope

You may be interested in conducting a hypothesis test for the slope of a
regression line as another way to assess how well the line fits. If the
slope is zero or close to it, the regression line is basically flat,
signifying that no matter the value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>, you’ll always estimate
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> by using its mean. This means that
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> and
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> aren’t related at all, so a specific
value of <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> doesn’t help you predict a
specific value for <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>. You can also
test to see if the slope is some value other than zero, but that’s
atypical. So for all intents and purposes, I use the hypotheses Ho:
<span class="zSymbolMedium">β</span> = 0 versus Ha:
<span class="zSymbolMedium">β</span> ≠ 0, where
<span class="zSymbolMedium">β</span> is the slope of the true model.

To conduct a hypothesis test for the slope of a simple linear regression
line, you follow the basic steps of any hypothesis test. You take the
statistic <span class="zCheltItalic">(b)</span> from your data, subtract
the value in Ho (in this case it’s zero), and standardize it by dividing
by the standard error (see Chapter 3 for more on this process).

Using the formula for standard error for
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span>, the test statistic for the
hypothesis test of whether or not the slope equals zero is
![466469-eq0403.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0403_fmt.png), where
![466469-eq0404.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0404_fmt.png). On the
Minitab output from Figure 4-2, the test statistic is located right next
to the SE Coef column; it’s cleverly marked T. In this case T = 7.78.
Compare this value to <span class="zCheltItalic">t\*</span> = 2.228 from
the t-table. Because T \> <span class="zCheltItalic">t\*</span>, you
have strong evidence to reject Ho and conclude that the slope of the
regression line for the textbook-weight data is not zero. (In fact, it
has to be greater than that, according to your data.)

You can also just find the exact
<span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-value on the output, right next to
the T column, in the column is marked P. The
<span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-value for the test for slope in this
case is 0.000, which means it’s less than 0.001. You conclude that the
slope of this line is not zero, so textbook weight is significantly
related to student weight. (See Chapter 3 to brush up on
<span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-values.)

![technicalstuff.eps](9780470543887/images/technicalstuff_fmt.png) To
test to see whether the slope is some value other than zero, just plug
that value in for
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">0</span> in
the formula for the test statistic. Also, you may conduct one-sided
hypothesis tests to see whether the slope is strictly greater than zero
or strictly less than zero. In those cases, you find the same test
statistic but compare it to the value
<span class="zCheltItalic">t\*</span> where the area to the right (or
left, respectively) is <span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span>.

Inspecting the y-intercept

The <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept is the place where the
regression line <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> =
<span class="zCheltItalic">a</span> +
<span class="zCheltItalic">bx</span> crosses the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-axis and is denoted by
<span class="zCheltItalic">a</span> (see the earlier section “The
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept of the regression line”).
Sometimes the <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept can be
interpreted in a meaningful way, and sometimes not. This differs from
slope, which is always interpretable. In fact, between the two elements
of slope and intercept, the slope is the star of the show, with the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y-</span>intercept serving as the somewhat
less famous but still noticeable sidekick.

There are times when the <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept
makes no sense. For example, suppose you use rain to predict bushels per
acre of corn; if you have zero rain, you have zero corn, but if the
