regression line crosses the <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-axis
somewhere else besides zero (and it most likely will), the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept will make no sense.
Another situation is where no data were collected near the value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> = 0; interpreting the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept at that point is not
appropriate. For example, using a student’s score on midterm 1 to
predict her score on midterm 2, unless the student didn’t take the exam
at all (in which case it doesn’t count), she’ll get at least some
points.

Many times, however, the <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept
is of interest to you and has a value that you can interpret, such as
when you’re talking about predicting coffee sales using temperature for
football games. Some games get cold enough to have zero and subzero
temperatures (like Packers games for example — Go Pack Go!).

Suppose I collect data on ten of my students who recorded their study
time (in minutes) for a 10-point quiz, along with their quiz scores. The
data have a strong linear relationship by all the methods used in this
chapter (for example, refer to the earlier section “Exploring
Relationships with Scatterplots and Correlations”). I went ahead and
conducted a regression analysis, and the results are shown in Figure
4-3.

Because there are students who (heaven forbid!) didn’t study at all for
the quiz, the <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept of 3.29
points (where study time <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> = 0) can be
interpreted safely. Its value is shown in the Coef column in the row
marked Constant (see the section “The
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept of the regression line”
for more information). The next step is to give a confidence interval
for the <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept of the regression
line, where you can take conclusions beyond just this sample of ten
students.

The formula for a 1 – <span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span> level
confidence interval for the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept
<span class="zCheltItalic">(a)</span> of a simple linear regression line
is ![466469-eq0405.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0405_fmt.png). The
standard error, SE<span class="zSubscript">a</span>, is equal to
![466469-eq0406.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0406_fmt.png), where
again the value of <span class="zCheltItalic">t\*</span> comes from the
<span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-distribution with
<span class="zCheltItalic">n</span> – 2 degrees of freedom whose area to
the right is equal to <span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span> ÷ 2. Using
the output from Figure 4-3 and the
<span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-table, I’m 95 percent confident that
the quiz score <span class="zCheltItalic">(y)</span> for someone with a
study time of <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> = 0 minutes is 3.29
<span class="zSymbolMedium">± </span>2.306
<span class="Times-Sign">\*</span> 0.4864, which is anywhere from 2.17
to 4.41, on average. Note that 2.306 comes from the t-table with 10 – 2
= 8 degrees of freedom and 0.4864 is the SE for the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept from Figure 4-3. (So
studying for zero minutes for my quiz is not something to aspire to.)

By the way, to find out how much time studying affected the quiz score
for these students, you can get an estimate of the slope on the output
from Figure 4-3 that the coefficient for slope is 0.1793, which says
each minute of studying is related to an increase in score of 0.1793 of
a point, plus or minus the margin of error, of course. Or, 10 more
minutes relates to 1.793 more points. On a 10-point quiz, it all adds
up!

<div class="story">

**Figure 4-3:** Regression analysis for study time and quiz score data.

</div>

![466469-fg0403.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-fg0403_fmt.png)

![technicalstuff.eps](9780470543887/images/technicalstuff_fmt.png)
Testing a hypothesis about the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept isn’t really something
you’ll find yourself doing much because most of the time you don’t have
a preconceived notion about what the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept would be (nor do you
really care ahead of time). The confidence interval is much more useful.
However, if you do need to conduct a hypothesis test for the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept, you take your
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept, subtract the value in Ho,
and divide by the standard error, found on the computer output in the
row for Constant and the column for SE Coef. (The default value is to
test to see whether the <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept is
zero.) The test is in the T column of the output, and its
<span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-value is shown in the P column. In
the study time and quiz score example, the
<span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-value is 0.000, so the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept is significantly different
from zero. All this means is that the line crosses the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-axis somewhere else.

Building confidence intervals for the average response

When you have the slope and
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept for the best-fitting
regression line, you put them together to get the line
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> =
<span class="zCheltItalic">a</span> +
<span class="zCheltItalic">bx</span>. The value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> here really represents the average
value of <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> for a particular value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>. For example, in the textbook-weight
data, Figure 4-2 shows the regression line
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> = 3.69 +
0.11337<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> where
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> = average student weight and
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> = average textbook weight. If you
put in 100 pounds for <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>, you get
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> = 3.69 + 0.1137
<span class="Times-Sign">\*</span> 100 = 15.02 pounds of textbook weight
for the group averaging 100 pounds. This number, 15.02, is an estimate
of the average weight of textbooks for children of this weight.

But you can’t stop there. Because you’re getting an estimate of the
average textbook weight using <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>, you
also need a margin of error for <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> to
go with it, to create a confidence interval for the average
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> at a given
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> that generalizes to the population.

Take your estimate, <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>, which you get
by plugging your given <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> value into
the regression line, and then add and subtract the margin of error for
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>. The formula for a 1 –
<span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span> confidence interval for the mean of
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> for a given value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> (call it
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>\*) is equal to
![466469-eq0407.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0407_fmt.png), where
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> is the value of the equation of the
line when you plug in <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>\* for
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>. The standard error for
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> is equal to
![466469-eq0408.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0408_fmt.png).
Luckily Minitab does these calculations for you and reports a confidence
interval for the mean of <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> for a given
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>\*.

![computeroutput.eps](9780470543887/images/computeroutput_fmt.png) To
find a confidence interval for the mean value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> using Minitab, you ask for a
regression analysis (see instructions in the earlier section “Finding
the best-fitting line to model your data”) and click on Options. You see
a box called Prediction Intervals for New Observations; enter the value
of <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>\* that you want, and just below
that, put in your confidence level (the default is 95 percent). Even
though this box is labeled Prediction Intervals, it finds both a
confidence interval and a prediction interval for you as well.
(Prediction intervals are different from confidence intervals, and I
discuss them in the next section.) On the computer output, the
confidence interval is labeled 95% CI.

Returning to the textbook-weight example, the computer output for
finding a 95 percent confidence interval for the average textbook weight
for 100-pound children is shown in Figure 4-4. The result is (14.015,
16.048) pounds. I’m 95 percent confident that the average textbook
weight for the group of children averaging 100 pounds is between 14.015
and 16.048 pounds. (Get out those rolling backpacks, kids!)

![warning_bomb.eps](9780470543887/images/warning_bomb_fmt.png) You
should only make predictions for the average value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> for
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> values that are within the range of
where the data was collected. Failure to do so will result in the
statistical no-no called extrapolation (see the later section “Knowing
the Limitations of Your Regression Analysis”).

Making the band with prediction intervals

Suppose instead of the mean value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>, you want to take a guess at what
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> would be for some future value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>. Because you’re looking into the
future, you have to make a prediction, and to do that, you need a range
of likely values of <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> for a given
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>\*. This is what statisticians call a
<span class="zCheltItalic">prediction interval.</span>

The formula for a 1 – <span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span> level
prediction interval for <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> at a given
value <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>\* is
![466469-eq0410.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0410_fmt.png). Again,
Minitab easily makes these calculations for you.

![computeroutput.eps](9780470543887/images/computeroutput_fmt.png) To
find a 1 – <span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span> level prediction
interval for the value of <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> for a
given <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>\* using Minitab, you ask for a
regression analysis (see instructions in the earlier section “Finding
the best-fitting line to model your data”) and click Options. In the box
Prediction Intervals for New Observations, enter the value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> that you want, and just below that,
put in your confidence level (the default is 95 percent). On the
computer output, the prediction interval is labeled 95% PI, and it
appears right next to the confidence interval for the mean of
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> for that same
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>\*.

Predicting textbook weight using student weight

For the textbook-weight data, suppose you’ve already made your
regression line and now a new student comes on the scene. You want to
predict this student’s textbook weight. This means you want a prediction
interval rather than a confidence interval, because you want to predict
the textbook weight for one person, not the average weight for a group.

Suppose this new student weighs 100 pounds. To find the prediction
interval for the textbook weight for this student, you use
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>\* = 100 pounds and let Minitab do
its thing.

The computer output in Figure 4-4 shows the 95 percent prediction
interval for textbook weight for a single 100-pound child is (11.509,
18.533) pounds. Note this is wider than the confidence interval of
(14.015, 16.048) for the mean textbook weight for 100-pound children
found in the earlier section “Building confidence intervals for the
average response.” This difference is due to the increased variability
in looking at one child and predicting one textbook weight.

<div class="story">

**Figure 4-4:** Prediction interval of textbook weight for a 100-pound
child.

</div>

![466469-fg0404.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-fg0404_fmt.png)

Comparing prediction and confidence intervals

Note that the formulas for prediction intervals and confidence intervals
are very similar. In fact, the prediction interval formula is exactly
the same as the confidence interval formula except it adds a 1 under the
square root. Because of this difference in the formulas, the margin of
error for a prediction interval is larger than for a confidence
interval.

This difference also makes sense from a statistical point. A prediction
interval has more variability than a confidence interval because it’s
harder to make a prediction about <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>
for a single value of <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>\* than it is
to estimate the average value of <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> for
a given <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>\*. (For example, individual
test scores vary more than average test scores do.) A prediction
interval will be wider than a confidence interval; it will have a larger
margin of error.

A similarity between prediction intervals and confidence intervals is
that their margin of error formulas both contain
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>\*, which means the margin of error
in either case depends on which value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>\* you use. It turns out in both
cases that if you use the mean value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> as your
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>\*, the margin of error for each
interval is at its smallest because there’s more data around the mean of
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> than at any other value. As you move
away from the mean of <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>, the margin of
error increases for each interval.

Checking the Model’s Fit (The Data, Not the Clothes!)

After you’ve established a relationship between
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> and
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> and have come up with an equation of
a line that represents that relationship, you may think your job is
done. (Many researchers erringly stop here, so I’m depending on you to
break the cycle!) The most-important job remains to be completed:
checking to be sure that the conditions of the model are truly met and
that the model fits well in more specific ways than the scatterplot and
correlation measure (which I cover in the earlier section “Exploring
Relationships with Scatterplots and Correlations”).

This section presents methods for defining and assessing the fit of a
simple linear regression model.

Defining the conditions

Two major conditions must be met before you apply a simple linear
regression model to a data set:

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) The
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>’s must have an approximately normal
distribution for each value of <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>.

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) The
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>’s must have a constant amount of
spread (standard deviation) for each value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>.

Normal y’s for every x

For any value of <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>, the population of
possible <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-values must have a normal
distribution. The mean of this distribution is the value for
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> that’s on the best-fitting line for
that <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>-value. That is, some of your
data fall above the best-fitting line, some data fall below the best
fitting line, and a few may actually land right on the line.

![tip.eps](9780470543887/images/tip_fmt.png) If the regression model is
fitting well, the data values should be scattered around the
best-fitting line in such a way that about 68 percent of the values lie
within one standard deviation of the line, about 95 percent of the
values lie within two standard deviations of the line, and about 99.7
percent of the values lie within three standard deviations of the line.
This specification, as you may recall from your Stats I course, is
called the <span class="zCheltItalic">68-95-99.7 rule,</span> and it
applies to all bell-shaped data (for which the normal distribution
applies).

You can see in Figure 4-5 how for each
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>-value, the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-values you may observe tend to be
located near the best-fitting line in greater numbers, and as you move
away from the line, you see fewer and fewer
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-values, both above and below the
line. More than that, they’re scattered around the line in a way that
reflects a bell-shaped curve, the normal distribution. This indicates a
good fit.

Why does this condition makes sense? The data you collect on
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> for any particular
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>-value vary from individual to
individual; for example, not all students’ textbooks weigh the same,
even for students who weigh the exact same amount. But those values
aren’t allowed to vary any way they want to. To fit the conditions of a
linear regression model, for each given value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>, the data should be scattered around
the line according to a normal distribution. Most of the points should
be close to the line, and as you get farther from the line, you can
expect fewer data points to occur. So condition number one is that the
data have a normal distribution for each value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>.

<div class="story">

**Figure 4-5:** Conditions of a simple linear regression model.

</div>

![466469-fg0405.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-fg0405_fmt.png)

Same spread for every x

In order to use the simple linear regression model, as you move from
left to right on the <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>-axis, the
spread in the <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-values around the line
should be the same, no matter which value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> you’re looking at. This requirement
is called the <span class="zCheltItalic">homoscedasticity
condition.</span> (How they came up with that mouthful of a word just
for describing the fact that the standard deviations stay the same
across the <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>-values, I’ll never know.)
This condition ensures that the best-fitting line works well for all
relevant values of <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>, not just in
certain areas.

You can see in Figure 4-5 that no matter what the value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> is, the spread in the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-values stays the same throughout. If
the spread got bigger and bigger as <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>
got larger and larger, for example, the line would lose its ability to
fit well for those large values of <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>.

Finding and exploring the residuals

To check to see whether the <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-values
come from a normal distribution, you need to measure how far off your
predictions were from the actual data that came in. These differences
are called <span class="zCheltItalic">errors,</span> or
<span class="zCheltItalic">residuals.</span> To evaluate whether a model
fits well, you need to check those errors and see how they stack up.

<span class="Icon-w-3-lines-of-text-baseline">![tip.eps](9780470543887/images/tip_fmt.png)</span>
In a model-fitting context, the word error doesn’t mean “mistake.” It
just means a difference between the data and the prediction based on the
model. The word I like best to describe this difference is residual,
however. It sounds more upbeat.

The following sections focus on finding a way to measure these residuals
that the model makes. You also explore the residuals to identify
particular problems that occurred in the process of trying to fit a
straight line to the data. In other words, you can discover that looking
at residuals helps you assess the fit of the model and diagnose problems
that caused a bad fit, if that was the case.

Finding the residuals

A <span class="zCheltItalic">residual</span> is the difference between
the observed value <span class="zCheltItalic">ŷ</span> of
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> (from the best-fitting line) and the
predicted value of <span class="zCheltItalic">y, also known as
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span></span> (from the data set). Its
notation is (<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> –
<span class="zCheltItalic">ŷ</span>). Specifically, for any data point,
you take its observed <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-value (from
the data) and subtract its expected
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-value (from the line). If the
residual is large, the line doesn’t fit well in that spot. If the
residual is small, the line fits well in that spot.

For example, suppose you have a point in your data set (2, 4) and the
equation of the best-fitting line is <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>
= 2<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> + 1. The expected value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> in this case is (2
<span class="Times-Sign">\*</span> 2) + 1 = 5. The observed value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> from the data set is 4. Taking the
observed value minus the estimated value, you get 4 – 5 = –1. The
residual for that particular data point (2, 4) is –1. If you observe a
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-value of 6 and use the same straight
line to estimate <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>, then the residual
is 6 – 5 = +1.

<span class="Icon-w-3-lines-of-text-baseline">![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png)</span>
In general, a positive residual means you underestimated
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> at that point; the line is below the
data. A negative residual means you overestimated
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> at that point; the line is above the
data.

Standardizing the residuals

Residuals in their raw form are in the same units as the original data,
making them hard to judge out of context. To make interpreting the
residuals easier, statisticians typically
<span class="zCheltItalic">standardize</span> them — that is, subtract
the mean of the residuals (zero) and divide by the standard deviation of
all the residuals. The residuals are a data set just like any other data
set, so you can find their mean and standard deviation like you always
do. Standardizing just means converting to a
<span class="zCheltItalic">Z</span>-score so that you see where it falls
on the standard normal distribution. (See your Stats I text or
<span class="zCheltItalic">Statistics For Dummies</span> for info on
Z-scores.)

Making residual plots

You can plot the residuals on a graph called a
<span class="zCheltItalic">residual plot.</span> (If you’ve standardized
the residuals, you call it a <span class="zCheltItalic">standardized
residual plot.</span>) Figure 4-6 shows the Minitab output for a variety
of standardized residual plots, all getting at the same idea: checking
to be sure the conditions of the simple linear regression model are met.

<div class="story">

**Figure 4-6:** Standard-ized residual plots for textbook-weight data.

</div>

![466469-fg0406.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-fg0406_fmt.png)

Checking normality

If the condition of normality is met, you can see on the residual plot
lots of (standardized) residuals close to zero; as you move farther away
from zero, you can see fewer residuals.
<span class="zCheltBoldItalic">Note:</span> You shouldn’t expect to see
a standardized residual at or beyond +3 or –3. If this occurs, you can
consider that point an outlier, which warrants further investigation.
(For more on outliers, see the section “Scoping for outliers” later in
this chapter.)

![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png) The residuals
should also occur at random — some above the line, and some below the
line. If a pattern occurs in the residuals, the line may not be fitting
right.

The plots in Figure 4-6 seem to have an issue with the very last
observation, the one for 12th graders. In this observation, the average
student weight (142) seemed to follow the pattern of increasing with
each grade level, but the textbook weight (16.06) was less than for 11th
graders (20.79) and is the first point to break the pattern.

You can also see in the plot in the upper-right corner of Figure 4-6
that the very last data value has a standardized residual that sticks
out from the others and has a value of –3 (something that should be a
very rare occurrence). So the value you expected for
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> based on your line was off by a
factor of 3 standard deviations. And because this residual is negative,
what you observed for <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> was much lower
than you may have expected it to be using the regression line.

The other residuals seem to fall in line with a normal distribution, as
you can see in the upper-right plot of Figure 4-6. The residuals
concentrate around zero, with fewer appearing as you move farther away
from zero. You can also see this pattern in the upper-left plot of
Figure 4-6, which shows how close to normal the residuals are. The line
in this graph represents the equal-to-normal line. If the residuals
follow close to the line, then normality is okay. If not, you have
problems (in a statistical sense, of course). You can see the residual
with the highest magnitude is –3, and that number falls outside the line
quite a bit.

The lower-left plot in Figure 4-6 makes a histogram of the standardized
residuals, and you can see it doesn’t look much like a bell-shaped
distribution. It doesn’t even look
<span class="zCheltItalic">symmetric</span> (the same on each side when
you cut it down the middle). The problem again seems to be the residual
of –3, which skews the histogram to the left.

The lower-right plot of Figure 4-6 plots the residuals in the order
presented in the data set in Table 4-1. Because the data was ordered
already, the lower-right residual plot looks like the upper-right
residual plot in Figure 4-6, except the dots are connected. This
lower-right residual plot makes the residual of –3 stand out even more.

Checking the spread of the y’s for each x

The graph in the upper-right corner of Figure 4-6 also addresses the
homoscedasticity condition. If the condition is met, then the residuals
for every <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>-value have about the same
spread. If you cut a vertical line down through each
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>-value, the residuals have about the
same spread (standard deviation) each time, except for the last
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>-value, which again represents grade
12. That means the condition of equal spread in the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-values is met for the
textbook-weight example.

![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png) If you look at
only one residual plot, choose the one in the upper-right corner of
Figure 4-6, the plot of the fitted values (the values of
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> on the line) versus the standardized
residuals. Most problems with model fit will show up on that plot
because a residual is defined as the difference between the observed
value of <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> and the fitted value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>. In a perfect world, all the fitted
values have no residual at all; a large residual (such as the one where
the estimated textbook weight is 20 pounds for students averaging 142
pounds; see Figure 4-1) is indicated by a point far off from zero. This
graph also shows you deviations from the overall pattern of the line;
for example, if large residuals are on the extremes of this graph (very
low or very high fitted values), the line isn’t fitting in those areas.
On balance, you can say this line fits well at least for grades 1
through 11.

Using r<span class="zSuperscript">2</span> to measure model fit

One important way to assess how well the model fits is to use a
statistic called the <span class="zCheltItalic">coefficient of
determination,</span> or
<span class="zCheltItalic">r</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>.
This statistic takes the value of the correlation,
<span class="zCheltItalic">r</span>, and squares it to give you a
percentage. You interpret
<span class="zCheltItalic">r</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
as the percentage of variability in the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> variable that’s explained by, or due
to, its relationship with the <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>
variable.

The <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-values of the data you collect
have a great deal of variability in and of themselves. You look for
another variable <span class="zCheltItalic">(x)</span> that helps you
explain that variability in the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-values. After you put that
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variable into the model and find
that it’s highly correlated with <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>,
you want to find out how well this model did at explaining why the
values of <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> are different.

![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png) Note that you
have to interpret
<span class="zCheltItalic">r</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
using different standards than those for interpreting
<span class="zCheltItalic">r</span>. Because squaring a number between
–1 and +1 results in a smaller number (except for +1, –1, and 0, which
stay the same or switch signs), an
<span class="zCheltItalic">r</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
of 0.49 isn’t too bad, because it’s the square of
<span class="zCheltItalic">r</span> = 0.7, which is a fairly strong
correlation.

![tip.eps](9780470543887/images/tip_fmt.png)

The following are some general guidelines for interpreting the value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">r</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>:

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) If the model containing
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> explains a lot of the variability in
the <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-values, then
<span class="zCheltItalic">r</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
is high (in the 80 to 90 percent range is considered to be extremely
high). Values like 0.70 are still considered fairly high. A high
percentage of variability means that the line fits well because there’s
not much left to explain about the value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> other than using
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> and its relationship to
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>. So a larger value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">r</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
is a good thing.

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) If the model containing
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> doesn’t help much in explaining the
difference in the <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-values, then the
value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">r</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
is small (closer to zero; between, say, 0.00 and 0.30 roughly). The
model, in this case, wouldn’t fit well. You need another variable to
explain <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> other than the one you
already tried.

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) Values of
<span class="zCheltItalic">r</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
that fall in the middle (between, say, 0.30 and 0.70) mean that
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> does help somewhat in explaining
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>, but it doesn’t do the job well
enough on its own. In this case, statisticians would try to add one or
more variables to the model to help explain
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> more fully as a group (read more
about this in Chapter 5).

For the textbook-weight example, the value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">r</span> (the correlation coefficient) is
0.93. Squaring this result, you get
<span class="zCheltItalic">r</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span> =
0.8649. That number means approximately 86 percent of the variability
you find in average textbook weights for all students
(<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-values) is explained by the average
student weight (<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>-values). This
percentage tells you that the model of using year in school to estimate
backpack weight is a good bet.

In the case of simple linear regression, you have only one
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variable, but in Chapter 5, you can
see models that contain more than one
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variable. In that situation, you use
<span class="zCheltItalic">r</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
to help sort out the contribution that those
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variables as a group bring to the
model.

Scoping for outliers

Sometimes life isn’t perfect (oh really?), and you may find a residual
in your otherwise tidy data set that totally sticks out. It’s called an
<span class="zCheltItalic">outlier,</span> and it has a standardized
value at or beyond +3 or –3. It threatens to blow the conditions of your
regression model and send you crying to your professor.

Before you panic, the best thing to do is to examine that outlier more
closely. First, can you find an error in that data value? Did someone
report her age as 642, for instance? (After all, mistakes do happen.) If
you do find a certifiable error in your data set, you remove that data
point (or fix it if possible) and analyze the data without it. However,
if you can’t explain away the problem by finding a mistake, you must
think of another approach.

If you can’t find a mistake that caused the outlier, you don’t
necessarily have to trash your model; after all, it’s only one data
point. Analyze the data with that data point, and analyze the data again
without it. Then report and compare both analyses. This comparison gives
you a sense of how influential that one data point is, and it may lead
other researchers to conduct more research to zoom in on the issue you
brought to the surface.

In Figure 4-1, you can see the scatterplot of the full data set for the
textbook-weight example. Figure 4-7 shows the scatterplot for the data
set minus the outlier. The scatterplot fits the data better without the
outlier. The correlation increases to 0.993, and the value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">r</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
increases to 0.986. The equation for the regression line for this data
set is <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> = 1.78 +
0.139<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>.

The slope of the regression line doesn’t change much by removing the
outlier (compare it to Figure 4-2, where the slope is 0.113). However,
the <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept changes: It’s now 1.78
without the outlier compared to 3.69 with the outlier. The slopes of the
lines are about the same, but the lines cross the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-axis in different places. It appears
that the outlier (the last point in the data set) has quite an effect on
the best-fitting line.

<div class="story">

**Figure 4-7:** Scatterplot of textbook-weight data minus the outlier.

</div>

![466469-fg0407.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-fg0407_fmt.png)

Figure 4-8 shows the residual plots for the regression line for the data
set without the outlier. Each of these plots shows a much better fit of
the data to the model compared to Figure 4-6. This result tells you that
the data for grade 12 is influential in this data set and that the
outlier needs to be noted and perhaps explored further. Do students peak
when they’re juniors in high school? Or do they just decide when they’re
seniors that it isn’t cool to carry books around? (A statistician’s job
isn’t to wonder why, but to do and analyze.)

<div class="story">

**Figure 4-8:** Residual plots for textbook-weight data minus the
outlier.

</div>

![466469-fg0408.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-fg0408_fmt.png)

Knowing the Limitations of Your Regression Analysis

The bottom line of any data analysis is to make the correct conclusions
given your results. When you’re working with a simple linear regression
model, there’s the potential to make three major errors. This section
shows you those errors and tells you how to avoid them.

Avoiding slipping into cause-and-effect mode

In a simple linear regression, you investigate whether
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> is related to
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>, and if you get a strong correlation
and a scatterplot that shows a linear trend, then you find the
best-fitting line and use it to estimate the value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> for reasonable values of
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>.

![warning_bomb.eps](9780470543887/images/warning_bomb_fmt.png) There’s a
fine line, however (no pun intended), that you don’t want to cross with
your interpretation of regression results. Be careful to not
automatically interpret slope in a cause-and-effect mode when you’re
using the regression line to estimate the value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> using
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>. Doing so can result in a leap of
faith that can send you into the frying pan. Unless you have used a
controlled experiment to get the data, you can only assume that the
variables are correlated; you can’t really give a stone-cold guarantee
about why they’re related.

In the textbook-weight example, you estimate the average weight of the
students’ textbooks by using the students’ average weight, but that
doesn’t mean increasing a particular child’s weight causes his textbook
weight to increase. For example, because of the strong positive
correlation, you do know that students with lower weights are associated
with lower total textbook weights, and students with higher weights tend
to have higher textbook weights. But you can’t take one particular
third-grade student, increase his weight, and presto — suddenly his
textbooks weigh more.

The variable underlying the relationship between a child’s weight and
the weight of his backpack is the grade level of the student from an
academic standpoint; as grade level increases, so might the size and
number of his books, as well as the homework coming home. Student grade
level drives both student weight and textbook weight. In this situation,
student grade level is what statisticians call a
<span class="zCheltItalic">lurking variable;</span> it’s a variable that
wasn’t included in the model but is related to both the outcome and the
response. A lurking variable confuses the issue of what’s causing what
to happen.

![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png) If the collected
data was the result of a well-designed experiment that controls for
possible confounding variables, you can establish a cause-and-effect
relationship between <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> and
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> if they’re strongly correlated.
Otherwise, you can’t establish such a relationship. (See your Stats I
text or Statistics For Dummies for info regarding experiments.)

Extrapolation: The ultimate no-no

Plugging values of <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> into the model
that fall outside of the reasonable boundaries of
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> is called
<span class="zCheltItalic">extrapolation.</span> And one of my
colleagues sums up this idea very well: “Friends don’t let friends
extrapolate.”

When you determine a best-fitting line for your data, you come up with
an equation that allows you to plug in a value for
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> and get a predicted value for
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>. In algebra, if you find the
equation of a line and graph it, the line typically has an arrow on each
end indicating it goes on forever in either direction. But that doesn’t
work for statistical problems (because statistics represents the
<span class="zCheltItalic">real</span> world). When you’re dealing with
real-world units like height, weight, IQ, GPA, house prices, and the
weight of your statistics textbook, only certain numbers make sense.

So the first point is, don’t plug in values for
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> that don’t make any sense. For
example, if you’re estimating the price of a house
<span class="zCheltItalic">(y)</span> by using its square footage
<span class="zCheltItalic">(x)</span>, you wouldn’t think of plugging in
a value of <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> like 10 square feet or
100 square feet, because houses simply aren’t that small.

You also wouldn’t think about plugging in values like 1,000,000 square
feet for <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> (unless your “house” is the
Ohio State football stadium or something). It wouldn’t make sense.
Likewise, if you’re estimating tomorrow’s temperature using today’s
temperature, negative numbers for <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>
could possibly make sense, but if you’re estimating the amount of
precipitation tomorrow given the amount of precipitation today, negative
numbers for <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> (or
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> for that matter) don’t make sense.

![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png) Choose only
reasonable values of <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> for which you
try to make estimates about <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> — that
is, look at the values of <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> for which
your data was collected, and stay within those bounds when making
predictions. In the textbook-weight example, the smallest average
student weight is 48.5 pounds, and the largest average student weight is
142 pounds. Choosing student weights between 48.5 and 142 to plug in for
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> in the equation is okay, but
choosing values less than 48.5 or more than 142 isn’t a good idea. You
can’t guarantee that the same linear relationship (or any linear
relationship for that matter) continues outside the given boundaries.

Think about it: If the relationship you found actually continued for any
value of <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>, no matter how large, then
a 250-pound lineman from OSU would have to carry 3.69 + 0.113
<span class="Times-Sign">\*</span> 250 = 31.94 pounds of books around in
his backpack. Of course this would be easy for him, but what about the
rest of us?

Sometimes you need more than one variable

A simple linear regression model is just what it says it is: simple. I
don’t mean easy to work with, necessarily, but simple in the uncluttered
sense. The model tries to estimate the value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> by only using one variable,
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>. However, the number of real-world
situations that can be explained by using a simple, one-variable linear
regression is small. Often one variable just can’t do all the
predicting.

If one variable alone doesn’t result in a model that fits well enough,
you can try to add more variables. It may take many variables to make a
good estimate for <span class="zCheltItalic">y,</span> and you have to
be careful in how you choose them. In the case of stock market prices,
for example, they’re still looking for that ultimate prediction model.

As another example, health insurance companies try to estimate how long
you’ll live by asking you a series of questions (each of which
represents a variable in the regression model). You can’t find one
single variable that estimates how long you’ll live; you must consider
many factors: your health, your weight, whether or not you smoke,
genetic factors, how much exercise you do each week, and the list goes
on and on and on.

The point is that regression models don’t always use just one variable,
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>, to estimate
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>. Some models use two, three, or even
more variables to estimate <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>. Those
models aren’t called simple linear regression models; they’re called
<span class="zCheltItalic">multiple linear regression models</span>
because of their employment of multiple variables to make an estimate.
(You explore multiple linear regression models in Chapter 5.)

</div>

</div>

<span id="10_466469-ch05.html"></span>

<div id="10_466469-ch05.html_x10_466469-ch05.html">

<div class="Basic-Text-Frame">

Chapter 5

Multiple Regression with Two X Variables

In This Chapter

![arrow](9780470543887/images/arrow.png) Getting the basic ideas behind
a multiple regression model

![arrow](9780470543887/images/arrow.png) Finding, interpreting, and
testing coefficients

![arrow](9780470543887/images/arrow.png) Checking model fit

<span class="char-style-override-1">T</span>he idea of regression is to
build a model that estimates or predicts one quantitative variable
<span class="zCheltItalic">(y)</span> by using at least one other
quantitative variable <span class="zCheltItalic">(x)</span>. Simple
linear regression uses exactly one <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>
variable to estimate the <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> variable.
(See Chapter 4 for all the information you need on simple linear
regression.) <span class="zCheltItalic">Multiple linear
regression,</span> on the other hand, uses more than one
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variable to estimate the value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>.

In this chapter, you see how multiple regression works and how to apply
it to build a model for <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>. You see all
the steps necessary for the process, including determining which
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variables to include, estimating
their contributions to the model, finding the best model, using the
model for estimating <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>, and assessing
the fit of the model. It may seem like a mountain of information, but
you won’t regress on the topic of regression if you take this chapter
one step at a time.

Getting to Know the Multiple Regression Model

Before you jump right into using the multiple regression model, get a
feel for what it’s all about. In this section, you see the usefulness of
multiple regression as well as the basic elements of the multiple
regression model. Some of the ideas are just an extension of the simple
linear regression model (see Chapter 4). Some of the concepts are a
little more complex, as you may guess because the model is more complex.
But the concepts and the results should make intuitive sense, which is
always good news.

Discovering the uses of multiple regression

One situation in which multiple regression is useful is when the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> variable is hard to track down —
that is, its value can’t be measured straight up, and you need more than
one other piece of information to help get a handle on what its value
will be. For example, you may want to estimate the price of gold today.
It would be hard to imagine being able to do that with only one other
variable. You may base your estimate on recent gold prices, the price of
other commodities on the market that move with or against gold, and a
host of other possible economic conditions associated with the price of
gold.

Another case for using multiple regression is when you want to figure
out what factors play a role in determining the value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>. For example, you want to find out
what information is important to real estate agents in setting a price
for a house going on the market.

Looking at the general form of the multiple regression model

The general idea of simple linear regression is to fit the best straight
line through that data that you possibly can and use that line to make
estimates for <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> based on certain
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>-values. The equation of the
best-fitting line in simple linear regression is
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> =
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">0</span> +
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span><span class="zCheltItalic">x</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span>,
where
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">0</span> is
the <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept and
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span> is
the slope. (The equation also has the form
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> =
<span class="zCheltItalic">a</span> +
<span class="zCheltItalic">bx</span>; see Chapter 4.)

In the multiple regression setting, you have more than one
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variable that’s related to
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>. Call these
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variables
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span>,
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span><span class="zSubscript">2</span>, .
. .
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span><span class="zSubscript">k</span>. In
the most basic multiple regression model, you use some or all of these
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variables to estimate
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> where each
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variable is taken to the first
power. This process is called finding the best-fitting linear function
for the data. This linear function looks like the following:
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> =
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">0</span> +
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span><span class="zCheltItalic">x</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span> +
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">2</span><span class="zCheltItalic">x</span><span class="zSubscript">2</span> +
. . . +
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">k</span><span class="zCheltItalic">x</span><span class="zSubscript">k</span>,
and you can call it the <span class="zCheltItalic">multiple (linear)
regression model.</span> You use this model to make estimates about
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> based on given values of the
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variables.

![technicalstuff.eps](9780470543887/images/technicalstuff_fmt.png) A
<span class="zCheltItalic">linear</span> function is an equation whose
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> terms are taken to the first power
only. For example <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> =
2<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span> +
3<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span><span class="zSubscript">2</span> +
24<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span><span class="zSubscript">3</span>
is a linear equation using three <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>
variables. If any of the <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> terms are
squared, the function is a <span class="zCheltItalic">quadratic</span>
one; if an <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> term is taken to the
third power, the function is a <span class="zCheltItalic">cubic</span>
function, and so on. In this chapter, I consider only linear functions.

Stepping through the analysis

Your job in conducting a multiple regression analysis is to do the
following (the computer can help you do steps three through six):

<span class="zCheltBold">1. Come up with a list of
possible</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic"> x
</span><span class="zCheltBold">variables that may be helpful in
estimating</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic"> y.</span>

<span class="zCheltBold"> 2. Collect data on
the</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic"> y
</span><span class="zCheltBold">variable and
your</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic"> x
</span><span class="zCheltBold">variables from step one.</span>

<span class="zCheltBold"> 3. Check the relationships between
each</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic"> x
</span><span class="zCheltBold">variable
and</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic"> y
</span><span class="zCheltBold">(using scatterplots and correlations),
and use the results to eliminate
those</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic"> x
</span><span class="zCheltBold">variables that aren’t strongly related
to</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic"> y.</span>

<span class="zCheltBold"> 4. Look at possible relationships between
the</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic"> x
</span><span class="zCheltBold">variables to make sure you aren’t being
redundant (in statistical terms, you’re trying to avoid the problem of
multicolinearity).</span>

If two <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variables relate to
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> the same way, you don’t need both in
the model.

<span class="zCheltBold">5. Use those
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">x</span><span class="zCheltBold">
variables (from step four) in a multiple regression analysis to find the
best-fitting model for your data.</span>

<span class="zCheltBold">6. Use the best-fitting model (from step five)
to predict
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">y</span><span class="zCheltBold">
for given
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">x</span><span class="zCheltBold">-values
by plugging those
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">x</span><span class="zCheltBold">-values
into the model.</span>

I outline each of these steps in the sections to follow.

Looking at x’s and y’s

The first step of a multiple regression analysis comes way before the
number crunching on the computer; it occurs even before the data is
collected. Step one is where you sit down and think about what variables
may be useful in predicting your response variable
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>. This step will likely take more
time than any other step, except maybe the data-collection process.
Deciding which <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variables may be
candidates for consideration in your model is a deal-breaking step,
because you can’t go back and collect more data after the analysis is
over.

![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png) Always check to
be sure that your response variable,
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>, and at least one of the
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variables are quantitative. For
example, if <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> isn’t quantitative but
at least one <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> is, a logistic
regression model may be in order (see Chapter 8).

Suppose you’re in the marketing department for a major national company
that sells plasma TVs. You want to sell as many TVs as you can, so you
want to figure out which factors play a role in plasma TV sales. In
talking with your advertising people and remembering what you learned in
those business classes in college, you know that one powerful way to get
sales is through advertising. You think of the types of advertising that
may be related to sales of plasma TVs and your team comes up with two
ideas:

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) <span class="zCheltBold">TV
ads: </span>Of course, how better to sell a TV than through a TV ad?

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png)
<span class="zCheltBold">Newspaper sales:</span> Hit ’em on Sunday when
they’re reading the paper before watching the game through squinty eyes
that are missing all the good plays and the terrible calls the referees
are making.

By coming up with a list of possible <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>
variables to predict <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>, you have just
completed step one of a multiple regression analysis, according to the
list in the previous section. Note that all three variables I use in the
TV example are quantitative (the TV ad and newspaper sales variables and
the TV sales response variable), which means you can go ahead and think
about a multiple regression model by using the two types of ads to
predict TV sales.

Collecting the Data

Step two in the multiple regression analysis process is to collect the
data for your <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> and
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> variables. To do this, make sure
that for each individual in the data set, you collect all the data for
that individual at the same time (including the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-value and all
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>-values) and keep the data all
together for each individual, preserving any relationships that may
exist between the variables. You must then enter the data into a table
format by using Minitab or any other software package (each column
represents a variable and each row represents all the data from a single
individual) to get a glimpse of the data and to organize it for later
analyses.

To continue with the TV sales example from the preceding section,
suppose that you start thinking about all the reams of data you have
available to you regarding the plasma TV industry. You remember working
with the advertising department before to do a media blitz by using,
among other things, TV and newspaper ads. So you have data on these
variables from a variety of store locations. You take a sample of 22
store locations in different parts of the country and put together the
data on how much money was spent on each type of advertising, along with
the plasma TV sales for that location. You can see the data in Table
5-1.

![tb0501](9780470543887/images/9780470466469-tb0501.png)

In reviewing this data, the question is whether the amount of money
spent on these two forms of advertising can do a good job of estimating
sales (in other words, are the ads worth the money?). And if so, do you
need to include spending for both types of ads to estimate sales, or is
one of them enough? Looking at the numbers in Table 5-1, you can see
that higher sales may be related at least to higher amounts spent on TV
advertising; the situation with newspaper advertising may not be so
clear. So will the final multiple regression model contain both
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variables or only one? In the
following sections, you can find out.

Pinpointing Possible Relationships

The third step in doing a multiple regression analysis (see the list in
the “Stepping through the analysis” section) is to find out which (if
any) of your possible <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variables are
actually related to <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>. If an
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variable has no relationship with
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>, including it in the model is
pointless. Data analysts use a combination of scatterplots and
correlations to examine relationships between pairs of variables (as you
can see in Chapter 4). Although you can view these two techniques under
the heading of looking for relationships, I walk you through each one
separately in the following sections to discuss their nuances.

Making scatterplots

You make scatterplots in multiple linear regression to get a handle on
whether your possible <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variables are
even related to the <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> variable you’re
studying. To investigate these possible relationships, you make one
scatterplot of each <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variable with
the response variable <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>. If you have
<span class="zCheltItalic">k</span> different
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variables being considered for the
final model, you make <span class="zCheltItalic">k</span> different
scatterplots.

![computeroutput.eps](9780470543887/images/computeroutput_fmt.png) To
make a scatterplot in Minitab, enter your data in columns, where each
column represents a variable and each row represents all the data from
one individual. Go to Graph\>Scatterplots\>Simple. Select your
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> variable on the left-hand side, and
click Select. That variable appears in the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-variable box on the right-hand side.
Then select your <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variable on the
left-hand side, and click Select. That variable appears in the
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>-variable box on the right-hand side.
Click OK.

Scatterplots of TV ad spending versus TV sales and newspaper ad spending
versus TV sales are shown in Figure 5-1.

<div class="story">

**Figure 5-1:** Scatterplots of TV and newspaper ad spending versus
plasma TV sales.

</div>

![466469-fg0501.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-fg0501_fmt.png)

You can see from Figure 5-1a that TV spending does appear to have a
fairly strong linear relationship with sales. This observation provides
evidence that TV ad spending may be useful in estimating plasma TV
sales. Figure 5-1b shows a linear relationship between newspaper ad
spending and sales, but the relationship isn’t as strong as the one
between TV ads and sales. However, it still may be somewhat helpful in
estimating sales.

Correlations: Examining the bond

The second portion of step three involves calculating and examining the
correlations between the <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variables
and the <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> variable. (Of course, if a
scatterplot of an <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variable and the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> variable fails to come up with a
pattern, then you drop that <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variable
altogether and don’t proceed to find the correlation.)

Whenever you employ scatterplots to explore possible linear
relationships, correlations are typically not far behind. The
<span class="zCheltItalic">correlation coefficient</span> is a number
that measures the strength and direction of the linear relationship
between two variables, <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> and
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>. (See Chapter 4 for the lowdown on
correlation.)

This step involves two parts:

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) Finding and interpreting
the correlations

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) Testing the correlations to
see which ones are statistically significant (thereby determining which
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variables are significantly related
to <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>)

Finding and interpreting correlations

You can calculate a set of all possible correlations between all pairs
of variables — which is called a <span class="zCheltItalic">correlation
matrix</span> — in Minitab. You can see the correlation matrix output
for the TV data from Table 5-1 in Figure 5-2. Note the correlations
between the <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> variable (sales) and
each <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variable, as well as the
correlation between TV ads and newspaper ads.

<div class="story">

**Figure 5-2:** Correlation values and
<span class="zUnivItalic">p</span>-values for the TV sales example.

</div>

![466469-fg0502.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-fg0502_fmt.png)

![computeroutput.eps](9780470543887/images/computeroutput_fmt.png)
Minitab can find a correlation matrix between any pairs of variables in
the model, including the <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> variable
and all the <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variables as well. To
calculate a correlation matrix for a group of variables in Minitab,
first enter your data in columns (one for each variable). Then go to
Stat\>Basic Statistics\>Descriptive Statistics\>Correlation. Highlight
the variables from the left-hand side for which you want correlations,
and click Select.

![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png) To find the
values of the correlation matrix from the computer output, intersect the
row and column variables for which you want to find the correlation, and
the top number in that intersection is the correlation of those two
variables. For example, the correlation between TV ads and TV sales is
0.791, because it intersects the TV row with the Sales column in the
correlation matrix in Figure 5-2.

Testing correlations for significance

By the rule-of-thumb approach from Stats I (also reviewed in Chapter 4),
a correlation that’s close to 1 or –1 (starting around
<span class="zSymbolMedium">± </span>0.75) is strong; a correlation
close to 0 is very weak/nonexistent; and around
<span class="zSymbolMedium">± </span>0.6 to 0.7, the relationships
become moderately strong. The correlation between TV ads and TV sales of
0.791 indicates a fairly strong positive linear relationship between
these two variables, based on the rule-of-thumb. The correlation between
newspaper ads and TV sales seen in Figure 5-2 is 0.594, which is
moderate by my rule-of-thumb.

Many times in statistics a rule-of-thumb approach to interpreting a
correlation coefficient is sufficient. However, you’re in the big
leagues now, so you need a more precise tool for determining whether or
not a correlation coefficient is large enough to be statistically
significant. That’s the real test of any statistic: not that the
relationship is fairly strong or moderately strong in the sample, but
whether or not the relationship can be generalized to the population.

Now, that phrase <span class="zCheltItalic">statistically
significant</span> should ring a bell. It’s your old friend the
hypothesis test calling to you (see Chapter 3 for a brush-up on
hypothesis testing). Just like a hypothesis test for the mean of a
population or the difference in the means of two populations, you also
have a test for the correlation between two variables within a
population.

![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png) The null
hypothesis to test a correlation is Ho:
<span class="zSymbolMedium">ρ</span> = 0 (no relationship) versus Ha:
<span class="zSymbolMedium">ρ</span>
<span class="zSymbolMedium">≠</span> 0 (a relationship exists). The
letter <span class="zSymbolMedium">ρ</span> is the Greek version of
<span class="zCheltItalic">r</span> and represents the true correlation
of <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> and
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> in the entire population;
<span class="zCheltItalic">r</span> is the correlation coefficient of
the sample.

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) <span class="zCheltBold">If
you can’t reject Ho based on your data,</span> you can’t conclude that
the correlation between <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> and
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> differs from zero, indicating you
don’t have evidence that the two variables are related and
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> shouldn’t be in the multiple
regression model.

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) <span class="zCheltBold">If
you can reject Ho based on your data,</span> you conclude that the
correlation isn’t equal to zero, so the variables are related. More than
that, their relationship is deemed to be statistically significant —
that is, the relationship would occur very rarely in your sample just by
chance.

Any statistical software package can calculate a hypothesis test of a
correlation for you. The actual formulas used in that process are beyond
the scope of this book. However the interpretation is the same as for
any test: If the <span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-value is smaller
than your predetermined value of <span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span>
(typically 0.05), reject Ho and conclude
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> and
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> are related. Otherwise you can’t
reject Ho, and you conclude you don’t have enough evidence to indicate
that the variables are related.

![computeroutput.eps](9780470543887/images/computeroutput_fmt.png) In
Minitab, you can conduct a hypothesis test for a correlation by clicking
on Stat\>Basic Statistics\>Correlation, and checking the Display
<span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-values box. Choose the variables you
want to find correlations for, and click Select. You’ll get output in
the form of a little table that shows the correlations between the
variables for each pair with the respective
<span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-values under each one. You can see
the correlation output for the ads and sales example in Figure 5-2.

Looking at Figure 5-2, the correlation of 0.791 between TV ads and sales
has a <span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-value of 0.000, which means
it’s actually less than 0.001. That’s a highly significant result, much
less than 0.05 (your predetermined <span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span>
level). So TV ad spending is strongly related to sales. The correlation
between newspaper ad spending and sales was 0.594, which is also found
to be statistically significant with a
<span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-value of 0.004.

Checking for Multicolinearity

You have one more very important step to complete in the
relationship-exploration process before going on to using the multiple
regression model. You need to complete step four: looking at the
relationship between the <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variables
themselves and checking for redundancy. Failure to do so can lead to
problems during the model-fitting process.

![warning_bomb.eps](9780470543887/images/warning_bomb_fmt.png)
<span class="zCheltItalic">Multicolinearity</span> is a term you use if
two <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variables are highly correlated.
Not only is it redundant to include both related variables in the
multiple regression model, but it’s also problematic. The bottom line is
this: If two <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variables are
significantly correlated, only include one of them in the regression
model, not both. If you include both, the computer won’t know what
numbers to give as coefficients for each of the two variables because
they share their contribution to determining the value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>. Multicolinearity can really mess up
the model-fitting process and give answers that are inconsistent and
often not repeatable in subsequent studies.

To head off the problem of multicolinearity, along with the correlations
you examine regarding each <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variable
and the response variable <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>, also find
the correlations between all pairs of
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variables. If two
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variables are highly correlated,
don’t leave them both in the model, or multicolinearity will result. To
see the correlations between all the <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>
variables, have Minitab calculate a correlation matrix of all the
variables (see the section “Finding and interpreting correlations”). You
can ignore the correlations between the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> variable and the
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variables and only choose the
correlations between the <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variables
shown in the correlation matrix. Find those correlations by intersecting
the rows and columns of the <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>
variables for which you want correlations.

![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png) If two
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variables
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span> and
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span><span class="zSubscript">2</span> are
strongly correlated (that is, their correlation is beyond +0.7 or –0.7),
then one of them would do just about as good a job of estimating
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> as the other, so you don’t need to
include them both in the model. If
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span> and
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span><span class="zSubscript">2</span>
aren’t strongly correlated, then both of them working together would do
a better job of estimating sales than either variable alone.

For the ad-spending example, you have to examine the correlation between
the two <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variables, TV ad spending
and newspaper ad spending, to be sure no multicolinearity is present.
The correlation between these two variables (as you can see in Figure
5-2) is only 0.058. You don’t even need a hypothesis test to tell you
whether or not these two variables are related; they’re clearly not.

The <span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-value for the correlation
between the spending for the two ad types is 0.799 (see Figure 5-2),
which is much, much larger than 0.05 ever thought of being and therefore
isn’t statistically significant. The large
<span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-value for the correlation between
spending for the two ad types confirms your thoughts that both variables
together may be helpful in estimating
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> because each makes its own
contribution. It also tells you that keeping them both in the model
won’t create any multicolinearity problems. (This completes step four of
the multiple regression analysis, as listed in the “Stepping through the
analysis” section.)

Finding the Best-Fitting Model for Two x Variables

After you have a group of <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variables
that are all related to <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> and not
related to each other (refer to previous sections), you’re ready to
perform step five of the multiple regression analysis (as listed in the
“Stepping through the analysis” section). You’re ready to find the
best-fitting model for the data.

In the multiple regression model with two
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variables, you have the general
equation <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> =
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">0</span> +
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span><span class="zCheltItalic">x</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span> +
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">2</span><span class="zCheltItalic">x</span><span class="zSubscript">2</span>,
and you already know which <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variables
to include in the model (by doing step four in the previous section);
the task now is to figure out which coefficients (numbers) to put in for
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">0</span>,
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span>,
and
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">2</span>, so
you can use the resulting equation to estimate
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>. This specific model is the
<span class="zCheltItalic">best-fitting multiple linear regression
model.</span> This section tells you how to get, interpret, and test
those coefficients in order to complete step five in the multiple
regression analysis.

![technicalstuff.eps](9780470543887/images/technicalstuff_fmt.png)
Finding the best-fitting linear equation is like finding the
best-fitting line in simple linear regression, except that you’re not
finding a line. When you have two <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>
variables in multiple regression, for example, you’re estimating a
best-fitting plane for the data.

Getting the multiple regression coefficients

In the simple linear regression model, you have the straight line
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> =
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">0</span> +
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span><span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>;
the coefficient of <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> is the slope, and
it represents the change in <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> per unit
change in <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>. In a multiple linear
regression model, the coefficients
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span>,
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">2</span>,
and so on quantify in a similar matter the sole contribution that each
corresponding <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variable
(<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span>,
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span><span class="zSubscript">2</span>)
makes in predicting <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>. The coefficient
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">0</span>
indicates the amount by which to adjust all these values in order to
provide a final fit to the data (like the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept does in simple linear
regression).

Computer software does all the nitty-gritty work for you to find the
proper coefficients
(<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">0</span>,
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span>,
and so on) that fit the data best. The coefficients that Minitab settles
on to create the best-fitting model are the ones that, as a group,
minimize the sum of the squared residuals (sort of like the variance in
the data around the selected model). The equations for finding these
coefficients by hand are too unwieldy to include in this book; a
computer can do all the work for you. The results appear in the
regression output in Minitab. You can find the multiple regression
coefficients
(<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">0</span>,
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span>,
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">2</span>, .
. . ,
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">k</span>) on
the computer output under the column labeled
<span class="zCheltItalic">COEF.</span>

![computeroutput.eps](9780470543887/images/computeroutput_fmt.png) To
run a multiple regression analysis in Minitab, click on
Stat\>Regression\>Regression. Then choose the response variable
<span class="zCheltItalic">(y)</span> and click on Select. Then choose
your predictor variables (<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>
variables), and click Select. Click on OK, and the computer will carry
out the analysis.

For the plasma TV sales example from the previous sections, Figure 5-3
shows the multiple regression coefficients in the
<span class="zCheltItalic">COEF</span> column for the multiple
regression model. The first coefficient (5.257) is just the constant
term (or
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">0</span>
term) in the model and isn’t affiliated with any
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variable. This constant just sort of
goes along for the ride in the analysis; it’s the number that you tack
on the end to make the numbers work out right. The second coefficient in
the <span class="zCheltItalic">COEF</span> column is 0.162; this value
is the coefficient of the
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span> (TV
ad amount) term, also known as
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span>.
The third coefficient in the <span class="zCheltItalic">COEF</span>
column is 0.249, which is the value for
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">2</span> in
the multiple regression model and is the coefficient that goes with
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span><span class="zSubscript">2</span>
(newspaper ad amount).

<div class="story">

**Figure 5-3:** Regression output for the ads and plasma TV sales
example.

</div>

![466469-fg0503.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-fg0503_fmt.png)

Putting these coefficients into the multiple regression equation, you
see the regression equation is Sales = 5.267 + 0.162 (TV ads) + 0.249
(Newspaper ads), where sales are in millions of dollars and ad spending
is in thousands of dollars.

So you have your coefficients (no sweat, right?), but where do you go
from here? What does it all mean? The next section guides you through
interpretation.

Interpreting the coefficients

In simple linear regression (covered in Chapter 4), the coefficients
represent the slope and <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept of
the best-fitting line and are straightforward to interpret. The slope in
particular represents the change in <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>
due to a one-unit increase in <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>
