In this situation, the explanatory variable,
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>, is day, and the response variable,
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>, is the number of people who know
the secret. Looking at Figure 7-2, you can see a pattern between the
values of <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> and
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>. But this pattern isn’t linear. It
curves upward. If you tried to fit a line to this data set, how well
would it fit?

<div class="story">

**Figure 7-2:** A scatter-plot showing the spread of a secret over a
six-day period.

</div>

![466469-fg0702.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-fg0702_fmt.png)

To figure this out, look at the correlation coefficient between
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> and
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>, which is found on Figure 7-2 to be
0.906 (see Chapter 4 for more on correlation). You can interpret this
correlation as a strong, positive (uphill) linear relationship between
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> and
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>. However, in this case, the
correlation is misleading because the scatterplot appears to be curved.

![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png) If the
correlation looks good (close to +1 or –1), don’t stop there. As with
any regression analysis, it’s very important to take into account both
the scatterplot and the correlation when making a decision about how
well the model being considered would fit the data. The contradiction in
this example between the scatterplot and the correlation is a red flag
that a straight-line model isn’t the best idea.

![warning_bomb.eps](9780470543887/images/warning_bomb_fmt.png) The
correlation coefficient measures only the strength and direction of the
linear relationship between <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> and
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> (see Chapter 4). However, you may
run into situations (like the one shown in Figure 7-2) where a
correlation is strong, yet the scatterplot shows a curve would fit
better. Don’t rely solely on either the scatterplot or the correlation
coefficient alone to make your decision about whether to go ahead and
fit a straight line to your data.

The bottom line here is that fitting a line to data that appear to have
a curved pattern isn’t the way to go. Instead, explore models that have
curved patterns themselves.

The following sections address two major types of nonlinear (or curved)
models that are used to model curved data: polynomials (that are not
straight lines — that is, curves like quadratics or cubics), and
exponential models (that start out small and quickly increase, or the
other way around). Because the pattern of the data in Figure 7-2 starts
low and bends upward, the correct model to fit this data is an
exponential regression model. (This model is also appropriate for data
that start out high and bend down low.)

Handling Curves in the Road with Polynomials

One major family of nonlinear models is the
<span class="zCheltItalic">polynomial</span> family. You use these
models when a polynomial function (beyond a straight line) best
describes the curve in the data. (For example, the data may follow the
shape of a parabola, which is a second-degree polynomial.) You typically
use polynomial models when the data follow a pattern of curves going up
and down a certain number of times.

For example, suppose a doctor examines the occurrence of heart problems
in patients as it relates to their blood pressure. She finds that
patients with very low or very high blood pressure had a higher
occurrence of problems, while patients whose blood pressure fell in the
middle, constituting the normal range, had fewer problems. This pattern
of data has a U-shape, and a para-bola would fit this data well.

In this section, you see what a polynomial regression model is, how you
can search for a good-fitting polynomial for your data, and how you can
assess polynomial models.

Bringing back polynomials

You may recall from algebra that a
<span class="zCheltItalic">polynomial</span> is a sum of
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> terms raised to a variety of powers,
and each <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> is preceded by a constant
called the <span class="zCheltItalic">coefficient</span> of that term.
For example, the model <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> =
2<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> +
3<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span> +
6<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span><span class="zSuperscript">3</span>
is a polynomial. The general form for a polynomial regression model is
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> =
<span class="zSymbolMedium">β</span><span class="zSubscript">0</span> +
<span class="zSymbolMedium">β</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span><span class="zCheltItalic">x</span><span class="zSuperscript">1</span> +
<span class="zSymbolMedium">β</span><span class="zSubscript">2</span><span class="zCheltItalic">x</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span> +
<span class="zSymbolMedium">β</span><span class="zSubscript">3</span><span class="zCheltItalic">x</span><span class="zSuperscript">3</span> +
. . . +
<span class="zSymbolMedium">β</span><span class="zSubscript">k</span><span class="zCheltItalic">x</span><span class="zSuperscript">k</span> +
<span class="zSymbolMedium">ε</span>. Here,
<span class="zCheltItalic">k</span> represents the total number of terms
in the model. The <span class="zSymbolMedium">ε</span> represents the
error that occurs simply due to chance. (Not a bad kind of error, just
random fluctuations from a perfect model.)

Here are a few of the more common polynomials you run across when
analyzing data and fitting models. Remember, the simplest model that
fits is the one you use (don’t try to be a hero in statistics — save
that for Batman and Robin). The models I discuss in this book are some
of your old favorites from algebra: second-, third-, and fourth-degree
polynomials.

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png)
<span class="zCheltBold">Second-degree (or quadratic) polynomial:</span>
This model is called a <span class="zCheltItalic">second-degree</span>
(or <span class="zCheltItalic">quadratic</span>)
<span class="zCheltItalic">polynomial,</span> because the largest
exponent is 2. An example model is <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> =
2<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> +
3<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>.
A second-degree polynomial forms a parabola shape — either an
upside-down or right-side up bowl; it changes direction one time (see
Figure 7-3).

<div class="story">

**Figure 7-3:** Example of a second-degree polynomial.

</div>

![466469-fg0703.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-fg0703_fmt.png)

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png)
<span class="zCheltBold">Third-degree polynomial:</span> This model has
3 as the highest power of <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>. It
typically has a sideways S-shape, changing directions two times (see
Figure 7-4).

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png)
<span class="zCheltBold">Fourth-degree polynomial:</span> Fourth-degree
polynomials involve
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span><span class="zSuperscript">4</span>.
They typically change directions in curvature three times to look like
the letter W or the letter M, depending on whether they’re upside down
or right-side up (see Figure 7-5).

In general, if the largest exponent on the polynomial is
<span class="zCheltItalic">n</span>, the number of curve changes in the
graph is typically <span class="zCheltItalic">n</span> – 1. For more
information on graphs of polynomials, refer to your algebra textbook or
<span class="zCheltItalic">Algebra For Dummies</span> by Mary Jane
Sterling (Wiley).

<div class="story">

**Figure 7-4:** Example of a third-degree polynomial.

</div>

![466469-fg0704.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-fg0704_fmt.png)

![technicalstuff.eps](9780470543887/images/technicalstuff_fmt.png) The
nonlinear models in this chapter involve only one explanatory variable,
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>. You can include more explanatory
variables in a nonlinear regression, raising each separate variable to a
power, but those models are beyond the scope of this book. I give you
information on basic multiple regression models in Chapter 5.

<div class="story">

**Figure 7-5:** Example of a fourth-degree polynomial.

</div>

![466469-fg0705.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-fg0705_fmt.png)

Searching for the best polynomial model

![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png) When fitting a
polynomial regression model to your data, you always start with a
scatterplot so you can look for patterns; the scatterplot will give you
some idea of the type of model that may work. Always start with the
simplest model possible and work your way up as needed. Don’t plunge in
with a high-order polynomial regression model right off the bat. Here
are a couple of reasons why:

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png)
<span class="zCheltBold">High-order polynomials are hard to interpret,
and their models are complex.</span> For example, with a straight line,
you can interpret the values of the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-intercept and slope easily, but
interpreting a tenth-degree polynomial is difficult (and that’s putting
it mildly).

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png)
<span class="zCheltBold">High-order polynomials tend to cause
overfitting.</span> If you’re fitting the model as close as you can to
every single point in a data set, your model may not hold for a new data
set, meaning that your estimates for <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>
could be way off.

![computeroutput.eps](9780470543887/images/computeroutput_fmt.png) To
fit a polynomial to a data set in Minitab, go to
Stat\>Regression\>Fitted Line Plot\> and click on the type of regression
model you want: linear, quadratic, or cubic. (It doesn’t go beyond a
third-degree polynomial, but these options should cover 90 percent of
the cases where a polynomial is appropriate.) Click on the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> variable from the left-hand box, and
click Select; this variable will appear in the Response
<span class="zCheltItalic">(y)</span> box. Click on the
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variable from the left-hand box, and
click Select; it will appear in the Predictor
<span class="zCheltItalic">(x)</span> box. Click OK.

Following are steps that you can use to see if a polynomial fits your
data. (Statistical software can jump in and fit the models for you after
you tell it which ones to fit.)

<span class="zCheltBold"> 1. Make a scatterplot of your data, and look
for any patterns, such as a straight line or a curve.</span>

<span class="zCheltBold"> 2. If the data resemble a straight line, try
to fit a first-degree polynomial (straight line) to the data first:
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">y</span><span class="zCheltBold">
=
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">b</span><span class="zCheltBold"><span class="zSubscript">0</span> +
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">b</span><span class="zCheltBold"><span class="zSubscript">1</span></span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">x</span><span class="zCheltBold">.</span>

If the scatterplot doesn’t show a linear pattern, or if the correlation
isn’t close to +1 or –1, move to step three.

<span class="zCheltBold"> 3. If the data resemble the shape of a
parabola, try to fit a second-degree polynomial:
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">y</span><span class="zCheltBold">
=
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">b</span><span class="zCheltBold"><span class="zSubscript">0</span> +
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">b</span><span class="zCheltBold"><span class="zSubscript">1</span></span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">x</span><span class="zCheltBold"> +
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">b</span><span class="zCheltBold"><span class="zSubscript">2</span></span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">x</span><span class="zCheltBold"><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>.</span>

If the data fit the model well, stop here and refer to the later section
“Assessing the fit of a polynomial model.” If the model still doesn’t
fit well, move to step four.

<span class="zCheltBold"> 4. If you see curvature that’s more complex
than a parabola, try to fit a third-degree polynomial:
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">y</span><span class="zCheltBold">
=
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">b</span><span class="zCheltBold"><span class="zSubscript">0</span> +
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">b</span><span class="zCheltBold"><span class="zSubscript">1</span></span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">x</span><span class="zCheltBold"> +
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">b</span><span class="zCheltBold"><span class="zSubscript">2</span></span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">x</span><span class="zCheltBold"><span class="zSuperscript">2</span> +
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">b</span><span class="zCheltBold"><span class="zSubscript">3</span></span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">x</span><span class="zCheltBold"><span class="zSuperscript">3</span>.</span>

If the data fit the model well, stop here and refer to the later section
“Assessing the fit of a polynomial model.” If the model still doesn’t
fit well, move to step five.

<span class="zCheltBold"> 5. Continue trying to fit higher-order
polynomials until you find one that fits or until the order of the
polynomial (largest exponent) simply gets too large to find a reliable
pattern.</span>

![tip.eps](9780470543887/images/tip_fmt.png) How large is too large?
Typically, if you can’t fit the data by the time the degree of the
polynomial reaches three, then perhaps a different type of model would
work better. Or you may determine that you observe too much scatter and
haphazard behavior in the data to try to fit any model.

Minitab can do each of these steps for you up to degree two (that’s step
three); from there, you need a more sophisticated statistical software
program, such as SAS or SPSS. However, most of the models you need to
fit go up to the second-degree polynomials.

Using a second-degree polynomial to pass the quiz

The first step in fitting a polynomial model is to graph the data in a
scatterplot and see whether the data fall into a particular pattern.
Many different types of polynomials exist to fit data that have a curved
type of pattern. One of the most common patterns found in curved data is
the quadratic pattern, or second-degree polynomial, which goes up and
comes back down, or goes down and comes back up, as the
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> values move from left to right (see
Figure 7-3). The second-degree polynomial is the simplest and most
commonly used polynomial beyond the straight line, so it deserves
special consideration. (After you master the basic ideas based on
second-degree polynomials, you can apply them to polynomials with higher
powers.)

Suppose 20 students take a statistics quiz. You record the quiz scores
(which have a maximum score of ten) and the number of hours students
reported studying for the quiz. You can see the results in Figure 7-6.

Looking at Figure 7-6, it appears that three camps of students are in
this class. Camp 1, on the left end of the
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>-axis, understands the stuff (as
reflected in their higher scores) but didn’t have to study hardly at all
(see that their study time on the
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>-axis is low). Camp 3 also did very
well on the quiz (as indicated by their high quiz scores) but had to
study a great deal to get those grades (as seen on the far-right end of
the <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>-axis). The students in the
middle, Camp 2, didn’t seem to fare well.

All in all, based on the scatterplot, it does appear that study time may
explain quiz scores on some level in a way indicative of a second-degree
polynomial. So a quadratic regression model may fit this data.

<div class="story">

**Figure 7-6:** Scatterplot showing study time and quiz scores.

</div>

![466469-fg0706.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-fg0706_fmt.png)

![warning_bomb.eps](9780470543887/images/warning_bomb_fmt.png) Suppose a
data analyst (not you!) doesn’t know about polynomial regression and
just tries to fit a straight line to the quiz-score data. In Figure 7-7,
you can see the data and the straight line that he tried to fit to the
data. The correlation as shown in the figure is –0.033, which is
basically zero. This correlation means that no linear relationship lies
between <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> and
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>. It doesn’t mean that no
relationship is present at all, just that it’s not a linear relationship
(see Chapter 4 for more on linear relationships). So trying to fit a
straight line here was indeed a bad idea.

<div class="story">

**Figure 7-7:** Trying to fit a straight line to quadratic data.

</div>

![466469-fg0707.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-fg0707_fmt.png)

After you know that a quadratic polynomial seems to be a good fit for
the data, the next challenge is finding the equation for that particular
parabola that fits the data from among all the possible parabolas out
there.

Remember from algebra that the general equation of a parabola is
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> =
<span class="zCheltItalic">ax</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span> +
<span class="zCheltItalic">bx</span> +
<span class="zCheltItalic">c</span>. Now you have to find the values of
<span class="zCheltItalic">a</span>,
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span>, and
<span class="zCheltItalic">c</span> that create the best-fitting
parabola to the data (just like you find the
<span class="zCheltItalic">a</span> and the
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span> that create the best-fitting line to
data in a linear regression model). That’s the object of any regression
analysis.

Suppose that you fit a quadratic regression model to the quiz-score data
by using Minitab (see the Minitab output in Figure 7-8 and the
instructions for using Minitab to fit this model in the previous
section). On the top line of the output, you can see that the equation
of the best-fitting parabola is quiz score = 9.82 – 6.15
<span class="Times-Sign">\*</span> (study time) + 1.00
<span class="Times-Sign">\*</span> (study
time)<span class="zSuperscript">2</span>. (Note that
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> is quiz score and
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> is study time in this example
because you’re using study time to predict quiz score.)

<div class="story">

**Figure 7-8:** Minitab output for fitting a parabola to the quiz-score
data.

</div>

![466469-fg0708.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-fg0708_fmt.png)

The scatterplot of the quiz-score data and the parabola that was fit to
the data via the regression model is shown in Figure 7-9. From algebra,
you may remember that a positive coefficient on the quadratic term (here
<span class="zCheltItalic">a</span> = 1.00) means the bowl is right-side
up, which you can see is the case here.

Looking at Figure 7-9, it appears that the quadratic model fits this
data pretty well, because the data fall close to the curve that Minitab
found. However, data analysts can’t live by scatterplots alone, so the
next section helps you figure out how to assess the fit of a polynomial
model in more detail.

<div class="story">

**Figure 7-9:** The parabola appears to fit the quiz-score data nicely.

</div>

![466469-fg0709.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-fg0709_fmt.png)

Assessing the fit of a polynomial model

You make a scatterplot of your data, and you see a curved pattern. So
you use polynomial regression to fit a model to the data; the model
appears to fit well because the points follow closely to the curve
Minitab found, but don’t stop there. To make sure your results can be
generalized to the population from which your data was taken, you need
to do a little more checking beyond just the graph to make sure your
model fits well.

To assess the fit of any model beyond the usual suspect, a scatterplot
of the data, you look at two additional items, typically in this order:
the value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">R</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
adjusted and the residual plots.

![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png) All three
assessments must agree before you can conclude that the model fits. If
the three assessments don’t agree, you’ll likely have to use a different
model to fit the data besides a polynomial model, or you’ll have to
change the units of the data to help a polynomial model fit better.
However, the latter fix is outside the scope of Stats II, and you
probably won’t encounter that situation.

In the following sections, you take a deeper look at the value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">R</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
adjusted and the residual plots and figure out how you can use them to
assess your model’s fit. (You can find more info on the scatterplot in
the section “Starting out with Scatterplots” earlier in this chapter.)

Examining R<span class="zSuperscript">2</span> and
R<span class="zSuperscript">2</span> adjusted

Finding
<span class="zCheltItalic">R</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>,
the <span class="zCheltItalic">coefficient of determination</span> (see
Chapter 5 for full details), is like the day of reckoning for any model.
You can find
<span class="zCheltItalic">R</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
on your regression output, listed as “R-Sq” right under the portion of
the output where the coefficients of the variables appear. Figure 7-8
shows the Minitab output for the quiz-score data example; the value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">R</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
in this case is 91.7 percent.

The value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">R</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
tells you what percentage of the variation in the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-values the model can explain. To
interpret this percentage, note
<span class="zCheltItalic">R</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
is the square of r, the correlation coefficient (see Chapter 5). Because
values of r beyond ± 0.80 are considered to be good,
<span class="zCheltItalic">R</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
values above 0.64 are considered pretty good also, especially for models
with only one <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variable.

You can consider values of
<span class="zCheltItalic">R</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
over 80 percent good, and values under 60 percent aren’t good. Those in
between I’d consider so-so; they could be better. (This assessment is
just my rule of thumb; opinions may vary a bit from one statistician to
another.)

However, you can find such a thing in statistics as too many variables
spoiling the pot. Every time you add another
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variable to a regression model, the
value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">R</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
automatically goes up, whether the variable really helps or not (this is
just a mathematical fact). Right beside
<span class="zCheltItalic">R</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
on the computer output from any regression analysis is the value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">R</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
adjusted, which adjusts the value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">R</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
down a notch for each variable (and each power of each variable) entered
into the model. You can’t just throw a ton of variables into a model
whose tiny increments all add up to an acceptable
<span class="zCheltItalic">R</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
value without taking a hit for throwing everything in the model but the
kitchen sink.

![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png) To be on the safe
side, you should always use
<span class="zCheltItalic">R</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
adjusted to assess the fit of your model, rather than
<span class="zCheltItalic">R</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>,
especially if you have more than one <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>
variable in your model (or more than one power of an
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variable). The values of
<span class="zCheltItalic">R</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
and
<span class="zCheltItalic">R</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
adjusted are close if you have only a couple of different variables (or
powers) in the model, but as the number of variables (or powers)
increases, so does the gap between
<span class="zCheltItalic">R</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
and
<span class="zCheltItalic">R</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
adjusted. In that case,
<span class="zCheltItalic">R</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
adjusted is the most fair and consistent coefficient to use to examine
model fit.

In the quiz-score example (analysis shown in Figure 7-8), the value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">R</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
adjusted is 90.7 percent, which is still a very high value, meaning that
the quadratic model fits this data very well. (See Chapter 6 for more on
<span class="zCheltItalic">R</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
and
<span class="zCheltItalic">R</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
adjusted.)

Checking the residuals

You’ve looked at the scatterplot of your data and the value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">R</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
is high. What’s next? Now you examine how well the model fits each
individual point in the data to make sure you can’t find any spots where
the model is way off or places where you missed another underlying
pattern in the data.

A <span class="zCheltItalic">residual</span> is the amount of error, or
leftover, that occurs when you fit a model to a data set. The residuals
are the distances between the predicted values in the model and the
observed values of the data themselves. For each observed
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-value in the data set, you also have
a predicted value from the model, typically called
<span class="zCheltItalic">y-hat,</span> denoted ŷ. The residual is the
difference between the values of <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> and
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-hat. Each
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-value in the data set has a
residual; you examine all the residuals together as a group, looking for
patterns or unusually high values (indicating a big difference between
the observed <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> and the predicted
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> at that point; see Chapter 4 for the
full info on residuals and their plots).

In order for the model to fit well, the residuals need to meet two
conditions:

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png)
<span class="zCheltBold">The residuals are independent.</span> The
independence of residuals means that you don’t see any pattern as you
plot the residuals. The residuals don’t affect each other and should be
random.

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png)
<span class="zCheltBold">The residuals have a normal distribution
centered at zero, and the standardized residuals follow suit.</span>
Having a normal distribution with mean zero means that most of the
residuals should be centered around zero, with fewer of them occurring
the farther from zero you get. You should observe about as many
residuals above the zero line as below it. If the residuals are
standardized, this means that as a group their standard deviation is 1;
you should expect about 95 percent of them to lie between –2 and +2,
following the 68-95-99.7 Rule (see your Stats I text).

You determine whether or not these two conditions are met for the
residuals by using a series of four graphs called
<span class="zCheltItalic">residual plots.</span> Most statisticians
prefer to standardize the residuals (meaning they convert them to
<span class="zCheltItalic">Z</span>-scores by subtracting their mean and
dividing by their standard deviation) before looking at them, because
then they can compare the residuals with values on a
<span class="zCheltItalic">Z</span>-distribution. If you take this step
also, you can ask Minitab to give you a series of four standardized
residual plots with which to check the conditions. (See Chapter 4 for
full details on standardized residuals and residual plots.)

Figure 7-10 shows the standardized residual plots for the quadratic
model, using the quiz-score data from the previous sections.

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) The upper-left plot shows
that the standardized residuals resemble a normal distribution because
your data and the normal distribution match up pretty well, point for
point.

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) The upper-right plot shows
that most of the standardized residuals fall between –2 and +2 (see
Chapter 4 for more on standardized residuals).

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) The lower-left plot shows
that the residuals bear some resemblance to a normal distribution.

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) The lower-right plot
demonstrates how the residuals have no pattern. They appear to occur at
random.

When taken together, all these plots suggest that the conditions on the
residual are met to apply the selected quadratic regression model.

<div class="story">

**Figure 7-10:** Standard-ized residual plots for the quiz-score data,
using the quadratic model.

</div>

![466469-fg0710.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-fg0710_fmt.png)

Making predictions

After you’ve found the model that fits well, you can use that model to
make predictions for <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> given
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>: Simply plug in the desired
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>-value, and out comes your predicted
value for <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>. (Make sure any values you
plug in for <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> occur within the range
of where data were collected; if not, you can’t guarantee the model
holds.)

Returning to the quiz-score data from previous sections, can you use
study time to predict quiz score by using a quadratic regression model?
By looking at the scatterplot and the value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">R</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
adjusted (review Figures 7-8 and 7-9, respectively), you can see that
the quadratic regression model appears to fit the data well. (Isn’t it
nice when you find something that fits?) The residual plots in Figure
7-10 indicate that the conditions seem to be met to fit this model; you
can find no major patterns in the residuals, they appear to center at 1,
and most of them stay within the normal boundaries of standardized
residuals of –2 and +2.

Considering all this evidence together, study time does appear to have a
quadratic relationship with quiz score in this case. You can now use the
model to make estimates of quiz score given study time. For example,
because the model (shown in Figure 7-8) is
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> = 9.82 –
6.15<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> +
1.00<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>,
if your study time is 5.5 hours, then your estimated quiz score is 9.82
– 6.15 <span class="Times-Sign">\*</span> 5.5 + 1.00
<span class="Times-Sign">\*</span> 5.52 = 9.82 – 33.83 + 30.25 = 6.25.
This value makes sense according to what you see on the graph in Figure
7-6 if you look at the place where <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> =
5.5; the <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-values are in the vicinity
of 6 to 7.

![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png) As with any
regression model, you can’t estimate the value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> for
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>-values outside the range of where
data was collected. If you try to do this, you commit a no-no called
extrapolation. It refers to trying to make predictions beyond where your
data allows you to. You can’t be sure that the model you fit to your
data actually continues ad infinitum for any old value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>. In the quiz-score example (see
Figure 7-6), you really can’t estimate quiz scores for study times
higher than six hours using this model because the data doesn’t show
anyone studying more than six hours. The model likely levels off after
six hours to a score of ten, indicating that studying more than six
hours is overkill. (You didn’t hear that from me though!)

Going Up? Going Down? Go Exponential!

Exponential models work well in situations where a
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> variable either increases or
decreases exponentially over time. That means the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> variable either starts out slow and
then increases at a faster and faster rate or starts out high and
decreases at a faster and faster rate.

Many processes in the real world behave like an exponential model: for
example, the change in population size over time, average household
incomes over time, the length of time a product lasts, or the level of
patience one has as the number of statistics homework problems goes up.

In this section, you familiarize yourself with the exponential
regression model and see how to use it to fit data that either rise or
fall at an exponential rate. You also discover how to build and assess
exponential regression models in order to make accurate predictions for
a response variable <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>, using an
explanatory variable <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>.

Recollecting exponential models

Exponential models have the form <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> =
<span class="zSymbolMedium">αβ</span><span class="zSuperscript">x</span>.
These models involve a constant, <span class="zSymbolMedium">β</span>,
raised to higher and higher powers of
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> multiplied by a constant,
<span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span>. The constant
<span class="zSymbolMedium">β</span> represents the amount of curvature
in the model. The constant <span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span> is a
multiplier in front of the model that shows where the model crosses the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-axis (because when
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> = 0,
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> =
<span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span> <span class="Times-Sign">\*</span>
1).

![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png) An exponential
model generally looks like the upper part of a hyperbola (remember those
from advanced algebra?). A hyperbola is a curve that crosses the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-axis at a point and curves downward
toward zero or starts at some point and curves upward to infinity (see
Figure 7-11 for examples). If β is greater than 1 in an exponential
model, the graph curves upward toward infinity. If β is less than 1, the
graph curves downward toward zero. All exponential models stay above the
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>-axis.

For example, the model <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> = 1
<span class="Times-Sign">\*</span> 3<span class="zSuperscript">x</span>
is an exponential model. Here, suppose you make
<span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span> = 1, indicating that the model
crosses the <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-axis at 1 (because
plugging <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> = 0 into the equation gives
you 1). You set the value of <span class="zSymbolMedium">β</span> equal
to 3, indicating that you want a bit of curvature to this model. The
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-values curve upward quickly from the
point (0, 1). For example, when <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> = 1,
you get 1 <span class="Times-Sign">\*</span>
3<span class="zSuperscript">1</span> = 3; for
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> = 2, you get 1
<span class="Times-Sign">\*</span> 3<span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
= 9; for <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> = 3, you get 1
<span class="Times-Sign">\*</span> 3<span class="zSuperscript">3</span>
= 27; and so on. Figure 7-11a shows a graph of this model. Notice the
huge scale needed on the <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-axis when
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> is only 10.

Now suppose you let <span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span> = 1 and
<span class="zSymbolMedium">β</span> = 0.5. These values give you the
model <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> = 1
<span class="Times-Sign">\*</span>
0.5<span class="zSuperscript">x</span>. This model takes 0.5 (a fraction
between 0 and 1) to higher and higher powers starting at 1 ∗ 0.50 = 1,
which makes the <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-values smaller and
smaller, never reaching zero but always getting closer. (For example,
0.5 to the second power is 0.25, which is less than 0.50, and 0.50 to
the tenth power is 0.00098.) Figure 7-11b shows a graph of this model.

<div class="story">

**Figure 7-11:** The exponential regression model for different values
of <span class="zSymbolMedium">β</span>.

</div>

![466469-fg0711.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-fg0711_fmt.png)

Searching for the best exponential model

Finding the best-fitting exponential model requires a bit of a twist
compared to finding the best-fitting line by using simple linear
regression (see Chapter 4). Because fitting a straight-line model is
much easier than fitting an exponential model directly from data, you
transform the data into something for which a line fits. Then you fit a
straight-line model to that transformed data. Finally you undo the
transformation, getting you back to an exponential model.

For the transformation, you use
<span class="zCheltItalic">logarithms</span> because they’re the inverse
of exponentials. But before you start sweating, don’t worry; these math
gymnastics aren’t something you do by hand — the computer does most of
the grunt work for you.

The exponential model looks like this (if you’re using base 10):
![466469-eq0701.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0701_fmt.png); note
the equation of the line is in the exponent. Follow these steps for
fitting an exponential model to your data and using it to make
predictions:

![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png) The math magic
used in these steps is courtesy of the definition of logarithm, which
says ![466469-eq0703.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0703_fmt.png).
Suppose you have the equation
log<span class="zSubscript">10</span><span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>
= 2 + 3<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>.

If you take ten to the power of each side, you get
![466469-eq0704.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0704_fmt.png). By the
definition of logarithm, the tens cancel out on the left side and you
get <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> =
10<span class="zSuperscript">2+3<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span></span>.
This model is exponential because <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> is
in the exponent. You can take step two up another notch to include the
general form of the straight line model
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> =
b<span class="zSubscript">0</span> +
b<span class="zSubscript">1</span><span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>.
Using the definition of logarithm on this line, you get
![466469-eq0705.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0705_fmt.png).

<span class="zCheltBold"> 1. Make a scatterplot of the data and see
whether the data appears to have a curved pattern that resembles an
exponential curve.</span>

If the data follows an exponential curve, proceed to step two;
otherwise, consider alternative models (such as multiple regression in
Chapter 5).

Chapter 4 tells you how to make a scatterplot in Minitab. For more
details on what shape to look for, refer to the previous section.

<span class="zCheltBold"> 2. Use Minitab to fit a line to the
log(</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">y</span><span class="zCheltBold">)
data.</span>

![computeroutput.eps](9780470543887/images/computeroutput_fmt.png) In
Minitab, you go to the regression model (curve fit). Under Options,
select Logten of <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>. Then select Using
scale of logten to give you the proper units for the graph.

Understanding the basic idea of what Minitab does during this step is
important; being able to calculate it by hand isn’t. Here’s what Minitab
does:

1\. Minitab applies the log (base 10) to the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-values. For example, if
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> is equal to 100,
log<span class="zSubscript">10</span>100 equals 2 (because 10 to the
second power equals 100). Note that if the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-values fell close to an exponential
model before, the log(<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>) values will
fall close to a straight-line model. This phenomenon occurs because the
logarithm is the inverse of the exponential function, so they basically
cancel each other out and leave you with a straight line.

2\. Minitab fits a straight line to the
log(<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>) values by using simple linear
regression (see Chapter 4). The equation of the best-fitting straight
line for the log(<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>) data is
log(<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>) =
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">0</span> +
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span><span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>.
Minitab passes this model on to you in its output, and you take it from
there.

<span class="zCheltBold"> 3. Transform the model back to an exponential
model by starting with the straight-line model,
log(</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">y</span><span class="zCheltBold">)
=
<span class="zCheltBoldItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">0</span> +
<span class="zCheltBoldItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span></span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">x</span><span class="zCheltBold">,
that was fit to the
log<span class="zSubscript">10</span>(</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">y</span><span class="zCheltBold">)
data and then applying ten to the power of the left side of the equation
and ten to the power of the right side.</span>

By the definition of logarithm, you get
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> on the left side of the model and
ten to the power of
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">0</span> +
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span><span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>
on the right side. The resulting exponential model for
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> is
![466469-eq0702.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0702_fmt.png).

<span class="zCheltBold"> 4. Use the exponential model in step three to
make predictions for
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">y</span><span class="zCheltBold">
(your original variable) by plugging your desired value of
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">x</span><span class="zCheltBold">
into the model.</span>

Only plug in values for <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> that are in
the range of where the data are located.

<span class="zCheltBold"> 5. Assess the fit of the model by looking at
the scatterplot of the
log(</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">y</span><span class="zCheltBold">)
data, checking out the value of
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">R</span><span class="zCheltBold"><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
(adjusted) for the straight-line model for
log(</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">y</span><span class="zCheltBold">),
and checking the residual plots for the
log(</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">y</span><span class="zCheltBold">)
data.</span>

The techniques and criteria you use to do this are the same as those I
discuss in the previous section “Assessing the fit of a polynomial
model.”

If these steps seem dubious to you, stick with me. The example in the
next section lets you see each step firsthand, which helps a great deal.
In the end, actually finding predictions by using an exponential model
is a lot easier to do than it is to explain.

Spreading secrets at an exponential rate

Often, the best way to figure something out is to see it in action.
Using the secret-spreading example from Figure 7-2, you can work through
the series of steps from the preceding section to find the best-fitting
exponential model and use it to make predictions.

Step one: Check the scatterplot

Your goal in step one is to make a scatterplot of the secret-spreading
data and determine whether the data resemble the curved function of an
exponential model. Figure 7-2 shows the data for the spread of a number
of people knowing the secret, as a function of the number of days. You
can see that the number of people who know the secret starts out small,
but then as more and more people tell more and more people, the number
grows quickly until the secret isn’t a secret anymore. This is a good
situation for an exponential model, due to the amount of upward
curvature in this graph.

Step two: Let Minitab do its thing to log(y)

In step two, you let Minitab find the best-fitting line to the
log(<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>) data (see the section
“Searching for the best exponential model” to find out how to do this in
Minitab). The output for the analysis of the secret-spreading data is in
Figure 7-12; you can see that the best-fitting line is
log(<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>) = –0.19 + 0.28
<span class="Times-Sign">\*</span> <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>,
where <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> is the number of people
knowing the secret and <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> is the number
of days.

<div class="story">

**Figure 7-12:** Minitab fits a line to the
log(<span class="zUnivItalic">y</span>) for the secret-spreading data.

</div>

![466469-fg0712.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-fg0712_fmt.png)

Step three: Go exponential

After you have your Minitab output, you’re ready for step three. You
transform the model log(<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>) = –0.19 +
0.28 <span class="Times-Sign">\*</span>
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> into a model for
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> by taking 10 to the power of the
left-hand side and 10 to the power of the right-hand side. Transforming
the log(<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>) equation for the
secret-spreading data, you get <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> =
10<span class="zSuperscript">–0.19 +
0.28<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span></span>.

Step four: Make predictions

By using the exponential model from step three, you can move on to step
four: Make predictions for appropriate values of
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> (within the range of where data was
collected). Continuing to use the secret-spreading data, suppose you
want to estimate the number of people knowing the secret on day five
(see Figure 7-2). Just plug <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> = 5 into
the exponential model to get <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> =
10<span class="zSuperscript">–0.19 + 0.28
</span><span class="Times-Sign">\*</span><span class="zSuperscript">
5</span> = 10<span class="zSuperscript">1.21</span> = 16.22. Looking
back at Figure 7-2, you can see that this estimate falls right in line
with the data on the graph.

Step five: Assess the fit of your exponential model

Now that you’ve found the best-fitting exponential model, you have the
worst behind you. You’ve arrived at step five and are ready to further
assess the model fit (beyond the scatterplot of the original data) to
make sure no major problems arise.

In general, to assess the fit of an exponential model, you’re really
looking at the straight-line fit of
log(<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>). Just use these three items (in
any order) in the same way as described in the earlier section
“Assessing the fit of a polynomial model”:

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png)
<span class="zCheltBold">Check the scatterplot of the
log(</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">y</span><span class="zCheltBold">)
data to see how well it resembles a straight line.</span> You assess the
fit of the log(<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>) for the
secret-spreading data first through the scatterplot shown in Figure
7-13. The scatterplot shows that the model appears to fit the data well,
because the points are scattered in a tight pattern around a straight
line.

<span class="Icon-w-3-lines-of-text-baseline">![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png)</span>
During this process the data were transformed also. You started with
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> and
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> data, and now you have
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> and
log(<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>) for your data. You see
<span class="zCheltItalic">x, y,</span> and
log(<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>) for the secret-spreading data
in Table 7-2.

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png)
<span class="zCheltBold">Examine the value of
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">R</span><span class="zCheltBold"><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
adjusted for the model of the best-fitting line for
log(</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">y</span><span class="zCheltBold">),
done by Minitab.</span> The value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">R</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
adjusted for this model is found in Figure 7-13 to be 91.6 percent. This
value also indicates a good fit because it’s very close to 100 percent.
Therefore, 91.6 percent of the variation in the number of people knowing
the secret is explained by how many days it has been since the
secret-spreading started. (Makes sense.)

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png)
<span class="zCheltBold">Look at the residual plots from the fit of a
line to the
log(</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">y</span><span class="zCheltBold">)
data.</span> The residual plots from this analysis (see Figure 7-14)
show no major departures from the conditions that the errors are
independent and have a normal distribution. Note that the histogram in
the lower-left corner doesn’t look all that bell-shaped, but you don’t
have a lot of data in this example, and the rest of the residual plots
seem okay. So, you have little cause to really worry.

<div class="Basic-Text-Frame">

Chapter 8

Yes, No, Maybe So: Making Predictions by Using Logistic Regression

In This Chapter

![arrow](9780470543887/images/arrow.png) Knowing when logistic
regression is appropriate

![arrow](9780470543887/images/arrow.png) Building logistic regression
models for yes or no data

![arrow](9780470543887/images/arrow.png) Checking model conditions and
making the right conclusions

<span class="char-style-override-1">E</span>veryone (even yours truly)
tries to make predictions about whether or not a certain event is going
to happen. For example, what’s the chance it’s going to rain this
weekend? What are your team’s chances of winning the next game? What’s
the chance that I’ll have complications during this surgery? These
predictions are often based on
<span class="zCheltItalic">probability,</span> the long-term percentage
of time an event is expected to happen.

In the end, you want to estimate <span class="zCheltItalic">p,</span>
the probability of an event occurring. In this chapter, you see how to
build and test models for <span class="zCheltItalic">p</span> based on a
set of explanatory <span class="zCheltItalic">(x)</span> variables. This
technique is called <span class="zCheltItalic">logistic
regression,</span> and in this chapter, I explain how to put it to use.

Understanding a Logistic Regression Model

In a logistic regression, you’re estimating the probability that an
event occurs for a randomly selected individual versus the probability
that the event doesn’t occur. In essence, you’re looking at yes or no
data: yes it occurred (probability =
<span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>); or no, it didn’t occur
(probability = 1 – <span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>). Yes or no data
that come from a random sample have a binomial distribution with
probability of success (the event occurring) equal to
<span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>.

In the binomial problems you saw in Stats I, you had a sample of size
<span class="zCheltItalic">n</span> trials, you had yes or no data, and
you had a probability of success on each trial, denoted by
<span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>. In your Stats I course, for any
binomial problem the value of <span class="zCheltItalic">p</span> was
somehow given to be a certain value, like a fair coin has probability p
= 0.50 for coming up heads. But in Stats II, you operate under the much
more realistic scenario that it’s not. In fact, because
<span class="zCheltItalic">p</span> isn’t known, your job is to estimate
what it is and use a model to do that.

![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png) To estimate
<span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>, the chance of an event occurring,
you need data that come in the form of yes or no, indicating whether or
not the event occurred for each individual in the data set.

Because yes or no data don’t have a normal distribution, which is a
condition needed for other types of regression, you need a new type of
regression model to do this job; that model is
<span class="zCheltItalic">logistic regression.</span>

How is logistic regression different from other regressions?

You use logistic regression when you use a quantitative variable to
predict or guess the outcome of some categorical variable with only two
outcomes (for example, using barometric pressure to predict whether or
not it will rain).

A logistic regression model ultimately gives you an estimate for
<span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>, the probability that a particular
outcome will occur in a yes or no situation (for example, the chance
that it will rain versus not). The estimate is based on information from
one or more explanatory variables; you can call them
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span>,
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span><span class="zSubscript">2</span>,
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span><span class="zSubscript">3</span>, .
. .
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span><span class="zSubscript">k</span>.
(For example,
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span> =
humidity,
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span><span class="zSubscript">2</span> =
barometric pressure,
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span><span class="zSubscript">3</span> =
cloud cover, . . . and
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span><span class="zSubscript">k</span> =
wind speed.)

Because you’re trying to use one variable
<span class="zCheltItalic">(x)</span> to make a prediction for another
variable <span class="zCheltItalic">(y)</span>, you may think about
using regression — and you would be right. However, you have many types
of regression to choose from, and you need to determine what kind is
most appropriate here. You need the type of regression that uses a
quantitative variable <span class="zCheltItalic">(x)</span> to predict
the outcome of some categorical variable
<span class="zCheltItalic">(y)</span> that has only two outcomes (yes or
no).

So being the good Stats II student that you are, you go to your trusty
list of statistical techniques, and you look under regression — and
immediately see more than one type.

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) You see simple linear
regression. No, you use that when you have one quantitative variable
predicting another (see Chapter 4).

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) Multiple regression? No,
that method just expands simple linear regression to add more
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variables (see Chapter 5).

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) Nonlinear regression? Well
no, that still works with two quantitative variables; it’s just that the
data form a curve, not a line.

But then you come across logistic regression, and . . . eureka! You see
that logistic regression handles situations where the
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variable is numerical and the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> variable is categorical with two
possible categories. Just what you’re looking for!

![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png) Logistic
regression, in essence, estimates the probability of
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> being in one category or the other,
based on the value of some quantitative variable,
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>. For example, suppose you want to
predict someone’s height based on gender. Because gender is a
categorical variable, you use logistic regression to make these
predictions. Suppose a 1 indicates a male. People who receive a
probability of more than 0.5 of being male (based on their heights) are
predicted to be male, and people who receive a probability of less than
0.5 of being male (based on their heights) are predicted to be female.

![tip.eps](9780470543887/images/tip_fmt.png) In this chapter, I present
only the case where you use one explanatory variable to predict the
outcome. You can extend the ideas in exactly the same way as you can
extend the simple linear regression model to a multiple regression
model.

Using an S-curve to estimate probabilities

In a simple linear regression model, the general form of a straight line
is <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> =
<span class="zSymbolMedium">β</span><span class="zSubscript">0</span> +
<span class="zSymbolMedium">β</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span><span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>
and <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> is a quantitative variable. In
the logistic regression model, the <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>
variable is categorical, not quantitative. What you’re estimating,
however, is not which category the individual lies in, but rather what
the probability is that the individual lies in a certain category. So,
the model for logistic regression is based on estimating this
probability, called <span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>.

If you were to estimate <span class="zCheltItalic">p</span> using a
simple linear regression model, you may think you should try to fit a
straight line, <span class="zCheltItalic">p</span> =
<span class="zSymbolMedium">β</span><span class="zSubscript">0</span> +
<span class="zSymbolMedium">β</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span><span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>.
However, it doesn’t make sense to use a straight line to estimate the
probability of an event occurring based on another variable, due to the
following reasons:

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png)
<span class="zCheltBold">The estimated values of
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">p</span><span class="zCheltBold">
can never be outside of \[0, 1\], which goes against the idea of a
straight line (a straight line continues on in both directions).</span>

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) <span class="zCheltBold">It
doesn’t make sense to force the values of
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">p</span><span class="zCheltBold">
to increase in a linear way based on
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">x</span><span class="zCheltBold">.</span>
For example, an event may occur very frequently with a range of large
values of <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> and very frequently with a
range of small values of <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>, with very
little chance of the event happening in an area in between. This type of
model would have a U shape rather than a straight-line shape.

To come up with a more appropriate model for
<span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>, statisticians created a new
function of <span class="zCheltItalic">p</span> whose graph is called an
S-curve. The <span class="zCheltItalic">S-curve</span> is a function
that involves <span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>, but it also involves
<span class="zCheltItalic">e</span> (the natural logarithm) as well as a
ratio of two functions.

The values of the S-curve always fit between 0 and 1, which allows the
probability, <span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>, to change from low to
high or high to low, according to a curve that’s shaped like an S. The
general form of the logistic regression model based on an S-curve is
![466469-eq0801.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0801_fmt.png).

Interpreting the coefficients of the logistic regression model

![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png) The sign on the
parameter
<span class="zSymbolMedium">β</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span>
tells you the direction of the S-curve. If
<span class="zSymbolMedium">β</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span> is
positive, the S-curve goes from low to high (see Figure 8-1a); if
<span class="zSymbolMedium">β</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span> is
negative, the S-curve goes from high to low (Figure 8-1b).

<div class="story">

**Figure 8-1:** Two basic types of S-curves.

</div>

![466469-fg0801.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-fg0801_fmt.png)

The magnitude of
<span class="zSymbolMedium">β</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span>
(indicated by its absolute value) tells you how much curvature is in the
model. High values indicate a steep curvature, and low values indicate
gradual curvature. The parameter
<span class="zSymbolMedium">β</span><span class="zSubscript">0</span>
just shifts the S-curve to the proper location to fit your data. It
shows you the cutoff point where
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>-values change from high to low
probability and vice versa.

The logistic regression model in action

Often, the best way to figure something out is to see it in action. In
this section, I give you an example of a situation where you can use a
logistic regression model to estimate a probability. (I expand on this
example later in this chapter; for now, I’m just setting up a scenario
for logistic regression.)

Suppose movie marketers want to estimate the chance that someone will
enjoy a certain family movie, and you believe age may have something to
do with it. Translating this research question into
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>’s and
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>’s, the response variable
<span class="zCheltItalic">(y)</span> is whether or not a person will
enjoy the movie, and the explanatory variable
<span class="zCheltItalic">(x)</span> is the person’s age. You want to
estimate <span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>, the chance of someone
enjoying the movie.

You collect data on a random sample of 40 people, shown in Table 8-1.
Based on your data, it appears that younger people enjoyed the movie
more than older people and that at a certain age, the trend switches
from liking the movie to disliking it. Armed with this data, you can
build a logistic regression model to estimate
<span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>.

Carrying Out a Logistic Regression Analysis

The basic idea of any model-fitting process is to look at all possible
models you can have under the general format and find the one that fits
your data best.

The general form of the best-fitting logistic regression model is
![466469-eq0802.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0802_fmt.png), where
![466469-eq0803.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0803_fmt.png) is the
estimate of <span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>,
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">0</span> is
the estimate of
<span class="zSymbolMedium">β</span><span class="zSubscript">0</span>,
and <span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span>
is the estimate of
<span class="zSymbolMedium">β</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span>
(from the previous section “Using an S-curve to estimate
probabilities”). The only values you have a choice about to form your
particular model are the values of
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">0</span> and
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span>.
These values are the ones you’re trying to estimate through the logistic
regression analysis.

To find the best-fitting logistic regression model for your data,
complete the following steps:

<span class="zCheltBold"> 1. Run a logistic regression analysis on the
data you collected (see the next section).</span>

<span class="zCheltBold"> 2. Find the coefficients of constant and
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">x</span><span class="zCheltBold">,
where
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">x</span><span class="zCheltBold">
is the name of your explanatory variable.</span>

These coefficients are
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">0</span> and
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span>,
the estimates of
<span class="zSymbolMedium">β</span><span class="zSubscript">0</span>
and
<span class="zSymbolMedium">β</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span> in
the logistic regression model.

<span class="zCheltBold"> 3. Plug the coefficients from step one into
the logistic regression model: </span>

<span class="zCheltBold">
</span>![466469-eq0802.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0802_fmt.png).

This equation is your best-fitting logistic regression model for the
data. Its graph is an S-curve (for more on the S-curve, see the section
“Using an S-curve to estimate probabilities” earlier in this chapter).

In the sections that follow, you see how to ask Minitab to do the above
steps for you. You also see how to interpret the resulting computer
output, find the equation of the best-fitting logistic regression model,
and use that model to make predictions (being ever mindful that all
conditions are met).

Running the analysis in Minitab

<span class="Icon-w-2-lines-of-text-baseline">![computeroutput.eps](9780470543887/images/computeroutput_fmt.png)</span>
Here’s how to perform a logistic regression using Minitab (other
statistical software packages are similar):

<span class="zCheltBold"> 1. Input your data in the spreadsheet as a
table that lists each value of the
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">x</span><span class="zCheltBold">
variable in column one, the number of yeses for that value of
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">x</span><span class="zCheltBold">
in column two, and the total number of trials at that
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">x</span><span class="zCheltBold">-value
in column three.</span>

These last two columns represent the outcome of the response variable
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>. (For an example of how to enter
your data, see Table 8-1 based on the movie and age data.)

<span class="zCheltBold"> 2. Go to Stat\>Regression\>Binary Logistic
Regression.</span>

<span class="zCheltBold"> 3. Beside the Success option, select your
variable name from column two, and beside Trial, select your variable
name for column three.</span>

<span class="zCheltBold"> 4. Under Model, select your variable name from
column one, because that’s the column containing the explanatory
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">(x)</span><span class="zCheltBold">
variable in your model.</span>

<span class="zCheltBold"> 5. Click OK, and you get your logistic
regression output.</span>

When you fit a logistic regression model to your data, the computer
output is composed of two major portions:

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png)
<span class="zCheltBold">The model-building portion:</span> In this part
of the output, you can find the coefficients
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">0</span> and
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span>. (I
describe coefficients in the next section.)

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png)
<span class="zCheltBold">The model-fitting portion:</span> You can see
the results of a Chi-square goodness-of-fit test (see Chapter 15) as
well as the percentage of concordant and discordant pairs in this
section of the output. (A <span class="zCheltItalic">concordant
pair</span> means the predicted outcome from the model matches the
observed outcome from the data. A <span class="zCheltItalic">discordant
pair</span> is one that doesn’t match.)

In the case of the movie and age data, the model-building part of the
Minitab output is shown in Figure 8-2. The model-fitting part of the
Minitab output from the logistic regression analysis is in Figure 8-4.

In the following sections, you see how to use this output to build the
best-fitting logistic regression model for your data and to check the
model’s fit.

<div class="story">

**Figure 8-2:** The model-building part of the movie and age data’s
logistic regression output.

</div>

![466469-fg0802.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-fg0802_fmt.png)

Finding the coefficients and making the model

After you have Minitab run a logistic regression analysis on your data,
you can find the coefficients
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">0</span> and
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span> and
put them together to form the best-fitting logistic regression model for
your data.

Figure 8-2 shows part of the Minitab output for the movie enjoyment and
age data. (I discuss the remaining output in the section “Checking the
fit of the model.”) The first column of numbers is labeled Coef, which
stands for the coefficients in the model. The first coefficient,
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">0</span>, is
labeled Constant. The second coefficient is in the row labeled by your
explanatory variable, <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>. (In the movie
and age data, the explanatory variable is age. This age coefficient
represents the value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span> in
the model.)

According to the Minitab output in Figure 8-2, the value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">0</span> is
4.87 and the value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span> is
–0.18. After you’ve determined the coefficients
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">0</span> and
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span>
from the Minitab output to find the best-fitting S-curve for your data,
you put these two coefficients into the general logistic regression
model: ![466469-eq0802.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0802_fmt.png).

For the movie and age data, you get
![466469-eq0804.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0804_fmt.png), which
is the best-fitting logistic regression model for this data set.

The graph of the best-fitting logistic regression model for the movie
and age data is shown in Figure 8-3. Note that the graph is a
downward-sloping S-curve because higher probabilities of liking the
movie are affiliated with lower ages and lower probabilities are
affiliated with higher ages.

The movie marketers now have the answer to their question. This movie
has a higher chance of being well liked by kids (and the younger, the
better) and a lower chance of being well liked by adults (and the older
they are, the lower the chance of liking the movie).

The point where the probability changes from high to low (that is, at
the ![466469-eq0803.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0803_fmt.png) =
0.50 mark) is between ages 25 and 30. That means that the tide of
probability of liking the movie appears to turn from higher to lower in
that age range. Using calculus terms, this point is called the
<span class="zCheltItalic">saddle point</span> of the S-curve, which is
the point where the graph changes from concave up to concave down, or
vice versa.

<div class="story">

**Figure 8-3:** The best-fitting S-curve for the movie and age data.

</div>

![466469-fg0803.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-fg0803_fmt.png)

Estimating p

You’ve determined the best-fitting logistic regression model for your
data, obtained the values of
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">0</span> and
<span class="zCheltItalic">b</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span>
from the logistic regression analysis, and know the precise S-curve that
fits your data best (check out the previous sections). You’re now ready
to estimate <span class="zCheltItalic">p</span> and make predictions
about the probability that the event of interest will happen, given the
value of the explanatory variable <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>.

To estimate <span class="zCheltItalic">p</span> for a particular value
of <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>, plug that value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> into your equation (the best-fitting
logistic regression model) and simplify it by using your algebra skills.
The number you get is the estimated chance of the event occurring for
that value of <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>, and it should be a
number between 0 and 1, being a probability and all.

Continuing with the movie and age example from the preceding sections,
suppose you want to predict whether a 15-year-old would enjoy the movie.
To estimate <span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>, plug 15 in for
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> in the logistic regression model
![466469-eq0802.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0802_fmt.png) to get
![466469-eq0805.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0805_fmt.png).

That answer means you estimate there’s a 90 percent chance that a
15-year-old will like the movie. You can see in Figure 8-3 that when
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> is 15,
<span class="zCheltItalic">p</span> is approximately 0.90. On the other
hand, if the person is 50 years old, the chance he’ll like this movie is
![466469-eq0806.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0806_fmt.png), or
0.02 (shown in Figure 8-3 for <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> = 50),
which is only a 2 percent chance.

Checking the fit of the model

![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png) The results you
get from a logistic regression analysis, as with any other data
analysis, are all subject to the model fitting appropriately.

To determine whether or not your logistic regression model fits, follow
these steps (which I cover in more detail later in this section):

<span class="zCheltBold"> 1. Locate the
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">p</span><span class="zCheltBold">-value
of the goodness-of-fit test (found in the Goodness-of-Fit portion of the
computer output; see Figure 8-4 for an example). If the
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">p</span><span class="zCheltBold">-value
is larger than 0.05, conclude that your model fits, and if the
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">p</span><span class="zCheltBold">-value
is less than 0.05, conclude that your model doesn’t fit.</span>

<span class="zCheltBold"> 2. Find the
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">p</span><span class="zCheltBold">-value
for the
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">b</span><span class="zCheltBold">1
coefficient (it’s listed under
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">P</span><span class="zCheltBold">
in the row for your column one (explanatory) variable in the
model-building portion of the output; see Figure 8-2 for an example). If
the
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">p</span><span class="zCheltBold">-value
is less than 0.05, the
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">x</span><span class="zCheltBold">
variable is statistically significant in the model, so it should be
included. If the
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">p</span><span class="zCheltBold">-value
is greater than or equal to 0.05, the
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">x</span><span class="zCheltBold">
vari-able isn’t statistically significant and shouldn’t be included in
the model.</span>

<span class="zCheltBold"> 3. Look later in the output at the percentage
of concordant pairs. This percentage reflects the proportion of time
that the data and the model actually agree with each other. The higher
the percentage, the better the model fits.</span>

![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png) The conclusion in
step one based on the <span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-value may seem
backward to you, but here’s what’s happening: Chi-square goodness-of-fit
tests measure the overall difference between what you expect to see via
your model and what you actually observe in your data. (Chapter 15 gives
you the lowdown on Chi-square tests.) The null hypothesis (Ho) for this
test says you have a difference of zero between what you observed and
what you expected from the model; that is, your model fits. The
alternative hypothesis, denoted Ha, says that the model doesn’t fit. If
you get a small <span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-value (under 0.05),
reject Ho and conclude the model doesn’t fit. If you get a larger
<span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-value (above 0.05), you can stay
with your model.

![warning_bomb.eps](9780470543887/images/warning_bomb_fmt.png) Failure
to reject Ho here (having a large
<span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-value) only means that you can’t say
your model doesn’t fit the population from which the sample came. It
doesn’t necessarily mean the model fits perfectly. Your data could be
unrepresentative of the population just by chance.

Fitting the movie model

You’re ready to check out the fit of the movie data to make sure you
still have a job when the box office totals come in.

Step one: p-value for Chi-squared

Using Figure 8-4 to complete the first step of checking the model’s fit,
you can see many different goodness-of-fit tests. The particulars of
each of these tests are beyond the scope of this book; however, in this
case (as with most cases), each test has only slightly different
numerical results and the same conclusions.

All the <span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-values in column four of
Figure 8-4 are over 0.80, which is much higher than the 0.05 you need to
reject the model. After looking at the
<span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-values, the model using age to
predict movie likeability appears to fit this data.

<div class="story">

**Figure 8-4:** The model-fitting part of the movie and age data’s
logistic regression output.

</div>

![466469-fg0804.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-fg0804_fmt.png)

Step two: p-value for the x variable

For step two, you look at the significance of the
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variable age. Back in Figure 8-2,
you can see the constant for age, –0.18, and farther along in its row,
you can see that the <span class="zCheltItalic">Z</span>-value is –3.52;
this <span class="zCheltItalic">Z</span>-value is the test statistic for
testing Ho:
<span class="zSymbolMedium">β</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span> =
0 versus Ha:
<span class="zSymbolMedium">β</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span>
<span class="zSymbolMedium">≠</span> 0. The
<span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-value is listed as 0.000, which
means it’s smaller than 0.001 (a highly significant number). So you know
that the coefficient in front of <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>,
also known as
<span class="zSymbolMedium">β</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span>,
is statistically significant (not equal to zero), and you should include
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> (age) in the model.

Step three: Concordant pairs

To complete step three of the fit-checking process, look at the
percentage of concordant pairs reported in Figure 8-4. This value shows
the percentage of times the data actually agreed with the model (87.3).
To determine concordance, the computer makes predictions as to whether
the event should have occurred for each individual based on the model
and compares those results to what actually happened.

![tip.eps](9780470543887/images/tip_fmt.png) The logistic regression
model is for <span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>, the probability of the
event occurring, so if <span class="zCheltItalic">p</span> is estimated
to be \> 0.50 for some value of <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>, the
computer predicts that the event will occur (versus not occurring). If
the estimated value of <span class="zCheltItalic">p</span> is \< 0.50
for a particular <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span>-value, the computer
predicts that it won’t occur.
