For the movie and age data, the percentage of concordant pairs (that is,
the percentage of times the model made the right decision in predicting
what would happen) is 87.3 percent, which is quite high.

![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png) The percentage of
concordant pairs was obtained by taking the number of concordant pairs
and dividing by the total number of pairs. I’d start getting excited if
the percentage of concordant pairs got over 75 percent; the higher, the
better.

Figure 8-5 shows the logistic regression model for the movie and age
data, with the actual values of the observed data added as circles. The
S-curve shows the probability of liking the movie for each age level,
and the computer will predict “1” = they will like the movie, if
![466469-eq0803.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0803_fmt.png) \>
0.50. Circles indicate whether the people of those age levels actually
liked the movie (<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> = 1) or not
(<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> = 0).

Much of the time, the model made the right decision; probabilities above
0.50 are associated with more circles at the value of 1, and
probabilities below 0.50 are associated with more circles at the value
of zero. It’s the outcomes that have <span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>
near 0.50 that are hard to predict because the results can go either
way.

<div class="story">

**Figure 8-5:** Actual observed values (0 and 1) compared to the model.

</div>

![466469-fg0805.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-fg0805_fmt.png)

<div class="sidebar">

Which method to use to compare? Sorting out similar situations

Data come in a variety of forms, and each form has its own analysis to
use to make comparisons. It can get difficult to decide which type of
analysis to use when.

It may help to sort out some situations that sound similar but have
subtle differences that lead to very different analyses. You can use the
following list to compare these subtle, but important, differences:

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) <span class="zUnivBold">If
you want to compare three or more groups of numerical variables,</span>
use ANOVA (see Chapter 10). For only two groups, use a
<span class="zUnivItalic">t</span>-test (see Chapters 3 and 9).

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) <span class="zUnivBold">If
you want to estimate one numerical variable based on another,</span> use
simple linear regression (see Chapter 4).

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) <span class="zUnivBold">If
you want to estimate one numerical variable using many other numerical
variables,</span> use multiple regression (see Chapter 5).

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) <span class="zUnivBold">If
you want to estimate a categorical variable with two categories by using
a numerical variable,</span> use logistic regression, which is the focus
of this chapter, of course.

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) <span class="zUnivBold">If
you want to compare two categorical variables to each other,</span> head
straight for a Chi-square test (see Chapter 14).

</div>

All this evidence helps confirm that your model fits your data well. You
can go ahead and make predictions based on this model for the next
individual that comes up, whose outcome you don’t know (see the section
“Estimating <span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>” earlier in this
chapter).

</div>

</div>

<span id="14_466469-pp03.html"></span>

<div id="14_466469-pp03.html_x14_466469-pp03.html">

<div class="story">

Part III

Analyzing Variance with ANOVA

<div class="image">

![466469-pp0301.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-pp0301_fmt.png)

</div>

In this part . . .

<span class="char-style-override-1">Y</span>ou get all the nuts and
bolts you need to understand one-way and two-way analyses of variance
(also known as ANOVA), which compare the means of several populations at
one time based on one or two different characteristics. You see how to
read and understand ANOVA tables and computer output, and you get to go
behind the scenes to understand the big ideas behind the formulas used
in ANOVA. Finally, you see lots of different multiple comparison
procedures to zoom in on which means are different. (Don’t sweat it. I
always present formulas only on a need-to-know basis.)

</div>

</div>

<span id="15_466469-ch09.html"></span>

<div id="15_466469-ch09.html_x15_466469-ch09.html">

<div class="Basic-Text-Frame">

Chapter 9

Testing Lots of Means? Come On Over to ANOVA!

In This Chapter

![arrow](9780470543887/images/arrow.png) Extending the
<span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-test for comparing two means by
using ANOVA

![arrow](9780470543887/images/arrow.png) Utilizing the ANOVA process

![arrow](9780470543887/images/arrow.png) Carrying out an
<span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-test

![arrow](9780470543887/images/arrow.png) Navigating the ANOVA table

<span class="char-style-override-1">O</span>ne of the most commonly used
statistical techniques at the Stats II level is
<span class="zCheltItalic">analysis of variance</span> (affectionately
known as ANOVA). Because the name has the word
<span class="zCheltItalic">variance</span> in it, you may think that
this technique has something to do with variance — and you would be
right. Analysis of variance is all about examining the amount of
variability in a <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> (response) variable
and trying to understand where that variability is coming from.

One way you can use ANOVA is to compare several populations regarding
some quantitative variable, <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>. The
populations you want to compare constitute different groups (denoted by
an <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variable), such as political
affiliations, age groups, or different brands of a product. ANOVA is
also particularly suitable for situations involving an experiment in
which you apply certain treatments <span class="zCheltItalic">(x)</span>
to subjects and measure a response
<span class="zCheltItalic">(y)</span>.

In this chapter, you start with the
<span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-test for two population means, the
precursor to ANOVA. Then you move on to the basic concepts of ANOVA to
compare more than two means: sums of squares, the
<span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-test, and the ANOVA table. You apply
these basics to the <span class="zCheltItalic">one-factor</span> or
<span class="zCheltItalic">one-way ANOVA,</span> where you compare the
responses based only on one treatment variable. (In Chapter 11, you can
see the basics applied to a two-way ANOVA, which has two treatment
variables.)

Comparing Two Means with a t-Test

The <span class="zCheltItalic">two-sample t-test</span> is designed to
test to see whether two population means are different. The conditions
for the two-sample <span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-test are the
following:

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) The two populations are
independent. In other words, their outcomes don’t affect each other.

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) The response variable
<span class="zCheltItalic">(y)</span> is a quantitative variable,
meaning its values have numerical meaning and represent quantities of
some kind.

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) The
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-values for each population have a
normal distribution. However, their means may be different; that’s what
the <span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-test determines.

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) The variances of the two
normal distributions are equal.

![tip.eps](9780470543887/images/tip_fmt.png) For large sample sizes when
you know the variances, you use a
<span class="zCheltItalic">Z</span>-test for the two population means.
However, a <span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-test allows you to test
two population means when the variances are unknown or the sample sizes
are small. This occurs quite often in situations where an experiment is
performed and the number of subjects is limited. (See your Stats I text
or Statistics For Dummies (Wiley) for info on the Z-test.)

Although you’ve seen <span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-tests before in
your Stats I class, it may be good to review the main ideas. The
<span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-test tests the hypotheses Ho:
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span> =
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span><span class="zSubscript">2</span>
versus Ha:
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span> is
<span class="zSymbolMedium">≤</span>,
<span class="zSymbolMedium">≥</span>, or
<span class="zSymbolMedium">≠</span>
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span><span class="zSubscript">2</span>,
where the situation dictates which of these hypotheses you use.
(<span class="zCheltBoldItalic">Note:</span> With ANOVA, you extend this
idea to <span class="zCheltItalic">k</span> different means from
<span class="zCheltItalic">k</span> different populations, and the only
version of Ha of interest is <span class="zSymbolMedium">≠</span>.)

![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png) To conduct the
two-sample <span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-test, you collect two
data sets from the two populations, using two independent samples. To
form the test statistic (the
<span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-statistic), you subtract the two
sample means and divide by the <span class="zCheltItalic">standard
error</span> (a combination of the two standard deviations from the two
samples and their sample sizes). You compare the
<span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-statistic to the
<span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-distribution with
<span class="zCheltItalic">n</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span> +
<span class="zCheltItalic">n</span><span class="zSubscript">2</span> – 2
degrees of freedom and find the
<span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-value. If the
<span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-value is less than the predetermined
<span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span> level, say 0.05, you have enough
evidence to say the population means are different. (For information on
hypothesis tests, see Chapter 3.)

For example, suppose you’re at a watermelon seed-spitting contest where
contestants each put watermelon seeds in their mouths and spit them as
far as they can. Results are measured in inches and are treated with the
reverence of the shot-put results at the Olympics. You want to compare
the watermelon seed-spitting distances of female and male adults. Your
data set includes ten people from each group.

You can see the results of the <span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-test
in Figure 9-1. The mean spitting distance for females was 47.8 inches;
the mean for males was 56.5 inches; and the difference (females – males)
is –8.71 inches, meaning the females in the sample spit seeds at shorter
distances, on average, than the males. The
<span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-statistic for the difference in the
two means (females – males) is <span class="zCheltItalic">t</span> =
–2.23, which has a <span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-value of 0.039
(see the last line of the output in Figure 9-1). At a level of
<span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span> = 0.05, this difference is
significant (because 0.039 \< 0.05). You conclude that males and females
differ with respect to their mean watermelon seed-spitting distance. And
you can say males are likely spitting farther because their sample mean
was higher.

<div class="story">

**Figure 9-1:** A <span class="zUnivItalic">t</span>-test comparing mean
watermelon seed-spitting distances for females versus males.

</div>

![466469-fg0901.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-fg0901_fmt.png)

Evaluating More Means with ANOVA

When you can compare two independent populations inside and out, at some
point two populations will not be enough. Suppose you want to compare
more than two populations regarding some response variable
<span class="zCheltItalic">(y).</span> This idea kicks the
<span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-test up a notch into the territory
of ANOVA. The ANOVA procedure is built around a hypothesis test called
the <span class="zCheltItalic">F-test,</span> which compares how much
the groups differ from each other compared to how much variability is
within each group. In this section, I set up an example of when to use
ANOVA and show you the steps involved in the ANOVA process. You can then
apply the ANOVA steps to the following example throughout the rest of
the chapter.

Spitting seeds: A situation just waiting for ANOVA

Before you can jump into using ANOVA, you must figure out what question
you want answered and collect the necessary data.

Suppose you want to compare the watermelon seed-spitting distances for
four different age groups: 6–8 years old, 9–11, 12–14, and 15–17. The
hypotheses for this example are Ho:
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span> =
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span><span class="zSubscript">2</span> =
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span><span class="zSubscript">3</span> =
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span><span class="zSubscript">4</span>
versus Ha: At least two of these means are different, where the
population means <span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span> represent those
from the age groups, respectively.

Over the years of this contest, you’ve collected data on 200 children
from each age group, so you have some prior ideas about what the
distances typically look like. This year, you have 20 entrants, 5 in
each age group. You can see the data from this year, in inches, in Table
9-1.

![tb0901](9780470543887/images/9780470466469-tb0901.png)

Do you see a difference in distances for these age groups based on this
data? If you were to just combine all the data, you would see quite a
bit of difference (the range of the combined data goes from 38 inches to
47 inches). And you may suspect that older kids can spit farther.

Perhaps accounting for which age group each contestant is in does
explain at least some of what’s going on. But don’t stop there. The next
section walks you through the official steps you need to perform to
answer your question.

Walking through the steps of ANOVA

You’ve decided on the quantitative response variable
<span class="zCheltItalic">(y)</span> you want to compare for your
<span class="zCheltItalic">k</span> various population (or treatment)
means, and you’ve collected a random sample of data from each population
(refer to the preceding section). Now you’re ready to conduct ANOVA on
your data to see whether the population means are different for your
response variable, <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>.

The characteristic that distinguishes these populations is called the
<span class="zCheltItalic">treatment variable, x</span>. Statisticians
use the word <span class="zCheltItalic">treatment</span> in this context
because one of the biggest uses of ANOVA is for designed experiments
where subjects are randomly assigned to treatments, and the responses
are compared for the various treatment groups. So statisticians often
use the word <span class="zCheltItalic">treatment</span> even when the
study isn’t an experiment and they’re comparing regular populations.
Hey, don’t blame me! I’m just following the proper statistical
terminology.

Here are the general steps in a one-way ANOVA:

<span class="zCheltBold"> 1. Check the ANOVA conditions, using the data
collected from each of the
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">k</span><span class="zCheltBold">
populations.</span>

See the next section, “Checking the Conditions” for the specifics on
these conditions.

<span class="zCheltBold"> 2. Set up the hypotheses Ho:
</span><span class="zCheltBold"><span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span></span><span class="zCheltBold">1
=
</span><span class="zCheltBold"><span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span></span><span class="zCheltBold">2
= . . . =
</span><span class="zCheltBold"><span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span></span><span class="zCheltBold">k
versus Ha: At least two of the population means are different.</span>

Another way to state your alternative hypothesis is by saying Ha: At
least two of
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span>,
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span><span class="zSubscript">2</span>, .
. .
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span><span class="zSubscript">k</span>
are different.

<span class="zCheltBold"> 3. Collect data from
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">k</span><span class="zCheltBold">
random samples, one from each population.</span>

<span class="zCheltBold"> 4. Conduct an
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">F</span><span class="zCheltBold">-test
on the data from step three, using the hypotheses from step two, and
find the
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">p</span><span class="zCheltBold">-value.</span>

See the section “Doing the <span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-Test”
later in this chapter for these instructions.

<span class="zCheltBold"> 5. Make your conclusions: If you reject Ho
(when your
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">p</span><span class="zCheltBold">-value
is less than 0.05 or your predetermined
</span><span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span><span class="zCheltBold">
level), you conclude that at least two of the population means are
different; otherwise, you conclude that you didn’t have enough evidence
to reject Ho (you can’t say the means are different).</span>

If these steps seem like a foreign language to you, don’t fear — I
describe each in detail in the sections that follow.

Checking the Conditions

Step one of ANOVA is checking to be sure all necessary conditions are
met before diving into the data analysis. The conditions for using ANOVA
are just an extension of the conditions for a
<span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-test (see the section “Comparing Two
Means with a <span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-Test”). The following
conditions all need to hold in order to conduct ANOVA:

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) The
<span class="zCheltItalic">k</span> populations are independent. In
other words, their outcomes don’t affect each other.

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) The
<span class="zCheltItalic">k</span> populations each have a normal
distribution.

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) The variances of the
<span class="zCheltItalic">k</span> normal distributions are equal.

Verifying independence

To check the first condition, examine how the data were collected from
each of the separate populations. In order to maintain independence, the
outcomes from one population can’t affect the outcomes of the other
populations. If the data have been collected by using a separate random
sample from each population (<span class="zCheltItalic">random</span>
here meaning that each individual in the population had an equal chance
of being selected), this factor ensures independence at the strongest
level.

In the watermelon seed-spitting data (see Table 9-1), the data aren’t
randomly sampled from each age group because the data represent everyone
who participated in the contest. But, you can argue that in most cases
the seed-spitting distances from one age group don’t affect the
seed-spitting distances from the other age groups, so the independence
assumption is relatively okay.

Looking for what’s normal

The second ANOVA condition is that each of the
<span class="zCheltItalic">k</span> populations has a normal
distribution. To check this condition, make a separate histogram of the
data from each group and see whether it resembles a normal distribution.
Data from a normal distribution should look symmetric (in other words,
if you split the histogram down the middle, it looks the same on each
side) and have a bell shape. Don’t expect the data in each histogram to
follow a normal distribution exactly (remember, it’s only a sample), but
it shouldn’t be extremely different from a normal, bell-shaped
distribution.

Because the seed-spitting data contain only five children per age group,
checking conditions can be iffy. But in this case, you have past years’
data for 200 children in each age group, so you can use that to check
the conditions. The histograms and descriptive statistics of the
seed-spitting data for the four age groups are shown in Figure 9-2, all
in one panel, so you can easily compare them to each other on the same
scale.

Looking at the four histograms in Figure 9-2, you can see that each
graph resembles a bell shape; the normality condition isn’t being
severely violated here. (Red flags should come up if you see two peaks
in the data, a skewed shape where the peak is off to one side, or a flat
histogram, for example.)

![computeroutput.eps](9780470543887/images/computeroutput_fmt.png) You
can use Minitab to make histograms for each of your samples and have all
of them appear on one large panel, all using the same scale. To do this,
go to Graph\>Histogram and click OK. Choose the variables that represent
data from each sample by highlighting them in the left-hand box and
clicking Select. Then click on Multiple Graphs, and a new window opens.
Under the Show Graph Variables option, check the following box: In
separate panels of the same graph. On the Same Scales for Graphs option,
check the box for <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> and the box for
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>. This option gives you the same
scale on both the <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> and
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> axes for all the histograms. Then
click OK.

<div class="story">

**Figure 9-2:** Checking ANOVA conditions by using histograms and
descriptive statistics.

</div>

![466469-fg0902.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-fg0902_fmt.png)

Taking note of spread

The third condition for ANOVA is that the variance in each of the
<span class="zCheltItalic">k</span> populations is the same;
statisticians call this the <span class="zCheltItalic">equal variance
condition.</span> You have two ways to check this condition on your
data:

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) Calculate each of the
variances from each sample and see how they compare.

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) Create one graph showing
all the boxplots of each sample sitting side by side. This type of graph
is called a <span class="zCheltItalic">side-by-side boxplot.</span> (See
your Stats I text or my book <span class="zCheltItalic">Statistics For
Dummies</span> (Wiley) for more information on boxplots.)

If one or more of the calculated variances is significantly different
from the others, the equal variance condition is not likely to be met.
What does <span class="zCheltItalic">significantly different</span>
mean? A hypothesis test for equal variances is the statistical tool used
to handle this question; however, it falls outside the scope of most
Stats II courses, so for now you can make a judgment call. I always say
that if the differences in the calculated variances are enough for you
to write home about (say they differ by 10 percent or more), the equal
variance condition is likely not to be met.

Similarly, if the lengths of one or more of the side-by-side boxplots
looks different enough for you to write home about, the equal variance
condition is not likely to be met. (But listen, if you really do write
home about any of your statistical issues, you may want to spice up your
life a bit.)

![technicalstuff.eps](9780470543887/images/technicalstuff_fmt.png) The
length of the box portion of a boxplot is called the
<span class="zCheltItalic">interquartile range.</span> You calculate it
by taking the third quartile (the 75th percentile) minus the first
quartile (the 25th percentile.) See your Stats I text or
<span class="zCheltItalic">Statistics For Dummies</span> for more info.

Table 9-2 shows an example of four small data sets with each of their
calculated variances shown in the last row. Note that the variance of
Data Set 4 is significantly smaller than the others. In this case, it’s
safe to say that the equal variance condition is not met.

![tb0902](9780470543887/images/9780470466469-tb0902.png)

Figure 9-3 shows the side-by-side boxplots for these same four data
sets. You see that the boxplot for Data Set 4 has an interquartile range
(length of the box) that’s significantly smaller than the others. I
calculated the actual interquartile ranges for these four data sets;
they’re 5.50, 5.75, 6.00, and 2.50, respectively. These findings confirm
the conclusion that the equal variance condition is not met, due to
group 4’s much smaller variability.

<div class="story">

**Figure 9-3:** Examining side-by-side boxplots to check the equal
variance condition.

</div>

![466469-fg0903.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-fg0903_fmt.png)

![computeroutput.eps](9780470543887/images/computeroutput_fmt.png) To
find descriptive statistics (including the variance and interquartile
range) for each sample, go to Stat\>Basic Statistics\>Display
Descriptive Statistics. Click on each variable in the left-hand box for
which you want the descriptive statistics, and click Select. Click on
the Statistics option, and a new window appears with tons of different
types of statistics. Click on the ones you want and click off the ones
you don’t want. Click OK. Then click OK again. Your descriptive
statistics are calculated.

To find side-by-side boxplots in Minitab, go to Graph\>Boxplot. A window
appears. Click on the picture for Multiple Y’s, Simple, and then click
OK. Highlight the variables from the left-hand side that you want to
compare, and click Select. Then click OK.

![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png) Note that you
don’t need the sample sizes in each group to be equal to carry out
ANOVA; however, in Stats II, you’ll typically see what statisticians
call a <span class="zCheltItalic">balanced design,</span> where each
sample from each population has the same sample size. (As I explain in
Chapter 3, for more precision in your data, the larger the sample sizes,
the better.)

For the seed-spitting data, the variances for each age group are listed
in Figure 9-2. These variances are close enough to say the equal
variance condition is met.

Setting Up the Hypotheses

Step two of ANOVA is setting up the hypotheses to be tested. You’re
testing to see if all the population means can be deemed equal to each
other. The null hypothesis for ANOVA is that all the population means
are equal. That is, Ho:
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span> =
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span><span class="zSubscript">2</span> =
. . . =
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span><span class="zSubscript">k</span>,
where
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span> is
the mean of the first population,
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span><span class="zSubscript">2</span> is
the mean of the second population, and so on until you reach
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span><span class="zSubscript">k</span>
(the mean of the
<span class="zCheltItalic">k</span><span class="zSuperscript">th</span>
population).

![tip.eps](9780470543887/images/tip_fmt.png) What appears in the
alternative hypothesis (Ha) must be the opposite of what’s in the null
hypothesis (Ho). What’s the opposite of having all
<span class="zCheltItalic">k</span> of the population’s means equal to
each other? You may think the opposite is that they’re all different.
But that’s not the case. In order to blow Ho wide open, all you need is
for at least two of those means to not be equal. So, the alternative
hypothesis, Ha, is that at least two of the population means are
different from each other. That is, Ha: At least two of
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span>,
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span><span class="zSubscript">2</span>, .
. .
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span><span class="zSubscript">k</span>
are different.

Note that Ho and Ha for ANOVA are an extension of the hypotheses for a
two-sample <span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-test (which only compares
two independent populations). And even though the alternative hypothesis
in a <span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-test may be that one mean is
greater than, less than, or not equal to the other, you don’t consider
any alternative other than <span class="zSymbolMedium">≠</span> in
ANOVA. (Statisticians use more in-depth models for the others. Aren’t
you glad someone else is doing it?)

![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png) You only want to
know whether or not the means are equal — at this stage of the game
anyway. After you reach the conclusion that Ho is rejected in ANOVA, you
can proceed to figure out how the means are different, which ones are
bigger than others, and so on, using multiple comparisons. Those details
appear in Chapter 10.

Doing the F-Test

Step three of ANOVA is collecting the data, and it includes taking
<span class="zCheltItalic">k</span> random samples, one from each
population. Step four of ANOVA is doing the
<span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-test on this data, which is the
heart of the ANOVA procedure. This test is the actual hypothesis test of
Ho:
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span> =
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span><span class="zSubscript">2</span> =
. . . =
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span><span class="zSubscript">k</span>
versus Ha: At least two of
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span>,
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span><span class="zSubscript">2</span>, .
. .
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span><span class="zSubscript">k</span>
are different.

You have to carry out three major steps in order to complete the
<span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-test.
<span class="zCheltBoldItalic">Note:</span> Don’t get these steps
confused with the main ANOVA steps; consider the
<span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-test a few steps within a step:

<span class="zCheltBold"> 1. Break down the variance of
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">y</span><span class="zCheltBold">
into sums of squares.</span>

<span class="zCheltBold"> 2. Find the mean sums of squares.</span>

<span class="zCheltBold"> 3. Put the mean sums of squares together to
form the
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">F</span><span class="zCheltBold">-statistic.</span>

I describe each step of the <span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-test in
detail and apply it to the example of comparing watermelon seed-spitting
distances (see Table 9-1) in the following sections.

![tip.eps](9780470543887/images/tip_fmt.png) Data analysts rely heavily
on computer software to conduct each step of the
<span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-test, and you can do the same. All
computer software packages organize and summarize the important
information from the <span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-test into a
table format for you.

This table of results for ANOVA is called (what else?) the
<span class="zCheltItalic">ANOVA table.</span> Because the ANOVA table
is a critical part of the entire ANOVA process, I start the following
sections out by describing how to run ANOVA in Minitab to get the ANOVA
table, and I continue to reference this section as I describe each step
of the ANOVA process.

Running ANOVA in Minitab

![computeroutput.eps](9780470543887/images/computeroutput_fmt.png) In
using Minitab to run ANOVA, you first have to enter the data from the
<span class="zCheltItalic">k</span> samples. You can enter the data in
one of two ways:

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png)
<span class="zCheltBold">Stacked data:</span> You enter all the data
into two columns. Column one includes the number indicating what sample
the data value is from (1 to <span class="zCheltItalic">k</span>), and
the responses <span class="zCheltItalic">(y)</span> are in column two.
To analyze this data, go to Stat\>ANOVA\>One-Way Stacked. Highlight the
response <span class="zCheltItalic">(y)</span> variable, and click
Select. Highlight the factor (population) variable, and click Select.
Click OK.

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png)
<span class="zCheltBold">Unstacked data:</span> You enter data from each
sample into a separate column. To analyze the data entered this way, go
to Stat\>ANOVA\>One-Way Unstacked. Highlight the names of the columns
where your data are located, and click OK.

I typically use the unstacked version of data entry just because I think
it helps visualize the data. However, the choice is up to you, and the
results come out the same no matter which method you choose, as long as
you’re consistent.

Breaking down the variance into sums of squares

Step one of the <span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-test is splitting up
the variability in the <span class="zCheltItalic">y</span> variable into
portions that define where the variability is coming from. Each portion
of variability is called a sum of squares. The term
<span class="zCheltItalic">analysis of variance</span> is a great
description for exactly how you conduct a test of
<span class="zCheltItalic">k</span> population means. With the overall
goal of testing whether <span class="zCheltItalic">k</span> population
(or treatment) means are equal, you take a random sample from each of
the <span class="zCheltItalic">k</span> populations.

You first put all the data together into one big group and measure how
much total variability there is; this variability is called the
<span class="zCheltItalic">sums of squares total,</span> or SSTO. If the
data are really diverse, SSTO is large. If the data are very similar,
SSTO is small.

You can split the total variability in the combined data set (SSTO) into
two parts:

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png)
<span class="zCheltBold">SST:</span> The variability between the groups,
known as the <span class="zCheltItalic">sums of squares for
treatment</span>

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png)
<span class="zCheltBold">SSE:</span> The variability within the groups,
known as the <span class="zCheltItalic">sums of squares for error</span>

Splitting up the variability in your data results in one of the most
important equalities in ANOVA:

SSTO = SST + SSE

![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png) The formula for
SSTO is the numerator of the formula for
<span class="zCheltItalic">s</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>,
the variance of a single data set, so
![466469-eq0901.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0901_fmt.png), where
<span class="zCheltItalic">i</span> and
<span class="zCheltItalic">j</span> represent the
<span class="zCheltItalic">j</span><span class="zSuperscript">th</span>
value in the sample from the
<span class="zCheltItalic">i</span><span class="zSuperscript">th</span>
population and
![466469-eq0906.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0906_fmt.png) is the
<span class="zCheltItalic">overall sample mean</span> (the mean of the
entire data set). So, in terms of ANOVA, SSTO is the total squared
distance between the data values and their overall mean.

The formula for SST is
![466469-eq0902.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0902_fmt.png), where
<span class="zCheltItalic">n</span><span class="zSubscript">i</span> is
the size of the sample coming from the
<span class="zCheltItalic">i</span><span class="zSuperscript">th</span>
population and
![466469-eq0907.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0907_fmt.png) is the
overall sample mean. SST represents the total squared distance between
the means from each sample and the overall mean.

The formula for SSE is
![466469-eq0903.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0903_fmt.png), where
<span class="zCheltItalic">x</span><span class="zSubscript">ij</span> is
the
<span class="zCheltItalic">j</span><span class="zSuperscript">th</span>
value in the sample from the
<span class="zCheltItalic">i</span><span class="zSuperscript">th</span>
population and
![466469-eq0904.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0904_fmt.png) is the
mean of the sample coming from the
<span class="zCheltItalic">i</span><span class="zSuperscript">th</span>
population. This formula represents the total squared distance between
the values in each sample and their corresponding sample means. Using
algebra, you can confirm (with some serious elbow grease) that SSTO =
SST + SSE.

![computeroutput.eps](9780470543887/images/computeroutput_fmt.png) The
Minitab output for the watermelon seed-spitting contest for the four age
groups is shown in Figure 9-4. Under the Source column of the ANOVA
table, you see Factor listed in row one. The factor variable (as
described by Minitab) represents the treatment or population variable.
In column three of the Factor row, you see the SST, which is equal to
89.75. In the Error row (row two), you locate the SSE in column three,
which equals 56.80. In column three of the Total row (row three), you
see the SSTO, which is 146.55. Using the values of SST, SSE, and SSTO
from the Minitab output, you can verify that SST + SSE = SSTO.

<div class="story">

**Figure 9-4:** ANOVA Minitab output for the watermelon seed- spitting
example.

</div>

![466469-fg0904.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-fg0904_fmt.png)

Now you’re ready to use these sums of squares to complete the next step
of the <span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-test.

Locating those mean sums of squares

After you have the sums of squares for treatment, SST, and the sums of
squares for error, SSE (see the preceding section for more on these),
you want to compare them to see whether the variability in the
<span class="zCheltItalic">y</span>-values due to the model (SST) is
large compared to the amount of error left over in the data after the
groups have been accounted for (SSE). So you ultimately want a ratio
that somehow compares SST to SSE.

To make this ratio form a statistic that they know how to work with (in
this case, an <span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-statistic),
statisticians decided to find the means of SST and SSE and work with
that. Finding the mean sums of squares is the second step of the
<span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-test, and the mean sums are as
follows:

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png)
<span class="zCheltBold">MST</span> is the
<span class="zCheltItalic">mean sums of squares for treatments,</span>
which measures the mean variability that occurs between the different
treatments (the different samples in the data). What you’re looking for
is the amount of variability in the data as you move from one sample to
another. A great deal of variability between samples (treatments) may
indicate that the populations are different as well.

You can find MST by taking SST and dividing by
<span class="zCheltItalic">k</span> – 1 (where
<span class="zCheltItalic">k</span> is the number of treatments).

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png)
<span class="zCheltBold">MSE</span> is the
<span class="zCheltItalic">mean sums of squares for error,</span> which
measures the mean within-treatment variability. The
<span class="zCheltItalic">within-treatment variability</span> is the
amount of variability that you see within each sample itself, due to
chance and/or other factors not included in the model.

You can find MSE by taking SSE and dividing by
<span class="zCheltItalic">n</span> –
<span class="zCheltItalic">k</span> (where
<span class="zCheltItalic">n</span> is the total sample size and
<span class="zCheltItalic">k</span> is the number of treatments). The
values of <span class="zCheltItalic">k</span> – 1 and
<span class="zCheltItalic">n</span> –
<span class="zCheltItalic">k</span> are called the
<span class="zCheltItalic">degrees of freedom</span> (or df) for SST and
SSE, respectively.

![computeroutput.eps](9780470543887/images/computeroutput_fmt.png)
Minitab calculates and posts the degrees of freedom for SST, SSE, MST,
and MSE in the ANOVA table in columns two and four, respectively.

From the ANOVA table for the seed-spitting data in Figure 9-4, you can
see that column two has the heading DF, which stands for degrees of
freedom. You can find the degrees of freedom for SST in the Factor row
(row two); this value is equal to <span class="zCheltItalic">k</span> –
1 = 4 – 1 = 3. The degrees of freedom for SSE is found to be
<span class="zCheltItalic">n</span> –
<span class="zCheltItalic">k</span> = 20 – 4 = 16. (Remember, you have
four age groups and five children in each group for a total of
<span class="zCheltItalic">n</span> = 20 data values.) The degrees of
freedom for SSTO is <span class="zCheltItalic">n</span> – 1 = 20 – 1 =
19 (found in the Total row under DF). You can verify that the degrees of
freedom for SSTO = degrees of freedom for SST + degrees of freedom for
SSE.

The values of MST and MSE are shown in column four of Figure 9-4, with
the heading MS. You can see the MST in the Factor row, which is 29.92.
This value was calculated by taking SST = 89.75 and dividing it by
degrees of freedom, 3. You can see MSE in the Error row, equal to 3.55.
MSE is found by taking SSE = 56.80 and dividing it by its degrees of
freedom, 16.

By finding the mean sums of squares, you’ve completed step two of the
F-test, but don’t stop here! You need to continue to the next section in
order to complete the process.

Figuring the F-statistic

The test statistic for the test of the equality of the
<span class="zCheltItalic">k</span> population means is
![466469-eq0905.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq0905_fmt.png). The
result of this formula is called the
<span class="zCheltItalic">F-statistic.</span> The
<span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-statistic has an
<span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-distribution, which is equivalent to
the square of a <span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-test (when the
numerator degrees of freedom is 1; see more on this interesting
connection between the t- and F-distributions in Chapter 12). All
<span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-distributions start at zero and are
skewed to the right. The degree of curvature and the height of the
curvature of each <span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-distribution is
reflected in two degrees of freedom, represented by
<span class="zCheltItalic">k</span> – 1 and
<span class="zCheltItalic">n</span> –
<span class="zCheltItalic">k</span>. (These come from the denominators
of MST and MSE, respectively, where <span class="zCheltItalic">n</span>
is the total sample size and <span class="zCheltItalic">k</span> is the
total number of treatments or populations.) A shorthand way of denoting
the <span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-distribution for this test is
<span class="zCheltItalic">F</span><span class="zSubscript">(<span class="zCheltItalic">k</span>
– 1, <span class="zCheltItalic">n</span> –
<span class="zCheltItalic">k</span>) </span>.

In the watermelon seed-spitting example, you’re comparing four means and
have a sample size of five from each population. Figure 9-5 shows the
corresponding <span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-distribution, which
has degrees of freedom 4 – 1 = 3 and 20 – 4 = 16; in other words
<span class="zCheltItalic">F</span><span class="zSubscript">(3,
16)</span> .

![computeroutput.eps](9780470543887/images/computeroutput_fmt.png) You
can see the <span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-statistic on the Minitab
ANOVA output (see Figure 9-4) in the Factor row, under the column
indicated by F. For the seed-spitting example, the value of the
<span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-statistic is 8.43. This number was
found by taking MST = 29.92 divided by MSE = 3.55. Then locate 8.43 on
the <span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-distribution in Figure 9-5 to
see where it stands in terms of its
<span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-value. (Turns out it’s waaay out
there; more on that in the next section.)

<div class="story">

**Figure 9-5:** <span class="zUnivItalic">F</span>-distribution with (3,
16) degrees of freedom.

</div>

![466469-fg0905.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-fg0905_fmt.png)

![warning_bomb.eps](9780470543887/images/warning_bomb_fmt.png) Be sure
to not to exchange the order of the degrees of freedom for the
<span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-distribution. The difference between
<span class="zCheltItalic">F</span><span class="zSubscript">(3,
16)</span> and
<span class="zCheltItalic">F</span><span class="zSubscript">(16,
3)</span> is a big one.

Making conclusions from ANOVA

If you’ve completed the <span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-test and
found your <span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-statistic (step four in
the ANOVA process), you’re ready for step five of ANOVA: making
conclusions for your hypothesis test of the
<span class="zCheltItalic">k</span> population means. If you haven’t
already done so, you can compare the
<span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-statistic to the corresponding
<span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-distribution with
(<span class="zCheltItalic">k</span> – 1,
<span class="zCheltItalic">n</span> –
<span class="zCheltItalic">k</span>) degrees of freedom to see where it
stands and make a conclusion. You can make the conclusion in one of two
ways: the <span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-value approach or the
critical-value approach. The approach you use depends primarily on
whether you have access to a computer, especially during exams. I
describe these two approaches in the following sections.

Using the p-value approach

![computeroutput.eps](9780470543887/images/computeroutput_fmt.png) On
Minitab ANOVA output (see Figure 9-4), the value of the
<span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-statistic is located in the Factor
row, under the column noted by F. The associated
<span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-value for the
<span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-test is located in the Factor row
under the column headed by P. The
<span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-value tells you whether or not you
can reject Ho.

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) <span class="zCheltBold">If
the
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">p</span><span class="zCheltBold">-value
is less than your predetermined
</span><span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span><span class="zCheltBold">
(typically 0.05), reject Ho.</span> Conclude that the
<span class="zCheltItalic">k</span> population means aren’t all equal
and that at least two of them are different.

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) <span class="zCheltBold">If
the
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">p</span><span class="zCheltBold">-value
is greater than
</span><span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span><span class="zCheltBold">,
then you can’t reject Ho.</span> You don’t have enough evidence in your
data to say the <span class="zCheltItalic">k</span> population means
have any differences.

The <span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-statistic for comparing the mean
watermelon seed-spitting distances for the four age groups is 8.43. The
<span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-value as indicated in Figure 9-4 is
0.001. That means the results are highly statistically significant. You
reject Ho and conclude that at least one pair of age groups differs in
its mean watermelon seed-spitting distances. (You would hope that a
17-year-old could do a lot better than a 6-year-old, but maybe those
6-year-olds have a lot more spitting practice than 17-year-olds do.)

Using Figure 9-5, you see how the
<span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-statistic of 8.43 stands on the
<span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-distribution with (4 – 1, 20 – 4) =
(3, 16) degrees of freedom. You can see that it’s way off to the right,
out of sight. It makes sense that the
<span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-value, which measures the
probability of being beyond that
<span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-statistic, is 0.001.

Using critical values

If you’re in a situation where you don’t have access to a computer (as
is still the case in many statistics courses today when it comes to
taking exams), finding the exact
<span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-value for the
<span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-statistic isn’t possible using a
table. You just choose the <span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-value of
the <span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-statistic that’s closest to
yours. However, if you do have access to a computer while doing homework
or an exam, statistical software packages automatically calculate all
<span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-values exactly, so you can see them
on any computer output.

![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png) To approximate
the <span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-value from your
<span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-statistic in the event you don’t
have a computer or computer output available, you find a cutoff value on
the <span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-distribution with
(<span class="zCheltItalic">k</span> – 1,
<span class="zCheltItalic">n</span> –
<span class="zCheltItalic">k</span>) degrees of freedom that draws a
line in the sand between rejecting Ho and not rejecting Ho. This cutoff,
also known as the <span class="zCheltItalic">critical value,</span> is
determined by your predetermined <span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span>
(typically 0.05). You choose the critical value so that the area to its
right on the <span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-distribution is equal
to <span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span>.

<span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-distribution tables are available in
various statistics textbooks and Web sites for other values of
<span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span>; however,
<span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span> = 0.05 is by far the most common
<span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span> level used for the
<span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-distribution and is sufficient for
your purposes.

This table of values for the
<span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-distribution is called the
<span class="zCheltItalic">F-table,</span> and students typically
receive these with their exams. For the seed-spitting example, the
<span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-statistic has an
<span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-distribution with degrees of freedom
(3, 16), where 3 = <span class="zCheltItalic">k</span> – 1, and 16 =
<span class="zCheltItalic">n</span> –
<span class="zCheltItalic">k</span>. To find the critical value, consult
an <span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-table (Table A-5 in the
appendix). Look up the degrees of freedom (3, 16), and you’ll find that
the critical value is 3.2389 (or 3.24). Your
<span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-statistic for the seed-spitting
example is 8.43, which is well beyond this critical value (you can see
how 8.43 compares to 3.24 by looking at Figure 9-5). Your conclusion is
to reject Ho at level <span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span>. At least two
of the age groups differ on mean seed-spitting distances.

![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png) With the critical
value approach, any <span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-statistic that
lies beyond the critical value results in rejecting Ho, no matter how
far from or close to the line it is. If your
<span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-statistic is beyond the value found
in the <span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-table you consult, then you
reject Ho and say at least two of the treatments (or populations) have
different means.

What’s next?

After you’ve rejected Ho in the <span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-test
and concluded that not all the populations means are the same, your next
question may be: Which ones are different? You can answer that question
by using a statistical technique called
<span class="zCheltItalic">multiple comparisons.</span> Statisticians
use many different multiple comparison procedures to further explore the
means themselves after the <span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-test has
been rejected. I discuss and apply some of the more common multiple
comparison techniques in Chapter 10.

Checking the Fit of the ANOVA Model

As with any other model, you must determine how well the ANOVA model
fits before you can use its results with confidence. In the case of
ANOVA, the model basically boils down to a treatment variable (also
known as the population you’re in) plus an error term. To assess how
well that model fits the data, see the values of
<span class="zCheltItalic">R</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
and
<span class="zCheltItalic">R</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
adjusted on the last line of the ANOVA output below the ANOVA table. For
the seed-spitting data, you see those values at the bottom of Figure
9-4.

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png)
<span class="zCheltBold">The value of
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">R</span><span class="zCheltBold"><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
measures the percentage of the variability in the response variable
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">(y)</span><span class="zCheltBold">
explained by the explanatory variable
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">(x)</span><span class="zCheltBold">.</span>
In the case of ANOVA, the <span class="zCheltItalic">x</span> variable
is the factor due to treatment (where the treatment can represent a
population being compared). A high value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">R</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
(say, above 80 percent) means this model fits well.

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png)
<span class="zCheltBold">The value of
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">R</span><span class="zCheltBold"><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
adjusted, the preferred measure, takes
</span><span class="zCheltBoldItalic">R</span><span class="zCheltBold">2
and adjusts it for the number of variables in the model.</span> In the
case of one-way ANOVA, you have only one variable, the factor due to
treatment, so
<span class="zCheltItalic">R</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
and
<span class="zCheltItalic">R</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
adjusted won’t be very far apart. For more on
<span class="zCheltItalic">R</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
and
<span class="zCheltItalic">R</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
adjusted, see Chapter 6.

For the watermelon seed-spitting data, the value of
<span class="zCheltItalic">R</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
adjusted (as found in the last row of Figure 9-4) is only 53.97 percent.
That means age group (shown to be statistically significant by the
<span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-test; see the section “Making
conclusions from ANOVA”) explains just over half of the variability in
the watermelon seed-spitting distances. Because of that connection, you
may find other variables you can examine in addition to age group,
making an even better model for predicting how far those seeds will go.

As you see in Figure 9-1, the results of the
<span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-test done to compare the spitting
distances of males and females in the section “Comparing Two Means with
a <span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-Test” show that males and females
were significantly different on mean seed-spitting distances (p-value =
0.039 \< 0.05). So I would venture a guess that if you include gender as
well as age group, thereby creating what statisticians call a
<span class="zCheltItalic">two-factor ANOVA</span> (or
<span class="zCheltItalic">two-way ANOVA</span>), the resulting model
would fit the data even better, resulting in higher values of
<span class="zCheltItalic">R</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
and
<span class="zCheltItalic">R</span><span class="zSuperscript">2</span>
adjusted. (Chapter 11 walks you through the two-way ANOVA.)

<div class="sidebar">

Upfront rejection is the best policy for most refusal letters

Many medical and psychological studies use designed experiments to
compare the responses of several different treatments, looking for
differences. A <span class="zUnivItalic">designed experiment</span> is a
study in which subjects are randomly assigned to treatments
(experimental conditions) and their responses are recorded. The results
are used to compare treatments to see which one(s) work best, which ones
work equally well, and so on.

Ohio State University researchers conducted one such experiment using
ANOVA to determine the most effective way to write a rejection letter.
(Is there really a best way to say “no” to someone? Turns out the answer
is “yes.”) The experiment tested three traditional principles of writing
refusal letters:

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) Using a buffer, which is a
neutral or positive sentence that delays the negative information

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) Placing the reason before
the refusal

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) Ending the letter on a
positive note as a way of reselling the business

Subjects were randomly assigned to treatments, and their responses to
the rejection letters were compared (likely on some sort of scale such
as 1 = very negative to 7 = very positive with 4 being a neutral
response).

You can analyze this scenario by using ANOVA because it compares three
treatments (forms of the rejection letters) on some quantitative
variable (response to the letter). You can argue that response to the
letter isn’t a continuous variable, however it has enough possible
values that ANOVA isn’t unreasonable. The data were also shown to have a
bell shape.

The null hypothesis would be Ho: Mean responses to the three types of
rejection letters are equal versus Ha: At least two forms of the
rejection letter resulted in different mean responses.

In the end, the researchers did find some significant results; the
different ways the rejection letter was written affected the
participants differently (so the F-test was rejected). Using multiple
comparison procedures (see Chapter 10), you could go in and determine
which forms of the rejection letters gave different responses and how
the responses differed.

In case you have to write a rejection letter at some point, the
researchers recommend the following guidelines:

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) Don’t use buffers to begin
negative messages.

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) Give a reason for the
refusal when it makes the sender’s boss look good.

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) Present the negative
positively but clearly; offer an alternative or compromise if possible.

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) A positive ending isn’t
necessary.

</div>

</div>

</div>

<span id="16_466469-ch10.html"></span>

<div id="16_466469-ch10.html_x16_466469-ch10.html">

<div class="Basic-Text-Frame">

Chapter 10

Sorting Out the Means with Multiple Comparisons

In This Chapter

![arrow](9780470543887/images/arrow.png) Knowing when and how to follow
up ANOVA with multiple comparisons

![arrow](9780470543887/images/arrow.png) Comparing two well-known
multiple comparison procedures

![arrow](9780470543887/images/arrow.png) Taking additional procedures
into consideration

<span class="char-style-override-1">I</span>magine this: You’re
comparing the means of not two, but <span class="zCheltItalic">k</span>
independent populations, and you find out (using ANOVA; see Chapter 9)
that you reject Ho: All the population means are equal, and you conclude
Ha: At least two of the population means are different. Now you gotta
know — which of those populations are different? Answering this question
requires a follow-up procedure to ANOVA called
<span class="zCheltItalic">multiple comparisons,</span> which makes
sense because you want to compare the multiple means you have to see
which ones are different.

In this chapter, you figure out when you need to use a multiple
comparison procedure. Two of the most well-known multiple comparison
procedures are Fisher’s LSD (least significant difference) and Tukey’s
test. They can help you answer that burning question: So some of the
means are different, but which ones are different? In this chapter, I
also tell you about other comparison procedures that you may encounter
or want to try.

<span class="zCheltBoldItalic">Note:</span> For those individuals who
come up with new multiple comparison procedures, the procedures are
generally named after them. (It’s like having a star named after you but
less romantic and a whole lot more work.)

Following Up after ANOVA

The main reason folks use ANOVA to analyze data is to find out whether
there are any differences in a group of population means. Your null
hypothesis is that there are no differences, and the alternative
hypothesis is that there’s at least one difference somewhere between two
of the means. (Note it doesn’t say that all the means have to be
different.)

If it’s established that at least two of the population means are
different, the next natural question is: “Okay, which ones are
different?” Although this is a very simple-sounding question, it doesn’t
have a simple answer. The concept of means being different can be
interpreted in hundreds of ways. Is one larger than all the others? Are
three pairs of them different from each other and the rest all the same?
Statisticians have worked long and hard to come up with a wide range of
choices of procedures to explore and find differences of all types in
two or more population means. This family of procedures is called
<span class="zCheltItalic">multiple comparisons.</span>

This section starts off with an example in which the ANOVA procedure was
used and Ho was rejected, leading you to the next step: multiple
comparisons. You then get an overview of how and why multiple comparison
procedures work.

Comparing cellphone minutes: An example

Suppose you want to compare the average number of cellphone minutes used
per month for various age groups, where the age groups are defined as
the following:

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) Group 1: 19 years old and
under

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) Group 2: 20–39 years old

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) Group 3: Adult males 40–59
years old

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) Group 4: Adult females 60
years old and over

You collect data on a random sample of ten people from each group (where
no one knows anyone else to keep independence), and you record the
number of minutes each person used their cellphone in one month. The
first ten lines of a hypothetical data set are shown in Table 10-1.

![tb1001](9780470543887/images/9780470466469-tb1001.png)

The means and standard deviations of the sample data are shown in Figure
10-1, as well as confidence intervals for each of the population means
separately (see Chapter 3 for info on confidence intervals). Looking at
Figure 10-1, it appears that all four means are different, with the
19-and-under group heading the pack, 40- to 59-year-olds not far behind,
with 20- to 39-year-olds and those over 60 bringing up the rear (in that
order).

Knowing that you can’t live by sample results alone, you decide that
ANOVA is needed to see whether any differences that appear in the
samples can be extended to the population (see Chapter 9). By using the
ANOVA procedure, you test whether the average cell minutes used is the
same across all groups. The results of the ANOVA, using the data from
Table 10-1, are shown in Figure 10-2.

<div class="story">

**Figure 10-1:** Basic statistics and confidence intervals for the
cellphone data.

</div>

![466469-fg1001.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-fg1001_fmt.png)

Looking at Figure 10-2, the <span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-test for
equality of all four population means has a
<span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-value of 0.000, meaning it’s less
than 0.001. That says at least two of these age groups have a
significant difference in their cellphone use (see Chapter 9 for info on
the <span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-test and its results).

<div class="story">

**Figure 10-2:** ANOVA results for comparing cellphone use for four age
groups.

</div>

![466469-fg1002.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-fg1002_fmt.png)

Okay, so what’s your next question? You just found out that the average
number of cellphone minutes used per month isn’t the same across these
four groups. This doesn’t mean all four groups are different (see
Chapter 9), but it does mean that at least two groups are significantly
different in their cellphone use. So your questions are

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) Which groups are different?

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png) How are they different?

Setting the stage for multiple comparison procedures

Determining which populations have differing means after the ANOVA
<span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-test has been rejected involves a
new data-analysis technique called <span class="zCheltItalic">multiple
comparisons.</span> The basic idea of multiple comparison procedures is
to compare various means and report where and what the differences are.
For example, you may conclude from a multiple comparison procedure that
the first population had a mean that was statistically lower than the
second population, but it was statistically higher than the mean of the
third population.

There are myriad different multiple comparison procedures out there; how
do you know which one you should use when? Two basic elements
distinguish multiple comparison procedures from each other. I call them
purpose and price.

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png)
<span class="zCheltBold">Purpose:</span> When you know that a group of
means aren’t all equal, you zoom in to explore the relationships between
them, depending on the purpose of your research. Maybe you just want to
figure out which means are equivalent and which are not. Maybe you want
to sort them into statistically equivalent groups from smallest to
largest. Or it may be important to compare the average of one group of
means to the average of another group of means. Different multiple
comparison procedures were built for different purposes; for the most
part, if you use them for their designed purposes, you have a better
chance of finding specific differences you’re looking for, if those
differences are actually there.

![check.png](9780470543887/images/check.png)
<span class="zCheltBold">Price:</span> Any statistical procedure you use
comes with a price: the probability of making a Type I error in your
conclusions somewhere during the procedure, due to chance. (A
<span class="zCheltItalic">Type I error</span> is committed when Ho is
rejected when it shouldn’t be; in other words, you think two means are
different but they really aren’t. See your Stats I textbook or my book
<span class="zCheltItalic">Statistics For Dummies</span> (Wiley) for
more info.) This probability of making at least one Type I error during
a multiple comparisons procedure is called the
<span class="zCheltItalic">overall error rate</span> (also known as the
experimentwise error rate (EER), or the familywise error rate). Small
overall error rates are of course desirable. Each multiple comparison
procedure has its own overall error rate; generally the more specific
the relationships are that you’re trying to find, the smaller your
overall error rate is, assuming you’re using a procedure that was
designed for your purpose.

In the next section, I describe two all-purpose multiple comparison
procedures: Fisher’s LSD and Tukey’s test.

![warning_bomb.eps](9780470543887/images/warning_bomb_fmt.png) Don’t
attempt to explore the data with a multiple comparison procedure if the
test for equality of the populations isn’t rejected. In this case, you
must conclude that you don’t have enough evidence to say the population
means aren’t all equal, so you must stop there. Always look at the
<span class="zCheltItalic">p</span>-value of the
<span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-test on the ANOVA output before
moving on to conduct any multiple comparisons.

Pinpointing Differing Means with Fisher and Tukey

You’ve conducted ANOVA to see whether a group of
<span class="zCheltItalic">k</span> populations has the same mean, and
you rejected Ho. You conclude that at least two of those populations
have different means. But you don’t have to stop there; you can go on to
find out how many and which means are different by conducting multiple
comparison tests.

In this section, you see two of the most well-known multiple comparison
procedures: <span class="zCheltItalic">Fisher’s LSD</span> (also known
as <span class="zCheltItalic">Fisher’s protected LSD</span> or
<span class="zCheltItalic">Fisher’s test</span>) and
<span class="zCheltItalic">Tukey’s test</span> (also known as
<span class="zCheltItalic">Tukey’s simultaneous confidence
intervals</span>).

![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png) Although I only
discuss two procedures in detail in this chapter, tons of other multiple
comparison procedures exist (see “So Many Other Procedures, So Little
Time!” at the end of this chapter). Although the other procedures’
methods differ a great deal, their overall goal is the same: to figure
out which population means differ by comparing their sample means.

Fishing for differences with Fisher’s LSD

In this section, I outline the original least significant difference
procedure (LSD) and R. A. Fisher’s improvement on it (aptly called
<span class="zCheltItalic">Fisher’s least significant difference
procedure,</span> or <span class="zCheltItalic">Fisher’s LSD</span>).
The LSD and Fisher’s LSD procedures both compare pairs of means using
some form of <span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-tests, but they do so
in different ways (see Chapter 3 or your Stats I textbook for more on
the <span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-test). You also see Fisher’s LSD
applied to the cellphone example from earlier in this chapter (see the
section “Following Up after ANOVA”).

The original LSD procedure

To use the original (pre-Fisher) LSD (short for
<span class="zCheltItalic">least significant difference</span>) simply
choose certain pairs of means in advance and conduct a
<span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-test on each pair at level
<span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span> = 0.05 to look for differences. LSD
doesn’t require an ANOVA test first (which is a problem that R. A.
Fisher later noticed). If <span class="zCheltItalic">k</span> population
means are all to be compared to each other in pairs using LSD, the
number of <span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-tests performed would be
represented by
![466469-eq1001.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq1001_fmt.png).

![technicalstuff.eps](9780470543887/images/technicalstuff_fmt.png)
Here’s how to count the number of
<span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-tests when all means are compared.
To start, you compare the first mean and the second mean, the first mean
and the third mean, and so on until you compare the first mean and the
<span class="zCheltItalic">k</span><span class="zSuperscript">th</span>
mean. Then compare the second and third, second and fourth, and so on
all the way down to the (<span class="zCheltItalic">k</span> –
1)<span class="zSuperscript">th</span> mean and the
<span class="zCheltItalic">k</span><span class="zSuperscript">th</span>
mean. The total number of pairs of means to compare equals
<span class="zCheltItalic">k</span> <span class="Times-Sign">\*</span>
(<span class="zCheltItalic">k</span> – 1). Because comparing the two
means in either order (mean one and mean two versus mean two and mean
one), gives you the same result regarding which one is largest, you
divide the total by 2 to avoid double counting. For example, if you have
four populations labeled A, B, C, and D, you have
![466469-eq1002.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-eq1002_fmt.png)
<span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-tests to perform: A versus B; A
versus C; A versus D; B versus C; B versus D; and C versus D.

![warning_bomb.eps](9780470543887/images/warning_bomb_fmt.png) The
original LSD procedure is very straightforward, easy to conduct, and
easy to understand. However, the procedure has some issues. Because each
<span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-test is conducted at
<span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span> level 0.05, each test done has a 5
percent chance of making a Type I error (rejecting Ho when you shouldn’t
have, as I explain in Chapter 3).

Although a 5 percent error rate for each test doesn’t seem too bad, the
errors have a multiplicative effect as the number of tests increases.
For example, the chance of making at least one Type I error with six
<span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-tests, each at level
<span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span> = 0.05, is 26.50 percent, which is
your overall error rate for the procedure.

![technicalstuff.eps](9780470543887/images/technicalstuff_fmt.png) If
you want or need to know how I arrived at the number 26.50 percent as
the overall error rate in that last example, here it goes: The
probability of making a Type I error for each test is 0.05. The chance
of making at least one error in six tests equals 1 – the probability of
making no errors in six tests. The chance of not making an error in one
test is 1 – <span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span> = 0.95. The chance of
no error in six tests is this quantity times itself six times, or
(0.95)<span class="zSuperscript">6</span>, which equals 0.735. Now take
1 – this quantity to get 1 – 0.735 = 0.2650 or 26.50 percent.

Using Fisher’s new and improved LSD

R. A. Fisher suggested an improvement over the regular LSD procedure,
and his procedure is called <span class="zCheltItalic">Fisher’s
LSD,</span> or <span class="zCheltItalic">Fisher’s protected LSD.</span>
It adds the requirement that an ANOVA
<span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-test must be performed first and
must be rejected before any pairs of means can be compared individually
or collectively. By requiring the
<span class="zCheltItalic">F</span>-test to be rejected, you’re
concluding that at least one difference exists in the means. Adding this
requirement, the overall error rate of Fisher’s LSD is somewhere in the
area of <span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span>, which is much lower than
what you get from the regular LSD procedure.

![warning_bomb.eps](9780470543887/images/warning_bomb_fmt.png) The
downside of Fisher’s LSD is that because each
<span class="zCheltItalic">t</span>-test is made at level
<span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span> and the overall error rate is also
near <span class="zSymbolMedium">α</span>, it’s good at finding
differences that really do exist, but it also makes some false alarms in
the process (mainly saying there’s a difference when there really
isn’t).

![computeroutput.eps](9780470543887/images/computeroutput_fmt.png) To
conduct Fisher’s LSD in Minitab, go to Stat\>ANOVA\>One-way or One-way
unstacked. (If your data appear in two columns with Column 1
representing the population number and Column 2 representing the
response, just click One-way because your data are stacked. If your data
are shown in <span class="zCheltItalic">k</span> columns, one for each
of the <span class="zCheltItalic">k</span> populations, click One-way
unstacked.) Highlight the data for the groups you’re comparing, and
click Select. Then click on Comparisons, and then Fisher’s. The
individual error rate is listed at 5 (percent), which is typical. If you
want to change it, type in the desired error rate (between 0.5 and
0.001), and click OK. You may type in your error rate as a decimal,
0.05, or as a number greater than 1, such as 5. Numbers greater than 1
are interpreted as a percentage.

An ANOVA procedure was done on the cellphone data presented in Table
10-1 to compare the mean number of minutes used for four age groups.
Looking at the output in Figure 10-2, you see Ho (all the population
means are equal) was rejected. The next step is to conduct multiple
comparisons by using Fisher’s LSD to see which population means differ.
Figure 10-3 shows the Minitab output for those tests.

The first block of results shows “Group 1 subtracted from” where Group 1
= age 19 and under. Each line after that represents the other age groups
(Group 2 = 20- to 39-year-olds, Group 3 = 40- to 59-year-olds, and Group
4 = age 60 and over). Each line shows the results of comparing the mean
for some other group minus the mean for Group 1.

For example, the first row shows Group 2 being compared with Group 1.
Moving to the right in that same row, you see the confidence interval
for the difference in these two means, which turns out to be –436.97 to
–323.03. Because zero isn’t contained in this interval, you conclude
that these two means are different in the populations also. Because this
difference
(<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span><span class="zSubscript">2</span> –
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span>)
is negative, you also can say that
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span><span class="zSubscript">2</span> is
less than
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span>.
Or, a better way to think of it may be that
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span> is
greater than
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span><span class="zSubscript">2</span>.
That is, Group 1’s mean is greater than Group 2’s mean.

<div class="story">

**Figure 10-3:** Output showing Fisher’s LSD applied to the cellphone
data.

</div>

![466469-fg1003.eps](9780470543887/images/466469-fg1003_fmt.png)

![remember.eps](9780470543887/images/remember_fmt.png)If two means are
equal, their difference equals zero, and a confidence interval for the
difference should contain zero. If zero isn’t included, you say the
means are different.

In this case, each subsequent row in the “Group 1 subtracted from”
section of Figure 10-3 shows similar results. None of the confidence
intervals contain zero, so you conclude that the mean cellphone use for
Group 1 is different from the mean cellphone use for any other group.

Moreover, because all confidence intervals are in negative territory,
you can conclude that the mean cellphone use for those users age 19 and
under is greater than all the others. (Remember, the mean for this group
is subtracted from the others, so a negative difference means its mean
is greater).

This process continues as you move down through the output until all six
pairs of means are compared to each other. Then you put them all
together into one conclusion. For example, in the second portion of the
output, Group 2 is subtracted from Groups 3 and 4. You see the
confidence interval for the “Group 3” line is (232.03, 345.97); this
gives possible values for Group 3’s mean minus Group 2’s mean. The
interval is entirely positive, so conclude that Group 3’s mean is
greater than Group 2’s mean (according to this data).

On the next line, the interval for Group 4 minus Group 2 is –299.97 to
–186.03. All these numbers are negative, so conclude Group 4’s mean is
less than Group 2’s. Combine conclusions to say that Group 3’s mean is
greater than Group 2’s, which is greater than Group 4’s.

In the cellphone example, none of the means are equal to each other, and
based on the signs of confidence intervals and the results of all the
individual pairwise comparisons, the following order of cellphone mean
usage prevails:
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span><span class="zSubscript">1</span> \>
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span><span class="zSubscript">3</span> \>
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span><span class="zSubscript">2</span> \>
<span class="zSymbolMedium">μ</span><span class="zSubscript">4</span>.
(Hypothetical data aside, it may be the case that 40- to 59-year-olds
use a lot of cellphone time because of their jobs.) Comparing these
results to the sample means in Figure 10-1, this ordering makes sense
and the means are separated enough to be declared statistically
significant.

Notice near the top of Figure 10-3 that you see “Simultaneous confidence
level = 80.32%.” That means the overall error rate for this procedure is
1 – 0.8032 = 0.1968, which is close to 20 percent, a bit on the high
side.

Separating the turkeys with Tukey’s test

The basic idea behind Tukey’s test is to provide a series of
simultaneous tests for differences in the means. It still examines all
